pages.title: Fallow: codebase analysis for TypeScript and JavaScript
items: Fallow: codebase analysis for TypeScript and JavaScript
Fallow is codebase analysis for TypeScript and JavaScript. It reports unused code, duplication, complexity, and architecture drift from one graph of your repo.
Fallow is codebase intelligence for TypeScript and JavaScript. One command reads your whole repository as one graph and shows:
where the code is hard to change (complexity hotspots and a health score)
where the architecture drifts (boundary rules and circular dependencies)
where the UI drifts from your design system (styling drift)
what nothing uses (unused files, exports, and dependencies)
To learn which code executed in production, add the optional runtime layer.
1Run fallow without installingnpx fallowThe first run needs no config.
2Read the resultsOne pass reports health, duplication, and unused code. For styling drift, run fallow audit or fallow health --css.

3Go deepernpx fallow dead-code
npx fallow dupes
npx fallow health
npx fallow fix --dry-run
Find unused files, exports, and dependencies, and remove them.
Find repeated logic before it spreads.
Rank code by complexity and health, and fix the worst first.
Confirm exact symbol use, class contracts, affected files, and the tests to run.
See hot paths and cold paths, and back a delete with production data.
Run mutation testing on changed code and find the changes that no test detects.
Start here. The CLI runs locally, in CI, and in agent loops.
Get real-time diagnostics, Code Lens, and one-click fixes in the editor.
Give Claude Code, Cursor, and other agents structured tool calls.
Static analysis tells you which code is connected to which. Production data from Fallow Cloud tells you which code actually ran. fallow health shows both.

Static analysis for TypeScript and JavaScript with fallow: unused code, duplication, complexity, architecture boundaries, styling drift, and runtime coverage.
Fallow shows you which code is unused, repeated, too complex, or in the wrong layer, and which code production actually runs. It works at two levels:
Static intelligence: structure, reachability, duplication, complexity, boundaries, and flags.
Production data (Fallow Cloud): the code that executed in production.

pages.title: Configuration
items: The Configuration pages of the Fallow documentation.
Configuration: Configure fallow for a TypeScript or JavaScript project. Fallow runs with no config. Add .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml to set entry points, ignores, and rules.
Rules & severity: Fallow rule severity decides what fails the CI build. Set each issue type to error, warn, or off, and adopt fallow in CI one issue type at a time.
Inline suppression: Suppress a fallow false positive with a fallow-ignore comment, a JSDoc tag such as @public or @internal, or @expected-unused. The rule stays on for other code.
Workspaces: Monorepo analysis with no workspace setup. Fallow detects npm, yarn, pnpm, and Deno workspaces, resolves cross-package imports, and supports per-package config.
Boundaries: Architecture boundaries for TypeScript and JavaScript. Fallow reports each import that crosses a layer. Start from a built-in preset or define your own zones.
Environment variables: Fallow environment variables set defaults for a whole CI job, editor, or MCP server. Reference for FALLOW_FORMAT, FALLOW_QUIET, and the other variables.

pages.title: Frameworks
items: The Frameworks pages of the Fallow documentation.
React & Next.js analysis: React and Next.js static analysis that finds wrong client and server directives, colliding routes, dead server actions, and unused or drilled props.
Built-in plugins: Built-in fallow plugins detect Next.js, Vite, Jest, Tailwind, ESLint, and many other tools, so fallow knows the files and exports that each tool uses.
Custom plugins: A custom fallow plugin stops false positives from an internal framework or unknown tool. Declare entry points, config files, and used exports in JSON or TOML.

pages.title: CLI reference
items: The CLI reference pages of the Fallow documentation.
fallow dead-code: Find unused files, exports, dependencies, and types in TypeScript and JavaScript. fallow dead-code traces code from your entry points and reports the rest.
fallow type-aware: Check that the optional fallow-type-aware companion is installed and compatible before you use --type-aware. The status command does not analyze the project.
fallow dupes: Find duplicate code in TypeScript and JavaScript projects. fallow dupes detects copy-pasted code blocks with suffix-array analysis and configurable thresholds.
fallow similar-code: Reference for fallow similar-code: flags, subcommands, and exit codes. Find functions that may do the same job with a pinned local model, then inspect and review them.
fallow viz: Visualize dead code, duplication, boundary violations, and complexity in your codebase. fallow viz writes one HTML map with a treemap and an import graph.
fallow health: Find complex functions and files and the best places to refactor first. fallow health combines cyclomatic and cognitive complexity, git churn, and coverage.
fallow license: Activate a fallow trial or license to turn on continuous runtime coverage. fallow license also shows status, refreshes a license, or removes the local token.
fallow cloud: Log in to Fallow Cloud from the CLI without copying an API key. fallow cloud login runs the device flow and stores a read-only key in the OS keychain.
fallow telemetry: Control what fallow sends and see the exact payload first. fallow telemetry manages opt-in telemetry, off by default: status, enable, disable, or inspect.
fallow coverage: Runtime coverage shows which code runs in production and which code you can delete. fallow coverage analyzes it and uploads source maps and the inventory.
fallow flags: Find feature flags in TypeScript and JavaScript code to review and retire them. fallow flags detects environment variable gates, SDK calls, and config toggles.
fallow security: Find security candidates in TypeScript and JavaScript: server secrets that reach client code, and untrusted values that reach dangerous sinks. Opt-in and local.
Security agent verification: Verify fallow security candidates with a coding agent and keep only the survivors that a verifier cannot dismiss. fallow itself makes no model calls.
fallow audit: Quality gate for pull requests. fallow audit gives one pass, warn, or fail verdict for the changed files from dead code, complexity, and duplication checks.
fallow mutation: Mutation testing for JavaScript and TypeScript. fallow mutation changes your code, runs Vitest, node:test, or bun test, and reports changes no test detects.
fallow impact: See what fallow has done in a project. fallow impact is a local-only report of current findings, the trend, commits stopped at the gate, and resolved findings.
fallow inspect: Get all context for one file or export before you edit it: trace, dead code, duplication, complexity, security, and optional Fallow Cloud production data.
fallow trace: See what calls an exported symbol and what it calls before you change it, or how one module comes to import another. fallow trace uses the module graph.
fallow trace-error: Map a runtime stack trace to the definitions in your code. fallow trace-error resolves each frame against the module graph, without reading source maps.
fallow decision-surface: Find the structural decisions in a code change that need a human judgment call. fallow decision-surface prints each one as a question with the expert to ask.
fallow explain: Learn what a fallow finding means and how to fix it. fallow explain prints the rationale, an example, fix guidance, and a docs link for one issue type.
fallow fix: Remove unused exports and dependencies automatically. fallow fix edits your TypeScript and JavaScript files in place, with a dry-run preview and JSON output.
fallow watch: Get dead code results each time you save a file. fallow watch re-runs dead code analysis in your TypeScript and JavaScript project when files change.
fallow init: Create a fallow config file with editor autocomplete and validation. fallow init generates a .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml file with schema support.
fallow agent: Set up fallow for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor with one command. It installs AGENTS.md, the skill, the MCP server, and a commit and push gate.
fallow hooks: Install, remove, and inspect the fallow-managed Git pre-commit hook and the Claude Code and Codex gate that runs fallow audit before git commit and git push.
fallow recommend: Get a proposed fallow config for your project and review it before you write it. fallow recommend is read-only and explains each decision behind the proposal.
fallow doctor: Check if fallow sees your project correctly before you trust its results. fallow doctor runs read-only checks on config, workspaces, plugins, and caches.
fallow guard: Check the architecture rules for a file before you edit it. fallow guard reports the boundary zone, allowed imports, forbidden calls, and rule-pack policies.
fallow architecture: Find import cycles and boundary violations, or inspect an opt-in shared-state inventory in TypeScript and JavaScript projects.
fallow rule-pack: Manage declarative fallow rule packs (policy as code). Create a pack from a template, list the configured rules, and test a pack against your project.
fallow rule-pack-schema: Print the JSON Schema of fallow rule pack files. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation of the policy rules in a rule pack.
fallow plugin-check: See why a custom fallow plugin does not activate or seeds no entries. plugin-check is a read-only dry run that shows the matches of each manifestEntries rule.
fallow plugin-schema: Print the JSON Schema of external fallow plugin files. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation while you write a fallow-plugin file.
fallow migrate: Migrate from knip, jscpd, or stylelint to fallow and keep your settings. fallow migrate converts your existing configuration to the fallow config format.
fallow list: Debug your fallow setup. fallow list shows the discovered files, entry points, active plugins, boundary zones, workspaces, and the import weight of each entry.
fallow workspaces: List the monorepo workspaces that fallow discovers, with diagnostics for malformed package.json files, unmatched globs, and missing tsconfig references.
fallow config: Print the resolved fallow configuration and the file that fallow loaded, to find out why a setting is not applied. It works like eslint --print-config.
fallow config-schema: Print the JSON Schema of the fallow config file. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation of .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, and fallow.toml.
fallow schema: Print the full fallow capability manifest as one JSON document: commands, issue types, MCP tools, plugins, and environment variables, for agents and tooling.
fallow suppressions: List every finding that your team chose to ignore, and why. fallow suppressions lists each fallow-ignore marker by file with its reason and a stale count.
fallow baselines prune: Remove stale entries from committed fallow baselines. One whole-project run prunes the dead-code, health, and duplication baselines and never adds an entry.
fallow report: Analyze once, then render every CI output from the saved JSON result. fallow report writes summaries, PR comments, annotations, and inline reviews.
fallow ci: Reference for fallow ci: post or update the sticky PR comment, post inline reviews, resolve fixed review threads, and post GitHub Check Runs from rendered fallow output.
fallow ci-template: Print the fallow GitLab CI template, or vendor it with its helper scripts into your repository so pipelines run without a download from GitHub.
Global flags: Global CLI flags that work the same on every fallow command: project root, config, output format, scope, cache, workspaces, score, trend, and snapshot options.

pages.title: Migration
items: The Migration pages of the Fallow documentation.
Migrating from knip: Migrate from knip to fallow. One command converts your knip config to a fallow config. See what the command migrates and what to check after the move.
Migrating from jscpd: Migrate from jscpd to fallow. One command converts your jscpd config to fallow duplication settings for TypeScript and JavaScript. See how detection modes map.
Migrating from stylelint: Convert the selector complexity rules of your stylelint config to fallow styling analysis. See what fallow migrates and which rules stay in stylelint.
Comparing with madge: Compare madge with fallow for circular dependencies, orphan files, and dependency graphs in TypeScript and JavaScript. See which madge command maps to which fallow command.

Comparing with dependency-cruiser: Compare dependency-cruiser rules with fallow boundaries, cycles, and dependency checks for TypeScript and JavaScript. See which rules map and which have no fallow equivalent.
Comparing with ts-prune: Compare ts-prune with fallow for unused exports in TypeScript. See which ts-prune option maps to which fallow setting, and how the two tools resolve symbols.

pages.title: Find unused exports and dead code in TypeScript
items: Find unused exports and dead code in TypeScript
Find unused files, exports, and dependencies to delete from a TypeScript or JavaScript project. Fallow also reports circular dependencies and unused members.
fallow dead-code tells you which files, exports, and dependencies you can delete. It builds a module graph from your entry points and reports everything that the graph does not reach.
The graph build is deterministic, so a developer, a CI pipeline, and a coding assistant get the same result for the same code.
Fallow reports these core issue types:

Fallow also has framework-specific rules, such as unused component props and route collisions, rules for Effect projects, such as unused Effect layers, and opt-in rules, such as private type leaks. To set the severity of a rule, see Rules & severity. To see the filter flag of each issue type, run fallow dead-code --help. For circular dependencies, boundary violations, and the other architecture findings, use fallow architecture.
Typical output with more than one issue type:

To report only some issue types, pass their flags:

fallow dead-code --unused-files
fallow dead-code --unused-exports --unused-types
fallow dead-code --unresolved-imports --unlisted-deps

When fallow reports a file as an unused file, it does not list the unused exports, unused types, unused class members, and unused enum members in that file. When you delete the file, you also remove these findings. Thus they add no information to the report. Other finding kinds in an unused file stay in the report, for example an unresolved import.
The report counts the hidden findings:
When the count is 0, all three outputs omit it. An example of the markdown note:
_3 findings in unused files are hidden; use `--show-cascade` to list them._

The codeclimate, compact, and github-annotations formats do not show the count. The markdown output with --group-by does not show it either. The summary counts and total_issues count only the findings in the report.
To list the hidden findings, use one of these options:
The --show-cascade flag, for one run of fallow, fallow dead-code, fallow audit, or fallow fix.
The showCascade config key, set to true.
The show_cascade parameter of the MCP tools analyze, check_changed, audit, fix_preview, and fix_apply, and of the combined call in Code Mode.
The showCascade option of the Node bindings.
The health vital signs and the health score still count the hidden findings. Bare fallow and fallow health give the same values with and without --show-cascade.
When an issue-type selection does not include unused files, fallow hides nothing. For example, fallow dead-code --unused-exports lists the unused exports of unused files.
A // fallow-ignore-file unused-file comment removes the file from the report. Fallow also hides the export and member findings of that file.
fallow fix does not fix a hidden finding. Delete the unused file, or pass --show-cascade to fix these findings too.
With --changed-since or --workspace, cascade_hidden counts only the findings in the scoped files.
A baseline that you saved with an older version still matches. A baseline that you save now does not contain the hidden findings.
A regression baseline that you saved with an older version counts the hidden findings. After the upgrade it allows more new findings than before. Save it again with --save-regression-baseline.
Optional props that callers never supply

Absent component props are optional props that a component reads but no inspected reachable caller supplies. Enable rules.absent-component-props with warn or error. The rule starts off because a default or a stable API can make an omitted prop intentional.

Fallow reports candidates only when it knows at least one reachable caller and can account for the component's callers statically. Unknown spreads, forwarding, dynamic use, and external package users prevent that conclusion. A finding includes the declaration, inspected callers, and whether a default exists. Review that evidence before changing the component. Fallow does not remove the prop or its conditional UI automatically.
Parameters that each call passes in one way

Constant parameters are function parameters that each visible call passes in the same way: the same literal value, or no value for an optional parameter. Enable the rule with --constant-parameters, or set rules.constant-parameters to warn or error. The rule starts off because a parameter can be a deliberate option.

Fallow reports a parameter only when it sees each caller of the function. Public API exports, entry-point exports, dynamic imports, a function used as a value, and other open cases prevent a finding. A finding includes the value, the count of calls, the inspected calls, and the count of conditions that test the parameter. Review that evidence before changing the function. Fallow does not change the function automatically.

Each finding has a stable finding_id. The id does not change when lines move, so you can track one finding across runs. See finding_id.
SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning and other static analysis tools.

A dead-code result has the key fallowFinding/v1 in partialFingerprints. Its value is the finding_id of the finding in JSON output, so you can join a SARIF result to its JSON finding. The keys tools.fallow.fingerprint/v1 and primaryLocationLineHash/v1 did not change, so GitHub code scanning keeps each open alert after an upgrade.

Some findings give one result for each location: an unlisted dependency gives one result for each import site, and a duplicate export gives one result for each location. These results do not have the fallowFinding/v1 key, because one id would identify more than one result. fallow report --from with a saved report from an older version also gives no key. Security results keep their own fallowSecurity/v2 key.

To post it as a PR comment, pipe it to gh pr comment:
fallow dead-code --format markdown | gh pr comment --body-file -
CodeClimate JSON, which GitLab Code Quality shows as inline MR annotations.

The fingerprint of a dead-code issue comes from its finding_id, so it does not change when lines move. GitLab Code Quality therefore keeps an issue open when you add lines above it. The same package unused in two workspaces gives two issues with two fingerprints. Duplication, health and security fingerprints did not change.

On the first run after the upgrade to this fingerprint form, GitLab Code Quality and other tools that key on the fingerprint show each dead-code finding as resolved and as new one time. After that run, a line shift keeps the issue. A saved report without finding ids, rendered with fallow report --from, keeps the old line-based fingerprint.
Add this job to GitLab CI:

fallow:
 script: npx fallow dead-code --format codeclimate > gl-code-quality-report.json
 artifacts:
 reports:
 codequality: gl-code-quality-report.json
To check only the files that changed since a git ref, pass --changed-since:

fallow dead-code --changed-since main
fallow dead-code --changed-since HEAD~5
In CI, this reports only the issues that a pull request adds.

To adopt fallow on an existing codebase, save the current issues as a baseline. Fallow then fails only on new issues:

# Save current issues as baseline
fallow dead-code --save-baseline fallow-baselines/dead-code.json

# Only fail on new issues (compared to baseline)
fallow dead-code --baseline fallow-baselines/dead-code.json

A dead-code baseline stores one line-free key for each finding: the rule, the path and the names. When you add lines above a finding, the baseline still hides it. Each saved entry hides one finding, so a second finding with the same key is new. A baseline from an earlier release still loads. Save it again once to get the line-free form. See Incremental.

A dead-code baseline also records whether node_modules existed when you saved it. Some findings need installed packages, so a run in the other install state can report baseline findings as new. Such a run adds a baseline-install-state-mismatch entry to workspace_diagnostics[] and prints a warning, also with --quiet. The entry has baseline_node_modules and run_node_modules (present or missing), and degrades_analysis: true. The comparison and the exit code do not change. To fix it, save and compare the baseline in the same install state. A baseline that you saved with an earlier release has no install state and gives no warning. Save it again once to get the check. dupes and health baselines do not record the install state.
To see why fallow counts an export, a file, or a dependency as used or unused, trace it:

fallow dead-code --trace src/utils.ts:formatDate
fallow dead-code --trace-file src/utils.ts
fallow dead-code --trace-dependency lodash
Fallow parses your code with Oxc and resolves bindings with scope analysis. It does not run the TypeScript compiler and does not use type information, which keeps the analysis fast.

flowchart TB A["Discovery
Entry points from package.json + plugins"] --> B["Parsing
Parallel with Oxc + oxc_semantic + rayon"] B --> C["Resolution
Import specifiers to file paths"] C --> D["Graph
Module graph with re-export chains"] D --> E["Analysis
Walk from entry points, report unreachable code"]

Fallow works best with isolatedModules: true, which esbuild, swc, and Vite require. oxc_semantic scope analysis finds import bindings that the file never reads. Older tsc-only projects without isolatedModules can still get edge cases with type-only imports.

A package that you only use from a package.json script is not an unused dependency. Fallow reads your scripts to find these packages. For "lint": "oxlint src/", fallow sees that the oxlint package supplies the oxlint binary and marks the package as used.
Fallow reads these parts of a script:

Binary names. Fallow maps commands such as tsc, vitest, or next to their packages (typescript, vitest, next). It does not report these packages as unused, even when no source file imports them. Fallow reads the bin fields of the installed packages in node_modules. It also reads the bin field of each declared workspace package, so a script that calls the binary of a workspace package credits that package without node_modules. When both name the same binary, the installed package takes priority. For other binaries, fallow uses a built-in table, for example napi to @napi-rs/cli and taplo to @taplo/cli.
--config arguments. When a script names a config file (for example jest --config jest.e2e.config.ts), fallow makes that file an entry point, so it does not report the file as unused.
File path arguments. Files that a script names directly (for example node scripts/seed.js) also become entry points.
Vite+ commands. vp, vpr and vpx credit vite-plus, and the subcommand decides how fallow reads the arguments. See Vite+.

Env wrappers and package manager runners. Fallow removes the cross-env, dotenv, env, npx, pnpx, yarn dlx, pnpm exec, npm exec --, yarn run, bun run, varlock run --, or dotenvx run -- prefix to find the real binary. The flags of these prefixes are also removed, for example dotenv -e .env.ci --, pnpm --filter web exec, and pnpm -r exec. yarn <bin>, yarn run <bin>, pnpm <bin>, and bun run <bin> count as the binary when no script has that name.

Script calls. A call such as npm run lint -- src/a.ts, npm run lint src/a.ts, yarn lint src/a.ts, or pnpm lint src/a.ts runs the lint script with the extra arguments. Fallow reads it as the script body plus those arguments, as the package manager does. As in npm 7 and later, npm forwards the positional arguments without -- and reads the --prefixed arguments before -- as npm config. npm config flags that take a value, such as --tag, --otp, or --node-options, also consume the next argument, so npm run lint --tag next src/a.ts forwards only src/a.ts. A declared script with the name of a tool runs instead of the tool: with "oxlint": "node tools/check.js", yarn oxlint src/a.ts keeps src/a.ts as an entry point.

Other workspace packages and directories. A command in a workspace package that it selects resolves its file arguments against the directory of that package. With the web package in packages/web, yarn workspace web node scripts/a.ts, pnpm --filter web exec tsx scripts/a.ts, npm exec -w web -- tsx scripts/a.ts, and a call of a web script such as npm run -w web gen -- scripts/a.ts make packages/web/scripts/a.ts an entry point. A pnpm filter can be a name, a name glob ('@acme/*'), a directory (./packages/*, {packages/web}), or an exclusion ('!web'). A selection of several packages resolves the file in each package where the file exists. This includes a command in every package: pnpm -r exec tsx scripts/a.ts, yarn workspaces foreach -A exec tsx scripts/a.ts (narrowed by --include and --exclude), yarn workspaces run gen scripts/a.ts, and npm --workspaces run gen -- scripts/a.ts. yarn workspaces foreach -A also runs in the root package, as yarn does, and its --include and --exclude match a workspace name or directory (. is the root). pnpm -w, a pnpm filter with the name or directory of the root package, and yarn workspace with the name of the root package also select the root package. An npm workspace name or directory does not select it, as in npm. --include-workspace-root adds the root package: in pnpm to -r and to a filter that only excludes packages (--filter '!web'), and in npm to every workspace selection (-w web, --workspaces), also with the short form -iwr. Without it, pnpm -r, yarn workspaces run, and npm --workspaces leave out the root package. From a workspace package, npm --workspaces selects only that package. A script call in the directory of a workspace package, such as pnpm -C packages/web run gen scripts/a.ts, npm --prefix packages/web run gen -- scripts/a.ts
In this example, fallow detects typescript, vite, vitest, and oxlint as used dependencies, and vitest.config.ts as an entry point.

A formatter or a linter reads its file arguments, but it does not run them. So the file arguments of these tools do not become entry points: oxlint src/, oxfmt --check ., eslint src/a.ts, and prettier --check "**/*.ts" keep every file that no import reaches reportable as unused. This applies to all the command forms in the list above: a direct call, a package manager runner, an env wrapper, and a script call. For example, with the script "lint": "oxlint", the call npm run lint -- src/a.ts does not make src/a.ts an entry point.

Fallow knows these tools: alex, Biome, CSpell, dependency-cruiser, dprint, EditorConfig checkers, ember-template-lint, ESLint (and eslint_d), HTMLHint, jscpd, JSHint, madge, markdownlint, markuplint, Oxfmt, Oxlint, Prettier, remark, Secretlint, Standard, Stylelint, textlint, TSLint, and XO.
The tool itself is still a used dependency, and its --config file is still tracked. A module that the tool loads through a flag also stays reachable:
A custom formatter, parser, or reporter: eslint -f ./tools/formatter.js, stylelint --custom-formatter ./fmt.js.
A rule directory: eslint --rulesdir ./rules, textlint --rulesdir ./rules. Fallow keeps the source files directly in that directory reachable.

A shell utility that copies, moves, deletes, searches or changes files runs none of its file arguments. So cp ./README.md ./lib makes neither README.md nor lib/index.ts an entry point, and an unused file in lib stays reportable. This applies to awk, cat, chmod, chown, cp, echo, grep, head, ln, ls, mkdir, mv, rimraf, rm, rmdir, sed, sleep, sort, tail, tee, touch, uniq, and wc. find, xargs, and the shells can run another program, so their arguments keep the normal rules: xargs node scripts/run.js keeps scripts/run.js as an entry point.
Turn off entry points for a command

Some other commands also read files as data. For example, a code generator that reads src/**/*.ts does not run those files. List such a command in ignoreCommandEntries, and its file arguments do not become entry points:

The command is still a used dependency, and its --config file is still tracked. The option applies to package.json scripts, CI files, and infrastructure files. It also applies when a script call runs the command, such as npm run gen -- src/input.ts with the script "gen": "my-codegen". To turn off entry points from all commands, use ["*"] and declare the real entry points in entry. ["*"] also drops the modules that a linter loads through a flag, such as eslint -f ./tools/fmt.js, so list those in entry too.

Worker processes and migration scripts often start from a Dockerfile or a CI job, not from an import. Fallow reads these infrastructure files and makes the source files they name entry points, so it does not report those files as unused.
Fallow looks for these files in the project root and in common subdirectories (config/, docker/, deploy/).
The rules for formatter and linter targets and for ignoreCommandEntries also apply here. A CI step such as npx oxlint src/ does not make src/ files entry points.

# Fallow detects scripts/migrate.ts and src/worker.ts as entry points
FROM node:20
RUN node scripts/migrate.ts
CMD ["node", "src/worker.ts"]

A GitHub Actions step runs in its working-directory. Fallow resolves the file arguments of the step in that directory. Fallow reads the value of the step, and the defaults.run.working-directory value of the job and of the workflow. The innermost value applies.

jobs:
 build:
 defaults:
 run:
 working-directory: packages/web
 steps:
 # Fallow makes packages/web/scripts/build.ts an entry point
 - run: tsx scripts/build.ts
 # Fallow makes scripts/check.ts in the project root an entry point
 - run: tsx $GITHUB_WORKSPACE/scripts/check.ts

A path that starts with $GITHUB_WORKSPACE/, ${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/, $\{\{ github.workspace \}\}/ or $\{\{ env.GITHUB_WORKSPACE \}\}/ resolves from the project root. A GitLab path that starts with $CI_PROJECT_DIR/ also resolves from the project root.
In a composite action, a path that starts with $\{\{ github.action_path \}\}/ resolves from the directory of the action.

When the directory is a workspace package, a script call such as npm run gen uses the scripts of that package. In another directory, the file arguments of a root script do not become entry points, because those paths are relative to the root.

A directory with a value that is known only at run time, such as ecosystem-ci/$\{\{ matrix.name \}\}, or a directory outside the project, such as $\{\{ runner.temp \}\}/x, makes no entry point for a relative path. A path such as ../patch.ts that leaves the run-time segment still resolves.
working-directory under with: is an input of an action. It does not change the directory of a run step.
The working directory changes only the file arguments. A binary in the step credits its package in every directory.
Fallow also finds the scripts that a workflow names in these places:

A matrix value. When a step is only run: $\{\{ matrix.project.command \}\}, Fallow reads the command values under project in the matrix: block of the same job, also under include:, as the commands of that step. The step working-directory applies to them.

An actions/github-script step. In the script: input, a path after ${process.env.GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/ or $\{\{ github.workspace \}\}/, and a require('./path'), resolve from the project root. A relative import('./path') resolves from the action itself, so Fallow does not read it.
A step env variable. When the whole value of a step env entry is an anchor such as $\{\{ github.action_path \}\}, a path that starts with that variable resolves like the anchor.

runs:
 using: composite
 steps:
 # Fallow makes .github/actions/setup/prepare-cache.mjs an entry point
 - run: node "$SETUP_ACTION_PATH/prepare-cache.mjs"
 shell: bash
 env:
 SETUP_ACTION_PATH: ${{ github.action_path }}
Fallow does not read env entries of the job or of the workflow for this.

Files that you load with a computed path, such as locale files or icons, are not unused. For import(`./locales/${lang}.json`), the target is not known at analysis time. Fallow converts the pattern into a glob and matches it against the project files.
Fallow marks the matched files as reachable, so it does not report them as unused. This covers locale files, icon sets, route modules, and other directories that follow a naming convention.
An import.meta.glob pattern can use the extglob groups @(..), ?(..), +(..), *(..) and !(..), as Vite does. A negated group excludes the files that match its alternatives:

// Loads every module in ./modules except the *.spec files
const modules = import.meta.glob("./modules/**/!(*.spec).{j,t}s");
A negative entry in an import.meta.glob array excludes files from every positive entry of the same call. Fallow can then report an excluded file as unused:

// ./pages/skip.js is not loaded, so fallow can report it as unused
const pages = import.meta.glob(["./pages/*.js", "!./pages/skip.js"]);
Fallow applies a negative entry that starts with ./, ../ or **. Other negative entries need the alias resolver of Vite, so fallow keeps the files.
Like Vite, fallow matches a ** entry from the common base directory of the positive entries. Next to ./pages/*.js, the entry !**/pages/a.js excludes nothing, because the match starts inside pages.

The static text of a template literal, a string concatenation, or a require.context directory matches only itself. Glob characters in that text, such as [, ], { or *, are not glob syntax. For example, import(`./[id]/${name}.js`) matches ./[id]/view.js, and import("./{group}/" + name) matches ./{group}/item.js.
When a dynamic import pattern is not a valid glob, fallow gives a warning, and the pattern matches no files.
A pattern match uses every value export of the matched file, default included. A type export (a type alias or an interface) of a matched file is used only by an import that names it.

A module path in new URL("./lib/sign.ts", import.meta.url) is not unused. A build tool or a script runner can load the module by that path and call its default export. So fallow uses the default export of the module. The other exports of the module stay reportable. A new URL() path that a Worker or SharedWorker constructor gets uses no export, because a worker runs the module as a script. A directory path, such as new URL("./services", import.meta.url), also uses no export.
Fallow cannot resolve a path that is fully computed at runtime (for example import(userInput)). Add those directories to entry in your config to make them entry points.
Fallow follows export * chains through any number of barrel files, so an export that you import through a barrel counts as used.

flowchart TB A["app.ts
import ﹛ add ﹜ from './src'"] --> B["src/index.ts
export * from './utils'"] B --> C["utils/index.ts
export * from './math'"] C --> D["utils/math.ts
export const add ✓"]
Here, fallow follows the import of add in app.ts through src/index.ts and utils/index.ts to utils/math.ts and marks add as used.
Multi-level chains. Fallow follows export * re-exports at any depth, up to the original declaration.
Cycles. Fallow detects circular re-export chains (for example, a re-exports from b and b re-exports from a) and stops without an error.
Mixed re-exports. Fallow tracks named re-exports (export { foo } from './bar') and namespace re-exports (export * from './bar').

When two export * sources supply the same name, ECMAScript treats the name
as ambiguous, and the barrel does not export it. Until you fix the collision,
Fallow does not report the declarations, members, components, or injections
that supply the name. Run fallow trace FILE:NAME to see the
source files and whether the collision is in the type namespace, the value
namespace, or both.

A namespace import does not mark every export as used. For import * as ns from './module', fallow looks for member accesses (ns.foo, ns.bar) and destructuring (const { foo, bar } = ns) in the importing file. Only those exports count as used.
This works for static imports, dynamic imports (const mod = await import('./x')), and require (const mod = require('./x')).

Fallow also uses oxc_semantic scope analysis to find imports whose binding the file never reads. If a file has import { foo } from './utils' and never uses foo, that import does not count as a reference to the foo export.

Some patterns use the whole object: Object.values(ns), { ...ns }, for (const k in ns), and rest destructuring (const { a, ...rest } = ns). Fallow cannot tell which members these patterns use, so it marks all exports as used.

The same narrowing applies to a namespace re-export (export * as ns from './module'). An export that no consumer reads through ns is an unused export, or an unused type for a type export. When the namespace object leaves the file, for example as a function argument (register(ns)), fallow cannot tell which members the receiver reads, so it marks all exports as used.
Fallow checks a TypeScript namespace (export namespace N { export const a = 1 }) as one export and reports its unused exported members as unused-namespace-members.
Fallow reports public class methods and properties that no code outside the class references. It takes class inheritance, decorators, and framework conventions into account.
Fallow handles these cases without configuration:
Inheritance. When code calls a parent class method through the parent type, fallow marks the child override as used.
Decorators. By default, fallow skips decorated members. Decorators such as @Get(), @Column(), and @Injectable() mean that a framework calls the member at runtime.
Framework lifecycle methods. Fallow never reports componentDidMount, ngOnInit, connectedCallback, and other framework lifecycle methods.
Whole-object patterns. Object.values(instance), Object.keys(), spread operators, and for..in loops mark all members as used.

Playwright fixtures. A test made with test.extend<T>(...) or mergeTests(...).extend<T>(...) credits the members of each fixture class that the test uses. Fallow reads test and mergeTests from @playwright/test and from playwright/test.

Some decorators do not mean that a framework calls the method, for example Playwright's @step("label") or your own @measure, @log, or @retry. List these names in ignoreDecorators. Fallow then checks a method that has only these decorators like an undecorated method.
Fallow still skips a method that has any decorator that is not in the list. A method with @step and @Inject stays framework-managed.
See ignoreDecorators for the matching rules and the unmatched-entry warning.
Class member detection uses syntactic analysis and does not run the TypeScript compiler. Fallow tracks member access through the import graph and does not resolve types.

Fallow tracks CSS and SCSS imports, so stylesheets that your code uses are not unused files. It resolves SCSS @use, @forward, and partials (_prefix files). It treats CSS Module class names as named exports and tracks them through styles.className accesses.
For details, see CSS, SCSS, and Tailwind analysis.

An entry point can also export helpers that nothing uses. Before v2.15.0, fallow marked all exports of an entry point as used. Since v2.15.0, fallow reports exports of an entry file that no other module in the project imports. A plugin or the entry config makes a file an entry point.

This helps most with framework convention files, such as Next.js pages and SvelteKit routes. The framework uses specific named exports (such as default, loader, or getStaticProps), and the file can also export helpers that nothing uses.
Fallow never reports an entry-point file as an unused file. It reports only the exports in that file that have zero references.

Code that is duplicated and unused is a good place to start the cleanup. fallow dead-code --include-dupes compares dead code findings with duplication analysis. Fallow reports clone instances in unused files, or that overlap unused exports, as combined high-priority findings.
When you delete a block that is duplicated and unused, you remove dead code and duplication in one change.
Clone instances in unused files. When no entry point reaches a file and the file has duplicated code, fallow raises the priority of the duplication finding.
Clone instances that overlap unused exports. When an unused export has code that is duplicated elsewhere, fallow reports both findings together.

fallow dead-code --circular-deps runs the full analysis (dead code, dependencies, boundaries, and cycles). All runs are cold, with fallow 2.100.0 on an Apple M5. The flag is now a deprecated alias for fallow architecture --cycles, which runs the same analysis.
Fallow finds cycles in the module graph that dead code analysis already builds, so cycle detection does not build a second graph.
Full reference for the fallow dead-code command and its flags.
Control which issue types are errors, warnings, or disabled.
Remove the dead code that fallow finds.

pages.title: Type-aware unused code checks for TypeScript
items: Type-aware unused code checks for TypeScript
Type-aware analysis confirms with the TypeScript checker that a symbol is unused before you delete it, with evidence for symbol usage and affected tests.
Type-aware mode lets you delete or refactor TypeScript code with exact TypeScript checker evidence. It follows exact symbol identity across aliases, re-exports, packages, and tests.
The default fallow analysis is Rust-native and syntactic. It does not need Node.js or the TypeScript compiler. Add --type-aware when a cleanup or refactor depends on exact TypeScript symbol identity.
The optional companion adds these project-wide capabilities:
Exact symbol-use confirmation for existing dead-code candidates.
Symbol traces with namespaces, aliases, and re-export hops.
Package API surfaces and private type leaks across files.
Exact consumers, affected files, and targeted tests.
Public-signature type coupling, as advisory findings.
Use this pass when a real cleanup or refactor decision depends on TypeScript identity. For fast everyday feedback, keep the normal syntactic run.

fallow type-aware status --format json --quiet
fallow dead-code --unused-class-members --type-aware --format json --quiet
fallow fix --type-aware --dry-run --format json --quiet
fallow dead-code --type-aware --symbol-impact src/api.ts:Client --format json --quiet
fallow health --type-aware --type-coupling --format json --quiet
fallow dead-code --constant-parameters --type-aware --format json --quiet
Keep tsc --noEmit for compiler correctness and Oxlint for local lint rules. Fallow does not emit TypeScript diagnostics or repeat local typed lint findings.
Type-aware fallow answers project-wide questions that those tools do not:
Is this exact declaration used through an alias or re-export?
Which production files and tests depend on this exported symbol?
Does a public signature expose a package-private type?
Which public types couple packages or modules together?
Does a default value of a parameter ever apply, and which calls does a class method have? The opt-in constant-parameter rule reads this evidence when --type-aware is on.

Every semantic result reports complete, partial, or unavailable. Fallow removes a dead-code candidate only when the checker resolves the exact identity of its declaration. When the analysis is partial or unavailable, fallow keeps the original finding and reports a stable omission reason.

fallow fix --type-aware offers a class-member removal only when two conditions are true: every owning project returns complete negative evidence, and the declaration guard still matches. Always preview with --dry-run.

Evidence that the checker can see does not prove that a published API has no external consumers. For library boundaries, package exports, publicPackages, visibility tags, and explicitly selected consumer projects stay authoritative.
To fail the CI job when semantic evidence is incomplete, use --type-aware-require complete:
When automatic project selection misses a consumer, add a --type-aware-project flag for each project. The flag is repeatable:

Svelte language tooling creates virtual TypeScript modules for .svelte files. TypeScript-Go does not yet expose the plugin integration that fallow needs to build the same virtual modules. Fallow still supports default component imports, and named exports backed by declarations that the checker can see.

A selected project can use a named import, named re-export, or wildcard re-export whose .svelte target does not resolve. In that case, fallow abstains with svelte-virtual-module-exports and reports the project and the affected semantic queries as unavailable. In best-effort mode, fallow keeps the syntactic result as advisory evidence. With --type-aware-require complete, the run fails.

For authoritative Svelte and TypeScript diagnostics, run svelte-check. Do not rewrite valid component exports only to satisfy fallow. Keep the Svelte project configuration as it is, and rely on the omission reason until TypeScript-Go provides a supported virtual-module host integration.
Keep the feature opt-in for each repository:
Start with best-effort. Use complete only when partial or unavailable semantic evidence must fail the run.

Type-aware analysis builds an additional TypeScript Program and scans checker symbols. On the current public release corpus, the added time is about 92 ms at the median and 2.3 seconds at P95. Large projects can take longer. Editor sessions reuse the loaded Program. One-shot CLI and CI runs pay the cold setup cost each time.

The fallow npm package does not install the companion, because it brings TypeScript 7 (about 30 MB). Install fallow-type-aware at the same version as fallow when you use --type-aware, mutation --typecheck, or the typeAware config:

The fallow launcher finds the companion next to the fallow package, or in the project root when both packages are in the same node_modules tree. So pnpm projects work too. A global fallow needs a global companion (npm install --global fallow-type-aware@<fallow version>). npx and other package runners do not use the project companion. Start both packages together (npx -p fallow@<version> -p fallow-type-aware@<version> fallow), or set FALLOW_TYPE_AWARE_BIN to its executable. The GitHub Action and the GitLab template install the companion themselves.
fallow type-aware status checks discovery, package version, protocol version, and backend version. It does not analyze the project.

Set FALLOW_TYPE_AWARE_BACKEND=tsrs to run the semantic pass on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 checker, instead of the default TypeScript-Go backend. The environment variable is the only way to select the backend. There is no typeAware.backend config key, and the config file rejects it as an unknown field. The backend stays opt-in while tsrs is a 0.x release.

Fallow accepts any tsrs from 0.18.0 up to (not including) 1.0.0, so you can reuse the tsrs that your project already installs. It must be where fallow-type-aware can resolve it. To install the version that Fallow tests:

npm install --save-dev tsrs@0.20.1-ts7.1.0-beta
FALLOW_TYPE_AWARE_BACKEND=tsrs npx fallow type-aware status
Select the backend on each surface
Fallow reads the variable once per process. Every Fallow process that you start inherits it from its parent.
For MCP, use an env block like this:

The VS Code extension bundles a companion that holds only the default backend. That companion cannot load tsrs. With only the backend variable set, the type-aware pass is unavailable and Fallow shows conservative syntactic findings. To use tsrs in VS Code, set both variables and start the editor from that shell:

An existing FALLOW_TYPE_AWARE_BIN takes precedence over the bundled companion. Use an absolute path, because Fallow resolves a relative path from the working directory. The project must have tsrs installed where that companion can resolve it. The extension has no setting for the backend.

Run fallow type-aware status in the same environment as the surface. It names the backend and the version that ran. _meta.type_aware in the JSON output names them too. The command does not read the config file. A version outside the supported range makes the type-aware pass unavailable, and type-aware status names the range. An unknown backend value also makes the pass unavailable, and type-aware status names the known values.
The tsrs backend refines findings, but its evidence never makes a fix eligible. Guarded fixes need the evidence of the default backend at the version that Fallow tests.
tsrs 0.18.0 has no Windows or macOS x64 binaries. Use 0.20.0 or later on those platforms.
The default backend also accepts any TypeScript 7 release that a package manager override selects.
Fallow will consider a config key when tsrs reaches 1.0 or when the default backend moves to TypeScript 7.1 with corpus evidence for tsrs.
Refine cleanup findings and run exact symbol queries.
See where the default syntactic analysis stops and the optional semantic analysis starts.

pages.title: Detect duplicate code in JavaScript and TypeScript
items: Detect duplicate code in JavaScript and TypeScript
Detect duplicate code in TypeScript and JavaScript. Fallow finds copy-pasted code and shows which copies to extract first, with the same binary and config.

fallow dupes finds duplicated code blocks in your whole codebase and ranks them, so you know which copies to extract first. It runs in the same audit as the dead code, dependency, complexity, and architecture checks. For raw duplication scans, jscpd v5 is faster on the current README benchmark fixtures.

Most dead-code analysis tools find only unused exports and unreachable files. Fallow also detects duplication in the same binary, with the same module graph. You can therefore compare dead code with duplication in one pass.

fallow dead-code --include-dupes finds code blocks that are duplicated and unused. These are the best blocks to clean up first. When you delete one, you remove dead code and duplication in one change.
One run for duplication and dead code also gives you:
One tool, one config, one CI step. You do not install and configure a separate duplication detector.
Shared file discovery. The same ignore patterns, entry points, and workspace config apply to both analyses.
Combined findings. Fallow reports clone families in unused files as combined findings.
The same output formats. JSON, SARIF, markdown, compact, and CodeClimate output work the same way for duplication and for dead code.
Only exact token-for-token clones. Fallow applies no normalization. The code must be character-identical after tokenization.
Use it to find exact copies with no changes.
The default mode. Strict and mild modes give identical results, because AST-based tokenization already removes whitespace and comments before the comparison.
Start with this mode for general detection.
Matches clones also when string literal values differ. Variable names must still match.
Use it to find copied code where only the strings (URLs, messages, labels) changed.
Finds clones with renamed variables and different literal values. Token-type normalization matches code with the same structure.
The broadest mode. Finds code that someone copied and then changed with new variable names and values.

dupes --mode semantic still compares normalized code structure. To find
complete functions that can have the same intent with a different structure,
use the separate, opt-in fallow similar-code
workflow. Its model-backed results are always unverified, and you must review them.
To also report function-scoped clones with small structural edits, add --near:

Near-miss detection uses semantic token normalization. Every pair in a group must have at least 80% shingle similarity. It runs next to exact clone detection. It is opt-in, because it does more work and can report code that a person must review. To turn it on by default, set duplicates.near to true, or use fallow.duplication.near in VS Code.

note: module wiring excluded from clone detection (--no-ignore-imports to include it)

✗ 27,255 lines (19.4%) duplicated across 398 files (0.23s)
Each group header shows the line count, the instance count, the spread (when it is above 0), and the dup: handle of the group.
In semantic mode, fallow also matches copies with renamed identifiers and changed literal values. The output has the same shape. It does not list the renamed identifiers:

note: module wiring excluded from clone detection (--no-ignore-imports to include it)

● Duplicates (2 clone groups)

 196 lines 2 instances spread 1 dup:c4e07b19
 src/lib/dutch-holidays.ts:193-388
 src/lib/dutch-holidays.ts:401-596

 src/features/forecasting/server/procedures/analytics.ts:141-181

 src/features/forecasting/server/procedures/income.ts:590-631
