 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/duplication/#clone-groups

✗ 94,457 lines (67.2%) duplicated across 775 files (3.74s)

fallow dupes --min-tokens 50 # Minimum tokens per clone (default: 50)
fallow dupes --min-lines 5 # Minimum lines per clone (default: 5)
fallow dupes --min-occurrences 3 # Only report clones repeated 3+ times (default: 2)
fallow dupes --threshold 5 # Fail if duplication exceeds 5%
fallow dupes --fail-on-issues # Fail if any clone group remains
fallow dupes --skip-local # Only cross-directory duplicates
By default, fallow reports every duplicated pair (minOccurrences: 2). If you follow the "rule of three" and refactor logic only when it appears in three or more places, raise the threshold:

Fallow rejects values below 2, because a single occurrence is not a duplicate. A higher value skips pairs that can depend on context, and keeps the copies that are worth an abstraction. The VS Code extension has the same control as the fallow.duplication.minOccurrences setting.

Fallow ranks clone groups so the most expensive copies come first. It multiplies the duplicated token count by the occurrence count, then adds a spread boost. Spread is the maximum directory-tree distance between copies. For copies in the same file, each 250 lines between them count as one spread step. The boost is at most 15%, so larger and more repeated clones stay the main priority.
The default report and --top use this order. The JSON output has spread on every clone group, and similarity on near-miss groups.
When a clone group is intentional, add it to duplicates.ignoredClones. Fallow still reports all other duplication findings:

Each entry is the fingerprint of the group plus its instance count. Copy the fingerprint from the human listing or from clone_groups[].fingerprint in JSON, then add :<instance_count>. After a token change or a new copy, fallow reports the group again. An edit that changes only formatting keeps the same fingerprint.

When fallow hides reviewed groups, the JSON output sets stats.clone_groups_ignored. When work limits skip candidate comparisons in a near-miss run, fallow sets stats.near_candidates_skipped. The near-miss result can then be incomplete.

Ordinary dup:<8hex> handles and widened dup:<16hex> handles do not change. When groups have the same full content fingerprint, their handles use dup:<16hex>-rN. A collision handle stays the same when you produce an identical report from another checkout location. It can change when the colliding groups change.

Older numeric collision handles such as dup:<16hex>-1 still load in ignoredClones, but they no longer hide or select a group. With a baseline that has these handles, the affected findings also appear again. To migrate:
Copy its reported handle into your configuration, or refresh the baseline.
Do not replace -1 with -r1 without a review. The number can point to a different group.
Before you add -rN keys to ignoredClones, upgrade every runner that reads a shared configuration. Older binaries reject that syntax.

Earlier versions gave every clone group whose code does not parse on its own the same handle, dup:c77b3abb6f87acd9-rN. An example is a clone that stops before the closing brace of a function. The number followed report order, so in the next run it could point to a different group. Now each of these groups gets its own handle from its tokens. A baseline that still has the old keys prints a note on stderr in human output, and sets baseline_staleness.format to legacy in JSON. To migrate, save the baseline again. Review each group that an ignoredClones entry with this handle hid, then copy its new handle into your configuration.
Fallow puts clone groups with the same set of files into a clone family and suggests a refactoring:
Extract function: the clones are in the same file.
Extract module: the clones are in more than one file.
To compare TypeScript and JavaScript files, pass --cross-language. Fallow removes type annotations before it compares:
Fallow converts .ts files to their .js equivalent for the comparison. This finds clones where someone converted one copy from TypeScript to JavaScript, or the reverse.

Two files with the same imports are not copy-paste. By default, fallow removes this module wiring from the token stream. This covers ES imports, re-export declarations, and top-level static require() binding declarations.
To count module wiring as clone candidates again, use the command-line flag:
Or set it in the config:

A symlinked file or directory in the project gives a clone of the same code under two paths. This is not copy-paste. Fallow marks such an instance with is_symlink: true in JSON output and (symlink) in human output. To report only duplication between real files, use the command-line flag:
Or set it in the config:
The duplication statistics then count only real files. See Symlinked files for the details.
To check duplication only in the files that changed since a git ref, pass --changed-since:
In CI, this reports only the duplication that a pull request adds.
To add duplication limits to an existing codebase, save the current duplication as a baseline. Fallow then fails only on new duplication:

# Save current duplication as baseline
fallow dupes --save-baseline fallow-baselines/dupes.json

# Fail only on new duplication
fallow dupes --baseline fallow-baselines/dupes.json --fail-on-issues
Without --fail-on-issues (or --ci), the run reports the new clone groups and exits 0. See exit codes.
To see all clones of one code location, trace it:
All runs are cold (no cache), with fallow 2.100.0 on an Apple M5. Warm runs are faster again.
Fallow runs duplication in the same audit pass as the dead code, dependency, complexity, CSS, framework, and security checks.
Fallow finds clones with a suffix array and an LCP array. This avoids a quadratic comparison of each pair.
Full reference for the fallow dupes command and its flags.
Set default duplication thresholds and modes in your config file.
Find functions that are written differently and can have the same intent.
How to read clone groups and families.

pages.title: Find semantically similar functions in TypeScript
items: Find semantically similar functions in TypeScript
Find similar functions in JavaScript and TypeScript that may do the same job under other names and syntax. A pinned local model finds them; a person decides.

fallow similar-code finds functions that may do the same kind of work, even
when their code looks different. Use the results to find logic that you can
possibly consolidate and that fallow dupes does not find.

fallow dupes finds exact, normalized, and near-miss copies. Similar-code
discovery compares the meaning of complete functions. Run it after
fallow dupes.

Every result is an unverified candidate. A similarity score is not a
probability. It does not prove that the behavior matches, and it does not
mean that a refactor is safe. Inspect both functions and their tests before
you decide.

The fallow npm package does not install the native companion. Install it at
the same version as fallow:

The fallow launcher finds the package, verifies it, and passes its binary to
fallow, which checks the signature again. A global fallow needs a global
companion. For npx, start both packages together:
npx -p fallow@<version> -p fallow-similar-code@<version> fallow similar-code.
An MCP client that starts npx fallow-mcp needs the same pair.
To check whether the companion and its pinned model are ready, run:
The first download needs your explicit confirmation:

Before it asks, setup shows the model, the license, and the download size.
Use --yes only when you already approved the download and need a command
without a prompt. Project config and agents cannot approve setup for you.

After setup, the analysis runs offline and function source stays on your
machine. The companion receives size-limited source over local process input
and does not save it. Fallow stores derived vectors in a user-local cache with
a separate namespace for each project, so later runs are faster.
The JSON output has its own top-level format:

The score has meaning only for the pinned model and the current settings. Use
it to rank review work. Do not use it to compare projects or to set a general
quality bar.
The top level of the output also records:
The exact companion, model revision, artifact digest, and parameters.

An empty candidate list proves that there are no candidates only when
completion.status is "complete". A "partial" run tells you which limit
or provider problem made the result incomplete.

fallow similar-code --file src/orders/normalize.ts
fallow similar-code --changed-since main
fallow similar-code --workspace @acme/orders
fallow similar-code --threshold 0.88 --min-lines 6 --top 20

--file keeps only the pairs that include the selected file. --changed-since
and the workspace options scope the project in the same way as other fallow
analyses.

Copy the candidate_id from the discovery output. Pass the saved discovery
JSON with --candidates:

fallow similar-code inspect similar-code:candidate:v1:... \
 --candidates similar-code.json --format json --quiet

Run this command from the same project root. Inspect reads the candidate from
the discovery JSON, so you do not repeat the discovery options. The human
discovery output prints this inspect command for each candidate. MCP callers
pass the candidate_id and the candidate snapshot from the
find_similar_code response to inspect_similar_code.

Inspect first reproduces the candidate against your current source. If either
function changed since discovery, you do not review a stale result. Inspect
then adds size-limited evidence, where it is available:
Syntax clues such as async behavior, throws, awaits, and possible side effects.

Every evidence source has an availability state. Fallow reports missing
context as missing. It does not treat absent evidence as a positive verdict.

Fallow never changes the raw candidate document. After a person or agent
inspects the code, they write a separate verdict:
To join the two documents, run:

fallow similar-code review \
 --candidates similar-code.json \
 --verdicts verdicts.json \
 --require-verdict-for-each-candidate \
 --format json --quiet

Review matches a verdict to a candidate by candidate_id first. A verdict
with an unknown candidate_id matches by its review_key. The review_key
hashes only the two function sources. When a function is copied verbatim into
two files, two candidates can therefore share one review_key. The rules are:

Verdicts that match by candidate_id can repeat a review_key. Write one
verdict for each candidate to pass --require-verdict-for-each-candidate.

A review_key must be unique only among the verdicts that match by
review_key.

Review does not apply a review_key verdict that matches more than one
candidate.

A duplicate candidate_id, or a review_key that does not match its
candidate_id, fails the review.

Each of the three judgments is yes, no, or unknown, and each answers a
different question:

Use null when you cannot answer. refactor_safe: true requires
behaviorally_equivalent: true, and behaviorally_equivalent: true requires
candidate_worthy: true.

The available outcomes are same-responsibility, related-but-distinct,
intentional-duplication, unrelated, and needs-human-review.
The MCP server has two read-only tools:

find_similar_code returns unverified candidates, with provenance and
completion status.

inspect_similar_code reproduces one candidate and returns its evidence
packet.

Neither tool downloads a model, edits source, or produces a verdict. If setup
is missing, the agent should ask you to run fallow similar-code setup --local.
When tests, callers, behavior, or side effects are unclear, the agent should
return needs-human-review.

These fields change only candidate discovery. Config cannot choose a model,
provider, executable, download, or credential.
To clear the derived project vectors and keep the downloaded model, run:

Similar-code discovery does not run in bare fallow, audit, dupes, CI
gates, SARIF, LSP, VS Code diagnostics, or auto-fix. It is a review aid and
does not add a finding category. It accepts only the official pinned local
model and never sends source to a remote provider.
Find deterministic and near-miss copied structure.
Connect the read-only discovery and inspect tools.
Set project thresholds, minimum function sizes, and ignore globs.

pages.title: Enforce architecture boundaries in TypeScript
items: Enforce architecture boundaries in TypeScript and JavaScript. Define which directories may import from which, and fallow reports each import that breaks a rule.

Architecture boundaries catch a UI component that imports the database client, or one feature that imports another. You define zones and declare which zones may import from which. fallow architecture then reports each import that breaks a rule.

fallow architecture reports boundary violations together with import cycles and policy violations. To show only boundary issues, pass --boundaries. To see the rules for a file before you edit it, run fallow guard. fallow dead-code also reports boundary violations until the next major version. Its --boundary-violations flag is a deprecated alias for fallow architecture --boundaries.
A built-in preset is the fastest way to add boundaries. Fallow has four presets for common architecture patterns:
To see the zones and rules that the preset creates, run fallow list --boundaries:

Boundaries: 6 zones, 6 rules, 1 logical group

Zones:
 app 3 files src/app/**
 features/auth 7 files src/features/auth/**
 features/billing 5 files src/features/billing/**
 features 0 files src/features/**
 shared 8 files src/components/**, src/hooks/**, src/lib/**, src/utils/**, src/utilities/**, src/providers/**, src/shared/**, src/types/**, src/styles/**, src/i18n/**
 server 4 files src/server/**

Rules:
 features/auth → shared, server
 features/billing → shared, server
 app → features/auth, features/billing, features, shared, server
 features → shared, server, features/auth, features/billing
 server → shared
 shared (isolated, no imports allowed)

Logical groups:
 features 12 files (2 children + 0 fallback) autoDiscover: src/features
 children: features/auth, features/billing
The parent features zone holds only the top-level files in src/features/. Here it has none.
A common React and Next.js pattern. Feature modules cannot import each other. Shared utilities and server infrastructure are the base layers.
4 logical zones: app, features, shared, server. The features zone auto-discovers its immediate child directories, and each child becomes an isolated features/<name> zone.

Top-level files inside src/features/ (barrels, shared types) fall back to the parent features zone. The parent rule allows the discovered children. A barrel can therefore re-export features without false positives, and other top-level files still obey the features rule.

app → every feature, shared, server
features/<name> → shared, server
server → shared
shared (isolated)
The shared zone covers these directories: components, hooks, lib, utils, utilities, providers, shared, types, styles, i18n.
This preset matches the architecture from Bulletproof React, the most common pattern in React and Next.js projects.
Classic N-tier architecture with four layers. Infrastructure may import from domain and from application, which is common with dependency injection.

presentation → application
application → domain
domain (isolated)
infrastructure → domain, application
Ports and adapters pattern. The domain has zero outward dependencies. Adapters implement port interfaces.
Feature-Sliced Design with strict downward imports. Each layer may import only from the layers below it.
6 zones: app, pages, widgets, features, entities, shared

app → pages, widgets, features, entities, shared
pages → widgets, features, entities, shared
widgets → features, entities, shared
features → entities, shared
entities → shared
shared (isolated)
Preset zone patterns use {rootDir}/{zone}/**. Fallow reads the source root from tsconfig.json:
If tsconfig.json has no rootDir, fallow uses src.
For full control, define the zones and rules yourself:
A file belongs to the first zone whose pattern matches (first match wins).
A file that matches no zone is unrestricted. It can import from any zone, and any zone can import it.
Self-imports are always allowed. Files in the same zone can import each other.
A zone with no rule entry is unrestricted. It can import from any zone.
A zone with a rule and an empty allow list is isolated. It cannot import from other zones.

An import that does not run its target is not checked. require.resolve('./x') gives only a path, and a webpack asset loader request (raw-loader!./x.js) gives the text, the bytes or a URL of the file. Both keep the file in use, but no code crosses the boundary.

Boundary checks apply to every analyzed file, also a file that no entry point reaches. A script that only make, mise, or a CI step runs gets the same boundary findings as a reachable file. Such a file can also keep its unused-files finding.

A named or default import through a barrel file is judged against the zone of the module that declares the symbol. For example, src/shared/index.ts re-exports a symbol from src/core/. An import of that symbol from ui is then judged as an import from core, not from shared.
to_path and to_zone name the origin module. The optional via_path field names the barrel that the file imports directly.
Fallow reports one finding per importer and origin module. A direct import of the origin module wins over an import through a barrel.
When a re-export in the barrel itself breaks a rule of the barrel zone, only the barrel gets a finding.
Namespace imports (import * as x) and side-effect imports (import "./x") are judged by the direct target, not by the origin modules.
With autoDiscover, one logical zone creates one concrete zone per child directory. Use it to keep src/features/auth and src/features/billing apart without a zone and a rule for every feature.

If src/features/auth and src/features/billing exist, fallow expands this config to features/auth and features/billing. A rule for the logical features parent applies to every discovered feature. An explicit child rule, such as from: "features/auth", overrides the generated parent rule.

When the zone also has patterns, top-level files inside the auto-discover directory fall back to the parent zone. The parent rule allows the discovered children. For the full semantics, see Auto-discovered zones.

In a monorepo, each package usually has the same directory layout (packages/app/src/, packages/core/src/, ...). With patterns from the project root, you need one zone for each combination of layer and package:

Set root on a zone to limit its patterns to a subtree. Fallow checks that the file path starts with the root prefix. It removes that prefix and matches the patterns against the rest of the path. A file outside the subtree never matches the zone.
Here, packages/app/src/login.tsx is in ui and packages/core/src/order.ts is in domain. To add packages/billing/ later, add one zone entry with the same patterns: ["src/**"] and a different root.
Fallow normalizes trailing slashes and a leading ./, so "packages/app", "packages/app/", and "./packages/app/" are equivalent. It converts backslashes to forward slashes.

Do NOT repeat the root prefix in the patterns. Patterns are already relative to the root. When fallow resolves the config, it rejects root: "packages/app/" with patterns: ["packages/app/src/**"] and reports FALLOW-BOUNDARY-ROOT-REDUNDANT-PREFIX. Remove the root prefix from the pattern (patterns: ["src/**"]).

You can start from a preset and change some zones or rules. A zone with the same name replaces the preset zone. A rule with the same from replaces the preset rule. For examples, see Merging presets with custom config.
To suppress one finding, add an inline comment:
To suppress all boundary violations in a file:
To turn off boundary checks, set the rule severity to off:
The boundary-violation token and rule cover all boundary findings:
Fallow also accepts boundary-call-violation and boundary-call-violations as aliases. Each of the three tokens suppresses every boundary finding on that line or in that file.
To add boundaries to an existing codebase, start with "warn" severity. Fix the violations step by step, then switch to "error" when no violations remain.
All output formats include boundary violations:

── Architecture ─────────────────────────────────────

● Boundary violations (2)
 src/components/Button.tsx:1 → src/server/db/client.ts (shared → server)
 src/features/auth/login.ts:3 → src/features/billing/api.ts (features/auth → features/billing)
 Imports that cross defined architecture zone boundaries
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#boundary-violations

✗ 2 boundary violations (0.05s)

The full JSON output also has schema_version, version, elapsed_ms, and the arrays for all issue types. Each violation also has an actions array with fix and suppression hints. This example shows only boundary_violations.

When the violation comes from a re-export chain, to_path is the origin module and the optional via_path field names the barrel. A direct import has no via_path. The human output shows the barrel as via <path> after the zones.
CLI reference for import cycles, boundaries, and policy rules.
Set boundary violations to error, warn, or off.
Suppress single findings in source code.

pages.title: Remove unused exports and dependencies automatically
items: Remove unused exports and dependencies automatically
Remove unused exports, dependencies, enum members, and catalog entries from TypeScript and JavaScript with one command. Preview each change before you apply it.
fallow fix removes unused exports and unused dependencies from your codebase, so you do not have to delete them by hand.
In agent workflows, fallow fix --yes --format json removes dead code after code generation, with no prompt.
Always commit your changes before you run fallow fix. Then you can undo the fix with Git.

1Preview changesRun a dry run. It shows each removal and changes no files.fallow fix --dry-runWould remove export from src/components/Card/index.ts:1 `CardFooter`
Would remove export from src/providers/trpc-provider/index.tsx:12 `TRPCProvider`
Would remove export from src/server/jobs/queue.ts:61 `enqueueJobDelayed`
Would remove export from src/server/jobs/queue.ts:206 `sweepStuckProcessingJobs`
Would remove export from src/server/jobs/queue.ts:276 `getDeadLetterJobs`
Would remove `@trpc/react-query` from dependencies in package.json
Dry run complete. No files were modified.

2Review the outputMake sure that each proposed removal is safe. Look for exports that external packages use, and for dynamic imports that fallow cannot detect statically.fallow fix --dry-run --format json

3Apply fixesWhen the preview is correct, apply the changes. In an interactive terminal, fallow asks for confirmation before it writes.fallow fixIn CI or another non-TTY environment, use --yes to skip the confirmation:fallow fix --yesInfo.Agents usually apply fixes with fallow fix --yes --format json, which does not prompt. The JSON output lists each change, so the agent can verify the result.
4Verify the resultRun your build and tests to make sure that nothing broke.npm run build && npm test
Unused exports: fallow removes the export keyword and keeps the declaration. An exported enum that the file never references outside its own body is different: fallow deletes the entire enum block.
Unused dependencies: fallow removes them from package.json when no other workspace imports them.

Unused enum members: fallow removes them from the enum declaration. When every member of an exported enum is unused, fallow deletes the whole declaration in one pass, so no empty export enum X {} shell stays behind. Importers in other files then reference a name that no longer exists. Run your TypeScript build to find and fix them.

Duplicate exports: fallow adds ignoreExports rules to your fallow config file. When no config exists outside a monorepo subpackage, it creates .fallowrc.json. Pass --no-create-config to turn off this step.

Unused pnpm catalog entries: fallow removes them from pnpm-workspace.yaml line by line. It removes an object-form entry as one block. Fallow keeps the other comments and the style of the file, with these exceptions:

By default, fallow also removes a contiguous YAML comment block directly above the entry when that block clearly belongs to the entry. Set this with fix.catalog.deletePrecedingComments ("auto", "always", or "never").

When fallow removes the last entry of a catalog group, it rewrites the header to catalog: {} (or <name>: {}), not to a bare catalog:. pnpm rejects a null-valued catalog at install time with Cannot convert undefined or null to object.
After a successful catalog edit, fallow reminds you to run pnpm install, so that pnpm-lock.yaml stays in sync.

Auto-fix does not delete entire files. It removes a class method only when two conditions are true: type-aware analysis gives complete evidence that the method is unused, and the declaration still matches the analyzed source. Review other class members manually.

Sometimes fallow cannot read or fully parse a source file, or discovery skips source files. The affected findings then have reachability_caveats, and workspace_diagnostics lists the files and the reasons. You still see the finding, but fallow does not offer its removal in these places:

Caveats can apply to unused files, exports, types, dependencies, enum members, and class members. An import that fallow did not see can point outside the affected file, so a caveat can apply across the project. Fix the cause of the diagnostic and run the analysis again before you apply the proposed removal. A type-aware result does not override incomplete source evidence.
auto_fixable is per-finding, not per action type

Each action in the actions[] array of a finding has an auto_fixable bool. Fallow sets the value per finding. The same action type can have auto_fixable: true on one finding and auto_fixable: false on another. The guards that the fallow fix applier runs on each instance decide the value.
An agent that uses auto_fixable: true to find actions that are safe to apply without review must check the bool of each action. The action type alone is not enough.
These actions can change per instance:

remove-catalog-entry (unused-catalog-entries): true only when the hardcoded_consumers array of the finding is empty. When a workspace package still pins a hardcoded version of the same package, fallow fix skips the entry so that pnpm install does not break. The action then has auto_fixable: false.

remove-dependency vs move-dependency (dependency findings): when the used_in_workspaces array of the finding is not empty, the primary action changes to move-dependency with auto_fixable: false. fallow fix does not remove a dependency that another workspace imports. When no other workspace uses the dependency, the action stays remove-dependency with auto_fixable: true.

add-to-config for ignoreExports (duplicate-exports): true when fallow fix can safely apply the action. Today that means one of these:

A fallow config file already exists.
No config exists, and the working directory is NOT inside a monorepo subpackage. The applier then creates .fallowrc.json with the same content that fallow init writes, and adds the new rules to it.

The value is false inside a monorepo subpackage that has no config at the workspace root. The applier does not split the configuration into one file for each package. It points you to the workspace root instead. From pre-commit hooks, CI bots, and fallow watch, pass --no-create-config to fallow fix to turn off config creation. The action then has auto_fixable: false, and fallow skips it when it applies fixes.

update-catalog-reference (unresolved-catalog-references): always false today. The applier that switches catalogs does not exist yet. The field can vary per finding, so a later release can enable it without a schema change.
All suppress-line and suppress-file actions have auto_fixable: false.
For scripts, CI, and agent workflows, use JSON output:
fixes lists the proposed actions. In a dry run, total_fixed stays at 0 because fallow changes no files. Paths are relative to the project root.
Reference for the fallow fix command and its flags.
What fallow detects, before you auto-fix.

pages.title: CRAP scores for TypeScript with Vitest coverage
items: CRAP scores for TypeScript with Vitest coverage
Get CRAP scores per function for a TypeScript or JavaScript project with Vitest. Configure Vitest coverage, run fallow health, and gate new CRAP in CI.
CRAP (Change Risk Anti-Patterns) combines the cyclomatic complexity of a function with its test coverage. A complex function with few tests gets a high score. Fallow uses this formula:
CC is the cyclomatic complexity of the function. cov is the statement coverage of the function in percent.
Without coverage data, fallow estimates the coverage from the module graph. This guide shows how to give fallow the real coverage from Vitest, so that each function gets an exact score.

npx vitest run --coverage
npx fallow health --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30
Fallow reads the Istanbul coverage map that the Vitest json reporter writes to coverage/coverage-final.json. Both Vitest coverage providers write this file.
Then add an include pattern to vitest.config.ts:

Vitest 4 removed coverage.all. Vitest 4 and later ignore all: true and give no error. Use coverage.include to add the files that no test loads. In Vitest 3, coverage.all defaults to true, so you do not need include.
With Vitest 3 and the v8 provider, a file that no test loads gets a placeholder entry with no functions. Fallow cannot match this entry, so these functions use the static estimate.
When a source file is not in the coverage map, fallow uses the static estimate for its functions. The human output tells you how many functions matched:
CRAP scores use Istanbul coverage where matched (4/7 functions); the rest fall back to the static estimate.
Vitest excludes test files from coverage by default. The functions in test files therefore always use the estimate. That is expected.
Run the tests with coverage, then give the coverage file to fallow:

npx vitest run --coverage
npx fallow health --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30
--max-crap 30 is the default threshold. A function with a CRAP score of 30 or more is a finding, and fallow health exits with code 1. Change the value to make the gate stricter or less strict.
--coverage also accepts the coverage directory. A relative path resolves against the project root.
When you do not pass --coverage, fallow looks for the coverage file in this order:
coverage/coverage-final.json, then .nyc_output/coverage-final.json, in the project root.
When fallow finds the file in step 3, it prints a note:
note: using auto-detected coverage at /path/to/project/coverage/coverage-final.json; pass --coverage explicitly for deterministic CI scores
In CI, pass --coverage or set FALLOW_COVERAGE. An old coverage file on disk then cannot change the scores.

Vitest writes absolute file paths into coverage-final.json. When the tests ran in a different directory, for example in a Docker container or on another CI runner, the paths do not match your project. Fallow then matches no function and prints a note:
note: the coverage file describes 3 files that no analyzed file matched; check that it was generated for this project, or set --coverage-root.
Give the absolute prefix of the other checkout to --coverage-root. Fallow removes this prefix from each path and adds the project root:
You can also set FALLOW_COVERAGE_ROOT or health.coverageRoot. When the tests and fallow run in the same checkout, you do not need --coverage-root.
Both providers write an Istanbul coverage map, so fallow reads them in the same way. The JSON summary shows coverage_model: "istanbul" and coverage_input_format: "istanbul" for both.

Fallow counts the statements in each function body from the file on disk, and reads the counts from the coverage map. The coverage percent of a function can therefore differ from the Vitest text table.

The CRAP score of a function can change when you change the provider or the Vitest major version. For example, Vitest 3 with v8 records coverage per line, and Vitest 4 and later record it per statement. Use one provider and one Vitest version in CI, so that two runs give comparable scores.

● High complexity functions (2)
 CRAP scores use Istanbul coverage where matched (4/7 functions); the rest fall back to the static estimate.
 src/shipping.ts
 :1 shippingCost HIGH
 10 cyclomatic 9 cognitive 24 lines
 80.2 ! CRAP (11% tested)
 src/untested.ts
 :1 classify HIGH
 7 cyclomatic 6 cognitive 9 lines
 56.0 ! CRAP (0% tested)
The number before CRAP is the score of the function.
! marks the threshold that the function exceeds. Here, both functions exceed only the CRAP threshold.
(11% tested) is the statement coverage of the function from the coverage map. When this part is missing, the score comes from the static estimate.

With real coverage, fallow can find a function that the estimate does not find. In the example, a test imports shipping.ts, so the estimate counts shippingCost as tested. The coverage map shows that the test runs only the first return.
With --format json, each finding has an actions list. The first action that is not a suppression tells you what to do:

{
 "path": "src/shipping.ts",
 "name": "shippingCost",
 "cyclomatic": 10,
 "exceeded": "crap",
 "crap": 80.2,
 "coverage_pct": 11.11111111111111,
 "coverage_tier": "partial",
 "coverage_source": "istanbul",
 "actions": [
 {
 "type": "increase-coverage",
 "auto_fixable": false,
 "description": "Increase test coverage for `shippingCost` (file is reachable from existing tests; add targeted assertions for uncovered branches)"
 }
 ]
}
Untested complexity risk explains the formula and the score ranges.
fallow health fails on every function above the threshold, also on old code. To fail only on the CRAP that a change adds, use fallow audit. It compares the changed files with a base ref:

npx vitest run --coverage
npx fallow audit --base main --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30

Audit scope: 5 changed files vs main (2f5e578..HEAD)
...
 src/shipping.ts
 :1 shippingCost HIGH
 10 cyclomatic 9 cognitive 24 lines
 80.2 ! CRAP (11% tested)
...
✗ complexity: 1 finding · 5 changed files (0.85s)

The default gate is new-only. A new finding fails the audit with exit code 1. A finding that was on the base already does not fail it. When its CRAP score, cyclomatic complexity, or cognitive complexity increases, the finding is worsened, and the verdict is warn with exit code 0.
Use --worsened error to also fail on a worsened finding.
Use --gate all to fail on all findings in the changed files.

The audit uses the same coverage resolution as fallow health, and it supports --coverage-root. Run the tests before the audit, so that the coverage file describes the head of the change. Without coverage data, a CRAP score from the estimate cannot fail a new-only audit. See Estimated CRAP under new-only.
Show mutation scores next to CRAP

Coverage shows which code ran. It does not show if a test fails when the code is wrong. fallow mutation changes the code in small steps, runs your Vitest tests against each change, and saves a report. fallow health can then show the mutation score of each finding under its CRAP score:

npx fallow mutation --all
npx fallow health \
 --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json \
 --mutation-report .fallow/mutation/last-report.json

Mutation report: 2 of 2 findings matched. The score does not change CRAP or the health score.
 src/shipping.ts
 :1 shippingCost HIGH
 10 cyclomatic 9 cognitive 24 lines
 80.2 ! CRAP (11% tested)
 50% mutation score (2 killed, 2 survived, 25 no coverage)

fallow mutation needs a clean git worktree. Commit your changes first, or pass --allow-dirty. It runs your tests many times, so it is slower than a coverage run. fallow health only reads the saved report. The mutation score never changes the CRAP score or a gate. See Mutation report.
--coverage takes one coverage file. Fallow looks for the auto-detected file only in the project root, not in each package.
One coverage file for all packages
Use one Vitest config in the repository root that runs all packages as projects. Vitest then writes one coverage-final.json in the root:

npx vitest run --coverage
npx fallow health --coverage coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30

When each package runs its own Vitest, each package has its own coverage/coverage-final.json. Run fallow one time for each package. Use --workspace to scope the report to the package, and give the coverage file of that package:

npx fallow health --workspace @acme/billing \
 --coverage packages/billing/coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30
npx fallow health --workspace @acme/shipping \
 --coverage packages/shipping/coverage/coverage-final.json --max-crap 30
Do not give the coverage file of one package to a run for all packages. The functions of the other packages then use the estimate, and fallow can miss a finding there.
All health flags, the output formats, and the JSON fields.
The CRAP formula, the score ranges, and the file-level aggregation.
Gate only the findings that a change adds.
Check whether your tests fail when the code is wrong.

pages.title: Find cold code with production runtime coverage
items: Find cold code with production runtime coverage
Runtime coverage shows which functions production traffic runs and which never run. Fallow merges it into fallow health, so you delete cold code on evidence.
Runtime coverage tells you which functions ran when your deployed app handled real traffic. Use it to delete cold code with confidence and to spot changes to hot code in review.
Static analysis finds exports with no references and files that no test reaches. Runtime coverage adds the production view on top of fallow health.

fallow license activate --trial --email you@company.com
fallow coverage setup
fallow health --runtime-coverage ./coverage

When you enable runtime coverage, fallow merges runtime evidence into the health report. Each function gets a per-finding verdict. The verdict combines the static reachability signal with the invocations that fallow observed in production:
The report also has these fields:
Aggregate counts: functions_tracked, functions_hit, functions_unhit, functions_untracked, coverage_percent.

capture_policy: absent for a full capture. positive_only for a Fallow Cloud partial capture, which records only the functions that ran. For such a capture, functions_tracked, functions_unhit and coverage_percent are null, because the capture cannot see a function that did not run. functions_untracked then also counts the functions without a call.

An optional capture_quality block (window_seconds, instances_observed, lazy_parse_warning, untracked_ratio_percent). Sidecars on protocol 0.3 or newer emit it. It flags short-window captures in which lazy-parsed scripts may not appear.
id: a per-finding suppression id (fallow:prod:<hash>). The hash covers the current line.

stable_id (optional): a cross-surface id (fallow:fn:<hash>). The hash covers file + name + start line. One function has one value across findings, hot paths, blast radius, and importance, and across the V8, Istanbul, and oxc producers.

source_hash (optional): a content digest that does not change when a line moves. A function that moved but was not edited keeps the same value, so its baseline stays suppressed after a pure line shift.
line, the per-finding verdict, confidence, supporting evidence, and machine-readable actions.

discriminators (optional): the inputs behind the verdict, so an agent can reproduce the verdict without deriving it again. The block has:

tracking_state: called, never_called, or untracked.
The low_traffic_threshold and min_observation_volume in effect.
Every finding has an evidence block. It gives the reason for the verdict in machine-readable form:

test_only_reference covers the one case where production mode and static reachability disagree. Production mode drops test, spec, story, fixture, and benchmark files from discovery. An export that only those files call therefore reads as statically unused.

true: the function is unreachable in the production graph, but an excluded file still references it. It is not dead code, because a removal breaks the test that references it. Fallow reports it as review_required, not safe_to_delete, with the action "Only tests reference this export; delete the test usage together with the function or keep it".
false: fallow compared the production graph with the full tree and found no such reference.
null: the report ran without a production filter, so there is no second reachability answer.

A hot path tells you how often a function runs. The optimization_target block also tells you how much work each call does, so you know where speed work gives the largest gain. importance ranks the risk of a change. optimization_target ranks the speed gain.

The block counts come from the V8 dump. Node writes them under NODE_V8_COVERAGE, so a dump from a test run or a benchmark run gives the measured value. When the dump has block counts for the function, cost_basis is inner_iterations. When it has none (an Istanbul file, or a cloud pull), cost_basis is cognitive. Cognitive complexity is a static proxy for the work per call, not a measurement. On the cognitive basis, the work per call is at least 1.

One report can hold both bases. A dump with block counts also gives cognitive for a function that shares its start line with another function, or that fallow cannot map to a source line. Scores on the two bases do not compare, so sort by cost_basis first.

A hot path has no optimization_target block when it has no stable_id, or when no function in the checkout matches the stable_id. The optimization_target_unmatched warning gives the count of these hot paths in the output.

The runtime coverage pass selects hot paths by invocations, and --top keeps the busiest. A function with fewer invocations but a large amount of work per call can be absent from the list. Raise --top, or lower --min-invocations-hot, to see more candidates.
To list the best speed targets from the JSON output:

fallow health --runtime-coverage ./coverage --format json --quiet \
 | jq '.runtime_coverage.hot_paths
 | map(select(.optimization_target))
 | sort_by(.optimization_target.cost_basis != "inner_iterations",
 -.optimization_target.cost_score)
 | .[:10]
 | map({path, line, function, invocations, basis: .optimization_target.cost_basis,
 cost: .optimization_target.cost_score,
 per_call: .optimization_target.inner_iterations_per_call})'
The human output shows the cost at the end of each hot path line, for example (600 invocations, p100, cost 1,800 at 3.00 iterations/call).
Two flags control how strict fallow is when it assigns verdicts:
fallow health has three coverage options. Each answers a different question:
To find untested code, use --coverage-gaps. For more accurate CRAP scores, use --coverage. For evidence about the code that production runs, use --runtime-coverage.

If a V8 dump includes Node's source-map-cache, fallow remaps the supported source-map URLs before analysis. Supported URLs include file paths, relative paths, webpack://..., and vite://.... For an unsupported virtual scheme, fallow uses raw V8 handling and the run continues.

A remapped function count has a ceiling of 4,294,967,295 calls. The remap writes 32-bit counts, so a function that V8 counted more often than that reports the ceiling as its invocations. Only very hot helpers in long-running processes reach it.

Production runtime coverage records positions in your built bundle. Examples are a Next.js .next/server/chunks/*.js, an Electron out/main/index.js, a NestJS dist/, or a minified browser bundle. Bundle positions cannot map back to your TypeScript or JSX source on their own.

If you do not take one of the two steps below, the cloud records every function as unresolved. fallow coverage analyze --cloud then shows no attributable findings, and a coverage_unresolved warning explains why.

Upload source maps (for V8 coverage). After the build, upload the .map files in a CI step. The cloud uses them to map bundle positions back to source:
fallow coverage upload-source-maps --dir <build-dir> # e.g. dist, .next, out
Upload the maps for the same commit on which you collected the coverage. fallow coverage documents the flags, per-commit SHA matching, and CI snippets. When fallow coverage analyze --cloud finds built .map files on disk that you did not upload, it prints the exact command to run.

Instrument at build time with Istanbul (no maps needed). oxc-coverage-instrument rewrites your source and puts the original file and line positions in the coverage itself, so nothing needs remapping. The fallow project uses this path for its own code.
Optional: start a trial or activate a license with fallow license. A single local capture works without one.
Follow the generated recipe in docs/collect-coverage.md.
When coverage exists, run fallow coverage setup or fallow health --runtime-coverage <path> again.
fallow coverage setup is resumable. It does these steps:
Writes a collection recipe for your framework.
Detects an existing coverage artifact, when one is present.
In change review, runtime coverage shows which hot code a change touches:
When changed files touch hot runtime code, fallow can upgrade the overall verdict to hot-path-touched. PR review then has a stronger signal than static complexity alone.
For tighter line-level scoping, pass a pre-computed unified diff:

Fallow then flags a hot function only when the diff changes a line inside its [start_line, end_line] range, not anywhere in the file. The bundled GitHub Action and GitLab CI template already pre-compute the diff and pass it in. PR comments therefore show only the hot paths that the change touches.
Line-level hot-path matching needs protocol 0.5 or newer in the sidecar. Older sidecars report only a start line, so fallow uses file-level scoping.

Runtime coverage is part of Fallow Cloud, the paid product. A single local capture is free and needs no license. Continuous or multi-capture monitoring (for example, a V8 directory with more than one JSON file) needs a license with the runtime_coverage feature. To try it, start a 30-day trial with fallow license activate --trial --email <addr>.
Fallow verifies the license offline against a compiled-in Ed25519 public key. Only fallow license activate --trial and fallow license refresh need network access.
When a license expires, fallow gives you a grace period:

When a license is present, fallow checks it for every runtime coverage run, also for a single capture. An expired license past the grace period, an invalid token, or a license without the runtime_coverage feature stops the run with exit code 3. For details, see fallow license.
Runtime coverage merges into the standard health report and output formats.
Start a trial, inspect license status, refresh, or deactivate a local token.

pages.title: Analyze production code only, without tests
items: Analyze production code only, without tests
Production mode limits fallow findings to the code you ship. It excludes test files, story files, and devDependencies, and flags type-only dependencies.
Production mode limits the analysis to code that ships to users. Fallow ignores test and development files, so the report shows only the unused code and dependencies in your production build.
You can also set it in your config:

● Unused exports (2)
 src/utils/format.ts
 :12 formatCurrency
 :28 formatPercentage
 Exported symbols with no known consumers
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#unused-exports

● Unused dependencies (1)
 moment
 Listed in dependencies but never imported
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#unused-dependencies

● Type-only dependencies (1)
 zod → move to devDependencies (only imported via 'import type')
 Dependencies only used for type imports; consider moving to devDependencies
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#type-only-dependencies

✗ 4 issues (19ms, production mode, 623/847 files)
In production mode, fallow finds dependencies that your code imports only with import type:
import type { Config } from 'some-package'; // Type-only, erased at runtime
Move these packages to devDependencies. The compiler erases types, so production installs do not need them.
In a monorepo, production mode finds the dependencies in each package that belong in devDependencies. This keeps each package install small.
In combined mode (bare fallow) and in fallow audit, you can enable production mode for each analysis separately:

For one run, pass --production-health, --production-dead-code, or --production-dupes. In CI, set FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH=true or one of the related env vars. The global --production flag still enables production mode for every analysis.
Fallow applies these sources in order of precedence, highest first:

--production and the per-analysis flags can only enable production mode. --no-production turns it off for every analysis, and it overrides env vars and config. It conflicts with --production. Env vars and config can enable or disable production mode. Examples:

# Run health in production mode, dead-code and dupes on the full tree
fallow --production-health

# Same, via env var (useful in CI templates that pass env-only)
FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH=true fallow

# Per-analysis env wins over the global env, so this runs health in production
# mode even though the global env says off (the typical CI-template case)
FALLOW_PRODUCTION=false FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH=true fallow

# CLI flags beat env vars; this enables all three regardless of FALLOW_PRODUCTION_* env
fallow --production

# Turn production mode off for every analysis, even when config sets production: true
fallow --no-production
Run production mode in your CI pipeline.
Control which issue types are errors, warnings, or disabled.

pages.title: Analyze Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX, and HTML files
items: Analyze Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX, and HTML files
Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX, and HTML support: fallow counts files that only these file types, GraphQL, or CSS reference as used, with no plugin or config.

A file that only an HTML page, a Vue template, or a stylesheet references is not unused. Fallow analyzes more than .js and .ts files: it reads imports and exports from non-JavaScript file types, based on the file extension. You do not need a plugin or config.
Fallow finds .html files and reads the <script src> and <link> tags as module graph edges. This covers projects with HTML entry points, such as Parcel or setups with no framework.

Root-relative paths (for example <script src="/src/main.tsx">). Fallow resolves them against the directory of the HTML file first, then against the project root, then against public/ in the project root. html tagged templates in JS and TS files use the same order, without the public/ step (see the SSR layouts tab).
Fallow reads references to ./styles/main.css, ./vendor/lodash.js, and ./src/main.ts from this file.
The Parcel plugin adds index.html as an entry pattern, so fallow finds HTML entry files with no extra config.

Angular template complexity. fallow health reports the complexity of Angular templates as synthetic <template> findings. This covers standalone .html files that templateUrl references and inline @Component({ template: \...` })` literals. Fallow counts these template constructs:

Fallow reports an inline-template finding on the @Component decorator line. To suppress it, put // fallow-ignore-next-line complexity directly above the decorator. To suppress an external-template finding, put <!-- fallow-ignore-file complexity --> at the top of the .html file.

Fallow reads the <script> block of Vue and Svelte single-file components and analyzes it like a JS or TS module. It also reads the <template> section for component references, directives, and expressions. An import that only the template uses therefore counts as used.
<script src="./external.ts"> external script references (Vue only. In Svelte, a <script src> tag is runtime HTML and does not add an import.)
HTML comments (<!-- ... -->), which fallow removes before parsing
Component tags: <MyComponent> resolves to imported MyComponent
Custom directives: v-focus-trap resolves to imported vFocusTrap
v-on and v-bind object syntax (for example v-on="handlers")
Template expressions: \{\{ formatDate() \}\} marks formatDate as used
Namespace member access: utils.formatDate in a template marks the member as used
Component tags: <Button> resolves to imported Button
Directives: use:tooltip, transition:fade, animate:flip, in:fly, out:fade

Fallow reads imports of ref from vue, formatDate from @/utils/date, and FocusTrap from @/components/FocusTrap.vue. The template uses <FocusTrap> and formatDate, so fallow does not report them as unused, although the script block does not use them.
Svelte components export props implicitly. Fallow cannot tell props from utility exports, so it can miss unused exports in .svelte files. For details, see Limitations.

SSR frameworks such as Hono can render HTML from a tagged template literal (html`...`). Fallow reads <script src="..."> and <link rel="stylesheet|modulepreload" href="..."> in these templates as it does in plain HTML. Each one is an asset reference that keeps the target file reachable.
<link rel="stylesheet" href="./global.css"> inside html`...` tagged templates
<link rel="modulepreload" href="./vendor.js"> inside html`...` tagged templates
Root-relative paths (<link href="/static/style.css">). Fallow resolves them against the parent directory of the source file first, then against the project root

import { html } from 'hono/html'

export const Layout = ({ title, body }: { title: string; body: string }) => html`
 <!doctype html>
 <html>
 <head>
 <title>${title}</title>
 <link rel="stylesheet" href="/static/style.css" />
 <script defer src="/static/app.js"></script>
 </head>
 <body>${body}</body>
 </html>
`
Fallow reads references to /static/style.css and /static/app.js from this file and marks those files in static/ as reachable.

Fallow does not read <script src> and <link href> in JSX or TSX layouts. In JSX, these attributes are runtime HTML, not module imports, so they do not add a graph edge. If a JSX layout is the only reference to an asset, add the asset to entry or ignorePatterns.

In tagged templates, fallow matches only the bare identifier tag html. It ignores other tags, such as css, sql, and gql. It skips an asset reference that an interpolation splits (html`<script src="${base}/app.js">`), so it does not produce a broken specifier.

Plain JavaScript files can reference TypeScript types through JSDoc import() expressions. Fallow reads these references and marks the types as used, so untyped JS files do not cause false unused-export reports.

Fallow marks the Config and Result types from ./types.ts as used, although no import statement binds them. This works in all JSDoc tags (@param, @returns, @type, @typedef, @callback). Fallow also supports:
union annotations with more than one import() expression ({import('./a').A | import('./b').B})
Fallow reads only /** */ JSDoc blocks. It ignores single-star /* */ comments, because they are not JSDoc. The TypeScript compiler does the same.
Astro components start with a frontmatter block between two --- lines. Fallow analyzes the content of this block as TypeScript.

Fallow also follows the client scripts in the template body: <script src="..."> references and ESM import statements in inline <script> blocks. Astro bundles both into the page at build time, so their targets stay reachable.

fallow health scores the functions of each inline <script> block, including is:inline and define:vars scripts. Each finding has its line and column in the full .astro file. A block with a src attribute or a data type, such as application/ld+json, gets no score.

---
import Header from '../components/Header.astro'
import Footer from '../components/Footer.astro'
import type { Props } from './types'
---

<html>
 <body>
 <Header />
 <slot />
 <Footer />
 <script src="../scripts/analytics.ts"></script>
 <script>
 import '../scripts/hydrate'
 </script>
 </body>
</html>
Fallow reads imports of Header, Footer, and the Props type from this file. It also reads ../scripts/analytics.ts (external) and ../scripts/hydrate (inline ESM).
MDX files can contain JavaScript import and export statements next to Markdown content. Fallow adds these statements to the module graph.

import { CodeBlock } from '../components/CodeBlock'
import { Callout } from '../components/Callout'

export const meta = { title: 'Getting Started' }

# Getting Started

<CodeBlock language="bash">
 npm install fallow
</CodeBlock>
Fallow tracks the imports of CodeBlock and Callout, and the named export meta.
GraphQL documents can import fragments from other .graphql and .gql files with #import comments. Fallow reads these relative links and keeps the imported fragment files reachable.
Relative imports with no extension, such as #import "./fragment". Fallow tries .graphql and .gql

Fallow reads the reference to ./fragments/user-fields from query.graphql. Because the reference has no extension, fallow tries .graphql and .gql. It then marks fragments/user-fields.graphql as reachable.

Fallow reads only relative #import specifiers that start with ./ or ../. It ignores package specifiers and schema-loader syntax on purpose, because they do not point to a local document in the module graph.
Fallow treats the class names in CSS and SCSS module files (.module.css and .module.scss) as named exports. When a component imports styles from a CSS module, fallow knows which classes exist.
This file exports root, primary, and disabled as named exports.

When Tailwind is in your package.json, @apply and @tailwind directives mark the tailwindcss dependency as used. This prevents a false "unused dependency" report. A Tailwind v4 @plugin "pkg" directive marks its package or local plugin file as used.
React Native projects use a file extension per platform for each platform implementation. Fallow treats these files as variants of the same module.

src/
 Button.tsx # Default implementation
 Button.web.tsx # Web override
 Button.native.tsx # Native override
When another file imports ./Button, fallow resolves the import to all platform variants and marks each one as reachable.
How fallow builds the module graph and detects unused code.
Framework plugins that detect entry points for you.

pages.title: Find unused CSS Modules classes and Tailwind tokens
items: Find unused CSS Modules classes and Tailwind tokens
Find unused CSS Module classes and Tailwind tokens, and stop false unused-file reports for stylesheets. Fallow resolves SCSS partials, @use, and @forward.

Fallow reads your stylesheets, so it can report unused CSS Module classes and Tailwind tokens, and it does not report used stylesheets or Tailwind packages as unused. It resolves @use, @forward, SCSS partials (_prefix files), and Tailwind directives. You do not need to configure anything.
Fallow supports the full SCSS module system. Each import adds an edge to the module graph, and fallow follows re-exports through the dependency chain.
Fallow resolves SCSS partials with the standard convention. For @use 'components/button', it tries these candidates in order:
Fallow reads this file as follows:
It imports the sass:color built-in. Fallow ignores it, because it is not a project dependency.
It imports ./variables, which resolves to _variables.scss through the partial convention.
It imports ./mixins/responsive, which resolves to mixins/_responsive.scss.

Fallow also supports SCSS include paths, which frameworks such as Angular configure. When fallow cannot resolve a bare specifier such as @use 'variables' locally, it searches the configured include directories with the same partial and index conventions.

CSS Module class tracking finds the classes that no component uses. For files with the .module.css, .module.scss, .module.sass, or .module.less extension, fallow reads every class name in the selectors as a named export. A class that appears in more than one selector is one export, so it does not cause duplicate findings.
This file exports three named symbols: root, primary, and disabled.

When a component imports a CSS module, fallow tracks which classes the component accesses. A default import can use any local name. If the code passes or uses the whole imported object, fallow marks every class as used:
Here, fallow marks styles.root and styles.primary as used. No code references the disabled class, so fallow reports it as an unused export.

── Unused Code ─────────────────────────────────────

● Unused exports (1)
 src/Button.module.css
 :10 disabled
 Exported symbols with no known consumers
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#unused-exports

✗ 1 export (0.02s)
Run fallow dead-code --unused-exports to see the unused CSS module class names in your project.
When a CSS or SCSS file has an @apply or @tailwind directive, fallow adds a synthetic dependency on the tailwindcss package. This prevents a false "unused dependency" report.
Fallow finds the @tailwind and @apply directives and marks tailwindcss as a used dependency.

Tailwind v4 registers plugins in CSS with the @plugin directive. Fallow reads each @plugin target as a default import. A package plugin counts as a used dependency. For a relative plugin file, fallow marks the default export as used.

Fallow marks @tailwindcss/typography and daisyui as used dependencies. It marks ./tailwind-local-plugin.js as reachable and its default export as used. Fallow also reads the directive in Vue and Svelte <style> blocks. A package name with no extension, such as daisyui, stays a package specifier, also in .scss and .sass files. Fallow does not resolve it as a local partial, as it does for SCSS @use.

With fallow health --css, fallow also reports @theme design tokens in Tailwind v4 projects that you can possibly remove. A token is a cleanup candidate when fallow sees no reference to its generated utility.
Here, --color-brand counts as used, because bg-brand uses the generated utility suffix. Fallow reports --shadow-glow in css_analytics.unused_theme_tokens with a read-only verification action.
These also count as a use of a token:

The check is conservative. It runs only for Tailwind v4 projects. It reports nothing when Tailwind plugins or published CSS can use tokens in ways fallow cannot see. Each result is a candidate, never an auto-fix.
The other CSS cleanup signals follow the same rules. Each is a candidate with a read-only verification action:
These signals point a reviewer to a class, font, animation, or type-scale mismatch that is probably stale. They do not claim that it is always safe to delete.

Fallow counts the @keyframes blocks of SCSS and Less sources, also in a Vue or Svelte <style lang="scss"> block. A Sass or Less animation value can hold a variable or an interpolation that fallow cannot resolve, for example animation: #{$name} 1s. Such a value can name any @keyframes block that a Sass or Less source defines. Fallow then does not report these blocks as unreferenced. The summary field css_analytics.summary.keyframes_unchecked gives their count. The human output shows them as not checked on the @keyframes line. A @keyframes block in plain CSS is always checked.

A server-side template can apply a class that no JavaScript or TypeScript file uses. Fallow reads template files as class references, so such a class is not an unreferenced_css_classes candidate. Fallow always reads files with these extensions:

Fallow reads the full text of a template. Each class-like word in a template counts as a use of that class. A common word such as hidden or title in a template therefore also credits the class of that name. A Markdown file is different: it counts only when it has dynamic class syntax.

A class prefix before a {{ expression also counts. In grid--\{\{ columns \}\}, the prefix grid-- credits each class that starts with grid--. This rule also applies to .vue, .html, .md, and .astro files with dynamic class syntax.
For other template languages, add their extensions with the top-level markupExtensions key:

Fallow reads template files as text only. They do not join source discovery or the module graph, so fallow never reports them as unused files and does not follow their imports. The walk obeys .gitignore, ignorePatterns, and --max-file-size.

Before you change a token, you want to know what uses it. token_consumers answers this question: it lists the consumers of each token. On Tailwind v4 projects, fallow health --css --format json adds css_analytics.token_consumers. It is a reverse index over the same gated set of @theme tokens:
Each consumer location has a kind:
utility: a markup class that ends in -<name>, such as bg-brand
apply: a class inside an @apply body
css-var: a var(--token) read in regular CSS
theme-var: a var() reference inside another @theme token
consumers is a capped sample. consumer_count is the full total.

consumer_count is a static lower bound. The scan cannot see a computed class name such as bg-${color}. A 0 therefore means that fallow sees no consumer. These are the same tokens that unused_theme_tokens reports, and a 0 does not prove that the token is safe to delete. token_consumers gives context for a change. The cleanup candidate is still unused_theme_tokens.
token_consumers also covers CSS-in-JS token DEFINITIONS. You see the consumers of these tokens in the same way as for an @theme token:

JS objects define these tokens. Code uses them through member access across modules (import { vars } from './tokens'; vars.color.primary) or through Panda token('colors.brand') calls. The entry shape therefore depends on the origin:
The consumer kind and the token shape tell the origins apart:
Before it matches, the cross-file scan resolves each import to its defining file. A vars with the same name from an unrelated module never counts.
Two limits are stricter than for Tailwind:

The cross-file scan uses the shared import resolver of fallow. Relative imports, tsconfig paths aliases, and workspace package imports can resolve to the token definition. Dynamic import strings, unresolved aliases, generated package state, and computed token access still make consumer_count a lower bound.

CSS-in-JS has no dead-token finding that confirms the count (no equivalent of unused_theme_tokens). A CSS-in-JS consumer_count of 0 is a weaker signal that fallow sees no consumers. It does not mean that you can delete the token.
Fallow reports CSS-in-JS token consumers only when the project declares a CSS-in-JS library (@stylexjs/stylex, @vanilla-extract/css, or @pandacss/dev).
The Tailwind plugin also parses tailwind.config.{js,ts,cjs,mjs}:
Content globs. Fallow treats the globs in the content array as always-used file patterns.
Plugin packages. Plugins in require() calls or string arrays count as used dependencies.
Presets. Fallow tracks presets as referenced dependencies.
Imports. Fallow tracks imports in the config file (for example import defaultTheme from 'tailwindcss/defaultTheme').
Fallow marks tailwindcss, @tailwindcss/typography, and @tailwindcss/forms as used dependencies.
Each plain CSS @import statement adds an edge to the module graph. Fallow tracks relative paths and package imports.
Fallow resolves ./reset.css and ./typography.css as local files, and @fontsource/inter as a package dependency. It ignores remote URLs (https://...) and data URIs.

The styling health grade gives you one number for the quality of your CSS. fallow health --css computes it from the raw css_analytics: an A-F letter and a 0-100 score. Fallow scores it separately from the JavaScript and TypeScript code health score. The JSON output has it as styling_health. The human output shows a Styling health: line under CSS health.
The score starts at 100 and subtracts five capped penalties:

The grade gives design-token drift (inconsistent values) more weight than identical repetition, because design tokens exist to fix inconsistent values. The token_erosion value-drift signal counts only hardcoded literals. Fallow never counts var(--*) references and @theme definitions as distinct hardcoded values. A system that uses its scale through custom properties (box-shadow: var(--shadow-md)) therefore scores zero drift, however many tokens it defines. A system that hardcodes many one-off shadows, radii, and line heights gets a small penalty that grows slowly. The penalty points you toward tokens and never jumps sharply.

Some grades come from little CSS: few authored declarations, or mostly compile-time atomic CSS-in-JS such as StyleX or Panda. Fallow marks such a grade confidence: "low" and states the reason. You can then tell it from a grade for a full design system. Confidence is metadata only and never changes the score.

Styling health is descriptive-only. It never changes an exit code, a badge, or a CI result, and it never affects the JavaScript and TypeScript health_score. Use it to judge the state of your design system, not as a pass or fail gate.

formula_version increases each time the styling-health rubric changes. It is separate from the code-health formula version. You can therefore tell a score change from new weights apart from a change in your CSS. If you compare styling_health.score / grade over time (snapshot CIs, trend dashboards), check formula_version and make a new baseline when it increases.

pages.title: Debug fallow findings and false positives
items: Debug fallow findings and false positives
Debug fallow findings: trace why an export, file, dependency, or clone is reported or missed, profile slow runs, and fix the common false positives.

When fallow reports something you did not expect, or misses something you did expect, this page shows you how to find the cause. Trace flags show how fallow reached a result, and --performance shows where the run spends its time.
To see the full usage chain for one export, pass --trace FILE:EXPORT.

USED formatCurrency in src/utils/format.ts

 File: reachable
 Namespace: value
 Reason: Used by 2 file(s), re-exported through 1 barrel(s)

 2 direct reference(s):
 -> src/components/Price.ts (named import)
 -> src/pages/Checkout.ts (named import)

 Re-exported through:
 -> src/utils/index.ts as 'formatCurrency' (1 ref(s))
Fallow prints every file that imports formatCurrency, and every barrel that re-exports it. For an unused export, the status is UNUSED and the Reason line tells you why. Use it when:
Fallow reports an export as unused, and you expected it to be used.
You want to know which files depend on a symbol before you remove it.
Fallow does not resolve a re-export chain the way you expect.
To see all incoming and outgoing module graph edges for one file, pass --trace-file PATH.

Fallow shows every import in the file and every file that imports from it. When a Module Federation exposes entry makes the file an entry point, the trace names each config that exposes it. See Trace the Federation source.

When a file exists at the exact path from the project root, dead-code --trace and --trace-file take that file. In a monorepo, src/a.ts then never selects packages/x/src/a.ts. A short path that matches more than one file takes the first match, so pass the full project-relative path.
Fallow reports a file as unused, and you think something references it.
You want to check that an entry point reaches the file.
Fallow marks all exports of a file as unused. The cause can be that no entry point reaches the file.
To find every place that uses a package, pass --trace-dependency PACKAGE. This covers imports and script binaries.

Fallow lists each file that imports the package once, and marks a file as type-only when every import of the package in that file is type-only. import_count is the number of importing files. To see which imported names the code uses, and where, run fallow trace --dependency PACKAGE. When a package.json script or a CI config uses a binary of the package, fallow says so. When the name is a Module Federation remote alias, the trace names each config that declares it, and says that a remote container provides the name. Use it when:
Fallow reports a dependency as unused, and you think a script or a config file uses it.
You want to know which parts of your codebase depend on a package.
You want to know if you can remove a dependency.
To see all clone instances for one source location, pass dupes --trace FILE:LINE.
Fallow shows every other location in the same clone group as the code at that line. Use it when:
You want to find all copies of a duplicated block before you refactor.
You must decide whether to extract a shared function or module.
A duplication finding looks wrong, and you want to see the matched instances.
To see how long each pipeline stage takes, pass --performance.

┌─ Pipeline Performance ─────────────────────────────
│ discover files: 13.2ms (520 files)
│ workspaces: 2.1ms (0 workspaces)
│ plugin detection: 21.4ms (+10.5ms plugin globs under entry points)
│ script analysis: 3.0ms
│ parse/extract: 17.6ms (520 modules, 520 cached, 0 parsed)
│ cache update: 2.0ms
│ entry points: 12.3ms (92 entries)
│ root package 1.5ms
│ workspaces 0.0ms
│ plugin globs 10.5ms
│ compile 9.9ms
│ match 0.2ms
│ (other) 0.4ms
│ infrastructure 0.2ms
│ dynamic globs 0.0ms
│ dedup 0.0ms
│ (other) 0.0ms
│ resolve imports: 0.0ms
│ build graph: 5.1ms
│ analyze: 19.3ms
│ (other): 0.0ms
│ ────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ TOTAL: 61.4ms
│ rows are per-stage costs; several run outside or beside the TOTAL clock
├─ Process ──────────────────────────────────────────
│ startup: 1.3ms (thread pool 0.1ms)
│ config: 1.1ms
│ analysis: 97.0ms (the stage rows above)
│ after analysis: 0.2ms
│ output: 12.9ms
│ (other): 0.4ms
│ ────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ WALL: 112.9ms
│ work: 0 files read, 0 source bytes, 2481337 parse cache bytes
│ resolve: 0 specifier calls (0 unique), 0 resolver calls, 0 canonicalize calls
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────

The indented rows under entry points split that stage into parts. They are not added to the TOTAL sum. Fallow shows them only when the stage takes 5ms or more, so the box stays short for a fast project. When entry-point discovery is the slow stage, these rows show if the cost is plugin glob compilation, workspace traversal, or something else.

Read the rows as the cost of each stage, not as parts of TOTAL. TOTAL is the wall clock of the dead-code analysis, from workspace and plugin loading until the detectors finish. File discovery, parsing and the cache update run before that clock starts, so on a warm run the rows can add up to more than TOTAL. The (other) row is TOTAL minus the stage rows, with a minimum of 0.0ms.

In combined mode (fallow with no subcommand), the duplication stage can run at the same time as the rest of the pipeline. Fallow then marks it (concurrent). When the two passes share one file walk, duplication runs after the dead-code pass, and fallow marks it (after dead code). Fallow does not add it to TOTAL in either case. When duplication detection takes longer than the dead-code pass, this stage can be larger than TOTAL.
The Process section covers the time outside the pipeline stages. The rows are parts of one clock, so they add up: the rows plus (other) give WALL, the time from process start to the table.
startup is argument parsing and setup before the command runs. The thread pool is part of it.
config is the config load for the command.
analysis holds all the stage rows above it.
after analysis is the scope filters, rules, baselines and gates.
output is the report serialization and write.
dead-code prints the table after the report, so the output row is complete. In combined mode, the table prints before the health analysis and the report, so WALL covers only the time until then.
The work and resolve rows are exact counts, not times. They do not change from run to run on the same project and commit, so you can compare two runs with exact equality:
files and source bytes that the parse stage read from disk,
bytes of the parse cache that the run read,
specifier resolutions that the imports asked for, and the distinct specifiers per file,
calls into the module resolver and path canonicalize calls.

A resolver count of zero means that the run reused the module graph cache. More specifier calls than distinct specifiers means that some files import the same specifier more than once. The health timings show git_log_bytes next to the git churn row: the bytes of git log output that the churn stage read.
The analysis is slower than you expect, and you want to find the slow stage.
You want to check that the cache works. A high hit rate means that incremental runs are fast.
You want to compare the speed of different configuration options.
parse/extract runs on all cores. When the run parses many files in parallel, the line gets a (parallel: ~Nms CPU) suffix. The suffix is the total parse CPU time of all workers:

Here the stage took 382ms of wall-clock time and ~594ms of CPU time across cores. If the CPU time is much larger than the wall-clock time, the stage is CPU-bound and more cores make it faster. If the two are close, the stage is I/O-bound and more threads do not help. Fallow omits the suffix on warm or small runs, where there is little parse work.

In combined mode (fallow with no subcommand), the health breakdown reuses the files that the dead-code pass discovered and parsed. Its discover files and parse/extract rows therefore show (measured above). You find that cost in the Pipeline Performance box.

With --format json, the timings include parse_cpu_ms (total parse CPU time) and parse_cache_load_ms (the parse cache load, part of parse_extract_ms) next to the wall-clock fields. The health timings include shared_parse. These values change from run to run, so do not use them as a CI gate.
The JSON timings also carry these objects:

counters: the work counts, with the fields files_read, source_bytes_read, parse_cache_bytes_read, resolve_specifier_calls, unique_specifiers, oxc_resolve_calls and canonicalize_calls. The health timings carry git_log_bytes. These counts are stable, so a test can compare them exactly.
process: the process time in milliseconds, with the fields wall_ms, startup_ms, thread_pool_ms, config_ms, git_ms, analysis_ms, post_analysis_ms and output_ms.

spans: the span tree. Each span has a name, the parent span that holds it, its ms, and concurrent, which is true when the span runs at the same time as its siblings. The tree shows that file discovery, parsing and the cache update are siblings of the pipeline span, which is the TOTAL clock.
Fallow caches the parse result of each file, so later runs parse only the files that changed. The cache uses bincode serialization and xxh3 hashing.

# Run with caching (default)
fallow dead-code

# Skip the cache entirely
fallow dead-code --no-cache
You think that stale cache entries cause incorrect results.
You changed the fallow version and want a clean analysis.
You want to benchmark a full parse.
--performance shows cache statistics, including the number of cache hits and misses. On incremental runs, expect a high hit rate, because fallow parses only the changed files again.
