When a run has a cache but cannot reuse it, fallow prints the reason under the stage that did the extra work. You can therefore tell a refused cache from a first run:

│ parse/extract: 16.2ms (335 modules, 0 cached, 335 parsed) (parallel: ~98ms CPU)
│ parse cache not reused: cache format version changed

The module-graph cache reports a refusal on its own line, graph cache not reused, under build graph. Neither line appears when fallow reuses the cache. Neither line appears with --no-cache either, because you asked for a cold run. fallow doctor reports the same two states before you run an analysis.
Fallow resolves template literals and import.meta.glob. It cannot resolve a fully dynamic import such as import(variable).
Fix: Add the target directory to entry in your config:
Some frameworks use exports by their name, with no import. Examples are Next.js generateStaticParams and Remix loader functions.
Fix: The built-in plugins handle most frameworks. For a less common framework, create a custom plugin or use ignoreExports:

DI containers (NestJS, Angular, InversifyJS) resolve dependencies at runtime through decorators and metadata. Fallow skips decorated class members by default. An injected service can still look unused if only DI tokens reference it.
Fix: Add the DI-registered files as entry points, or suppress specific findings:

Some decorators do NOT mean that a framework calls the method, for example Playwright @step or your own @measure and @log. List them in ignoreDecorators. Fallow then checks a method that has ONLY those decorators like any other method:
Fallow still skips a method that has any decorator NOT in the list. A method with @step + @Inject is still skipped, as DI code needs.
Files that a build step collects by their default export
Some SDKs have a build step that finds files by what their default export calls. No import reaches these files. For example, a file holds only this code:

Fallow reports such files as unused. In a monorepo, the app packages that hold these files are often not in the workspaces of package.json or in pnpm-workspace.yaml. Then they get no plugins and no entry points of their own.
Fix: List the collected files in entry, and declare the nested app packages in workspaces.patterns:
Run fallow list --workspaces to make sure that fallow finds each app package. See Additional workspace patterns.
Entity properties that code uses only as a type

An ORM entity class can have properties that code reads only through a type, for example in a query result or in a DTO. Fallow does not resolve types, so these properties can look like unused class members. Fallow already skips decorated members, such as @Column() properties, and entities that a library reads by reflection.
Fix: Use one of these two options.
The first option keeps the check for the other members and classes. The second option is shorter, but it hides all unused class members in these files. See usedClassMembers and overrides.

Fallow does not report packages in peerDependencies, because the project that installs your package supplies them. Fallow does report a package in optionalDependencies that no file imports and no script uses. A package that loads at runtime without an import, such as a platform-specific binary, can therefore look unused.
Fix: If fallow reports such a package by mistake, add it to ignoreDependencies:
Config files not recognized as entry points
If fallow reports a config file (for example tailwind.config.ts) as unused, its framework plugin is possibly not active.
Fix: Run fallow list to see the active plugins. If fallow does not detect the plugin, add the config file to entry:
Files in a hidden directory are missing

If a file in a dot-prefixed directory never appears in a finding, fallow did not
look in that directory. Fallow skips hidden directories, except for a few
conventional names and the directories that an active framework plugin owns.
Check the diagnostics of the run:

Fix: To add the hidden directory to discovery, add a ! exception to
ignorePatterns, for example "!.claude/**". Fallow then analyzes the files
in the directory that the exception matches. Otherwise, if a file, an export or
a dependency that only the hidden directory uses reports as unused, add the
file to entry, the export to ignoreExports or the dependency to
ignoreDependencies. To analyze the directory on its own, run
fallow dead-code --root .claude. That run is separate and does not fix the
main run. If the directory holds tool state that you never want to analyze, add
it to ignorePatterns. For the full behavior, see
Known limitations.

When a health input does not load, the section that needs it reports nothing,
not zero. The run records the reason as a diagnostic entry. Each entry has a
message that ends with a next step. Fallow records the entry with or without
--quiet. To find these entries, select on degrades_analysis, not on a list
of kinds:

The two plugin kinds come from a config file, not from a health input. Every
run with a dead-code pass can include them: dead-code / check, health,
flags, audit and the bare combined run. A standalone fallow dupes includes
neither. The reason token sets are open too. For the keys that report one,
see Module Federation.

Fix: Read the message of the entry. fallow health shows
which sections report nothing, and what a section reports when it measured zero.
The kind set is open. Treat a kind that you do not recognize as one more
diagnostic, not as an error.
Full reference for the fallow dead-code command and its flags.
Suppress single findings with inline comments.

pages.title: Known limitations and false positives of fallow
items: Known limitations and false positives of fallow
Known limitations of fallow: where it can miss a finding or report a false positive, and how to work around it for runtime patterns and framework edge cases.

This page lists the patterns where fallow can miss a finding or report a false
positive, with a workaround for each.

The default fallow analysis is syntactic. It does not use the TypeScript
compiler or resolve types. The optional --type-aware
pass adds limited checker evidence for the project questions that fallow
answers. It does not make fallow a compiler or a general typed linter.
Each limitation below applies to a specific pattern. Most of them do not affect a standard TypeScript project with isolatedModules: true.

By default, fallow parses source code into syntax trees with Oxc, and uses
oxc_semantic for scope-aware binding analysis. It does not run the
TypeScript compiler or resolve type information, so the default path stays
fast. Add --type-aware for exact symbol identity,
private type leaks across files, targeted tests, and public type coupling.

Impact: Fallow handles type-only imports (import type { Foo }) correctly. It also tracks value imports that are used only as type annotations (e.g., import { Foo } followed by const x: Foo), with oxc_semantic reference counting. To detect conditional type exports or dead code behind generic interfaces, fallow needs real type resolution.

Workaround: Set isolatedModules: true in tsconfig.json. esbuild, swc, and Vite already require this setting, so most modern projects have it. With isolatedModules, every import is either an explicit import type or a real value import, so there is no ambiguity.

In Svelte components, an export let declaration defines a component prop and a regular export. Fallow cannot tell props (which consumers use through the template) apart from utility exports that can really be unused.
Impact: Fallow can miss some unused exports in .svelte files.
Workaround: There is no configuration workaround. Review Svelte component exports manually. Move utility functions into separate .ts files, where fallow can track them accurately.
This limitation applies only to export let prop detection. Since v2.15.0, fallow does track imports that the template uses. It counts these as used:
v-on and v-bind object syntax in Vue.

Fallow reads import directives and all SCSS syntax with regex extraction, not with a full parser. For CSS Module class names in standard CSS files, fallow uses a CSS parser (lightningcss). The parser does not read SCSS syntax, so .module.scss class names also come from regex extraction.
@plugin directives (Tailwind v4 plugin sources, package or relative)
composes: (CSS Modules composition). A class that another class composes can show as unused.
The scope of :global(). Fallow reads the class inside :global(.name) as a CSS Module class, so it can report a global class as unused.
Workaround: If fallow reports false positives for CSS files that use composes: or :global(), suppress them with ignorePatterns or inline comments.

Fallow tracks class member usage syntactically: it looks for direct references in source code. In NestJS and other DI frameworks, the DI container can call abstract class methods at runtime, with no direct reference in the source.
Impact: Fallow can report abstract class methods and properties that dependency injection uses as unused.
Workaround: In a project that uses DI a lot, disable unused-class-members:
If your package exports types for external consumers (e.g., ButtonProps, Config), fallow reports them as unused in your project. The finding is correct, because no internal file imports them.
Impact: Library authors get correct findings that add noise.
Workaround: Mark the public API files with ignoreExports:

The built-in fallow plugins parse config files (e.g., vite.config.ts, jest.config.js) with the Oxc AST parser. The parser handles static objects, arrays, and defineConfig() wrappers, but it cannot evaluate arbitrary JavaScript.
Workaround: Add the entry points that fallow misses to your fallow config manually:
Fallow does not detect auto-linked React Native native packages (installed via npx pod-install or auto-linking) as used. These packages can have no explicit import in JavaScript code.
Impact: Fallow can report auto-linked packages such as react-native-screens or react-native-gesture-handler as unused dependencies.
Workaround: Add auto-linked packages to ignoreDependencies:

Discovery skips directories whose names start with a dot. It traverses five
conventional names by default (.storybook, .vitepress, .well-known,
.changeset, .github). An active framework plugin can also add the hidden
directory that its framework owns. A hidden directory that a package.json
script names as a config or file argument (for example
tsx ./.scripts/build.ts) is also traversed. Fallow drops every other hidden directory
before it parses the contents. This keeps machine-written trees such as
.next, .turbo, and .venv out of the analysis, with no configuration.

Impact: Fallow does not analyze first-party source in a hidden directory,
for example agent hooks in .claude/hooks/ or plugins in .omp/extensions/.
Fallow cannot see its imports and exports. The directory produces no findings
of its own and does not mark the modules it imports as used.

Fallow reports the skip. For each hidden directory that holds source files
your project did not exclude, it writes a skipped-source-dotdir entry in
workspace_diagnostics[] and names the directory in one aggregated note on
stderr.

Workaround: To add the directory to traversal, add a ! exception to
ignorePatterns. Fallow then analyzes the files in the directory that the
exception matches:

Without an exception, a file, an export or a dependency that only the
hidden directory uses can report as unused. To stop that false positive, add
the file to entry, the export to ignoreExports or the dependency to
ignoreDependencies:

To analyze the hidden directory itself, point fallow at it. This run is
separate and does not fix the findings of the main run:

If the directory holds tool or agent scratch state that you never want
analyzed, add it to ignorePatterns. The note then stops:

Fallow does not report content that the run already excludes. A hidden
directory that .gitignore covers (including a global gitignore, which often
covers agent tooling) never produces the note.

Fallow does not read the <script setup> block of a VitePress Markdown page.
A module that only a .md page imports, such as docs/_data/team.ts, shows
as an unused file.
Workaround: Add the module to entry:
Suppress one false positive at a time in source code.
Config file reference for ignorePatterns, ignoreExports, and rules.
How agents handle false positives with config and suppression.

pages.title: Configure fallow with .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml
items: Configure fallow for a TypeScript or JavaScript project. Fallow runs with no config. Add .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml to set entry points, ignores, and rules.
Fallow works with no configuration. Add a config file when the defaults do not fit your project, for example to add entry points, ignore generated files, or change rule severity. To create one, run:

fallow init # Creates .fallowrc.json
fallow init --toml # Creates fallow.toml
Fallow looks for config files in this order:
.fallowrc.jsonc (same JSONC parser; editors detect the JSON-with-comments syntax from the extension)
Fallow checks each directory up to the workspace root, and the first match wins. .fallowrc.json and .fallowrc.jsonc behave the same. The .jsonc extension only tells editors to expect comments.

If one directory has more than one of these files, fallow loads the file with the higher precedence. It prints a warning on stderr that names the ignored file. An old config from a migration therefore cannot take effect without a message.

Fallow parses both JSON forms as JSONC, and the published schema declares this (allowComments, allowTrailingCommas). Editors that use the JSON language service, such as VS Code and Zed, therefore accept comments and trailing commas in a config that references schema.json.
The config fields that select files use the same glob rules. A single * and a ? match inside one path segment and do not match /. Only ** crosses directories, as in picomatch.
the files, exclude and allowedFiles globs of a rule pack
the framework[] fields usedExports[].pattern, manifestEntries[].manifests and detection.pattern

A glob in these fields, and in ignoreDependencies and ignoreUnresolvedImports, can be at most 512 bytes long. A longer glob makes the config load fail. The time to build a glob matcher grows with the square of the glob length.
Before fallow 3.34.0, a single * in these fields also matched /. If your config used * to match nested files, it now matches fewer files, and a run can show new findings. You have two choices:
If you mean one folder level, write the names in place of *, for example examples/{app,docs}. The glob then matches the same files, and the warning stops.
If you mean nested folders, change the single * to **, for example src/generated/** or **/*.test.ts. This keeps the old match.
fallow prints a warning on stderr for each glob that matches fewer files now. The warning names the field, the pattern, up to 3 of the files that no longer match, and the ** form, for example:

fallow: health.ignore glob "*.test.ts" matches 481 fewer files than before fallow 3.34.0. A single "*" or "?" now matches in one folder level only. These files no longer match: src/a/a.test.ts, src/b/b.test.ts, src/c/c.test.ts, and 478 more. To keep the one-level match and stop this warning, write the names in place of "*" or "?", for example "{name1,name2}". To match nested folders again, use "**/*.test.ts".
For entry and dynamicallyLoaded, a file that another entry source still declares, for example a plugin or package.json, does not count. When no file remains, fallow prints no warning.
--quiet hides the warning, and JSON output does not change.

Globs that match package names or import specifiers do not use these rules. In ignoreDependencies, ignoreUnresolvedImports and publicPackages, a * still matches /, so @scope/* and @* keep their match.
Extra entry point glob patterns. Fallow detects entry points from package.json (main, module, bin, exports) and from framework plugins. Add the files that fallow does not detect.
A single * matches inside one directory. src/workers/*.ts does not match src/workers/jobs/send.ts. Use src/workers/**/*.ts for nested files. See Path globs.
Glob patterns for entry points that do not run in production: dev scripts, setup files and other tooling. In a normal run, a support entry keeps its file and its imports reachable, the same as entry.

In production mode (--production, production: true or production: { "deadCode": true }), fallow leaves a file that only supportEntry matches out of the analysis. Its imports do not mark an export, a file or a dependency as used, and fallow reports no finding in the file. So production mode uses the files in entry, the framework production entries and the package.json entry points only.

A file that entry, a framework plugin or a package.json field also declares stays an entry point. A support file that production code imports stays a normal module. The glob syntax is the same as for entry.
Without an entry config, fallow still finds entry points in your package.json fields. These files are the roots of the module graph. Fallow treats all code that they reach as "used."

Fallow resolves the exports field recursively. It follows nested conditions such as "import", "require", "types", and "default" to their target files. It also includes subpath exports (for example "./utils").

When these fields point at output directories (dist/, build/, out/, esm/, cjs/), fallow maps the paths back to the same files in src/ and tries the source extensions. Fallow ignores output directories by default. Fallow also maps a lib/ path back to src/, but only when the lib/ file is not in the analyzed files: it is not on disk, or .gitignore or ignorePatterns excludes it. A package with hand-written source in lib/ keeps its lib/ entry.

Framework plugins add their own entry points to the package.json entry points. For example, Next.js adds pages/** and app/**/page.tsx, and Vitest adds **/*.test.ts. Run fallow list to see all detected entry points.
Glob patterns for files that fallow does not analyze at all.

The built-in ignores apply at any depth: **/node_modules/**, **/dist/**, **/build/**, **/coverage/**, and the minified-bundle globs. Since 3.26.0, the build default is recursive like the others. Fallow therefore also skips a nested build/ directory with hand-written source.

A source folder named build, for example the build step of a CLI in src/cli/build/, is then not analyzed. Its imports do not count, so a dependency that only this folder uses can be reported as unused. The run names the skipped folder in workspace_diagnostics with the kind excluded-by-default-ignore, and fallow list shows it too. To analyze the folder, add an exception such as "!src/**/build/**", as in the example below. Keep the built-in default for the build output itself.
A !-prefixed entry is an exception. It brings back files that a built-in default, one of your own patterns, or the hidden-directory skip removes:
Fallow applies the built-in defaults first, then your own patterns, then the ! exceptions.
An exception lifts only the paths that it matches. With !src/policy/coverage/**, a top-level coverage/ output directory stays excluded.
In a hidden directory that only an exception opens, fallow keeps only the files that an exception matches.
Paths under node_modules or .git cannot be lifted. A ! entry that names one of these segments is a config error (exit 2).
To see which built-in pattern removed files, and how many, run with --explain-skipped.

A line that you copy from .gitignore can match fewer files here. In .gitignore, src/generated/* also ignores the subfolders of src/generated, because git does not go into an ignored directory. Fallow matches each glob against the full file path, so in ignorePatterns the same line ignores only the files directly in src/generated. Use src/generated/** to ignore the subfolders too. See Path globs.

Glob patterns for files where fallow does not report dead-code findings. Fallow still discovers and parses matching files and keeps them in the module graph, so everything they import stays reachable. To remove files from the analysis fully, use ignorePatterns.

Patterns are relative to the project root and use / on every platform, including Windows. Matching is case sensitive. * and ? do not match /, so src/* covers only the files directly in src. Use src/** for the whole src subtree. See Path globs. Fallow rejects absolute paths, .. segments, and a bare "!" when it loads the config.
Order does not matter. A negation wins over any positive match, in any position in the array. An array with only negations hides every path except the paths that a negation matches.
Fallow hides findings before it applies rules, severities, and --fail-on-issues. A hidden finding therefore cannot fail a run and does not show in any output format.

Some findings belong to several files: circular dependencies, re-export cycles, package cycles (which belong to the files of their example imports), duplicate exports, prop drilling chains, and unlisted dependencies (which belong to their import sites). Fallow hides such a finding only when every owning file matches.
These findings stay visible even when their path matches:
Dependency findings that belong to a manifest (unused, dev, optional, type-only, test-only, catalog, override).
Architecture boundary violations and policy violations.
Framework correctness findings, such as client and server directives and route collisions.
A covered file that does not parse is broken on purpose, for example a syntax-error test fixture. Fallow therefore also hides its parse errors:
The run reports no source-parse-degraded or source-nesting-too-deep diagnostic and prints no parse warning for the file.
The file does not count for the parse error gate.
Other findings do not get the incomplete-import-graph or incomplete-file-analysis caveat because of the file, so their actions can be auto-fixable.

This also applies when the covered file is an entry point or is reachable. Use ignoreFindings this way only for files that are broken on purpose. A valid file that the parser cannot read, for example because of syntax that is newer than the parser, can hide an import. Another module can then read as unused, and no caveat shows this.
A pattern that matched no finding has no effect. The usual cause is a typo. Every output of fallow dead-code names such a pattern, see Unmatched config patterns.

Package names that fallow always treats as used and as available.
Fallow does not report listed dependencies as unused or as unlisted.
Use it for packages that the runtime provides, such as bun:sqlite, and for other dependencies that are available without a declaration.

An entry can also be a glob. An entry with *, ?, [ or { is a glob with the same syntax as ignorePatterns, and fallow matches it against the package name. An entry without these characters matches one package name exactly.
A glob applies to the same checks as an exact name: unused, unlisted, type-only, test-only and dev-in-production dependencies.
An invalid glob, for example @acme/[, stops the config load with an ignoreDependencies error.

A glob that matches no dependency that a package.json of the project declares has no effect. The usual cause is a typo in the scope. Every output of fallow dead-code names such a glob, see Unmatched config patterns.

Binary names that the unlisted-binaries rule does not report.
Use it for a binary that the operating system, the CI image, or a tool outside node_modules provides.

An entry with *, ?, [ or { is a glob, and fallow matches it against the binary name. An entry without these characters matches one binary name exactly. An invalid glob stops the config load with an ignoreBinaries error.
Command names whose file arguments do not become entry points.

Fallow reads the commands in package.json scripts, CI files, Dockerfiles, Procfiles, and fly.toml. A file that a command names, such as node scripts/seed.ts, normally becomes an entry point. Formatters and linters (ESLint, Prettier, Oxlint, Oxfmt, Biome, Stylelint, textlint, and similar tools) never make their targets entry points, so you do not have to list them. Use this field for another command that reads files as data:
A listed command is still a used dependency, and its --config file is still tracked.

A name matches the command after env, package-manager, and wrapper prefixes (cross-env, dotenv -e .env --, npx, pnpm exec, pnpm --filter web exec, yarn run, varlock run --, dotenvx run --). The match is on the exact file name.
A script call such as npm run gen -- src/input.ts or npm run gen src/input.ts matches the command in the body of the gen script.

"*" matches every command. Use ["*"] to turn off entry points from all commands, and declare the real entry points in entry. This also drops the modules that a linter loads through a flag, such as eslint -f ./tools/fmt.js. Add those modules to entry too.
The field does not change commands that a plugin reads from a tool config, such as Playwright webServer.command.

Entries that suppress unresolved-catalog-reference findings. This finding is a catalog: dependency or a catalog: pnpm override value that points at a catalog that does not declare the package. Most findings are in package.json, and JSON has no comments. // fallow-ignore-next-line cannot work there, so a config entry is the only way to suppress them.

package is required. Fallow compares it to the dependency key as an exact, case-sensitive string, so "@scope/*" matches nothing. For a pnpm override, package is the target package of the override: write child for "parent>child". catalog and consumer are optional. When you leave one out, it matches any value.
Fallow compares catalog to the normalized catalog name. "react": "catalog:" and "react": "catalog:default" are both default, and "catalog:react17" is react17.

consumer is a glob for the path of the package.json that uses the catalog. The path is relative to the project root and uses / on every platform: package.json for the root manifest, packages/app/package.json for a workspace member. For a pnpm override, the consumer is the file that declares the override: pnpm-workspace.yaml or the root package.json. The glob must match the whole path, and * and ? match across /.
All fields of one entry must match. Any matching entry in the array suppresses the finding.
Each unresolved-catalog-reference finding in fallow dead-code --format json output has an add-to-config action with package, catalog, and consumer already filled in.

This field changes only unresolved-catalog-reference. unused-catalog-entries and empty-catalog-groups do not change. To turn off the rule for a path, use overrides with "unresolved-catalog-references": "off". To turn it off everywhere, set rules.unresolved-catalog-references to "off".

ignoreFindings does not apply here, because findings that belong to a manifest stay visible when their path matches. A consumer value with invalid glob syntax, an absolute path, or a .. segment makes the config load fail.

Package-manager override entries that fallow does not report, for example a CVE pin that must stay. The field suppresses unused-dependency-override and misconfigured-dependency-override for matching entries in these places:
These findings are in manifests, not in source files. // fallow-ignore-next-line cannot work there, so a config entry is the only way to suppress them.

Fallow compares package to the target package of the override as an exact, case-sensitive string. It is not a glob and not the raw key. Write react-dom for "react>react-dom" and @types/react for "@types/react@<18".

Fallow removes the ** path segments from bun resolutions keys, so "**/trim-newlines" matches as trim-newlines. Fallow does not remove a **/ prefix from an overrides key. When fallow cannot parse a key, it compares the key as written, so "react>" needs { "package": "react>" }.

source is the label of the file that declares the override: "pnpm-workspace.yaml" or "package.json". It is not a path. Leave it out to match both. Any other value loads without an error and never matches. pnpm.overrides, npm overrides, and bun resolutions all report "package.json", so source cannot tell them apart.

Fallow skips a pnpm source that the declared pnpm version does not read. For example, pnpm 11 does not read pnpm.overrides. See override sources and the pnpm version. An entry for a skipped source matches nothing.

Fallow reads the resolutions of a bun project only when the root manifest declares no overrides key. When overrides exists, fallow ignores resolutions and never reports them, so an entry for them matches nothing.
Both fields must match. Any matching entry in the array suppresses the finding.

Both findings have an add-to-config action in JSON output, with package and source already filled in. An entry that matches nothing gives no warning. To turn off either finding fully, set rules.unused-dependency-overrides or rules.misconfigured-dependency-overrides to "off". ignoreFindings does not apply here, because findings that belong to a manifest stay visible when their path matches.

Glob patterns that fallow matches against the import specifier as written, not against a file path. Fallow never reports a matching specifier as unresolved-import. Use it for imports that fallow cannot resolve on disk:
Code that a later build step generates.
A package with an exports map that points at build artifacts that are not in the checkout.
A bundler alias that fallow does not model.

Matching is case-sensitive, and a pattern must match the whole specifier. * and ? match across /, but a trailing /** requires the separator. To match the package and its subpaths, list the bare package name and the subpath pattern. Fallow removes a leading ./ from each pattern and tries each specifier with and without its own ./. "./generated/x.js" and "generated/x.js" therefore cover the same imports.

A .. segment is allowed here, because these patterns match specifiers, not paths. The file-path glob fields do not allow it. There is no negation syntax and no ordering. Fallow suppresses a specifier if any pattern matches. A pattern with invalid glob syntax makes the config load fail, with a message that names the field and the pattern.

The field covers static imports, dynamic imports, and re-export sources, for value imports and type-only imports. Resolution and the module graph do not change, and neither does the dependency usage count. unlisted-dependency therefore does not change. For that finding, use ignoreDependencies, which matches package names as exact strings.

Each unresolved-import finding in JSON output has an add-to-config action for this field with the reported specifier. When you move an import here from an inline // fallow-ignore-next-line unresolved-import comment, delete the comment. The config check runs first, so fallow then reports the comment as stale-suppression.

Entries that tell fallow to ignore specific exports. Use them for public API packages. Use them also for UI libraries with namespace barrels (shadcn, Radix, bits-ui), where many components/ui/<name>/index.ts files export the same short names on purpose.

ignoreExports suppresses unused-export findings, duplicate-export grouping and duplicate-export-alias findings for matching files. For duplicate-export-alias, a listed name exempts the binding that has that name. Use exports: ["*"] to exclude every export from the matched files. Use a list of names to exclude only those names.

A per-file overrides.rules.duplicate-exports = "off" has no effect, because the rule spans multiple files. A duplicate-export finding groups N locations in N files. When fallow detects this override, it prints a warning at load time and points you to ignoreExports.

Suppress unused-export findings when the file that declares the export also uses it. Fallow still reports exports with no references at all. This is the same as the ignoreExportsUsedInFile option of knip.
For knip compatibility, fallow also accepts an object form:

Fallow reports type aliases and interfaces under the same unused-types issue. { "type": true }, { "interface": true }, and { "type": true, "interface": true } therefore behave the same: fallow suppresses any type export that the same file uses. The two fields exist only for knip-config compatibility.

A reference in the export specifier itself (export { foo }, export { foo as bar }, export default foo) does not count as a same-file use. Fallow still reports such an export when no other file and no other expression in the file references the binding.

Report unused exports in entry files (package.json main and exports, framework pages, and so on). By default, fallow marks these exports as used. This option finds typos in framework-convention exports, such as meatdata instead of metadata.
The global CLI flag --include-entry-exports does the same. When both are set, the CLI flag takes precedence.
To set the option for some workspaces only, use workspaces.settings.

The default export of a tool config file of an active plugin (for example tailwind.config.js, jest.config.js or next.config.mjs) counts as used, because the tool loads the file and reads that export. Named exports of a config file stay reportable, unless the tool reads them: every export of a Cucumber config file (each named export is a profile) and of vercel.ts counts as used. GraphQL Codegen codegen*, Serverless serverless.* and Vercel vercel.* files get this credit only at the project root and at the root of each workspace package, because these names also match ordinary source files. Gatsby gatsby-node, gatsby-browser and gatsby-ssr do not get the credit, because Gatsby reads named exports from them.

Also report the unused exports, unused types, unused class members, and unused enum members of a file that fallow reports as an unused file. The default is false. When you delete an unused file, you also remove these findings, so the report hides them and counts them in cascade_hidden.
The CLI flag --show-cascade does the same for one run. See Findings in unused files.

Use the TypeScript type checker for more exact results. With this option, fallow
gets checker evidence for exact symbol use, class contracts, cross-file private
type leaks, affected tests, and public-signature coupling. The option is off by
default, so the normal analysis stays fast and does not need the TypeScript
companion.

projects is optional and takes tsconfig paths relative to the project root.
With an empty list, fallow discovers the projects automatically. Start with
best-effort. It keeps conservative findings when the checker evidence is
partial or not available. Choose complete only when an incomplete checker pass
must fail the run.

This option does not replace tsc or Oxlint. For installation, performance,
safety, and library-consumer boundaries, see
Type-aware TypeScript analysis.

Configure the catalogue of fallow security. security.categories selects the candidate categories that run. security.requestReceivers adds the names of your own HTTP request objects to the built-in receiver allowlist (req, request, ctx, context, event).

requestReceivers only adds names. It does not replace the built-in names. Fallow trims the values and matches them case-insensitively for *.query, *.params, and *.body source reads. The field has no effect on *.searchParams.

Resolve framework auto-imports (Nuxt components) as real edges in the module graph. Frameworks such as Nuxt make components available to templates by file name, with no import statement: <Card001 /> resolves to components/Card001.vue.

Fallow always creates the edges for these tag references, so includeEntryExports counts a default export that a <Card /> tag uses. The rules below do not change this. A template tag or a composable call marks its file as used, whatever your nuxt.config says.
autoImports: true also removes the convention entry patterns. A convention file is then no longer an entry point, and fallow reports it as unused-file when nothing references it.
Fallow reads two settings from nuxt.config.ts or nuxt.config.js and handles each one separately:
imports: controls the composable, util, shared/utils, and shared/types patterns.
Fallow removes the patterns of a setting when the config does not have the key, or when the value scans no more than the Nuxt defaults:

components: false, components: null, components: [], components: true, or components: { dirs: [] }. components: true gives the same directories as a missing key. Other keys next to an empty dirs do not change the result.

imports: {}, imports: { dirs: [] }, or imports: { scan: false } with no imports.dirs or an empty array. The first two are the Nuxt defaults: imports.dirs starts empty, and Nuxt registers the convention directories itself.
Fallow reads every other shape as a custom layout. That setting keeps its entry patterns:

components: {}, the array form (components: [{ path: '~/ui' }]), and an object with no empty dirs. A non-empty dirs, or only a prefix or pathPrefix, keeps the patterns. Any other value is also custom.
imports: { scan: true }, a non-empty imports.dirs, and imports: { scan: false } next to a non-empty imports.dirs, which Nuxt scans either way.
imports: { autoImport: false } alone. It turns off the injection, not the scan, and the documented replacement (import { useThing } from '#imports') resolves to no file.
A config with a top-level extends, a spread or a repeated key in either object, or a config object that fallow cannot resolve statically.

A top-level property that fallow cannot read statically: a spread such as { ...base, devtools: {} }, a computed key such as ['imports'], an accessor, or a shorthand method. That property can configure either setting, so both settings keep their patterns for that root.
Only a top-level property counts when the config object is readable. A nested key, such as a routeRules path that ends in components or imports, does not keep a fallback on its own.
Two nested locations still count for a setting, because Nuxt reads them the same way as the top level:
$production, $development, $test, and each $env.<name> override, when it carries a nested components or imports key.
A hooks entry for components or imports, in the flat form ('components:dirs': fn) and in the nested form (components: { dirs() {} }), because Nuxt joins nested hook names with :.

An override object or a hooks object that fallow cannot read statically falls back to a text match for the components and imports keys, inside that object. An unrelated hook or override does not change the static reading.

For each setting that fallow reads as custom, it adds a plugin-effect-not-modeled entry to workspace_diagnostics[], one entry per config file and setting. The entry has plugin, key, and reason, with the config file in path. The entry does not make the analysis less complete, and fallow prints no warning for it. For the diagnostic kinds, see Debugging.

Fallow reads the config of each root separately: the project root and every workspace root, plus each local layer of that root. The config of the root, and of its local layers, that contains a pattern decides that pattern. One custom nuxt.config in a monorepo does not keep the patterns of another app.

Component names follow Nuxt. Nuxt names a component directly under components/global/ or components/islands/ after its own directory. components/global/Foo.vue is then <Foo>, and components/base/global/Card.vue stays <BaseGlobalCard>. Fallow removes the .client, .server, .global, and .island suffixes.

A name that you import or re-export by hand from #components or #imports marks its convention file as used, like a template tag. A member access on a namespace import, such as C.Card on import * as C from '#components', marks components/Card.vue as used. A file with export * from '#components' or export * from '#imports' passes on the names that its importers take from it. When fallow cannot read which names a file takes, for example a spread of the namespace, every name of that module counts as used. A plugin-effect-not-modeled diagnostic then names the file, with key set to the module. #layers/<name>/ resolves to a local layer by its $meta.name.

An auto-import name marks as used only the files of the app that renders or calls it, and of the layers that this app extends. In a monorepo, a <Card /> in one app does not keep the unused Card.vue of another app. See Nuxt auto-import scope.
Some component files stay entry points with autoImports on, because fallow cannot see how they render:
components/global/ files and *.global.vue files. A string reference such as resolveComponent('Name') can render a global component.

components/content/ files of the project and of each local layer, when @nuxt/content is in modules (as a string or as a ['@nuxt/content', { ... }] entry), or when a package layer such as docus registers it. Markdown content renders these components, and fallow does not read Markdown.
An OG image template that a defineOgImage('Name') or defineOgImageComponent('Name') call names with a static string counts as used. See Nuxt auto-import scope.
The default is false. Fallow tracks Pinia store auto-imports separately.

Decorator names that do not mean reflective use. By default, fallow skips every class member with a decorator. Fallow checks a member that has only listed decorators like a member with no decorators. A member with any decorator that is not in the list stays skipped, so framework defaults (NestJS, Angular, TypeORM) do not change.

Use this for utility decorators that do not mean runtime reflection. Examples are @step("label") from Playwright, internal labeling decorators such as @measure, @log, and @retry, and custom decorators that wrap a method for logging or tracing.

The behavior is conservative. A method with both @step and @Inject stays skipped, because @Inject is not in the list. Fallow applies the standard usage check only to methods where every decorator is in the list.

Bare entries ("step" or "decorators") match the leftmost segment of the decorator path. One bare "decorators" entry covers every @decorators.* decorator. Use this when an internal namespace has many utility decorators that are all non-reflective.
Dotted entries ("decorators.log") match the full dotted path exactly. A sibling such as @decorators.audit stays skipped, unless you also list "decorators.audit" or use the bare "decorators" form.
"@step" and "step" are the same. Fallow removes a leading @ before matching.

When an entry matches no decorator in the analyzed codebase, fallow prints one warning at the end of the run. usedClassMembers does the same for unmatched patterns. Remove unmatched entries, because they have no effect.

The default is an empty list, which keeps the behavior that skips all decorated members. Existing NestJS, Angular, and TypeORM projects see no change. The first run after you enable this option can report new unused-class-members findings on members that fallow skipped before.

Options for the unused-component-props rule. Some props stay in the public API but are not used inside the component. To stop fallow from reporting them, set ignorePattern to a regex. Fallow skips each prop where the local destructure binding name matches.

This supports the convention that a leading underscore marks an accepted but intentionally unused value. TypeScript noUnusedParameters and the varsIgnorePattern and argsIgnorePattern options of ESLint @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars use the same convention:

<script lang="ts">
 interface Props { stage: string; variant?: string }
 // `_stage` is exempted by `^_`; `variant` is still reported if unused.
 let { stage: _stage, variant }: Props = $props();
</script>
This applies to Vue, Svelte, Astro, React, and Preact props. The default behavior does not change: with no ignorePattern, fallow reports every unused prop.

Fallow matches the regex against the local destructure binding name (_stage in let { stage: _stage } = $props()). It does not match the public prop name that the finding reports (stage). When a prop has no alias, the local name is the public name.
Matching is unanchored (like RegExp.test in ESLint). _ with no anchor matches any prop that contains an underscore (on_click, aria_label). To match a leading underscore, use ^_.
An invalid regex makes the config load fail with a clear error.
When the pattern skips at least one prop, fallow prints a one-line note with the count. If the note does not show, your pattern matches nothing, which is often a typo.
The Angular rules unused-component-input and unused-component-output do not change, because their declarations are class fields, not destructured locals.
Names of class methods and properties that fallow never reports as unused. The names add to the built-in Angular and React lifecycle allowlist, for methods that third-party libraries call.

Use this when a library calls methods on your class at runtime through an interface or contract. Common examples are ag-Grid (agInit, refresh), TypeORM migrations (up, down), and Web Components (connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, attributeChangedCallback).
Each entry is one of these:
A plain member name, which applies to all classes.
A scoped object, which matches only classes with the configured extends or implements identifier in their heritage clause.
Strings can be exact names or glob patterns:

A name such as agInit is unique enough to suppress for all classes. A common name such as refresh or execute would hide real findings in unrelated classes, so scope it with implements or extends. A scoped rule needs at least one of extends or implements. Fallow rejects an object rule with no heritage field ({ "members": [...] }) at load time.

Heritage matching is syntactic. Fallow compares the identifier in the extends Foo or implements IBar clause of the source to the string in the rule. For a renamed import (import { IBar as IBaz }), use the identifier that the class declaration shows.
Fallow treats a member string that contains * or ? as a glob pattern. Exact strings keep their meaning.
"*" matches every member of a matching class.
"enter*" matches any member with a name that starts with enter.
"*Handler" matches any member with a name that ends with Handler.
"on*Event" combines a prefix and a suffix.
Use glob patterns for parser-generator listeners (ANTLR), generated bridges, and abstract framework base classes that call members by a name prefix.

When a glob pattern matches zero members in the codebase, fallow prints a WARN at the end of the run, so you can remove the entry. Exact-string entries give no warning, because they are common boilerplate that can match in some configurations and not in others.
The allowlist applies only to class methods and properties. Fallow still checks enum members with the same names.
For an allowlist that applies only when a library is installed, use a plugin file with the usedClassMembers field. For the plugin format, see Custom plugins.

Workspace packages with a public API. Fallow never reports exports, exported enum members, or exported class members from these packages as unused, also when no code in the repo imports them. Use it for library packages that other projects use.
Glob patterns for files that your code loads at runtime, for example with import(), lazy routes, or plugin systems. Fallow treats these files as entry points and does not report them as unused.
A single * matches inside one directory. src/plugins/*/index.ts matches src/plugins/alpha/index.ts, but not src/plugins/alpha/ui/index.ts. See Path globs.

File extensions of server-side templates that fallow health --css reads as CSS class references. Write each extension without the leading dot. Fallow always reads liquid, njk, hbs, handlebars, twig, and blade.php. Use this key for other template languages:
Each class-like word in a template counts as a use of that class, also a common word such as hidden or title.
An extension matches the end of a file name, and case does not matter. blade.php matches welcome.blade.php.
A value can contain only letters, digits, ., -, and _.

A value that ends in a script, stylesheet, data, or asset extension is a config error, for example module.css or d.ts. A value that ends in a markup extension that fallow already reads, such as page.html, is also a config error.
Template files do not join source discovery, so fallow never reports them as unused files.
The walk obeys .gitignore, ignorePatterns, health.ignore, and --max-file-size. It skips node_modules, vendor, and build output directories.
In extends, the list of the child config replaces the list of the parent.
Project settings for the separate fallow similar-code workflow:

The config cannot select the provider, model, executable, download, or credential.
The model setup always needs a separate, explicit action from you. For the
discovery, inspect, and verdict flow, see
Semantic similar code.
Project defaults for the opt-in fallow mutation command:

The section rejects unknown keys. No key starts a run. The option that keeps
mutants near file system, process, network, or database calls is the
--allow-side-effects flag only, so the config rejects allowSideEffects.
For the operators, statuses, and exit codes, see
fallow mutation.
Change coupling reads 12 months of git history when you do not pass --since. Hotspots keep their 6 month default. With --since, both read the same window.
Configuration for fallow audit, the command that reviews changed files:

[audit]
gate = "all"
worsened = "error"
css = true
cssDeep = true
cacheMaxAgeDays = 14
Configure the behavior of fallow fix.

auto removes a leading comment block when it clearly belongs to the deleted catalog entry. That is the case when the block directly follows the parent catalog: or catalogs.<name>: header, or follows a blank line. Use always to remove every adjacent leading comment block. Use never to keep leading comments for manual review.
Two mechanisms keep your comments, whatever the setting:

Add # fallow-keep to any line in a comment block to keep the whole block, also under always. This works like the fallow-ignore-next-line and fallow-ignore-file inline suppression comments:
catalog:
 # fallow-keep: audit trail, CVE-2024-XXXX
 react: ^18.2.0

Under auto, fallow keeps section banners. A banner is a comment where the text after # and optional whitespace starts with three or more of the same character: =, -, *, _, ~, +, or #:
catalog:
 # === React 18 production pins ===
 react: ^18.2.0
Under always, the banner rule does not apply. To keep banners with always, use # fallow-keep.
The JSON action in fixes[N] has two line fields:
line: the first deleted line (1-based). This is the leading comment when auto or always removes one.
entry_line: the original line of the catalog entry (1-based).
CI annotators and dedup caches that key on the entry position should use entry_line, which stays stable. Tools that point at the actual file edit should use line.

Enable production mode to analyze only the code that ships to users. The field takes the legacy boolean form, which applies to every analysis. It also takes a per-analysis object. For example, you can run health on production code only, and dead-code and duplication on the full tree:

The CLI flags --production, --production-dead-code, --production-health, and --production-dupes (bare combined runs and fallow audit) override the config. The matching env vars FALLOW_PRODUCTION, FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DEAD_CODE, FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH, and FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DUPES follow the same precedence order. A per-analysis env var takes precedence over the global env var. For the full order, see global flags.
Extra workspace patterns, added to the workspaces that fallow detects automatically (package.json workspaces, pnpm-workspace.yaml, a root Deno config, and tsconfig.json references). See Workspaces:

Each package that these patterns find gets its own plugins, entry points, and dependency checks. fallow list --workspaces, --workspace, --changed-workspaces, and --group-by package also use these packages. See Additional workspace patterns.
Inherit from one or more base config files. Use it to share one config across projects, or to keep a base config with per-project overrides.
The extends field accepts these source types:
Deep merge: fallow deep-merges object fields (such as rules). The child config overrides the base, and the child inherits the fields that it does not set.
Array replacement: array fields (such as entry and ignorePatterns) replace the base value. Fallow does not concatenate them. If the child sets entry, it overrides the base entry.
Cross-format support: a JSON config can extend a TOML config, and a TOML config can extend a JSON config.
Circular detection: fallow detects circular extends chains and reports an error.
Max depth: an extends chain can have 10 levels at most, to prevent accidental deep nesting.
String shorthand: you can pass one path as a string instead of an array: "extends": "./base.json".
Fallow resolves paths relative to the config file that contains the extends field.
URL sources must use https://. Fallow rejects plain HTTP. It fetches the config on every run, with no cache.
Timeout: 5 seconds by default. Change it with FALLOW_EXTENDS_TIMEOUT_SECS.
Body limit: 1 MB maximum response size.
Chaining: a config from a URL can extend other URLs or npm: packages. It cannot extend relative paths, because there is no file system location to resolve them against.
Fallow fetches URL extends on every run. If the remote server is slow or not available, your analysis fails. For important shared configs, use a versioned URL or an npm: package.
The lowest fallow version that this config needs, as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. It gives a clear upgrade message instead of an "unknown field" error on older fallow versions.
An unknown config key fails the run with exit 2. This catches mistakes such as ignorePaths instead of ignorePatterns. It also means that every new config field needs a coordinated upgrade.

When a team commits a field from a newer version, every runner on an older version breaks. The failure comes on the commit that adds the field, not on an upgrade. The error names the field, so the first guess is a typo.
With minimumVersion, the older runner shows a clear message instead.
A fallow binary below the minimum version stops before it reports any unknown field:

fallow.json requires fallow 3.21.0 or newer, running 3.19.0.
Upgrade fallow, or remove minimumVersion and the fields that need it.
Inherited through extends: a monorepo base config sets it once, and every config that extends the base inherits the minimum version.
Checked before unknown keys: the version message replaces the misleading field-name error. It does not only come first.
No other effect: at or above the minimum version, an unknown key still fails, because there it is a real typo.
Optional: unset by default. Without it, nothing changes.
Validated: a value that is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (for example v3.21) is a config error.
Set it in the same change that adds a field from a newer version. Do not set it in advance. A minimum version higher than the config needs blocks runners for no reason.

Fail the run with exit code 1 when fallow cannot parse a source file cleanly. Boolean, default false. It arms the parse-error gate on fallow dead-code, fallow health, fallow audit, and the bare fallow run. The --fail-on-parse-error flag arms the same gate for one run.

The gate is off by default, because the parser also rejects valid syntax that is newer than the parser. An older fallow version rejects this key as unknown, so set minimumVersion to the first release that has the key. See Parse error gate for the output and the CI behavior.
Apply different rules to specific file patterns. For example, relax rules in test files, or make them stricter in critical paths.
Each override object has these fields:

files: array of glob patterns, matched against paths relative to the project. A single * does not match /, so *.test.ts matches only test files at the project root. Use **/*.test.ts for test files at any depth.
rules: rule severities for the files that match the patterns.
When multiple overrides match the same file, the later override takes precedence.
Mark a config as sealed to make sure that no config from a parent directory can change it through extends. When sealed: true:
extends paths must be relative to the file.
extends paths must resolve inside the directory of the config (no ../ paths).
Fallow rejects npm: and https: extends with a clear error.
Library publishers who ship a .fallowrc.json in an npm package can make sure that the config is self-contained.
Monorepo sub-packages (for example a shared component library that multiple apps use) that do not inherit from the monorepo root config on purpose.
sealed: true does not change config discovery. Fallow already stops at the nearest config in the directory tree (first match wins). This option only limits what extends can reference.
Options for the circular-dependencies rule. The only option is ignoreLazyImports (default false).
With ignoreLazyImports: true, an import edge that loads its target on demand or on another thread does not take part in cycle detection. These edges are lazy:
a webpack inline request through a worker loader, such as worker-loader!./work.js (see inline loader requests)

These edges stay in the cycle graph: a top-level await import(), require(), an eager import.meta.glob, and an edge that also has a static import. Fallow removes the lazy edges before it counts the cycles of a group, so lazy cycles do not fill the cycle limit and hide a static cycle.
A top-level await import() in a Vue <script setup> block, a Svelte instance script, or an Astro frontmatter stays lazy, because that code runs for each component instance.
Options for projects that use the Effect library. The only option is schemaExportsAsTypes (default false).

An exported Effect schema defines a runtime value and a type (typeof User.Type). Some teams keep exported types as contracts and set "unused-types": "off". With schemaExportsAsTypes: true, fallow treats an unused schema export the same way: it reports the schema under unused types, not under unused exports. With "unused-types": "off", fallow does not report the schema.
Fallow finds a schema from the syntax of its declaration. These declarations are schemas:

a class that extends a Schema class factory: Schema.Class, Schema.TaggedClass, Schema.TaggedError, Schema.TaggedRequest (Effect 3), Schema.Error or Schema.Opaque (Effect 4), also when the class has a body
a class that extends a schema class of the same file, such as class Admin extends User.extend<Admin>("Admin")({...}) {}
a const whose value is a Schema constructor or member, such as Schema.Struct({...}), Schema.Literal("a") or Schema.String. A type name such as Schema.Schema or Schema.Top is not a constructor.

a const whose value is a pipe or annotation chain on a schema, such as Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId")) or User.pipe(Schema.extend(...)). Each pipe argument must be a Schema transform, such as Schema.brand(...), Schema.minLength(...), Schema.check(...) or a bare Schema.NullOr
a default export of a schema, such as export default Schema.Struct({...}). The finding has the export name default.
a re-export of a schema of another module, such as import { User } from "./schemas"; export { User } or export { User } from "./schemas", also through export * barrels

in a module that imports Effect, a chain on an imported schema, such as export const UserId = User.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId")) or User.annotations({...}), and an alias, such as export const Copy = User. This also applies to a default export.
A re-export of a value that is not a schema stays an unused export.

Schema must be an import from effect, effect/Schema or @effect/schema: a named import (import { Schema } from "effect", also with an alias) or a namespace import (import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"). A local object with the name Schema does not match.
a value that a schema function returns, such as Schema.decodeUnknownSync(User), Schema.is(User) or User.make({...})
a pipe with an argument that is not a Schema transform, such as User.pipe(Schema.decodeUnknownSync) or User.pipe((user) => ...)
a re-export of a schema from another file
a schema whose chain starts at a schema imported from another file

When a schema and its type alias with the same name (export type User = typeof User.Type) are both unused, fallow reports one unused type at the schema. An existing // fallow-ignore-next-line unused-export comment on a schema keeps its effect, and an unused-type comment also works. fallow fix does not remove these exports, the same as for other unused types, although the finding carries the remove-export action. In JSON output, the finding is in unused_types with is_type_only: false, because the export is a value. The finding moves to another issue type, so a saved baseline does not cover it. Save the baseline again when you turn on the option.
Fallow versions before this option reject the effect key. Set minimumVersion when the config is shared.
Define architecture boundary zones and import rules. Use a built-in preset, or define custom zones.
Available presets: layered, hexagonal, feature-sliced, bulletproof. For full control, define custom zones and rules.
For presets, custom zones, examples, and output formats, see Architecture boundaries.

Rule packs let you enforce project policies for calls, imports, exports, effects, and gdp-ts proof producers. A rule pack is a standalone JSON or JSONC file. Fallow loads packs as data only and never runs project code. Paths are relative to the project root. Fallow reports matches as policy-violation findings with the ID <pack>/<rule-id>.

A pack file declares version: 1, a unique name, and a non-empty rules array. Pack names and rule IDs must use ASCII letters, digits, ., _, or -, so that scoped suppression comments can name them without ambiguity.

banned-call rules match callee paths per segment, through imports. child_process.* covers named, namespace, and default imports from child_process and node:child_process. A pattern matches a call and a new expression, so Date covers Date() and new Date().
banned-import rules match import specifiers as written, per segment. moment covers moment/locale/nl, never moment-timezone.

An optional allowNames list on a banned-import rule bans a package and keeps some of its exports. Each entry is an exact imported name, with no globs. default allows a default import. The rule compares the source-side name, so import { Mesh as Vector3 } reports three: Mesh. A namespace import, a star re-export, and a side-effect import always report. Other rule kinds reject allowNames. See Policy violations.
banned-effect rules match effect classes from the security catalogue, such as network and database. These rules read calls only, not new expressions.
banned-export rules match exported names. A trailing * matches a name prefix.
gdp-proof-producer rules restrict calls to @gdp-ts/core.defineProof to allowedFiles globs. Optional proofKinds labels restrict the rule to those literal proof kinds.
Optional files and exclude globs limit where a rule applies.
An optional per-rule severity overrides the main rules."policy-violation" severity (default warn).
To suppress one rule, use // fallow-ignore-next-line policy-violation:<pack>/<rule-id> or the file-level form. Bare policy-violation still suppresses all rule-pack findings.
For editor autocomplete, point $schema at the schema in the npm package. This schema matches the fallow version that you installed:

The editor reads the path relative to the pack file. For a pack in the project root, use ./node_modules/fallow/rule-pack-schema.json. The package also exports the file as fallow/rule-pack-schema.json. Without the npm package, run fallow rule-pack-schema to print the schema, or point $schema at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/rule-pack-schema.json. An invalid or missing pack makes the config load fail with exit code 2. Fallow does not continue with a pack that enforces nothing.
Keep pack files in a committed directory such as rule-packs/. .fallow/ is the gitignored cache directory, so packs there are missing from the checkouts of your teammates.
Use a global producer rule to allow proof factories only in your authorization modules. Add a rule for a specific proof kind to require its factory to live in one owner file:

Add "rulePacks": ["rule-packs/gdp.json"] to your fallow config. Each matching rule reports independently. A call outside src/auth/** can violate both rules. A call in src/auth/other.ts violates only the owner rule.

allowedFiles must contain at least one project-root-relative glob. It grants producer permission. files, exclude, and zones limit where the rule checks code. Neither allowedFiles nor proofKinds applies to other rule kinds.

An absent or empty proofKinds checks every recognized factory call, including dynamic labels. A nonempty list matches exact static string labels; dynamic labels are skipped by that rule. Keep the global rule to restrict those calls too.

The rule checks every analyzed file, including files unreachable from entry points. Files excluded from discovery are outside its scope. It follows named and namespace imports, import aliases, and unambiguous project re-export chains to the gdp-ts factory. See Policy violations for supported forms and limits.

Inspect the configured permissions with fallow rule-pack list --format json or fallow guard src/routes/project.ts --format json. Use fallow rule-pack test rule-packs/gdp.json --format json to inspect matches while authoring the pack. This command exits successfully when it reports findings. For CI enforcement, run fallow architecture --policy. An error-severity finding exits with code 1.
For details on the issue type, see Policy violations.
Severity per issue type: error (fails CI with exit code 1), warn (reports but exits 0), or off (no detection). Each rule has its own default. See Rules for the default of each rule.
The complexity-cyclomatic, complexity-cognitive, complexity-crap, and complexity-file-lines rules decide if a complexity finding fails fallow health and fallow audit. See Complexity rules.

Styling audit findings use the same severity map. The styling rules are css-token-drift, css-duplicate-block, css-selector-complexity, css-dead-surface, and css-broken-reference. They default to warn, so they show in the output but do not change the verdict, unless you set them to error or off.

Rules and severity has the full list of issue types, with the default severities. It includes the pnpm catalog rules such as unused-catalog-entries and empty-catalog-groups. For per-glob severities, use the overrides field.

Customize feature flag detection. Fallow detects the SDKs of LaunchDarkly, Statsig, Unleash, GrowthBook, Split, PostHog, Vercel Flags, ConfigCat, Flagsmith, Optimizely, and Eppo by default. With this field you can:
fallow flags is the command that uses this configuration.
Module resolver configuration. It controls how fallow matches the exports and imports maps of package.json.

Use this for community conditions such as worker, edge-light, and deno, or for any custom condition that your bundler uses. The built-in set already has development. A package with a development branch therefore resolves to source with no config. This is common in monorepos, where development points at source and import points at compiled output.
With this config, a package.json like:
resolves ./api to src/api.worker.ts instead of dist/api.js.
For the full list of established condition names, see the Node.js community conditions reference.

Path to a CODEOWNERS file for --group-by owner. When unset, fallow looks for CODEOWNERS, .github/CODEOWNERS, .gitlab/CODEOWNERS, and docs/CODEOWNERS. Set this field when your file is in a different location.
Inline framework plugin definitions. Define custom entry points, ignored files, or test patterns without a separate plugin file.
Paths to external plugin files or directories. Fallow also finds *.toml, *.json, and *.jsonc files in .fallow/plugins/, and fallow-plugin-*.{toml,json,jsonc} in the project root, automatically.
Settings for the incremental cache. Use dir to move the extraction cache. Use maxSizeMb to limit its serialized size. Above the limit, fallow removes entries when it saves.

The default cache file is .fallow/cache.bin under the project root. When cache.dir is set, fallow stores the cache file in that directory. The directory must be inside the project root and outside .git. A relative path resolves from the project root. Fallow ignores another value, prints a warning and uses .fallow. To put the cache outside the project, set FALLOW_CACHE_DIR. When both are set, the env var FALLOW_CACHE_DIR overrides cache.dir.

The default limit is 256 MB. The limit applies to the serialized extraction cache. When a save goes past 80% of the limit, fallow removes the entries for the files that the latest run did not discover, until the cache is at 60%. An example is the test files after a --production run. Fallow keeps the entries of the latest run while they fit in the limit, so the cache can stay near the full limit. When they do not fit, fallow removes only the entries that go past the limit. A file that every run reads stays, also when it never changes. When both are set, the env var FALLOW_CACHE_MAX_SIZE overrides cache.maxSizeMb. Both values are in whole megabytes.

Fallow rebuilds the cache automatically when config that affects extraction
changes: the active plugin names and the inline framework definition names.
Fields that affect only detection, such as entry, ignorePatterns, and
severity overrides, do not invalidate the extraction cache.
--no-cache turns off the cache fully. This section then has no effect.

Regression baseline in the config. It stores the issue counts of a known-good state, so CI can fail when the counts go up. --save-regression-baseline (with no path argument) writes it, and --fail-on-regression reads it.
The count keys use camelCase, for example totalIssues and unusedExports. Fallow ignores snake_case keys such as unused_exports and treats a missing count as 0.

An ignoreDependencies glob that matches no declared dependency, or an ignoreFindings pattern that matches no finding, has no effect. The usual cause is a typo. fallow dead-code, fallow audit and the combined fallow run report such an entry in every output format. The presentation is different per format, but each format names the same entries.

fallow report --from shows the entries at the same place as the live run of the same format. The GitHub Action and the GitLab template post the job summary and the PR or MR comment, so the entries reach the pull request. They also write one warning with the entries to the job log. The integrations run fallow with --quiet, and they post a review only when it has new inline comments, so the log warning also covers a setup that posts only the review.
The MCP dead-code tool and the programmatic API carry the same workspace_diagnostics[] entries.
An entry is advisory. It does not change the exit code, and degrades_analysis is not set.
Fallow reports an ignoreDependencies glob only when the run shows dependency findings. These runs do not report it:
A run with an issue filter that does not include --unused-deps or --unlisted-deps, for example --unused-files.
A run with --file, because such a run drops dependency findings.
A run where every dependency rule is off.

Fallow compares an ignoreFindings pattern with every finding of the analysis, before issue filters and scope filters. A filtered run therefore does not make a pattern look unused. A run with no findings at all reports no ignoreFindings pattern.
A config entry can match and still change nothing, because fallow does the same without it. fallow dead-code, fallow audit and the combined fallow run report three such entries:
The entries use the same output places as unmatched config patterns, with these differences:
Markdown, the job summary, the PR comment and the review summary body show the entries in a separate Redundant config entries section.
The GitHub Action and the GitLab template do not write them to the job log.
An entry is advisory. It does not change the exit code.
The answer applies to the run only:
An ignorePatterns glob for generated output has an effect only when that output is on disk. Keep it when a build creates the output before fallow runs.
A glob that names a hidden directory, such as .cache/**, is never reported. A ! exception is not checked.
An entry pattern that matches no file is not reported.

An ignoreDependencies glob that matches no declared dependency is an unmatched config pattern, not a redundant entry. The redundant ignoreDependencies entries use the same dependency-report rules as the unmatched glob.
A --production run reports no redundant entry, because it checks fewer files and dependency sections.

Some overrides[].rules entries cannot change a result. fallow dead-code, fallow audit and the combined fallow run report each one as a workspace_diagnostics[] entry with the kind override-rule-ineffective. The entry changes no finding and no exit code. Each entry has these fields:
The message names the mechanism that works:
The entries use the same output places as unmatched config patterns, with these differences:
SARIF carries each entry as a toolConfigurationNotifications[] note with properties.setting set to overrides, plus rule, files and reason.
Markdown, the job summary, the PR comment and the review summary body show the entries in a separate Override rules with no effect section.
The LSP marks the key in overrides[].rules.

An issue-type flag can ask for a rule that the config sets to off. Fallow does not run that check, so a zero count for the rule measures nothing. fallow dead-code and fallow architecture then add one workspace_diagnostics[] entry for each such rule, with the kind requested-rule-off:

{
 "path": ".",
 "kind": "requested-rule-off",
 "rule": "unused-dependencies",
 "flag": "--unused-deps",
 "message": "unused-dependencies is off in config, so --unused-deps did not check it. Set the rule to \"error\" or \"warn\" to run this check."
}

An entry is advisory. It does not change the findings or the exit code. A script that passes --unused-deps with the rule at off still exits 0. To fail the script on a finding, set the rule to error. A rule at warn reports the finding, but it does not fail the run.
Fallow adds an entry only for an explicit selection:

The fallow dead-code filter flags, such as --unused-files and --stale-suppressions, and fallow architecture --cycles, --boundaries and --policy. --cycles checks circular-dependencies, re-export-cycle and package-cycle.

--unused-deps checks only unused-dependencies, unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies. The placement rules type-only-dependencies, test-only-dependencies and dev-dependencies-in-production give no entry, because off is the way to remove them from the selection.
--private-type-leaks, --absent-component-props, --constant-parameters and --deprecated-exports-in-use turn their rule on, so they give no entry.
Production mode turns unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies off. A production run gives no entry for these two rules.
A run with no selection, a bare fallow architecture, the bare fallow run and fallow audit give no entry.
The entries use the same output places as unmatched config patterns, with these differences:
Human, compact, CodeClimate and github-annotations print one Note: line on stderr for each entry. --quiet removes the line, and the machine formats keep the entry.
SARIF carries each entry as a toolConfigurationNotifications[] note with properties.setting set to rules, plus rule and flag.
Markdown, the job summary, the PR comment and the review summary body show the entries in a separate Requested checks that did not run section.
The LSP shows no diagnostic for the entry.
The MCP tools add one sentence to the root warnings[] array.
--lean keeps the first entry of the kind plus a count. Run without --lean to see each rule.
Add the $schema field to get autocomplete and validation in your editor:
To generate the schema locally, run:
Control issue severity for incremental CI adoption.
Suppress single findings in source code.
Add entry point detection for your own frameworks.
Get a proposed config for your project.
Print the resolved config and its file.

pages.title: Set fallow rule severity to error, warn or off
items: Set fallow rule severity to error, warn or off
Fallow rule severity decides what fails the CI build. Set each issue type to error, warn, or off, and adopt fallow in CI one issue type at a time.
Rules let you decide which findings fail CI. You set a severity per issue type, so you can adopt fallow one issue type at a time.
Start with all rules as warn. Promote one type at a time to error when you have fixed its findings.
When you do not configure a rule, it uses its default severity. The Default column in Available rule names shows the default of each rule. The defaults by group:

Default off (opt-in): private-type-leaks, deprecated-exports-in-use, absent-component-props, constant-parameters, prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, duplicate-prop-shape, coverage-gaps, feature-flags, require-suppression-reason, security-client-server-leak, security-sink, diverged-clone-sibling, and added-dependency.

Default warn:

Dependency hygiene: unused-dev-dependencies, unused-optional-dependencies, type-only-dependencies, test-only-dependencies, and dev-dependencies-in-production.

Framework components: unused-store-members, unprovided-injects, unrendered-components, unused-component-props, unused-component-emits, unused-component-inputs, unused-component-outputs, unused-svelte-events, unused-server-actions, and unused-load-data-keys.
Audit diff risk: weakened-tests, added-suppression, and test-only-branch.
Client and server directives: invalid-client-export, mixed-client-server-barrel, and misplaced-directive.
Styling: css-token-drift, css-duplicate-block, css-selector-complexity, css-dead-surface, and css-broken-reference.
pnpm cleanup: unused-catalog-entries, empty-catalog-groups, and unused-dependency-overrides.
Other: re-export-cycle, package-cycle, stale-suppressions, and policy-violation.
To print the resolved severity of every rule for your project, run fallow config.
In production mode, fallow sets unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies to off.
circular-dependencies and circular-dependency are the same rule. You can use either form in rules, overrides[].rules, and inline directives.

An overrides[].rules entry cannot change every rule. Ten rules read only the top-level severity, and most rules do not run when the top-level rule is off. Fallow reports each such entry as an override-rule-ineffective diagnostic. See Override rules with no effect.

A rule at off does not run, also when an issue-type flag such as --unused-deps asks for it. Fallow then prints a Note: line on stderr and adds a requested-rule-off diagnostic. The findings and the exit code do not change. See Requested rules that are off.

The rules complexity-cyclomatic, complexity-cognitive, complexity-crap, and complexity-file-lines decide if a complexity finding fails fallow health and fallow audit.
