The thresholds still decide which functions and files have a finding. The thresholds are health.maxCyclomatic, health.maxCognitive, health.maxCrap, health.maxFileLines, and health.thresholdOverrides.
A function above more than one threshold gets the most severe rule of those kinds. Fallow drops the finding only when all of these rules are off.
overrides[].rules can set the complexity rules for some files.
The rule applies before fallow health --min-severity. So a warn finding never fails the run, also when its band is at or above the --min-severity level.
--fail-on-issues (and --ci, which sets it) raises a warn complexity finding to error in fallow health and in the bare fallow run. fallow audit ignores --fail-on-issues and keeps its own verdict.
health.maxCrap: 0 stays the full off switch for CRAP. It also removes the CRAP signals of the file scores. complexity-crap: "off" hides the findings only, and keeps these signals.
After you set a kind to off, save the health baseline again. Its entries for the hidden findings no longer match, so they count as stale.
A thresholdOverrides row still lists the dimensions that its function breaches, also when a rule hides the finding.
Each complexity finding in the JSON output has an optional effective_severity field (error or warn). The severity field keeps the band (moderate, high, or critical).
A fallow version without these rules warns about an unknown rule name and ignores it. A shared config therefore works with an older binary, but its complexity findings still fail the run there.

The CI formats take the level of each finding from its rule severity. This includes the severity that an overrides[].rules entry sets for the file. For a complexity finding, the complexity-* rule sets the level, not the band. The band stays in the title and the message.

With the default rules, a moderate complexity finding is an ::error annotation and a SARIF error, because the finding fails the run. Error annotations come before warnings, so the max-annotations cap of the GitHub Action keeps the errors.

Each dead-code and complexity finding in the JSON output has the optional effective_severity field. fallow report --from reads it, so a saved report gives the same levels as the direct run. A saved report from an older version has no effective_severity. For such a report, report --from uses the earlier levels.

prop-drilling defaults to off. Set it to error to fail CI for a finding, or warn to keep it advisory even with --fail-on-issues. Error findings use the configured error level in CI formats. The editor still shows prop drilling as a hint. Saved JSON reports preserve their effective severity when rendered with fallow report --from.

Earlier versions treated prop-drilling: "error" as advisory. If you used that setting for non-gating reports, change it to warn when upgrading. This affects future analysis runs. An archived JSON report with effective_severity: "error" renders as an error even after you change the current config to warn.

thin-wrapper and duplicate-prop-shape findings stay advisory, also when their rules are error. Their SARIF level is warning at most. The human, json, sarif, compact, and markdown reports list these findings, and the editor shows them as hints. The pull request formats (codeclimate, github-annotations, github-summary, and the comment and review formats) do not list them.
In an existing codebase, adopt fallow in steps:
Start permissive. Set all rules to warn so you see issues without blocking CI.
Fix high-confidence rules first. Promote unresolved-imports and unlisted-dependencies to error. These rules almost never give false positives.
Fix unused files. Promote unused-files to error. You can safely remove unreachable files.
Fix unused exports. This is usually the largest category. Promote unused-exports to error when the count is manageable.

Enable the remaining rules. Promote unused-types, unused-enum-members, and unused-class-members as you clean up each category. Enable private-type-leaks only for packages where the public API or the declaration files matter.
Use baselines to enforce rules on new code without failing CI on existing issues.

To treat all warnings as errors for one run, pass --fail-on-issues. The config file stays the same. Use it for pre-merge gates on critical branches. In fallow health and the bare fallow run, it also raises warn complexity findings to error.

Exit code 0 does not always mean a clean run. The bare fallow run in a machine format, such as --format json, exits 0 on error-severity findings unless you pass --fail-on-issues. Read gate_outcomes to see each gate that failed.
When all findings of a run are warn, the run exits 0 and the human summary line shows a yellow ⚠. A red ✗ shows only when a gate fails the run, for example an error finding or --fail-on-issues.
A source file that fallow cannot parse does not change the exit code by default. To fail the run on such a file, see failOnParseError.
Reference for every field in the config file.
Set up fallow in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and more.

pages.title: Suppress fallow findings with inline comments
items: Suppress fallow findings with inline comments
Suppress a fallow false positive with a fallow-ignore comment, a JSDoc tag such as @public or @internal, or @expected-unused. The rule stays on for other code.

Inline suppression removes one finding from the report and keeps the rule on for the rest of the codebase. Use it for a false positive or an intentional exception. You add a comment or a JSDoc tag next to the code.

For broad patterns, use config-level rules. Keep inline suppression for single exceptions. For library exports that other projects use, add JSDoc visibility tags (@public, @internal, @beta, @alpha) instead of suppression comments.

Fallow never reports an export with a JSDoc visibility tag as unused. It recognizes @public, @internal, @beta, and @alpha. Use these tags for library APIs that external projects use, and for exports that you keep for a specific audience. These exports have no references in your repo, but they are part of your public API.
The tags work with all export types: named, default, classes, interfaces, enums, type aliases, and multi-specifier exports (export { foo, bar }).

The tags also work on a re-export statement: export { foo, bar } from "./impl", export * as ns from "./impl", and export { foo, bar } that forwards imported bindings. Fallow does not report a tagged re-export. The re-export counts as a use of its source export, the same as an export of an entry point. export * from "./impl" does not take a tag, because it exports no name of its own.
On a decorated class, put the JSDoc block before the first decorator, as TypeScript does. The block then applies to the export. This is also true for @deprecated.
A JSDoc block between a decorator and export does not apply to the export. A block before an earlier, unrelated statement does not apply either.
Fallow recognizes only /** */ JSDoc block comments. Line comments (// @public) and regular block comments (/* @public */) have no effect.

To mark an export as intentionally unused, add /** @expected-unused */. Fallow checks this tag for staleness, which it does not do for visibility tags (@public, @internal). If another module imports the export later, fallow reports the tag as a stale suppression.
The tag also works on a re-export statement, with the same forms as the visibility tags.
Get a finding when the export is used again (through the stale-suppressions rule).
The stale-suppressions rule (default: warn) sets the severity of stale @expected-unused tags. For details, see dead code explained.
To remove one function from the complexity report of fallow health, suppress complexity on it. The comment suppresses the cyclomatic and the cognitive metric together.
A file-level suppression removes all functions in the file from the complexity findings. File health scores do not change:

A marker can list more than one token. A token may not match a known issue kind, for example because of a typo or because a newer fallow release renamed the kind. The recognized tokens then still apply, and fallow reports each unknown token as a stale-suppression finding.
When a known kind is within edit distance 2, the finding includes a "Did you mean ...?" hint. An upgrade across a rename therefore never breaks the whole marker without a message.

In JSON output, the additive origin.kind_known field on stale_suppressions[].origin tells an unknown-kind token apart from a known token that is stale. The field is present and false only for an unknown kind. It is absent when fallow recognizes the kind.
A reason tells the next reader why a suppression exists. Add -- <reason> at the end of any suppression comment or @expected-unused tag:
By default, the reason is optional. Fallow records it in the suppression hygiene output. To require a reason on every suppression, enable the opt-in require-suppression-reason rule (default off):

With the rule at warn (or error to fail CI), fallow reports each fallow-ignore-* comment or @expected-unused tag without a -- <reason> as a missing-suppression-reason finding. You can then find the suppressions that have no reason and add one. For the rule reference, see Rules & Severity.
Use these tokens in suppression comments. The Scope column shows where each token works: line level (// fallow-ignore-next-line), file level (// fallow-ignore-file), or both.

Dependency findings (unused-dependencies, unused-dev-dependencies, unused-optional-dependencies, unlisted-dependencies, type-only-dependencies, test-only-dependencies, dev-dependencies-in-production) belong to package.json. A comment in a source file does not suppress them. Use ignoreDependencies for a package, or set the rule severity. For catalog and override findings, use ignoreCatalogReferences and ignoreDependencyOverrides.

fallow dead-code (dead code, dependency hygiene, and framework findings):
unused-file, unused-export, unused-type, private-type-leak, unused-enum-member, unused-class-member, unused-namespace-member, unused-store-member, unresolved-import, duplicate-export, circular-dependency, re-export-cycle, package-cycle, boundary-violation, policy-violation, policy-violation:<pack>/<rule-id>, the client and server directive tokens, the Next.js route tokens, the component tokens, prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, duplicate-prop-shape, unused-catalog-entry

fallow health (complexity, coverage, and styling with --css):
complexity, coverage-gaps, the css-* tokens

You can use circular-dependency and circular-dependencies in every place that takes a rule slug: inline directives, config rules, and overrides[].rules. The singular form is the standard form for inline directives. The plural form is the standard form for the rules config. Both forms work in both places.
For broad patterns, use the config (rules, ignoreExports). Use inline suppression for:
Do not suppress an issue that repeats across the codebase. If a pattern affects many files, configure it at the project level.
Control issue severity at the project level.
Reference for every config field, including ignoreExports and ignorePatterns.
List every suppression in the project.

pages.title: Configure fallow for a monorepo with workspaces
items: Configure fallow for a monorepo with workspaces
Monorepo analysis with no workspace setup. Fallow detects npm, yarn, pnpm, and Deno workspaces, resolves cross-package imports, and supports per-package config.

Fallow analyzes a monorepo as one project graph. When only a sibling package uses an export, fallow does not report it as unused. You do not configure workspaces, because fallow reads the npm, yarn, pnpm, and Deno workspace formats.
Fallow resolves cross-package imports through node_modules symlinks or Deno import maps. You can scope the output to one package or to a set of packages.
Workspace detection is automatic. Fallow finds and analyzes all packages if your repo has one of these:
A workspace field in a root deno.json or deno.jsonc.
A references field in the root tsconfig.json (TypeScript project references).
Fallow detects workspaces from these sources:

Fallow adds the packages from all sources together. When the repo declares no workspace patterns, fallow also scans the directories up to two levels below the root. It adds each directory with a package.json as a workspace package.

A directory with its own package.json and pnpm-workspace.yaml is an independent pnpm project, for example a docs site next to the packages. When no root workspace pattern declares such a directory, fallow still analyzes it as a workspace:
Its package.json owns its files and declares their dependencies.
Fallow does not report its directories as undeclared workspaces.
The members that the packages list of its pnpm-workspace.yaml declares are workspaces too. fallow list --workspaces shows them below the nested project root.
A catalog: or catalog:<name> reference in the project or its members resolves against the nested pnpm-workspace.yaml, not against the root catalog.

Fallow looks for these directories up to two levels below the root, and only when the root declares workspace patterns. Each one gets a nested-project-root diagnostic, which is information only. You do not need a workspaces.patterns entry for it. To leave the project out of the analysis, add it to ignorePatterns.

The unused-catalog-entries, empty-catalog-groups and unresolved-catalog-references findings of a nested project name the nested files. fallow fix removes an unused entry from the nested pnpm-workspace.yaml. A packages entry of the nested file whose directory does not exist gets a workspace-pattern-dir-missing diagnostic. Fallow then does not report the unused entries of that nested catalog. A member that a root workspace pattern declares keeps the root catalog. Fallow does not read the nested workspaces of npm and yarn projects.

A workspace pattern can name a directory that exists only in CI, for example a repository that a CI step clones into the workspace. When the directory does not exist, fallow reports a workspace-pattern-dir-missing diagnostic and does not report unused-catalog-entries, because the packages in that directory can use the entries. See workspace diagnostics.
Fallow reads a root deno.json or deno.jsonc the same way it reads package.json for npm. The workspace field lists member globs. It accepts the bare array form and the object form:

Fallow reads the name and exports of each member like the same fields in package.json. For example, @scope/lib with "exports": { ".": "./mod.ts" } resolves like an npm package export map. When a member directory has both a package.json and a deno.json, fallow takes the package identity from package.json.
Fallow resolves import maps (imports in the root or member configs) per package. An exact specifier match wins. If there is no exact match, the longest matching slash-prefix entry applies.
Deno workspace member names count as listed dependencies. When you import a sibling package by name, fallow does not report it as an unlisted dependency.

With a pure Deno root (no root package.json), fallow does not warn about a missing node_modules directory. If the root deno.json or deno.jsonc is malformed, fallow stops with an analysis error (exit 2). It does not continue with an empty workspace list.

When apps/web imports from @myorg/ui, fallow follows the node_modules symlink back to the workspace source files. Fallow canonicalizes symlinked paths, so it records the usage on the real source file.

// Resolves to packages/ui/src/Button.tsx via node_modules symlink
import { Button } from '@myorg/ui'

Fallow checks imports against the nearest valid package.json inside the project. This includes standalone nested packages omitted from explicit workspace patterns, such as scripts/tool/package.json. Recognizing that manifest for dependency checks does not add the package to the workspace list.

npm links workspace packages into node_modules during installation. That link lets an import resolve. Fallow also checks whether the importing package declares the dependency, including imports from the repository root.
For example, if src/index.ts imports @myorg/ui, the root manifest needs a dependency declaration even when packages/ui is already listed as a workspace:
Use a version that matches your workspace package and package-manager setup. Put a dependency used only by root tests or tooling in devDependencies instead.

A private package, or a test, config, or build script, may use a dependency declared in an ancestor manifest. Runtime source in a publishable package needs its own declaration. A package can import itself by name without declaring a dependency on itself.

If your project deliberately permits undeclared workspace imports, add the package name to ignoreDependencies. This suppresses dependency findings for that package; it does not add a declaration to package.json.
See unlisted dependencies for the rule and its alias behavior.

pnpm uses a content-addressable store with a .pnpm virtual store inside node_modules. Fallow detects these paths and maps them back to the workspace source files. Fallow also tracks cross-package usage correctly in the strict isolation mode of pnpm.

A dependency can be an alias of a workspace package: "vite": "workspace:@myorg/core@*". pnpm installs @myorg/core under the name vite. Fallow resolves vite/<subpath> through the exports of @myorg/core, also when another workspace member has the name vite. The usage counts for the declared dependency vite.

CI can clone an upstream repository into a directory that pnpm-workspace.yaml declares and .gitignore excludes. Fallow does not read the source files of such a member, so it does not report the dependencies of its package.json as unused. The member is still a workspace: imports and catalog references still reach its manifest.
Fallow resolves the exports field in the package.json of each package, including subpath patterns:
An import of @myorg/ui/icons resolves to packages/ui/src/icons/index.ts.

Packages often point exports or main at build output. Fallow maps these paths back to the source file, so usage counts against the code you edit. This applies to the dist, build, out, esm, and cjs directories. Fallow tries the same relative path under src/ with the source extensions .ts, .tsx, .mts, .cts, .js, .jsx, .mjs, and .cjs.

Fallow also maps lib/ targets back to src/, but only when the lib/ file is not in the analyzed files. This is the case before the build, or when .gitignore or ignorePatterns excludes lib/. A package with hand-written source in lib/ keeps its result. A relative import of a missing lib/ file stays an unresolved import.
Fallow maps dist/index.js back to src/index.ts (or .js, .tsx, and so on) if the source file exists.

The same rule applies to a nested path and to a type target. For example, dist/define/index.mjs maps to src/define/index.ts, and a types entry dist/index.d.ts maps to src/index.ts. When a tsconfig.json maps the output path to a file that does not exist, fallow also tries the file under src/.
Fallow finds the tsconfig.json file in each workspace package automatically. It uses the path aliases of a package to resolve imports in that package.

A framework plugin alias of a workspace package, such as SvelteKit $lib or Nuxt ~/, also applies only to the files of that package. An alias from the project root applies to all files. When the package has no target for the import, fallow reports an unresolved-import finding.
To see the issues of one or more workspaces only, pass -w or --workspace. Fallow still analyzes the full monorepo graph and filters only the reported issues.
A pattern has one of these forms:
Exact package name or workspace path: web, @myorg/ui, apps/web
Glob, matched against both the package name and the workspace path relative to the repo root: apps/*, @scope/*
Separate values with commas, or repeat the flag. Quote patterns that contain ! or glob characters, so that your shell does not expand them.

# Single package (back-compat with earlier fallow versions)
fallow dead-code -w @myorg/ui

# Multiple packages (comma-separated or repeated)
fallow dead-code -w web,admin
fallow dead-code -w web -w admin

# Glob: all apps, all scoped packages
fallow dead-code -w 'apps/*'
fallow dead-code -w '@myorg/*'

# Everything under apps/ except legacy
fallow dead-code -w 'apps/*,!apps/legacy'

# Everything except a workspace (negation only)
fallow dead-code -w '!apps/legacy'

● Unused exports (2)
 apps/web/src/Button.tsx
 :15 ButtonVariant
 apps/admin/src/Modal.tsx
 :8 ModalContext
 Exported symbols with zero references

✗ 2 issues (31ms, 1,247 files)
To scope the output to the workspaces that changed since a git ref, pass --changed-workspaces <REF> instead. You cannot combine it with --workspace.
For CI matrix jobs, combine --workspace with --changed-since. Fallow applies both filters, so you get only the changed files inside the matched workspaces.

In a monorepo, packages often follow different release branches. workspaces.changedSince maps a workspace root to its own Git ref. For a mapped package, check, dead-code, dupes and the editor report only the findings in files that changed since that ref. Unlisted packages and files outside every workspace stay in full scope.

Write each key as fallow list --workspaces prints the workspace root: relative to the project root, with / separators. A file belongs to its nearest workspace, so a nested workspace uses its own entry. A clone group or a cycle stays in the report when one of its files is in scope.
A global --changed-since replaces the map for one run.
--no-package-baselines or FALLOW_PACKAGE_BASELINES=false turns the map off, so every package is in full scope. In VS Code, set fallow.packageBaselines to false.
audit, health and security do not read the map. In a bare fallow run, the health section is not scoped by it.
A malformed key or ref is a config error and exits with code 2.

A key that names no workspace of the project, or a ref that Git cannot resolve (for example in a shallow CI clone), turns the whole map off for that run. Fallow prints a warning and reports every package in full scope. The report is wider than you asked for, never narrower. A run from a package subdirectory loads the parent config, so its keys name no workspace there, and the map turns off in the same way.

JSON reports list the applied refs in package_baselines, for example [{ "workspace_root": "packages/web", "reference": "main" }]. request_outcomes["package-baselines"] is applied when the map scoped the run, and not-applied with a reason and a message when it turned off. A narrowed run names package-baselines in baseline_staleness.scope_reasons.

The map applies to every run, so a baseline saved under it holds only the findings in changed files of the mapped packages. Fallow warns when it saves such a baseline and records the scope in the file. Save and gate a whole-project baseline with --no-package-baselines:

fallow dead-code --no-package-baselines --save-baseline fallow-baselines/dead-code.json
fallow dead-code --no-package-baselines --baseline fallow-baselines/dead-code.json --fail-on-stale-baseline
The GitHub Action and the GitLab template add --no-package-baselines to their whole-project baseline check for you.
workspaces.settings sets ignoreDependencies and includeEntryExports for some workspaces only. The global keys continue to apply to every workspace.

Write each key as fallow list --workspaces prints the workspace root, or as a glob over workspace roots. A single * matches inside one path segment. A file belongs to its deepest workspace, so a nested workspace uses its own keys.

ignoreDependencies: a workspace gets the global list plus the list of each key that selects it. An unused dependency uses the workspace of its package.json. An unlisted dependency uses the workspace of the file that imports it.

includeEntryExports: an exact root wins over a glob, and a glob with more literal segments wins over a shorter glob. A workspace that no key sets uses the global value. When two keys of the same precedence give different values, fallow warns and uses the global value.
The --include-entry-exports flag turns the check on in every workspace, also where a key sets false.
The root package uses only the global keys.
A key that selects no workspace has no effect, and fallow prints a warning. Fallow also warns about an unknown key under workspaces.
An older fallow version ignores workspaces.settings. Add minimumVersion to the config, so that an older binary stops with a clear message.
If fallow does not detect all your workspace packages, add patterns in your config:
These patterns add to the packages that fallow detects from package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml, a root Deno config, or tsconfig.json references.

Each package that these patterns find is a full workspace package. It gets its own plugins, entry points, and dependency checks. Use this for packages that the package manager does not declare, for example app packages in an Nx monorepo that only have a project.json and a package.json.
These commands and options use the packages from workspaces.patterns:
The analysis of every command that loads a config.

The base checkout of fallow audit and fallow security also uses them, and the scope-workspaces next step lists the packages that they declare. fallow init and fallow coverage setup read only the patterns in package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml, and the other manifests.
To make sure that fallow finds a package, run this command:
Reference for every field in the config file.
CLI reference for running analysis across workspaces.

pages.title: Configure architecture boundaries and zones
items: Architecture boundaries for TypeScript and JavaScript. Fallow reports each import that crosses a layer. Start from a built-in preset or define your own zones.

Boundaries stop imports that break your architecture, for example UI code that imports the database layer. You group files into zones with glob patterns. A rule says which zones a zone may import from. Fallow reports each forbidden import as a boundary-violation issue in fallow architecture output.
Two optional sections add checks beyond import direction:
coverage reports source files that are outside every zone.
calls bans specific callees per zone.
For preset descriptions, output formats, and suppression, see Architecture boundaries.
Fallow has four built-in presets for common architecture patterns:
When a preset is active, fallow reads compilerOptions.rootDir from tsconfig.json to find the source root for zone patterns. Preset zones become {rootDir}/{zone}/**.
Fallow finds the root in these steps:
Read tsconfig.json from the project root. JSONC with comments and trailing commas is supported.
Remove a leading ./ prefix and any trailing /.
Reject ., .., and absolute paths for security.
Use src if the field is missing, the file does not exist, or the value is rejected.
With the hexagonal preset, this config gives these zones:
rootDir detection applies only to presets. Custom zones use patterns exactly as written.
When no preset matches your architecture, define zones yourself. Each zone has these fields:
A file belongs to the first zone with a matching pattern (first match wins).
Files that match no zone are unrestricted. They can import from any zone, and any zone can import them.
Zone order is important. Put more specific patterns before broader ones.

Fallow warns when a zone matches no analyzed file (boundary zone '<zone>' matched 0 files). Usually the glob pattern does not match your directory structure. Run fallow list --boundaries to see the file count of each zone.

Use autoDiscover to make each feature module its own zone, without one zone entry per feature. Every immediate child directory becomes a zone. Rules can still name the parent zone, and fallow expands them to the discovered child zones.

If src/features/auth and src/features/billing exist, fallow list --boundaries shows features/auth and features/billing. Fallow checks imports between sibling features as cross-zone imports. An explicit child rule, such as from: "features/auth", overrides the generated parent rule, in any rule order.
When the zone also has patterns, fallow matches the discovered child zones first. Top-level files in the auto-discover directory then belong to the parent zone.

The parent rule automatically allows its discovered children. A src/features/index.ts barrel can therefore re-export feature modules without features → features/<child> violations. Other top-level files, such as src/features/types.ts, still follow the parent features rule. Generated child rules keep the original allow list exactly, so sibling features stay isolated.
To classify only the discovered child directories and leave top-level files unrestricted, remove patterns from the zone.
A rule says which zones a zone may import from. Each rule has these fields:
Self-imports are always allowed. Files in the same zone can import each other.
No rule entry means the zone is unrestricted. It can import from any zone.
Empty allow list means the zone is isolated. It cannot import from other zones.
Only zones with an explicit rule entry have restrictions.

Re-export chains: a named or default import through a barrel file is judged against the zone of the module that declares the symbol. The finding names the barrel in via_path. Namespace and side-effect imports are judged by the direct target. See re-export chains.
Every analyzed file: rules also apply to a file that no entry point reaches.
Start with rules for your lowest-level zones (the zones that should import from nothing). Then add rules for the zones above them.

Some TypeScript modules must share types but must not depend on each other at runtime. For example, a plugin system can declare a contribution interface in one feature. Other features then import only that type:
The compiler removes this import, so there is no runtime dependency. To allow it without adding the target zone to allow, add allowTypeOnly:
Whole-declaration type imports: import type { Foo } from '...'
Namespace type imports: import type * as ns from '...'
Inline-type imports where every named specifier has the type qualifier: import { type Foo } from '...'
Type-only re-exports: export type { Foo } from '...'
Mixed-specifier imports where at least one specifier is a value (import { type Foo, Bar }). The runtime dependency on Bar still gives a violation.
Side-effect imports (import '...'). These run the target at runtime.
allowTypeOnly is independent of allow. Fallow allows a type-only import if its target zone is in either list.
The default value is an empty list. Without the field, fallow behaves as before the field existed.
No preset (Layered, Hexagonal, FeatureSliced, Bulletproof) sets the field. Type-only crossings are opt-in per rule.
When you set preset together with zones or rules, fallow merges them:
Zones with the same name as a preset zone replace the preset zone fully.
Rules with the same from as a preset rule replace the preset rule.
Fallow adds new zones and rules after the preset zones and rules. A zone that replaces a preset zone also moves to the position of your zone in the list.
Use the hexagonal preset, but keep your domain code in src/core instead of src/domain:
This config keeps adapters and ports from the hexagonal preset and replaces the domain zone pattern with src/core/**. All three rules stay the same.
Zones restrict only the files they match. A file outside every zone has no restrictions, and fallow does not tell you about it. To find these files, enable coverage:
Coverage runs only when requireAllFiles is true. By default, unmatched files stay unrestricted, as before coverage existed.
Coverage checks every analyzed file, also a file that no entry point reaches.
Findings use the severity and the suppression token of the boundary-violation rule.
Combine coverage with forbidden calls. A file outside all zones then cannot escape a call policy.
For generated code, use allowUnmatched instead of file-level suppression comments. The config keeps the exception in one place that reviewers can see.
To ban specific calls in a zone, add a forbidden-call policy. For example, you can keep process execution and logging out of a domain layer:

Fallow reports each matching call or new expression as a boundary_call_violations finding. The finding names the callee as written, the matched pattern, and the zone. A new expression has the prefix new in callee, for example new Date for the pattern Date.

Per segment: matching compares whole name segments. It does not match substrings or globs.

fetch matches only fetch, never myfetch.
A trailing object.* matches any member: child_process.* matches child_process.exec.
A leading *.member matches any object: *.innerHTML matches el.innerHTML.
Import provenance: patterns match through imports. child_process.* covers import { execSync } from "node:child_process", the bare child_process specifier, namespace imports, and default imports.

Direct callee paths only, including optional chaining (cp?.exec() matches like cp.exec()). Fallow does not follow aliased or re-bound callees (const run = cp.exec; run()), computed members, or injected dependencies (this.client.exec()).

Zoned files only: rules apply only to files in a zone, also a file that no entry point reaches. Files outside all zones are unrestricted. To make sure every file is in a zone, combine with coverage.requireAllFiles.

One finding per call site: each call and each new expression gets its own finding, so Date() and new Date() on two lines give two findings. When several rules match, the first matching rule in config order wins. A fallow-ignore-next-line comment covers only the call site on its next line.
Fallow rejects patterns that match nothing useful, such as a bare *, when it loads the config. A rule for a zone that matches no files gives a warning during analysis.

Severity and suppression: forbidden-call findings use the boundary-violation rule (default error) and its suppression token. Fallow also accepts the aliases boundary-call-violation and boundary-call-violations. Each of these tokens suppresses all boundary findings on that line or in that file.

For a staged rollout, set "rules": { "boundary-violation": "warn" } while you triage existing forbidden calls. Then set it back to "error" to enforce them. This also makes import-direction violations warnings, because all boundary findings share one rule.
Run fallow list --boundaries to see the final configuration after preset expansion and merging. This is the fastest way to check your config.

Boundaries: 4 zones, 4 rules

Zones:
 app 3 files src/app/**
 features 12 files src/features/**
 shared 8 files src/components/**, src/hooks/**, src/lib/**, ...
 server 4 files src/server/**

Rules:
 app → features, shared, server
 features → shared, server
 server → shared
 shared (isolated, no imports allowed)
For scripts or MCP tools, use JSON output:
When you debug boundary violations, run fallow list --boundaries first. It shows the real zone patterns, file counts, and resolved rules. You see a wrong glob before you run the analysis.
Preset zone patterns are flat (src/<zone>/**). They do not work when packages have separate source directories. Define zones for each package:
In tRPC apps, the server router usually imports sub-routers from feature modules. With the bulletproof preset, this gives server -> features violations.
The cleanest fix is to suppress the file that combines the routers:
You can also add features to the server rule:
A wider server rule lets all server files import from features, not only the router. For one exception, use inline suppression.
Test files often import from any zone. Add a test zone above the preset layers:

The first matching zone wins. With a preset, fallow puts the preset zones first and adds your custom zones after them. This example therefore works only for test files outside the preset zone directories, such as src/__tests__/**. For a test file inside a zone directory (for example src/features/auth/auth.test.ts), the features zone of the preset matches first.
To put the test zone first, redeclare every preset zone after it. A zone with the same name as a preset zone replaces it, and fallow keeps the order of your list. The preset rules stay active:

A replacing zone uses only the patterns that you give. Copy all the preset patterns, as in this example. Run fallow list --boundaries to check the zone order. You can also use ignorePatterns to exclude test files from the analysis fully.
Presets, output formats, and inline suppression for boundary violations.
Set boundary-violation to error, warn, or off.
Suppress single findings in source code.

pages.title: Fallow environment variables for CI and editors
items: Fallow environment variables for CI and editors
Fallow environment variables set defaults for a whole CI job, editor, or MCP server. Reference for FALLOW_FORMAT, FALLOW_QUIET, and the other variables.
Environment variables change fallow defaults for every command in a shell, a CI job, or an MCP server. You set a value once and do not repeat the flag on each command.
Set the default output format, so you do not pass --format on every command.

export FALLOW_FORMAT=json
fallow dead-code # Outputs JSON without --format flag
When both are set, the --format CLI flag takes precedence over FALLOW_FORMAT.
Hide progress bars and status messages. Use it in CI or when you pipe the output.

export FALLOW_QUIET=1
fallow dead-code # No progress output, only results
This is the same as --quiet on every command.
A quiet run also hides the stderr warnings that repeat a workspace_diagnostics[] entry. See Quiet runs.
Path to the fallow binary. The MCP server (fallow-mcp) uses it to find the fallow CLI.

export FALLOW_BIN=/usr/local/bin/fallow
fallow-mcp # MCP server uses the specified binary
When not set, the default is fallow on PATH.
Timeout in seconds to fetch remote configs from https:// URLs in the extends field.

export FALLOW_EXTENDS_TIMEOUT_SECS=10
fallow dead-code # URL extends have 10s to respond
When not set, the default is 5 seconds.

Directory for the persistent analysis cache. The CLI, the language server, the MCP server and the Node bindings read it. When both are set, this variable takes precedence over the cache.dir config field. A relative path resolves from the project root. This variable can point outside the project. A cache.dir in the config file must be inside the project.

export FALLOW_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/fallow-cache
fallow dead-code # cache files are stored under /tmp/fallow-cache
By default, fallow stores the cache in .fallow/cache.bin under the project root. Set this variable in these cases:
CI has a dedicated cache volume.
Multiple workspace copies share one cache location.
--no-cache turns off the cache fully. This variable then has no effect.
One cache directory for several projects
An absolute path outside the project is one directory for every project. The hosts use it in two ways:

The CLI, the MCP server and the Node bindings write cache.bin and graph-cache.bin directly into the directory. The extraction cache keys on paths relative to the project root, so a CI job still gets cache hits when the checkout path changes. Use one directory for one project: when two projects share it, each run replaces the cache of the other project.

The language server writes into one subdirectory for each project root, for example web-3f2a9c1d8e7b6a50 (the folder name and a hash of the full root path). Two editor windows on two projects can share one FALLOW_CACHE_DIR and keep both caches.

Maximum size in megabytes of the extraction cache on disk (.fallow/cache.bin). When both are set, this variable takes precedence over the cache.maxSizeMb config field. The CLI, the language server, the MCP server and the Node bindings read this variable.

export FALLOW_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=64
fallow dead-code # cache capped at 64 MB

When not set, the default is 256 (MB). When the serialized cache grows past 80% of the limit, fallow removes the entries for the files that the latest run did not discover, until the cache is at 60%. An example is the test files after a --production run. Fallow keeps the entries of the latest run while they fit in the limit, so the cache can stay near the full limit. When they do not fit, fallow removes only the entries that go past the limit. A file that every run reads stays, also when it never changes. Use this variable on CI runners with disk quotas. Local machines with large disks rarely need it.
--no-cache turns off the cache fully. This variable then has no effect.
One cache directory for several projects
An absolute path outside the project is one directory for every project. The hosts use it in two ways:

The CLI, the MCP server and the Node bindings write cache.bin and graph-cache.bin directly into the directory. The extraction cache keys on paths relative to the project root, so a CI job still gets cache hits when the checkout path changes. Use one directory for one project: when two projects share it, each run replaces the cache of the other project.

The language server writes into one subdirectory for each project root, for example web-3f2a9c1d8e7b6a50 (the folder name and a hash of the full root path). Two editor windows on two projects can share one FALLOW_CACHE_DIR and keep both caches.

Set to false, 0, no or off (in any case) to ignore workspaces.changedSince for every run of the process. Every workspace package is then in full scope, as with --no-package-baselines. Other values keep the map, so a typo never widens a run. The CLI, the language server, the MCP server and the Node bindings read this variable.

export FALLOW_PACKAGE_BASELINES=false
fallow dead-code --save-baseline fallow-baselines/dead-code.json # whole-project baseline
Sets a fixed comparison base for fallow audit. It has an effect only when you pass neither --base nor --changed-since. The precedence is the --base flag, then FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE, then auto-detection.

export FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE=upstream/main
fallow audit # compares against upstream/main instead of the auto-detected base

When unset, fallow audit uses the git merge-base (fork point) as the base. It compares against the upstream of the branch, or the remote default (origin/HEAD, then origin/main, then origin/master). This works for most repositories. Set a fixed base in two cases:
Forks. On a fork, origin is your fork, which can be behind the real upstream. Set FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE=upstream/main to compare against the real upstream.

The agent gate. fallow hooks install --target agent generates a hook that runs bare fallow audit. Your team may work only in git worktrees and never update the local default branch. Then set the base with this variable. You do not edit the generated script, which a reinstall overwrites.
A malformed value (a ref with disallowed characters) stops the audit with exit code 2. Fallow does not ignore it, so you see a typo immediately.

Maximum age of a base-snapshot worktree cache that fallow audit keeps and reuses. The age is in whole days since the last reuse or since creation. The next fallow audit run removes older entries when it starts.

The same age applies to the base-snapshot files in the fallow cache directory (.fallow/cache/audit-base-v<N>/ by default), counted from the last use. After each save of a snapshot file, audit removes the older files and keeps only the newest 32 files.
When both are set, this variable takes precedence over the audit.cacheMaxAgeDays config field. In fallow audit-cache prune, the --max-age-days flag takes precedence over this variable.

export FALLOW_AUDIT_CACHE_MAX_AGE_DAYS=7
fallow audit --base origin/main # caches older than 7 days are reclaimed

When not set, the default is 30 days. Set 0 to turn off the age-based cleanup, for example on CI runners that clean /tmp with a separate process. The cap of 32 snapshot files stays. For an invalid value (not an integer, or negative), fallow uses the config field or the default and gives no message. A typo in a runner variable does not fail audits.

The cleanup runs once per fallow audit run. It looks only at base-snapshot cache entries that fallow owns, never at other content of the temp directory or the cache directory. It never removes a cache entry that another running fallow audit uses (a kernel flock(2) lock per entry).

When it removes caches, fallow writes one fallow: reclaimed N stale base-snapshot caches line to stderr, unless --quiet is set. To run the same cleanup on demand and see the decision for each entry, use fallow audit-cache prune.

Delete per-project fallow impact stores that have not changed in this many whole days. Impact keeps one small history file per project in your user config directory. When you delete a project from disk, its store stays. Set this variable so that a recorded run removes these stores.

export FALLOW_IMPACT_STORE_MAX_AGE_DAYS=90
fallow audit --base origin/main # impact stores untouched for 90+ days are reclaimed
When unset (the default), fallow keeps every store forever. 0 and invalid values also keep every store, so a typo never deletes history.

The age is the modification time of the store file. Each recorded run rewrites the file, so a project that you still track never expires. The cleanup never touches the project that you just recorded. It never deletes the advisory .lock sidecar files or the global impact.json opt-in toggle. Impact records only on developer machines (never in CI), so this cleanup is local only.

In a local terminal run, fallow can show a one-line upgrade hint when a cached latest-version check finds a newer release. Fallow does not show the hint for machine formats, CI, quiet runs, and non-TTY agent runs. Set FALLOW_UPDATE_CHECK=off to turn off the hint and the background latest-version check on that machine. DO_NOT_TRACK and FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED also turn them off.

The warnings that fallow writes to stderr have color only when stderr is a terminal. A pipe, a log file, or an agent session gets plain text without ANSI escape codes. Set NO_COLOR to a non-empty value to turn off color on a terminal. Set CLICOLOR_FORCE to a value other than 0 to turn on color also on a pipe. CLICOLOR_FORCE takes precedence. The report uses the same CLICOLOR_FORCE rule.

dead-code, health, dupes, bare fallow, and audit add a top-level next_steps[] array to their --format json output. The array lists read-only follow-up commands, based on the findings of the run. Bare fallow also prints a one-line Next: hint in human output on a TTY.

Set FALLOW_SUGGESTIONS=off (or 0, false, no, disabled) to hide them. Use this when a CI job compares raw JSON output against a snapshot. The CLI that the MCP server starts inherits the variable, so it also removes next_steps from MCP responses.

FALLOW_PRODUCTION is the same as the --production CLI flag. It turns on production mode for every analysis. The per-analysis variables (FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DEAD_CODE, FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH, FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DUPES) change one analysis in bare combined mode (fallow with no subcommand) or in fallow audit.

# Run combined mode with production-only health, full-tree dead-code and dupes
export FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH=true
fallow --format json --quiet
Config (production: true legacy form, or production: { health: true, ... } per-analysis form)

A per-analysis variable takes precedence over the global variable. For example, FALLOW_PRODUCTION=false FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH=true runs health in production mode and the other analyses in non-production mode.
A single subcommand such as fallow health rejects the per-analysis CLI flag, but it still reads FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH. For a subcommand, pass --production or set the per-analysis variable.
In CI, set FALLOW_FORMAT=json and FALLOW_QUIET=1 to get machine-readable output with no progress messages.

Path to Istanbul coverage data (coverage-final.json) or raw V8 coverage (a NODE_V8_COVERAGE directory, or one V8 coverage JSON file). With this data, fallow health, fallow audit, and bare fallow compute accurate CRAP scores per function. An explicit CLI flag or MCP tool parameter takes precedence. After that, the CLI and typed MCP routes read this variable, and then health.coverage from config.

Absolute prefix that fallow removes from Istanbul coverage paths before it matches files. Use it when the coverage comes from a different checkout root, such as CI or Docker. An explicit CLI flag or MCP tool parameter takes precedence. After that, the CLI and typed MCP routes read this variable, and then health.coverageRoot from config.

Maximum size in megabytes of one source file (default 5; 0 means no limit). Fallow skips larger source files before it parses them. This prevents out-of-memory failures on one large generated or bundled file. When both are set, the --max-file-size CLI flag takes precedence. Fallow always analyzes declaration files (.d.ts).

These variables change the review-github, review-gitlab, pr-comment-github, and pr-comment-gitlab output formats. The bundled GitHub Action and GitLab CI template set them for you. Set them yourself only when you render these formats outside the bundled integrations.
These variables configure the runtime coverage license and the connection to Fallow Cloud, the paid product. See fallow license and fallow coverage.
Set these in the env block of the MCP server. The CLI that the server starts inherits them. For the full reference, see MCP integration.
For the complete machine-readable list, see the environment_variables block of fallow schema.

pages.title: MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf
items: MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf
Connect fallow to Claude Code, Cursor, or Windsurf through MCP or the CLI. Your agent gets repeatable answers on unused code, duplication, and complexity.

Your coding agent writes code fast, but it cannot see the whole codebase at once. It cannot build a module graph, follow re-export chains, find duplication across thousands of files, or score complexity hotspots. Fallow does that analysis for the agent. The agent calls fallow through the CLI or MCP and gets the same complete result on every run.
Any agent that can run shell commands can use fallow. The CLI is the primary interface. MCP is an optional layer on top that adds typed tools.
To analyze a codebase, a tool must build the full import graph and walk it. An agent that reads files into its context window cannot do this.
Every AI coding agent can run shell commands, so you do not need MCP:

# Full dead code analysis with JSON output
fallow dead-code --format json

# Only check changed files (great for agent PR workflows)
fallow dead-code --changed-since main --format json

# Find code duplication
fallow dupes --format json

# Preview what auto-fix would remove
fallow fix --dry-run --format json

# Apply fixes (agents should use --yes to skip confirmation)
fallow fix --yes --format json

# Detect feature flags and environment gates
fallow flags --format json

# List project info (plugins, entry points, file count)
fallow list --format json
When an agent runs fallow, always use --format json. The agent can parse JSON output without guessing. The human-readable format also works, but it is less exact to parse.

To read fallow JSON output in TypeScript, use import type { CheckOutput, HealthOutput, DupesOutput, AuditOutput } from "fallow/types". These types cover the full output contract. Fallow generates them from the same schema it uses internally. SchemaVersion is fixed to a literal when the types are generated, so a major schema change causes a compile error at your call sites. Your code cannot drift out of sync without notice.
For agents that support MCP (Model Context Protocol), fallow-mcp gives each analysis as a structured tool. The agent gets typed inputs and outputs and does not parse CLI text.

The MCP server uses stdio transport and a hybrid adapter. It runs supported requests in process. For options that only the CLI command has, it starts a managed fallow CLI subprocess. Set FALLOW_BIN only when CLI-backed calls need a specific binary. The default is fallow in PATH.
The fallow npm package includes the fallow-mcp launcher. You can also install it with cargo install fallow-mcp, or download a binary from GitHub Releases.
Register the server with the Claude Code CLI. The CLI writes the configuration for you:

# Available in every project on this machine
claude mcp add fallow --scope user fallow-mcp

# This repository only, checked in for the whole team
claude mcp add fallow --scope project fallow-mcp

--scope project creates .mcp.json in the repository root. fallow agent install writes the same entry for each harness it detects. It first checks which launcher works. You can also write the file by hand:
Run claude mcp list to confirm fallow is registered.
Claude Code does not read mcpServers from .claude/settings.json. It ignores a server there and shows no error. Use .mcp.json or claude mcp add.
Cursor reads MCP servers from mcp.json. To use fallow in one project, create .cursor/mcp.json in the project root. To use it in all projects, create ~/.cursor/mcp.json in your home directory:
Any MCP-compatible client can connect to fallow-mcp over stdio transport:

# Start the MCP server directly
fallow-mcp

# With a custom fallow binary path
FALLOW_BIN=/usr/local/bin/fallow fallow-mcp
Configure your client to launch fallow-mcp as a stdio subprocess.

Installed fallow as a project devDependency? "command": "fallow-mcp" expects the binary on your PATH, as with a global install. A binary in node_modules/.bin/ is not on PATH, so the server fails to start with ENOENT. Start it through the runner of your package manager, which finds the binary in node_modules/.bin/:

The npm and Bun examples explicitly select the fallow package that provides the launcher. Start the agent from the project root, so the runner finds the local install. To use a specific fallow binary, you can still set FALLOW_BIN.

The MCP server analyzes a Rust workspace through cargo fallow. A root with a Cargo.toml and no package.json takes the Rust route. Each routed tool runs cargo-fallow and returns its report with language: "rust".
mutation_plan and mutation_inspect take a package parameter on this route. Neither tool compiles or runs tests.
A parameter that the Rust route cannot honor gives FALLOW_RUST_UNSUPPORTED_PARAMS.
project_info, mutation_tasks and code_execute give FALLOW_RUST_UNSUPPORTED_TOOL.
A missing binary gives FALLOW_RUST_BINARY_NOT_FOUND. Set CARGO_FALLOW_BIN to name the binary.
A root with both a Cargo.toml and a package.json keeps the JavaScript route. The result then has a warnings entry that points to cargo fallow.

When the response capabilities array has function_identity_v2, cloud runtime tools can add source-map confidence metadata. Function list responses use resolutionStatus and mappingQuality. Runtime-context responses use resolution_status and mapping_quality. These fields tell you how much to trust the source map. They do not tell you if the function ran.

analyze, check_changed, find_dupes, and check_health can write a baseline or snapshot file. These four tools therefore declare readOnlyHint: false and destructiveHint: false. A host that approves read-only tools without a confirmation now asks before it runs them. code_execute stays read-only.

The save_baseline, save_regression_baseline, and save_snapshot parameters write only inside the project root, its Git work tree, the CI workspace (GITHUB_WORKSPACE, CI_PROJECT_DIR), RUNNER_TEMP, or the system temp directory. Another path returns a tool error. See Save destinations.
Review parameters that each call passes in one way
To request constant parameters, pass issue_types: ["constant-parameters"] to analyze:
Each finding lists the function, the parameter, the reason, the value, and the inspected calls. Read the calls before you change the function. The findings are not auto-fixable.
Review optional props absent from callers
To request absent component props, pass issue_types: ["absent-component-props"] to analyze:

The rule is off by default. Selecting it opts in to findings about optional props that the component reads but no inspected reachable caller supplies. A finding includes its declaration and inspected callers. Review defaults and API intent before proposing an edit. Every action requires manual review; no action automatically removes a prop or conditional UI.
Some tools take more parameters than the common root, config, no_cache, and threads:
Every finding from every tool has a structured actions array. An agent can use it to apply fixes or suppressions in code:

Dead code (analyze, check_changed): a fix action (for example remove-export) and a suppress action. The auto_fixable flag tells the agent whether to call fix_apply or to handle the suggestion by hand. For the action types, see the dead-code CLI reference.

Health (check_health, audit): complexity findings and styling findings have an actions array. For complexity findings, a CRAP and coverage formula picks the primary action from coverage_tier, cyclomatic, and max_crap_threshold. The action types include refactor-function, add-tests, increase-coverage, and suppress-line. Styling findings have read-only verification and suppression actions for styling. When you pass --baseline or --save-baseline, or set health.suggestInlineSuppression: false, fallow leaves out suppress-line. It then adds a top-level actions_meta: { suppression_hints_omitted: true, reason } field (under health.actions_meta in combined-mode and audit output). Targets get apply-refactoring and a suppress action (when evidence exists). Hotspots get refactor-file and add-tests.
Duplication (find_dupes, audit): extract-shared and suppress actions on clone families and groups.
Audit (audit): the actions from all three parts (dead code, health, duplication).

The analyze, check_health, find_dupes, and audit responses (and combined output) also have a top-level next_steps[] array. It is separate from the per-finding actions[]. It lists read-only follow-up commands, based on the findings of the run. Each entry is { id, command, reason }:
You can run command as-is. It is never a fix or another command that changes files. Fallow gives the evidence. The agent decides on the change and applies it.

The stable kebab-case id (setup, impact-report, trace-unused-export, trace-clone, complexity-breakdown, scope-workspaces, audit-changed) names a verification step to run before you act. Through MCP, use the id to call the matching tool (trace_export, trace_clone, check_health with complexity_breakdown: true, audit) or a code_execute host call. Do not run the CLI command string in a shell.

A setup step (command: fallow agent install --dry-run) comes first, and only on projects with findings, no config, and no CI. By design, no tool runs it for you. Offer the user fallow init for a config. The dry run previews the agent guide, the skills, the MCP server, and the commit gate, and writes no files. Do not run a setup command that writes files without asking. The step goes away when a config exists or after fallow init --decline.

An impact-report step (command: fallow impact) shows at most once a week. It has the local value digest (commits contained at the gate, findings resolved) when impact tracking is enabled and the results are not zero. The impact store keeps the time of the last step, so the weekly limit is the same for all agents and sessions. The step can show even on a clean run. Tell the user the non-zero numbers in one line.
The array has no duplicates, is in priority order, and has at most three entries. When it is empty, fallow leaves it out. To turn it off, set FALLOW_SUGGESTIONS=off in the server env.

Fallow emits add-to-config actions for findings that you resolve with a new entry in the fallow config, such as unused-dependency, type-only-dependency, test-only-dependency, and duplicate-export. These actions have an optional value_schema field next to value:

The value_schema URL is a JSON Pointer fragment into the published fallow schema.json. An agent can fetch the linked schema to validate value before it writes the value into the config of a user. For example, it can reject a malformed { file, exports } rule object on the ignoreExports action. The field only adds information. Actions without a schema still work, and agents that ignore the field work as before.
CLI-backed tool calls run fallow with --quiet, so the caller gets nothing that the CLI writes to stderr. In its place, the root warnings[] array has plain sentences about the run:
each gate that reported fail or warn
diagnostics that made the analysis less complete
each request the run could not apply
requested rules that are off, in one sentence for all such rules

A request that made the report wider and an output file that the run did not write each get their own sentence. Only a wider report means that the findings cover more than you asked for. A request that the run applied to an empty scope also gets its own sentence. An empty scope cannot have findings. An empty result there means there was nothing to analyze. It does not mean the code is clean.

When the command cannot read a baseline file as its own format, that gets its own sentence, before the staleness sentence. Read baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format first, because such a file suppresses nothing. When the file names a writer that fallow knows, baseline_staleness.saved_by and the warning name the command that saved it. Pass another path, and do not save the baseline again. The sentence also says that the run would fail the --fail-on-stale-baseline gate. Every tool says this except audit, because the audit stale-baseline gate does not apply to the baselines it loads.

The typed in-process route reads the same fields, so a tool gives the same answer on both routes. The warnings do not move or remove other fields. gate_outcomes, baseline_staleness, workspace_diagnostics and request_outcomes stay where they are in the response. A run with nothing to report adds no warnings. A warning never makes the call an error.

The server also gives read-only reference material as MCP resources. A resource read starts no subprocess and runs no analysis, and your client can cache it by URI. The client reads resources with its own resource tool, for example ReadMcpResourceTool in Claude Code. Each payload is plain JSON. The server version is in _meta.fallow_version of each content item, so a cached copy shows its own version, and the schema resources stay valid strict JSON Schema. The catalogue is fixed at build time, so there are no subscriptions and no list-changed notifications.

{issue_type} takes the bare id (unused-export), the namespaced id (fallow/unused-export), or the CLI filter spelling. An unknown URI returns a structured error, and its data lists the known URIs. For an unknown issue type, data lists the nearest matches. The numeric code is -32002 for clients on protocol versions before 2026-07-28 and -32602 from that version on. So check data, not the code. fallow schema also publishes the same catalogue as mcp_resources.
To get a full picture of the codebase in one call, run fallow with no subcommand. It runs all analyses in one pass and returns one JSON object with dead_code, duplication, and health sections:
The combined output has all dead-code issue types, the duplication findings, and the health metrics. The combined envelope has its own schema_version, currently 15.
Diff and ref from the environment

FALLOW_DIFF_FILE and FALLOW_CHANGED_SINCE come from the server environment, not from the caller. When the server cannot use one of them, the call does not fail. It stands down to the full project, the same as the CLI:
A FALLOW_DIFF_FILE that cannot be read, or that is too large, gives a report at full scope.
A FALLOW_CHANGED_SINCE ref that does not resolve gives a report at full scope.

The response then has a not-applied entry in request_outcomes, with the reason token and the sentence of the CLI, and a sentence in warnings[]. An applied request gives an applied entry with scope_size. The typed route and the CLI route publish the same object, on the dead-code, dupes, health, flags, and combined responses.
A since or changed_since argument that the caller passes, and that does not resolve, still fails the call with FALLOW_CHANGED_FILES_FAILED, because the caller can fix it.
Some tools keep the hard error for a FALLOW_CHANGED_SINCE ref that does not resolve:
audit and decision_surface read the variable as their base ref, not as a request to narrow the report.
project_info, list_boundaries, and the trace tools have no request_outcomes in their response. A ref that stands down would make their result wider, and nothing in the response would say so.
The MCP server returns structured JSON errors from both routes:
Typed API timeout: returns the FALLOW_MCP_API_TIMEOUT code. The in-process analysis stops at its next stage boundary.

CLI exit code 1: the server treats it as success (issues found, not an error) and returns the full JSON output. One exception: a run that requires complete type-aware evidence (--type-aware-require complete, or typeAware.require: complete in the config) and reports it incomplete is an error.

CLI exit code 2+: the server passes through the structured JSON error that the CLI writes to stdout, when there is one. If there is no JSON, the server builds {"error": true, "message": "...", "exit_code": N} from stderr.
CLI timeout: kills the process tree and returns the FALLOW_MCP_SUBPROCESS_TIMEOUT code.

Output over the response cap: the default cap is 1,000,000 bytes. On both routes, the server returns isError: true with the FALLOW_MCP_SUBPROCESS_OUTPUT_LIMIT code. The context field is subprocess or typed. The optional narrow array lists the parameters of the tool that make its output smaller, for example issue_types, file and workspace on analyze, or top on find_dupes. Call the tool again with one of them. max_output_bytes on a call can only lower the cap. To set a different cap for all calls, set FALLOW_MCP_MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES in the server environment, up to 16 MiB.

Client cancel: when the client sends notifications/cancelled, a CLI call kills its process tree and a typed call stops at its next stage boundary. The client gets no response for the cancelled call, as the MCP specification requires.
code_execute applies the same exit-code rules to the calls in its snippet, so an incomplete type-aware run that requires complete evidence is also an error there.

The CLI is the primary interface. Any agent that can run shell commands can call fallow --format json --quiet. MCP is an optional layer that adds typed tools, so the agent does not parse CLI text. See CLI: the primary agent interface.

No. The server runs on your machine over stdio. Four tools make a network call to read production data from Fallow Cloud: get_cloud_runtime_context, get_cloud_review_packet, get_cloud_deployment_changes, and inspect_target when you set cloud: true. These calls send the repository name and selectors such as commit SHAs, file paths, and function names. They do not send source code. All other tools analyze only the local project.

Only fix_apply changes source files. Call fix_preview first to see the changes. The analysis tools that take a save_baseline parameter write a baseline file only when you pass that parameter. The fallow://tools resource lists the read-only flag of each tool.

The client cannot find fallow-mcp on the PATH. This happens when fallow is a project devDependency. Start the server through your package manager, for example npx --yes --package fallow fallow-mcp. See the devDependency note in MCP: structured tool calling.
Set FALLOW_TIMEOUT_SECS to a higher value in the server environment. The default is 120 seconds. See Environment variables.

pages.title: Fallow Agent Skills for Claude Code and Cursor
items: Fallow Agent Skills for Claude Code and Cursor
Install the fallow Agent Skills in Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or Gemini CLI. Your coding agent then runs fallow with the right flags and reads the output.
With the fallow skills installed, your coding agent runs the right fallow command for a request and reads the output correctly. It does not guess from general knowledge. The skills tell the agent:
They cover codebase health, cleanup analysis, circular dependencies, duplication, and complexity hotspots.
Skills work together with the CLI and MCP integrations. Skills tell the agent how to use fallow. The CLI and MCP give the agent the tools.

The commit gate of the plugin runs only in a project that uses fallow: a project with a fallow config file, or with a fallow dependency in package.json. It does nothing when fallow agent install already registered a gate for Claude Code or Codex. To turn it off, set FALLOW_PLUGIN_GATE=off in the environment of Claude Code.

If your project already has fallow installed from npm, you can skip the manual steps. fallow agent install writes the fallow and fallow-setup skills where Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor look for them. It also writes the MCP registration, an AGENTS.md task map, and the commit and push gate. Add --dry-run to see the plan first.

codex plugin marketplace add fallow-rs/fallow-skills
codex plugin add fallow@fallow-skills
In the Codex desktop app, this plugin also adds the Fallow app: a code health dashboard, a thread tab, composer attachments, and a config editor.

Inside a Claude Code session, fallow can write one <claude-code-hint /> line that asks Claude Code to offer the fallow plugin. Fallow writes the line to stderr, and only for human output without --quiet, outside CI, and when the project and the user have no fallow plugin or skill for Claude Code. The hint has no effect until the official Claude Code marketplace lists the plugin. Set FALLOW_CLAUDE_CODE_HINT=off to turn it off.
The skills follow the open Agent Skills specification, so any compatible agent can use them.
What agents can do after installation
After you install the skills, your agent can handle requests like these:
"Find all unused exports in this project". The agent runs fallow dead-code --format json --quiet --unused-exports and summarizes the findings.
"Are there any unused dependencies?" The agent runs a targeted analysis and suggests removals.
"Find code duplication in the codebase". The agent runs fallow dupes with the right mode and explains the clone families.
"Remove unused exports". The agent does a dry run first and shows the proposed changes. Then it applies them with --yes.
"Set up a code quality gate in CI". The agent writes a GitHub Actions workflow with baselines.
"Why is this export flagged?" The agent uses --trace to find the cause and suggests a suppression if needed.
Use all three together. Install the skill so the agent knows how to use fallow. Configure MCP for typed tool calls. Keep fallow in PATH as a CLI fallback.
