pages.title: Fallow app for Codex: code health dashboard
items: Fallow app for Codex: code health dashboard
The fallow app for the Codex desktop app shows a code health dashboard, a Code Health tab per thread, a branch audit, a cleanup form, and a config editor.

The Fallow plugin for Codex includes an app. In the Codex desktop app, it shows code health next to your conversations and lets Codex act on the findings you pick. The app runs the fallow CLI on your machine. No code leaves the machine.

codex plugin marketplace add fallow-rs/fallow-skills
codex plugin add fallow@fallow-skills
The app needs Node.js 20 or later on PATH, and fallow itself:
After the install, choose Set up on the plugin page. Codex checks the installation, asks for your defaults, and runs the first analysis.
The OpenAI plugin directory lists the skills-only version of the plugin. The app comes with the marketplace install above.
The plugin page has these settings:
Forms need Default permissions. When a thread runs in Full access mode, Codex declines forms without showing them. The app then shows a notice, and Codex asks you in chat instead.
Choose the config editor once. Codex opens JSON files in its own viewer by default. To edit .fallowrc.json and .fallowrc.jsonc in Fallow, choose Fallow Config under Settings, File type handlers.
Mentions in a new thread. Before the first message of a thread, @Fallow lists the findings of the last analyzed project and names it.
You can open a repository that you do not trust, so the app limits what that repository can run and read:
A fallow binary that the repository ships, and an npx download, run only inside the Codex sandbox of the thread. Outside the sandbox, the app only runs a fallow that you installed on PATH.
Fallow gets a short list of environment variables. Tokens and credentials in the Codex environment do not reach it.
The app reads source lines only from files that a report names.
In a thread, a folder that the model names must be inside the working directory of that thread.

The app stores its settings, recent projects, and the project of each thread in your user state folder. To find the project of a thread tab, it reads the first line of that thread's Codex session log, which holds the working directory. The config impact preview writes a draft next to the config file for the length of two fallow runs, then deletes it.
The skills in the same plugin, for Codex and other agents.
Stop the agent from committing code that fails fallow audit.

pages.title: Claude Code hooks to block commits that fail fallow
items: Claude Code hooks to block commits that fail fallow
A Claude Code PreToolUse hook runs fallow audit before git commit or git push. When the audit fails, the hook blocks the command and sends the findings back.
This gate stops Claude Code and Codex from committing or pushing code that fails fallow audit. The agent gets the findings, fixes the code, and tries again.

The gate is not a Git hook. It is a local PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool of the agent. When the agent runs git commit or git push, the hook runs fallow audit --format json --quiet --explain --gate-marker agent:
On pass or warn, the command continues.
On fail, the hook blocks the command and sends the JSON findings to the agent on stderr.
This is Option C (local agent gate) in the adoption rollout. Use it together with the shared CI gate from fallow audit. It does not replace the CI gate. See Adopt Fallow in an existing repo.

The command writes a project-level .claude/settings.json and .claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh. If your repo also has a .codex/ directory, the command also installs the Codex gate. An AGENTS.md file alone does not select Codex, because Cursor and fallow also write that file. When no .claude/ or .codex/ directory exists, the command installs the Claude Code gate. To remove the generated files later, run fallow hooks uninstall --target agent.
The output has one line for each path and says what changes:

fallow hooks install --target agent (install) (dry run):
 .claude/settings.json updated (1 handler added, 1 preserved)
 .claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh would create
With a .codex/ directory, the output also has lines for .codex/hooks.json, .codex/hooks/fallow-gate.sh, and AGENTS.md.

fallow agent install installs this gate together with the skill, the MCP registration, and an AGENTS.md task map for each harness it detects. The older fallow setup-hooks command is deprecated. It still works in all of fallow 3 with a warning, and the next major version removes it. See Deprecated fallow setup-hooks.
To install the gate once for all repos, pass --user. The installer writes to your home directory:
The handler command runs "$HOME"/.claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh, so it works in every repo that Claude Code opens.

For Codex, --user writes the gate to ~/.codex/hooks.json and ~/.codex/hooks/fallow-gate.sh. The user handler runs the audit from the git root of the session. With --user, fallow does not write the AGENTS.md block.
When a repo has both, the project-level install overrides the global one. Use this to give one repo a stricter or looser policy.
By default, the installer looks at the project directories:
With a .claude/ directory, it installs the Claude Code gate.
With a .codex/ directory, it installs the Codex gate.
With both, it installs both gates.
With neither, it installs the Claude Code gate.
To select one harness, pass --agent claude or --agent codex. The installer then writes only the files of that harness, also when the directory does not exist yet:
--agent also works on uninstall. Without it, uninstall removes the gate of each harness that it finds. It also finds an AGENTS.md routing block that an older fallow wrote without a .codex/ directory.
To add .claude/ to the .gitignore of the project, pass --gitignore-claude:

The installer creates .gitignore when it does not exist. It adds no line when .gitignore already has .claude or .claude/. The flag applies only when the installer writes the Claude Code gate, and a --dry-run does not change .gitignore. Use it when each developer installs the gate locally and the team does not commit .claude/.
fallow hooks install --target agent and fallow hooks uninstall --target agent take these flags. For the Git target and the full command reference, see fallow hooks.

fallow setup-hooks is the older form of the same installer. It prints a deprecation warning on stderr. It works in all of fallow 3, and the next major version removes it. Use fallow hooks install --target agent, or fallow agent install for the gate together with the skill and the MCP registration.
fallow setup-hooks takes the installer flags, and one more flag:

The gate script and fallow audit read paths from the current directory. An agent session can work in a package directory below the install root. The project handler thus walks up from the session directory to the nearest directory that holds the gate script, and runs the audit there. The audit then covers the full project, and not only the package.
The walk stops at the first .git entry. A nested worktree thus does not use the gate of the checkout around it. When the walk finds no gate script:
The Claude Code handler runs the script under $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.
The Codex handler exits 0 without output.
Run fallow agent install or fallow hooks install --target agent again to get the current handler.
Commit or push in another worktree
An agent can commit or push in another directory with git -C <dir> or cd <dir> && git .... The gate then audits the work tree of that directory, not the session directory.

A linked worktree shares its branches with the session checkout, so a push from a linked worktree can send the session branch. For such a push, the gate also audits the session checkout, unless git shows that the push cannot send the session branch. The gate audits only the linked worktree when all of these are true:
The push options are only -u, -q, --set-upstream, --force-with-lease and --force-if-includes.
Each refspec sends the branch that the linked worktree has checked out, for example git -C ../feature push -u origin feature or HEAD.
A push without a refspec has push.default unset or set to simple, current, upstream or nothing, and no remote has a push or mirror setting.

In all other cases, and when a git command fails, the gate audits the session checkout too. Unrelated findings in the session checkout, such as untracked build output, then block the push. After you update fallow, run fallow agent install again to get this behavior.

The hook blocks the git commit or git push only when fallow audit returns verdict: "fail". When local Impact tracking is enabled, the --gate-marker agent flag lets it record blocked-then-cleared containment events.

Audit defaults to gate=new-only. Only findings that the changeset introduces fail the gate. Inherited findings in touched files still show in attribution, and each of those issues has introduced: false. They do not change the verdict.
This default helps you adopt fallow on a legacy codebase. An agent that edits a 10-year-old file is not blocked by the old unused exports in it. Only new ones block it.
To gate every finding in changed files (strict mode), set the gate in your project config:

You can also edit .claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh to pass --gate all. But each fallow hooks install --target agent run regenerates the script and removes your edit. Use the config file for a permanent setting.
When the gate blocks, it writes a short message to stderr. Claude Code and Codex give this message to the agent as the reason for the block. The message has:
the line fallow-gate: blocked by fallow <version> at <binary>,
the verdict and the number of findings that caused the block,
one line for each of these findings, in the form <kind> <path>:<line> <name>,
the path of the full JSON report.

fallow-gate: blocked by fallow 3.43.1 at /usr/local/bin/fallow
fallow-gate: verdict fail, 2 finding(s) caused the block:
 unused-export src/utils.ts:12 formatDate
 complexity src/parser.ts:40 parse
fallow-gate: full report: /path/to/repo/.fallow/gate-report.json

With the default gate=new-only, the list holds only the findings that the changeset introduces. Inherited findings are not in the list, but they stay in the full report. With gate = "all", the list holds every finding that is not a warning. The message lists at most 50 findings and gives the count of the rest.

The gate writes the full report, the output of fallow audit --format json --explain, to .fallow/gate-report.json in the audited tree. The .fallow/ directory holds a .gitignore with *, so the report does not show in git status. Two env vars change this behavior:
Run fallow agent install or fallow hooks install --target agent again to get this message in an installed gate.

The hook runs fallow audit with no --base. Audit then uses the git merge-base (fork point) as the comparison base. It compares against the upstream of the branch, or else the remote default (origin/main). Audit finds the merge-base at run time, so a new branch from origin/main is gated only on its own changes.
Two setups need an explicit base. For these, set FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE. It takes effect because the gate passes no --base:
Forks. On a fork, origin is your fork, and it can be behind the real upstream. Set FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE=upstream/main to compare against the real upstream.
A non-default integration branch. If your team merges into develop or a release branch and not into main, set FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE=origin/develop.
Use the env var, not a script edit. Each fallow hooks install --target agent run regenerates fallow-gate.sh, so a reinstall removes script edits.

The gate requires a minimum fallow version, set by the FALLOW_GATE_MIN_VERSION env var (default 2.85.0). The gate passes --gate-marker agent, which v2.85.0 added. Older binaries reject this flag, and every audit would then fail open. So if the fallow on PATH is older than the floor, the gate blocks and shows an upgrade hint. This stops an old npm-global or ~/.cargo/bin/fallow from looking like a working gate.

# Raise the floor (require a newer fallow across your team)
export FALLOW_GATE_MIN_VERSION=3.0.0

# Disable (only do this if you know why)
export FALLOW_GATE_MIN_VERSION=

Each block logs the path and version of the binary that ran, for example fallow-gate: blocked by fallow 3.43.1 at /usr/local/bin/fallow. You can see which binary ran without more debugging. The header of the installed script also has # Installer version: X.Y.Z. Use it when the gate does not agree with your current fallow --version.
fallow hooks status shows what is installed and changes nothing. It checks four places:
Agents and scripts read the JSON form before they propose setup changes:

After installation, also run fallow agent status --format json to check gate readiness. It identifies missing readers, unverified launchers, edited scripts, and PATH version differences. Project trust and hook approval remain manual.

user_edited is true when a hook file exists but has lost the fallow generator marker, or when a managed block is broken. An agent then knows not to overwrite the file without asking. script_version and min_version_floor give the installer version and the version floor of the gate script. Tools use them to find an old gate.
It removes the fallow-gate handler from .claude/settings.json and .codex/hooks.json. When nothing else is left in .codex/hooks.json, it deletes that file.
It deletes each hook script that still has the generator marker. To also remove a user-edited script, pass --force.
It removes the managed block from AGENTS.md.
Handlers that you added outside fallow stay. To uninstall the global files at ~/.claude/ and ~/.codex/ in place of the project files, pass --user.
Uninstall is idempotent. A second run prints unchanged or not present and exits 0. It also supports a dry run: fallow hooks uninstall --target agent --dry-run.

fallow hooks install --target agent also finds and removes hook commands from older manual setups. These include absolute paths, ~/-based paths, and Windows drive paths. When you run it on an existing install, it upgrades the handler to the canonical form and leaves no duplicates.

fallow hooks install --target git is a different hook. It creates a shell-level Git pre-commit hook in .git/hooks/ that runs fallow on changed files. That hook checks human commits. The gate on this page checks agent commits. You can use both together.

Copy the canonical script from the fallow repo, crates/cli/src/setup_hooks/fallow-gate.sh, into .claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh. Leave out the # Installer version: line, because only the installer writes it. Use fallow hooks install --target agent when you can. Copy the script by hand only when you cannot run that command.

For the audit, the hook looks for fallow in this order: fallow on PATH, ./node_modules/.bin/fallow, yarn exec fallow (for Yarn Plug'n'Play), and npx --no-install fallow. Current gates prefer fallow's native JSON reader. jq remains a compatibility fallback for older installations. When neither reader is available, the gate prints a notice and lets the command continue without auditing.

In JSON mode, fallow audit reports invalid refs, non-Git directories, and config errors as { "error": true, ... } with exit code 2. The gate does not block on these errors. A new repo or a repo with empty history can then commit before the first successful audit.
This gate runs before Claude runs the shell command, so git push --no-verify does not bypass it. Keep fallow audit in CI as the shared gate for humans and for workflows outside Claude.
Codex has its own hooks. For Codex, the installer writes two files:
.codex/hooks.json with a PreToolUse handler. The matcher is ^Bash$.
.codex/hooks/fallow-gate.sh, the same gate script that Claude Code uses.
The installer merges the handler into an existing .codex/hooks.json and keeps all other hooks. Codex runs a project hook only after you trust it in /hooks. Until then, the gate does not run.

The installer also writes a routing block to AGENTS.md. The block tells agents to use fallow, and names the hook as the enforcement layer. Agents without a hook run the check themselves. The block starts like this:

## Fallow checks

Use fallow for code-quality, cleanup, and setup tasks in this repository. Fallow checks the changed code before each `git commit` and `git push`. In Claude Code and Codex, a PreToolUse hook from `fallow agent install` runs this check and blocks the command when the verdict is `fail`. Other agents run the check themselves: `fallow audit --format json --quiet --explain --gate-marker agent`. If the verdict is `fail`, fix the reported findings before you try again. A JSON runtime error such as `{ "error": true, ... }` does not block.

The rest of the block explains the audit gate default and includes the task-to-command matrix from fallow schema. It is between <!-- fallow:setup-hooks:start --> and <!-- fallow:setup-hooks:end --> markers. When you upgrade fallow and run the installer again, the block updates in place.
Why this works well with agents
fallow audit --explain gives Claude structured findings with docs links and fix guidance. Agent Skills teach the agent how to act on them. The loop is short:
Claude tries to commit or push.
The gate blocks only on fail-severity issues.
Claude reads the block message, which lists the findings that caused the block, and fixes the code. It can read the full JSON report for more detail.
See Option C: local agent gate next to warn-everywhere and error-plus-baselines.
Reference for verdicts, JSON output, and baselines.
Teach the agent what to do after the gate blocks.

pages.title: VS Code extension for unused code and duplication
items: VS Code extension for unused code and duplication
The fallow VS Code extension shows unused code, duplication, complexity hotspots, and boundary violations as you edit. Fix them with one-click quick fixes.

The VS Code extension shows fallow findings in your editor while you write code, so you can fix them before you commit. The fallow LSP server gives real-time diagnostics for unused code, duplication, complexity, and boundary violations.
Sidebar views and status-bar items cover more of fallow:
the audit verdict for changed files

Code Lens shows "imported by N files" above each export that other files import. N is the number of distinct importing files. Click the lens to peek the import locations. An export without importers gets no lens, because the unused-export diagnostic already reports it.
Real-time diagnostics for dead-code issue types. The LSP server updates them, with no separate CLI process
Code Lens with the number of importing files above each used export (click to peek the import locations)
Hover information with the number of files that import an export, unused status, and duplicate block locations
Quick-fix code actions to remove unused exports or delete unused files, or to copy the finding id of a dead-code or security diagnostic
Refactor actions to extract duplicates into shared functions
Tree views in the sidebar with an icon for each category, an issue count badge, and a welcome view
Status bar with color-coded severity, a tooltip with a breakdown, and command links
Diagnostic documentation links: click a diagnostic code to open its docs page
Related information: circular dependencies, duplicate exports, and code duplication diagnostics link to all related files
Fix preview with a searchable Quick Pick to review fixes and go to them
JSON schema for .fallowrc.json with autocomplete and validation
Getting Started walkthrough on first install

The extension also shows the rest of the fallow analysis. Each one is a sidebar view or a status-bar item. Most are on by default. The Security Candidates view is opt-in, and the Runtime Coverage view stays empty until you load a capture:

Health view (sidebar): the project health score and grade, the top complexity findings, hotspot and refactoring candidates, and the hidden change coupling pairs. Each pair shows its degree and its shared commits, and opens either file. The pairs need the git history, so they come with fallow.health.hotspots. A separate run computes the view when you need it. To turn it off, use fallow.health.enabled.

Security Candidates view (sidebar): local security candidates (client-server-leak, the tainted-sink CWE catalogue). These are unverified candidates to verify, never confirmed vulnerabilities. To turn it on, use fallow.security.enabled.
Runtime Coverage view (sidebar): hot paths and cleanup candidates (safe-to-delete or review-required) from a loaded coverage capture.
Audit verdict (status bar): pass, warn, or fail for your current change set, the same as fallow audit.
License management: activate, view the status of, refresh, and deactivate the fallow license for continuous or multi-capture runtime coverage in the editor.

Monorepo workspace scope (status bar): a picker that limits sidebar analysis to one package. The limit also applies to the Health, Security, and Audit views. The extension passes the package as --workspace.
1Install the extensionSearch for "fallow" in the VS Code extensions marketplace. You can also install from the command line:code --install-extension fallow-rs.fallow-vscode

2Binary resolutionThe extension finds the binary for you. It checks these places in order:
the fallow.lspPath setting
node_modules/.bin/ for a local devDependency (pnpm add -D fallow)

If it finds no binary, it downloads one from GitHub releases. Before it installs the download, the extension verifies the Ed25519 signature of the binary. When a release has no signature file, it compares the SHA-256 digest from the GitHub release. If the check fails, the extension does not install the binary.

The extension downloads the binary from the GitHub release of its own version. After an extension update, that release can take some minutes to appear. In that time, the extension keeps the verified binary that you already have and tells you once per session. When fallow.autoDownload is on, it retries in the background and offers a restart when the new binary is in place. When no binary is installed, the download prompt names the release that is not published yet.

3Getting Started walkthroughAfter the first install, a walkthrough opens with four steps: Run your first analysis, Explore the results, Fix an issue, and Configure rules. Each step links to its command. To open it again, use the Command Palette.
4Start codingOpen a TypeScript or JavaScript project. The extension starts and runs the analysis. Diagnostics show inline, and Code Lens annotations show above exports.

The status bar shows the current issue count and duplication percentage. When the LSP server completes an analysis, it sends a custom fallow/analysisComplete notification, and the status bar updates. No separate CLI process runs.
Color-coded background: red when there are unresolved imports (errors), yellow when there are other issues (warnings), and the default color when the project is clean
Rich tooltip: hover to see all issues by category, such as unused files, exports, dependencies, circular dependencies, and clone groups
Command links in tooltip: Run Analysis, Auto-Fix, and Show Output
You can turn each of these status-bar items on or off:
Health score segment with the project grade (toggle with fallow.health.statusBar)

Audit verdict for the current change set: pass, warn, or fail, color-coded, with a gating-candidate count (toggle with fallow.audit.statusBar.enabled). The count includes the diff-risk findings, and the tooltip shows a diff-risk row
License indicator showing the active license state (toggle with fallow.license.showStatusBar)
Workspace scope picker that shows the package the analysis is limited to in a monorepo (hidden in single-package projects)
Each diagnostic has a clickable diagnostic code, such as unused-export or unresolved-import. The code opens its documentation page at fallow.tools/docs.
Some diagnostics link to the other files in the issue. To go to a related location, click it in the Problems panel.
Circular dependencies: each file in the cycle is a related location, so you can follow the full cycle
Duplicate exports: links to the other files that export the same name
Code duplication: links to all other instances of the duplicated block
Prop drilling: links to each component that passes the prop and to the component that uses it
Duplicate prop shapes: links to the other components with the same prop shape

Each dead-code diagnostic has a quick fix, Copy Fallow finding id. It copies the stable finding_id of the finding to the clipboard, for example dc1:unused-export:81a349a3b9ea3b15. The id is the same as the finding_id field in fallow dead-code --format json, so you can find the same finding in a CLI or CI report. The id does not change when code above the finding moves.
A security candidate diagnostic has the same quick fix. It copies the security finding_id, which is the same id as in fallow security --format json and the MCP security_candidates tool.

The language server puts the id in the data.findingId key of each dead-code diagnostic, next to changedSince and the circular-dependency cycleId. A security candidate diagnostic has data.findingId next to its security object. Other LSP clients can read the id there.

Security candidate diagnostics are off by default. They are separate from the Security Candidates sidebar view. They show in the editor gutter only when you raise the security-sink or security-client-server-leak rule to warn or error in your fallow config. Each one is an unverified candidate to verify, shown as information and never as a red error. The hover shows the confidence signals first and points to fallow security --file for the full trace. A quick-fix dismisses the candidate.

The component health signals are off by default too. When you set prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, or duplicate-prop-shape to warn or error under rules, each finding shows as a hint on the component and in the sidebar tree. The hints do not add to the issue count. To hide one type in the editor, set it to false in fallow.issueTypes.

An ignoreDependencies glob or an ignoreFindings pattern that matches nothing has no effect. The editor marks the entry in .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, or .fallow.toml. For an extends chain, the diagnostic goes on the file that declares the list. See Unmatched config patterns. The editor marks a redundant config entry in entry, ignoreDependencies or ignorePatterns the same way.
The sidebar groups issues by type and duplicates by clone family. Each category has its own icon:
A badge on the sidebar icon shows the total issue count. Before the first analysis, a welcome view shows a "Run Analysis" button.
Click an item in the tree to open the file at its line and column.

Fallow: Preview Fixes (Dry Run) opens a searchable Quick Pick with each available fix, its type, and its file location. Select an item to go to it in the editor. To apply all fixes at once, choose Apply all fixes at the bottom.
After it applies fixes, the extension saves the changed files, restarts the LSP server, and runs the analysis again. The diagnostics then update.
The extension gives .fallowrc.json files autocomplete and validation from the published JSON schema. You do not need to set this up.
Adopting fallow on a legacy codebase
To hide existing issues and still flag new ones, run Fallow: Set Baseline at HEAD from the Command Palette. The command does three things:
It creates the local lightweight fallow-baseline tag at the current commit.
It writes fallow.changedSince to the workspace settings.
The command asks before it replaces another active baseline setting. It does not work in multi-root workspaces. It never moves an existing tag or pushes to a remote.
To share the baseline with your team, push the tag and commit the change to .vscode/settings.json:

git push origin refs/tags/fallow-baseline
git add .vscode/settings.json
git commit -m "chore: set fallow baseline"
To apply the same rule to pull requests, use the same tag in CI with fallow dead-code --changed-since fallow-baseline.

Shallow clones hide the baseline. actions/checkout@v4 defaults to fetch-depth: 1, and GitLab CI defaults to GIT_DEPTH: 50. If your baseline tag is older than the fetched history, --changed-since and fallow.changedSince fall back to the full scope with no error. The LSP logs a warning to the Fallow output channel. When you use a long-lived baseline tag, set fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout (or GIT_DEPTH: 0 in GitLab CI).
Use fallow from AI agents through the CLI and MCP.
Add fallow to your CI pipeline.
All issue types that the extension shows in real time.

pages.title: Fallow for Neovim: LSP diagnostics
items: Set up fallow in Neovim with the built-in LSP client. See unused code, duplication, circular dependencies, and complexity as you edit, with code actions.

Get fallow findings in Neovim while you edit, with the same results as the CLI and CI. Neovim's built-in LSP client starts fallow-lsp, the language server that the VS Code extension also uses. The editor does no analysis of its own.
The vim.lsp.config and vim.lsp.enable API below requires Neovim 0.11+. On older versions, attach fallow-lsp through nvim-lspconfig or a manual vim.lsp.start.

Real-time diagnostics for these issues:

unused files, exports, types, dependencies, and enum and class members
unresolved imports, unlisted dependencies, and duplicate exports

Opt-in security candidate diagnostics. These are off by default. To turn them on, raise the security-sink or security-client-server-leak rule to warn or error in your fallow config. Each candidate shows as an information squiggle. A candidate is unverified, so check it before you act. The hover shows the confidence signals first and points to fallow security --file for the full trace. A quick-fix dismisses the candidate.
Opt-in component health hints. When you raise prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, or duplicate-prop-shape to warn or error, each finding shows as a hint diagnostic on the component.
Config pattern checks. An ignoreDependencies glob or an ignoreFindings pattern that matches nothing gets an information diagnostic on its entry in the config file.
Hover information with the number of files that import an export, unused status, and duplicate block locations
Quick-fix code actions to remove unused exports or delete unused files

Finding ids. Each dead-code diagnostic has the stable finding_id of the finding in data.findingId. It is the same id as in fallow dead-code --format json, so you can join a diagnostic to a CLI or CI report. A security candidate diagnostic also has data.findingId, with the same id as in fallow security --format json.
Code lens with "imported by N files" above each used export, where Neovim shows code lens
1Install Fallow so fallow-lsp is on your PATHnpm install -g fallowYou can also add it as a project devDependency (npm install -D fallow) and point cmd at node_modules/.bin/fallow-lsp.
3Register and enable the serverAdd the configuration below to your Neovim config, then open a TypeScript or JavaScript project.
init_options is optional. cmd, filetypes, and root_markers are enough to attach the server.

To hide an issue type in the editor, set it to false in the LSP initialization options. Your project config does not change. The keys are fallow issue types in kebab-case, such as unused-exports, unresolved-imports, and circular-dependencies. To get the current list, a client can send the custom fallow/issueTypes request.

To see diagnostics only for files changed since a git ref, pass the ref as changedSince. This works like fallow dead-code --changed-since and the VS Code fallow.changedSince setting. Use it to adopt fallow on a legacy codebase without a flood of old findings:

The first analysis runs when you open the first file. To parse the project earlier, set prewarm. The server then parses the files when it starts, but publishes no diagnostics. The first analysis starts from the parsed files:
prewarm is off by default. It needs a package.json in the workspace root. It also needs a client that registers watched files, because the server keeps its project session only for such a client.

When the client registers watched files, the server keeps one project session between saves. A save then parses only the changed files. A change to package.json, a tsconfig file, or a fallow config file loads the session again. On a large repository the kept session holds more memory between saves: about 100 MB on the Next.js repository. To load a new session on each save, set FALLOW_LSP_REUSE_SESSION=0 for the server:

When diagnostics appear. Fallow uses the LSP 3.17 pull model and refreshes diagnostics on save. The first analysis runs when the server attaches. A buffer you just opened shows findings when that first pass completes, or after the next save. Some findings belong to files you have not opened, such as package.json for unlisted dependencies. Fallow pushes those findings, so you still see them.
Neovim runs cmd exactly as configured. If fallow-lsp is not on Neovim's PATH, point cmd at an absolute path:
Open a TypeScript or JavaScript project.

Confirm fallow is attached:
:lua vim.print(vim.lsp.get_clients({ name = "fallow" }))
Sidebar views, status bar, and fix preview in VS Code.
Use fallow from AI agents through the CLI and MCP.
All issue types the language server reports.

pages.title: Fallow in GitHub Actions and GitLab CI
items: Fallow in GitHub Actions and GitLab CI
Run fallow in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI on every pull request. Get SARIF upload, Code Quality reports, inline review comments, and baselines for changed code.

Run fallow in CI to catch changed-code risk, cleanup opportunities, duplication, and complexity issues on every push and pull request. CI catches the issues that get past agent workflows and editor review. You get the results as PR or MR comments, inline review, annotations, and a merge gate.

To roll out on TypeScript, start with type-aware analysis in best-effort
mode and check _meta.type_aware in the JSON output. Switch to complete
only when partial or unavailable semantic evidence must fail the job.
Type-aware analysis adds a slower semantic pass. See
Type-aware TypeScript analysis.

1Add the actionAdd fallow to your workflow file:name: Fallow analysis
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
 fallow:
 runs-on: ubuntu-26.04
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3
 with:

GitHub Code Scanning is free on public repositories (no GitHub Advanced Security needed). On private or internal repositories, it needs GitHub Advanced Security. On a public repository, the action always tries the upload, and the first upload sets up Code Scanning. On a private or internal repository without Advanced Security, the action warns and skips the SARIF upload. The job summary and the main fallow output are still available.
The upload needs permissions: security-events: write on the job. Without it, the upload step fails. On a public repository the job fails, so add the permission together with sarif: true.

PR summary comments use the native fallow pr-comment-github format. Inline review comments use review-github. When findings go away, fallow ci reconcile-review --provider github marks the old fallow review threads as resolved. A dead-code review thread stays open when you add lines above its finding, because its fingerprint comes from the finding_id.

GitHub inline review comments point to the current state of the PR file (side: RIGHT). Fallow does not yet model findings on deleted lines. In normal use, fallow diagnostics describe the current state of the code.
The action detects your package manager (npm, pnpm, or yarn) from the lock files. Review comments and annotations show the correct install and uninstall commands for your project.

3Code Quality reportsThe template generates a GitLab Code Quality report (CodeClimate format). GitLab shows the fallow findings as inline annotations on the MR diff. Mutation entries are then not in the report. When that older fallow cannot make the report either, for example with --report-path-prefix in FALLOW_ARGS, the job log shows a warning, the report is empty, and the job continues. 7Setup gotchas
The template sets GIT_STRATEGY: "fetch". A shared template that sets GIT_STRATEGY=none then cannot leave fallow without a working tree.
The template sets GIT_DEPTH: "0", so --changed-since can diff against the MR base SHA without shallow-clone problems.
For a private GitLab npm registry, create .npmrc during the job with ${CI_PROJECT_ID} and ${CI_JOB_TOKEN}. Do not commit tokens.
For pnpm projects with minimumReleaseAge, add fallow and @fallow-cli/* to minimumReleaseAgeExclude when you need a just-published fallow release at once.
To run the template with a fallow that you install yourself (for example a pnpm-catalog pin), do these steps:
Override image: with your base image.
Make sure that your install step puts fallow on the PATH of the job shell.

A plain pnpm install or npm install only writes node_modules/.bin/fallow. GitLab does not add that directory to PATH, so add it yourself. A job that uses extends: .fallow and defines its own before_script replaces the before_script of the template, because GitLab does not merge them. Use !reference to keep the install and script-prep block of the template:

fallow:
 extends: .fallow
 before_script:
 - export PATH="$CI_PROJECT_DIR/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"
 - !reference [.fallow, before_script]
 variables:
 FALLOW_SKIP_INSTALL: "true"

The job then skips npm install -g fallow and runs your exact binary, so CI gives the same result as your local lint gate. If you also enable FALLOW_COMMENT or FALLOW_REVIEW and your binary is a dev build whose --version is not an exact release (for example 2.3.0-dev), pin FALLOW_SCRIPTS_REF to a real tag or vendor ci/scripts/, so the template can still fetch the MR-integration scripts.
The GitLab template caches parse results for each branch in .fallow/, so incremental runs are fast.
A full .gitlab-ci.yml setup with summary comments, inline review, and Code Quality:

include:
 - remote: 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/ci/gitlab-ci.yml'

fallow:
 extends: .fallow
 variables:
 FALLOW_COMMENT: "true" # Rich MR summary with collapsible sections
 FALLOW_REVIEW: "true" # Inline discussions with suggestion blocks
 FALLOW_MAX_COMMENTS: "50" # Cap inline review comments (default: 50)
 FALLOW_CODEQUALITY: "true" # Code Quality report for MR annotations
 FALLOW_FAIL_ON_ISSUES: "true" # Fail pipeline on issues
 FALLOW_PRODUCTION: "true" # Exclude test/dev files
 # FALLOW_SCRIPTS_REF: "v1.0.0" # Pin scripts to a specific version
The template also does these things for you:
It detects your package manager (npm, pnpm, or yarn) from the lock files.
In MR pipelines, it limits the analysis to changed files with --changed-since.
It caches parse results for each branch, so incremental runs are fast.
It uploads Code Quality artifacts for inline MR annotations.
To run fallow without the action or the template, call it directly:

- run: npx fallow --ci # All analyses (dead code + dupes + health)
- run: npx fallow dead-code --ci # Dead code only
- run: npx fallow dupes --ci # Duplication only
- run: npx fallow health --ci # Complexity hotspots only
The --ci flag turns on SARIF output, fail-on-issues, and quiet mode together. You can also set them one by one:

The --ci and --fail-on-issues flags work on all commands: dead-code, architecture, dupes, health, and bare fallow. With dupes, and with a bare run that analyzes duplication, they fail the run when at least one clone group remains after the baseline and suppression filters. See fallow dupes exit codes. --sarif-file works only when the dead-code analysis runs. For dupes and health, use --format sarif --output-file <PATH>.
To post the results as a comment, use markdown output:

- run: npx fallow dead-code --format markdown | gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --body-file -
- run: npx fallow dupes --format markdown | gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --body-file -
- run: npx fallow health --format markdown | gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} --body-file -

Consuming review envelopes from your own code

Use this path when your CI runners cannot use remote includes, do not have jq, or cannot give API tokens to third-party binaries. Run fallow to get the typed review-github or review-gitlab envelope. Then POST the comments yourself from the job that already has the token. Fallow does the rendering, the fingerprints, and the DiffNote positions. Your code only loops over the comments and POSTs each one.

gh pr diff $PR_NUMBER | npx fallow audit --diff-stdin --format review-github
glab mr diff $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID | npx fallow audit --diff-stdin --format review-gitlab

Each entry under comments[] is fully rendered Markdown that you can POST as-is. Each body has a <!-- fallow-fingerprint:v3: <fingerprint> --> marker. This marker is the stable identifier that matches comments across runs. The top-level marker_regex is the canonical pattern to extract it. It matches the current v3 marker and the older v2 marker. Match a captured value against comments[].fingerprint and against comments[].legacy_fingerprint. Run it (with one capture group) against an existing PR or MR comment to get the fingerprint string. Fallow puts the multiline m flag in a separate field, marker_regex_flags, and not as (?m) in the pattern, because JavaScript RegExp rejects standalone inline flag groups. Pass both fields to your regex engine:

The top-level summary: { body, fingerprint } block has the sticky-summary comment. summary.body is byte-identical to the legacy top-level body field, which stays for v1 consumers. Match summary.fingerprint against existing comments to update the sticky summary in place, or create it. One fallow run gives both the summary and the inline comments, so you do not need a second fallow --format pr-comment-{github,gitlab} run.

When more than one finding is on the same path:line (for example, three unused-dependency variants on package.json:5), fallow merges them into one comment. The body has one paragraph for each finding, and the comment has fingerprint = "merged:<16-char hash of sorted constituent fingerprints>". This fingerprint changes when the set of findings changes. So the bundled wrappers (and fallow ci reconcile-review), which read only the primary fingerprint, skip the comment when its content is the same and post it again when the set changes. A comment with one finding keeps the bare 16-hex fingerprint shape.
To update comments in place and keep reviewer reply threads when the content changes, track the identity yourself:
Run fallow again against the new HEAD and compare the findings in each comment.
When the findings differ from the existing comment, call the edit endpoint of the provider: PATCH /pulls/comments/{id} on GitHub, or PUT /discussions/.../notes/{note_id} on GitLab.
The bundled fallow scripts do not do this. Only a consumer that needs to keep threads has to handle the extra work: auth scopes, retry semantics, and the 422 error when you edit a resolved thread.

A comment can also have a truncated: bool field. When it is true, fallow cut the body to fit under a conservative 65,536-byte cap. In practice, GitHub PR review comments reject larger bodies. GitLab note bodies accept up to 1,000,000 characters, as the GitLab application limits docs state. A truncated body always has all three of these signals: the typed truncated: true flag, an inline <!-- fallow-truncated --> HTML marker, and a > Body truncated by fallow. blockquote. Fallow keeps the closing fallow-fingerprint marker, so matching across runs still works.

For GitLab, each comment also has a position block with base_sha, start_sha, head_sha, position_type, old_path, new_path, and new_line. These are the fields that the GitLab discussions API expects. For renamed files (when you run fallow with --diff-file or --diff-stdin), old_path is the base-side filename from the rename from and rename to extended headers of the diff. Inline comments on renamed files then attach to the correct line through the GitLab discussion-position API. When the diff has no rename (the usual case), old_path is the head-side path.
Environment variables that feed the envelope
If neither CI_MERGE_REQUEST_DIFF_BASE_SHA nor FALLOW_GITLAB_BASE_SHA is set, the position block has null SHAs. You must then fill them from the diff_refs of the MR before you POST.

fallow audit --diff-stdin --format review-gitlab < diff.patch > plan.json

jq -c '.comments[]' plan.json | while read -r comment; do
 curl --silent --request POST \
 --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
 --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
 --data "$comment" \
 "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/merge_requests/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID/discussions"
done

If your runner also has no jq, parse the JSON in the language of your CI (Node, Python, Go) and POST each entry as-is. The shape under comments[].position matches the GitLab discussions API field for field, so you do not need to map fields.

To prevent duplicate threads on later pushes, fetch the existing MR discussions before you POST, and extract their fingerprints from the marker. The simplest sed extraction matches the marker prefix <!-- fallow-fingerprint:v2: or <!-- fallow-fingerprint:v3: and the fingerprint token. Then compare the results with comments[].fingerprint and comments[].legacy_fingerprint:

existing=$(curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
 "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/merge_requests/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID/discussions?per_page=100")

existing_fps=$(echo "$existing" | jq -r '.[].notes[].body? // empty' \
 | sed -n 's|.*fallow-fingerprint:v[23]: \([^ ]*\) .*|\1|p' \
 | sort -u)

# For each comment in plan.json, only POST when neither its fingerprint
# nor its legacy_fingerprint is already present in $existing_fps.

To resolve threads when a finding goes away between runs, use fallow ci reconcile-review --provider gitlab, if you can give fallow a token. If you cannot, use the same fingerprint comparison in your own script. Both paths use the same marker, so they give the same result. The bundled reconciler accepts v1 (<!-- fallow-fingerprint: <hash> -->), v2 (<!-- fallow-fingerprint:v2: <fingerprint> -->) and v3 (<!-- fallow-fingerprint:v3: <fingerprint> -->) markers. After an upgrade, it processes old comments with no extra steps.

Before the v3 marker, the fingerprint of a dead-code comment held the line of the finding. When you added lines above an unused export, the thread resolved and a new thread opened for the same finding. Now the fingerprint comes from the finding_id, and review comments end with <!-- fallow-fingerprint:v3: <fingerprint> -->. Duplication, health and security fingerprints did not change.

When the old line-based value is different, a comment has it in the optional legacy_fingerprint field. For one release, fallow ci post-review and fallow ci reconcile-review match an open thread with a v2 marker through this value:
They do not post a second thread for the same finding.
They do not resolve the v2 thread as stale.
A v2 thread stays open until its finding goes away or its old line-based value changes. The finding then gets one v3 thread, which stays open across line shifts.

The bundled GitHub Action and GitLab template use these commands, so the first run after the upgrade posts no duplicate threads. A script that posts from the envelope itself must match each captured marker value against fingerprint and legacy_fingerprint.
An older fallow binary does not read the v3 marker. Do not downgrade the binary after a run that wrote v3 markers on an open PR or MR, because the older binary posts duplicate threads.

The reconciler stops at the first failed provider change. When a provider target is gone or a change fails, the JSON output keeps the apply_errors array. It can also add apply_hint, failed_fingerprints, and unapplied_fingerprints. CI wrappers and custom integrations can then show a retry hint and know which old findings are still unresolved.

The envelope has the tag meta.schema, for example "fallow-review-envelope/v3". New fields are backwards-compatible, so ignore fields that you do not know. For a dead-code finding, fallow computes the fingerprint from its finding_id, so it stays the same when lines move. For other findings, fallow computes the fingerprint hash from rule_id + path + snippet. In both cases it stays the same when only whitespace or the body Markdown changes. Code written for v1 still works on v2 output, because the v1 top-level body field stays. Code written for v2 should validate the schema marker against ^fallow-review-envelope/v[0-9]+$, so it keeps working when fallow moves to v3.
The job fails when the overall duplication percentage is more than 5%.
To fail the job on any clone group, use --fail-on-issues:
To check duplication only in files that the PR or MR changes, use --changed-since:

Fallow works in any CI environment that can run Node.js or install fallow. The commands are the same everywhere:

# Run all analyses (no install needed)

The bare fallow run in a machine format (JSON, SARIF, CodeClimate, the GitHub formats, and the comment and review formats) exits 0 on findings, because the GitHub Action and the GitLab template read its output and not its exit code. The human, compact and markdown formats exit 1. fallow dead-code exits 1 on the same findings in every format. A bare machine run prints one [W] Exit code 0: line on stderr, also with --quiet. The line names each failing findings gate and the flag that enforces it. To see a failing gate that did not set the exit code, read gate_outcomes in the JSON output. See exit codes. With --fail-on-issues or --ci, the bare run exits 1 on error-severity findings in every format. When the run analyzes duplication, it also exits 1 when at least one clone group remains. fallow dupes without a gate flag exits 0. With --fail-on-issues or --ci, it exits 1 when at least one clone group remains.
In a PR or MR, the GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template check only the changed files. You do not need to configure this.
fallow mutation shows where your tests miss a small change in the code. The GitHub Action and the GitLab template can run it before the analysis. The step is off by default.

# GitHub Actions
- uses: actions/checkout@v6
- uses: actions/setup-node@v6

- run: npm ci
- uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3

# GitLab CI
fallow:
 extends: .fallow
