Scope and budget. The default scope is the lines that the pull request or merge request adds, with a 10m time budget. A run that the budget stops says "Partial run", and the next run continues from the result cache.

Change scope. A Resolve change scope step (GitLab: a block in the template) writes one diff before the mutation run. The mutation run, the analysis, the comment and the review all use that diff, so they look at the same lines.

Findings. A survived mutant on a changed line is a finding of the rule fallow/mutation-survived in the Tests group. It appears like the other findings: a row in the sticky comment, a workflow annotation, an inline review comment (with review-comments: true) and a GitLab Code Quality entry, 20 at most for each render. The finding names the mutant ID. Run fallow mutation inspect <mutant-id> to see the code.

One comment. The sticky comment, the review summary and the job summary get one "Mutation testing" section: the killed, survived, no-coverage and not-measured counts, the score, the budget state, the lines that no test reaches, and a note for survivors that have no finding (a changed file, or a line outside the diff). The comment shows no source code.

Check run. The Fallow check run gets a Mutation testing row and, with a minimum score, a Mutation score row. To make the score block a merge, require the Fallow / mutation-min-score check of --split-gates.

Clean worktree. fallow mutation refuses a dirty git worktree, and the CI step never passes --allow-dirty. Run code generation and build steps before the Fallow step, and commit or ignore each file that they write. A package manager store inside the project, such as .pnpm-store/, must be in .gitignore.

Exit codes. The analysis and the comment run first. Then a failed mutation-min-score fails the job with exit code 1, and a tool failure of fallow mutation (exit code 2) fails it with exit code 2 and the error message.

Forks and secrets. The step runs the tests of the checked-out code. On GitHub it runs only for the pull_request, push, schedule, workflow_dispatch, and merge_group events. It refuses pull_request_target, issue_comment, workflow_run, and other events that give the job the secrets of the base repository. Never check out the head of a fork pull request in a pull_request_target job. On GitLab, the job refuses a fork merge request pipeline that runs in the target project. The run removes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITLAB_TOKEN, the GitHub OIDC and runtime tokens, and the GITHUB_ENV, GITHUB_OUTPUT, GITHUB_PATH, GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, GITHUB_STATE and BASH_ENV variables from the environment of the tests. Other secrets in the job environment stay visible to your tests.
Cache. The result cache (.fallow/mutation/results.json) goes through actions/cache and the GitLab job cache, with a key on the lockfiles and the runner config. A fork pull request never saves it.

Report file. The step writes fallow-mutation.json and fallow-mutation-status.json. The GitLab job keeps them as artifacts. On GitHub, add an actions/upload-artifact step for the mutation-results output. The Action also has the outputs mutation-outcome, mutation-completion, mutation-score, and mutation-report-rendered. gates-failed (GitLab: FALLOW_GATES_FAILED) names mutation-min-score when the score gate fails.

Older fallow versions. fallow report --mutation-report renders the results. With a fallow version that does not have it, the run, the cache and the score gate still work, and the job summary says which version renders the results.

When more than one fallow review job posts to the same pull request or merge request (for example, one job per workspace in a CI matrix), give each job a stable review id. On GitHub, use the review-id Action input. On GitLab, use the FALLOW_REVIEW_ID variable. The id must be 1-64 characters from A-Za-z0-9._-.

A run only deduplicates and resolves comments with the same review id. A run without an id only sees comments without an id. So when you add an id to a new job, the threads of existing jobs do not change.
Without different ids, parallel jobs share one scope. Each job then deduplicates against the comments of the other jobs and resolves their threads as stale.

Fallow checks that the binary you run is the binary that the fallow release built. The fallow-rs/fallow GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template both install fallow with npm install -g fallow@<spec>. Each @fallow-cli/<platform> npm package has an Ed25519 .sig file next to each binary, and a SHA-256 digest in its package.json#fallowDigests field. Verification has two layers, and it runs in two separate places:

Ed25519 signature (offline, based on the signing key of the release workflow): the public key in the fallow npm wrapper verifies all three binaries (fallow, fallow-lsp, fallow-mcp). A tampered binary fails closed with a specific failure code (sig-invalid, digest-mismatch, binary-missing, sig-missing, or digest-unavailable).

SHA-256 digest (offline, based on the fallowDigests field of the platform package): the verifier checks that the SHA-256 of each binary matches the digest that the release wrote into the package.json of the platform package. A swapped binary with a valid signature would still fail the digest check.
Both layers run in these two places:

First run of fallow, fallow-lsp, or fallow-mcp: on the first run after an install or upgrade, the bin wrapper runs the Ed25519 and SHA-256 checks before it starts the platform binary. A small JSON sentinel file caches the verified state, so later runs skip verification on a cache hit. The sentinel is next to the platform binary, or in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/fallow/sentinels/ when the platform package directory is read-only (for example with yarn PnP or Docker layered images). fallow --version adds a last line verified: yes (<sentinel-path>), so vendor questionnaires and CI logs can confirm the integrity status with one command.

The Action installer runs both layers again (action/scripts/install.sh) after npm install -g --ignore-scripts. It loads the verifier from the checked-out Action tree, not from the installed npm package, so a tampered installer cannot validate itself. This adds defense in depth on CI runners, where the risk of secrets exposure is highest.
A failed verification writes a ::error:: annotation to the Action log and exits with a non-zero code. The workflow stops before any user code reads a swapped binary.

The npm wrapper used to run verification during postinstall. Fallow removed that hook before npm RFC 868 (npm/cli#9360) Phase 2. Phase 2 will block postinstall hooks by default, unless you add fallow to package.json#allowScripts. The first-run check gives exactly the same cryptographic guarantee: the same public key, the same offline fallowDigests lookup, and the same fail-closed behavior.
Three environment variables change how the first-run check works:

FALLOW_SKIP_BINARY_VERIFY=1 skips the Ed25519 and SHA-256 checks. Use it only when you replace the published binary on purpose (source builds, airgapped mirrors, signed-repack registries). fallow --version then shows verified: skipped (FALLOW_SKIP_BINARY_VERIFY is set), so CI logs and vendor audits still show the bypass.

FALLOW_VERIFY_CACHE_DIR=<path> puts the sentinel file in a writable directory when the platform package directory is read-only. The order is: the platform package directory, then this override, then $XDG_CACHE_HOME/fallow/sentinels/ (or %LOCALAPPDATA%\fallow\sentinels\ on Windows).
FALLOW_VERIFY_LOG=1 writes one structured stderr line for each outcome (fallow-verify outcome=ok cache=hit sentinel=...) for CI diagnostic logs.
To skip verification in the Action:

Do not set this in normal CI configurations. The public key fingerprint and the steps for manual out-of-band verification are in SECURITY.md in the main repo. The VS Code extension does its own Ed25519 verification on the binary it downloads. See the extension docs for details.
Analyze only the files that the current pull request or merge request changes:
The action does this with auto-changed-since, which is on by default. To turn it off and run a full analysis on PRs:
To compare against a custom ref in place of the PR base SHA:
The template does this in MR pipelines. To use a custom ref:
Does your codebase already have findings? With a baseline, fallow reports only new issues. See PR enforcement in the adoption guide.

Each gate that the run turned on writes a verdict to the analysis envelope. Both integrations read that verdict, not the CLI exit code. They ignore the exit code when stdout parses as JSON. A gate fails the build only when all three of these are true:
The input or variable for the gate asked for it.
The CLI marked the verdict as enforced.
Each gate has its own input:

These gates do not depend on fail-on-issues or FALLOW_FAIL_ON_ISSUES, which still gates on the issue count. command: audit is the exception: it gates on its verdict through fail-on-issues. So an audit job with fail-on-issues: false only reports.

When a gate concludes fail but its input is not set, it warns and does not fail. So a flag in args cannot override fail-on-issues: false. When a gate did not judge the run, it warns if its input asked for it. Each failing gate prints its own error line. The step exits once at the end, after it writes the outputs and artifacts, so the comment, annotation, and summary steps still run. The security gate keeps its documented exit code 8.

gates-failed, gates-warned, gates-skipped, and gates-passed list the gate names, comma-separated. The list always includes the default rule of the command (error-severity-findings, health-findings or audit-verdict). A run with findings names that rule in gates-failed, also when fail-on-issues: false keeps the job green. A job that analyzes duplication and passes --fail-on-issues or --ci in args or FALLOW_ARGS also lists duplication-findings. fail-on-issues governs this entry in the same way. The count gate already counts clone groups, so the result of the job does not change. To act on one gate, read its name. Do not treat a non-empty gates-failed as a failed job.
analysis-degraded tells you if the findings cover less than the whole project.
requests-unapplied names the requests that the run could not apply, each with its reason in parentheses, for example changed-since (git-failed).
baseline-path is the baseline that the run compared against, as the baseline input wrote it. It is empty for a baseline passed through args.
GitLab writes the same names, and FALLOW_REQUESTS_UNAPPLIED, to fallow-gates.env, and publishes that file through artifacts:reports:dotenv.

The sticky PR comment, the MR note, the inline review bodies, and the Check Run show the same verdict. They show the baseline notice as a blockquote, and one row for each gate that the run turned on. Each row gives the value that the gate measured and the threshold it compared against. A gate that the run did not enforce shows as neutral and does not change the Check Run conclusion. To make each gate a separate required check, post the decision sidecar yourself with fallow ci post-check-run --split-gates. That flag creates one Fallow / <gate> status context for each gate, in place of a single Fallow check. Neither integration passes this flag.

In combined mode, the CLI enforces the duplication threshold only with --fail-on-issues, and says so in the envelope. Without that flag, the integrations warn and do not fail. When --fail-on-issues comes through args or FALLOW_ARGS, the threshold fails the job only when fail-on-issues or FALLOW_FAIL_ON_ISSUES is true. To gate on the threshold alone, run the dupes command.

On a fallow older than 3.27.0, the envelope has no gate verdicts. For the regression, security, baseline, and semantic gates, both integrations then read the fields that those releases already had. threshold, min-score, and min-severity had no field, so these gates fail open with one warning. That warning shows only when the matching input is set.

On a fallow older than 3.28.0, the envelope has no request_outcomes, and baseline_staleness has no scope_reasons or unrecognised_format. requests-unapplied, baseline-scope-reasons, and baseline-unrecognised are then empty, and the warnings that read them do not show. The whole-project baseline re-read then uses the production, workspace, and changed-workspaces inputs.

When the findings of a run cover less than the whole project, the run warns once with Fallow ran with degraded inputs:, followed by the diagnostic kinds and their counts. Both integrations filter on degrades_analysis in workspace_diagnostics, so they also handle a kind that a later release adds. A run that analyzed no source file gets its own sentence. Its clean result means that the run measured nothing, not that it found nothing. By default, such a run warns and passes. To make it fail, set fail-on-empty-analysis or FALLOW_FAIL_ON_EMPTY_ANALYSIS.

When the run cannot apply a request that narrows the report, it warns with Fallow could not apply: and names each request with its reason. The report then covers more of the project than you asked for, so do not read it as limited to the change. The warning filters on affects: "scope", so a request that writes a file next to the report never shows in it. For the request names, statuses, and reasons, see request_outcomes.

When a dead-code or architecture run asks for a rule that the config sets to off, for example with --unused-deps in args or FALLOW_ARGS, the integrations write one warning to the job log. The warning starts with Fallow did not run these requested checks because their rules are off in config: and names each rule with its flag. The job summary and the comment show a Requested checks that did not run section. The result of the job does not change. See Requested rules that are off.

The action gives a separate warning when format: sarif or sarif: true produced no SARIF document. The warning says that the action uploads nothing, and that code scanning keeps the alerts of the previous upload. When the binary gives a reason in request_outcomes["sarif-file"], the warning shows it.

In the opposite case, the run warns with Fallow applied <request> over an empty scope. The run applied the request, and the remaining scope was empty. An empty scope cannot have findings, so a clean report there covered nothing. For example, a --changed-since run where only a README changed gives scope_size: 0. Check the diff or the ref that you gave the run before you trust a clean result. Both integrations check for scope_size: 0 together with status: "applied", and for affects: "scope". So a file written next to the report never triggers this warning. The comment, review, job summary, and annotation bodies also state this, on their request-outcome line.

A run that loads a baseline reports how much of the baseline still matches. When entries are stale, it warns in the log and the job summary. A scoped run cannot judge a whole-project baseline, so for a narrowed run the integrations first read the baseline again over the whole project. baseline_staleness.scope_reasons controls this:
The integrations read the baseline again when they added each narrowing channel themselves: diff, changed-since, changed-files, scope, file, and issue-type-filter.

For workspace and changed-workspaces, they do not judge the baseline and they name the channel, because these inputs define what you consider the project to be. The same rule applies to a scope that comes in through args or FALLOW_ARGS.

For production and include-entry-exports, the binary reports the channel only when the run and a dead-code baseline differ on that mode. The re-read keeps the mode, so a baseline saved with --production is judged in production mode. A baseline in another mode is not judged, and the integrations name the channel.

The action publishes the list as baseline-scope-reasons. To fail the build on a stale baseline, set fail-on-stale-baseline (GitHub) or FALLOW_FAIL_ON_STALE_BASELINE (GitLab). The baseline input and the save-baseline input must not name the same file, because the run saves before it compares. The integrations warn when they see this. The PR comment and the MR note show the gate line from fallow report, which states what each gate concluded.

A baseline that the command cannot read as its own format (baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format) suppresses nothing. It is a baseline that another command saved, or a file with no content for this command. Fallow does not report a baseline that you saved correctly on a project with nothing to record. dead-code, dupes, and health all report an unrecognised baseline, and all keep their exit code. The step log, the job summary, the PR comment, the MR note, and the Check Run show the sentence. The action publishes baseline-unrecognised, and the job summary names the file through baseline-path. When the file names the command that saved it, the action publishes that command as baseline-saved-by (dead-code, dupes, or health), and the step log, the job summary, and the comments name it. The GitLab template names it in the job log and the MR note. Such a file trips the baseline gate, which baseline-gate-trips also reports, so fail-on-stale-baseline fails the job. Each command has its own baseline format. See dead-code, dupes, and health.

command: audit does not judge the baselines it loads, because it analyzes only the files that changed against its base. For each loaded baseline, it prints one notice with the entry count and the unscoped command that can judge it. It rejects --fail-on-stale-baseline in args or FALLOW_ARGS with exit 2. For the baseline inputs of each analysis, see audit.

A run limited to the change says nothing about staleness, because it cannot judge a whole-project baseline. The PR comment, the MR note, and the Check Run come from the envelope of that run, so they show no baseline notice on a pull request. The step log and the job summary show the verdict of the whole-project re-read. The baseline rows below describe a run that could judge the baseline it loaded. The job summary and the Check Run exist on GitHub only. On GitLab, read the job log, the MR note, and the Code Quality report.

When the stale-baseline gate does not judge the run, every place in the table shows this through the gate inventory. Only the sentence that says why, and which channel narrowed the run, stays in the log.

The default combined run gates on the raw issue count: any finding in the changed files fails CI. This gives fast feedback, but it ignores rule severity. A project with unused-exports: warn (or any warn-tier rule) still fails CI when a PR touches a file with old warn-tier findings.
fallow audit gates on severity. It runs dead-code, complexity, and duplication analysis on the changed files and returns a verdict (pass, warn, or fail):
pass: no issues in changed files
warn: only warn-tier issues; CI does not fail
fail: error-tier issues found; CI fails

By default, audit runs in gate: new-only mode, so only findings that the current changeset introduces change the verdict. Old findings show in the PR comment as inherited (with a count), but they do not block the merge.

- uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3
 with:
 command: audit
 gate: new-only # default; fails only on findings introduced by this PR
 fail-on-issues: true
The action has the outputs outputs.verdict (pass, warn, or fail) and outputs.gate, so later steps can act on the verdict:

- uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3
 id: fallow
 with:
 command: audit

- name: Block release on regression
 if: steps.fallow.outputs.verdict == 'fail'
 run: exit 1

fallow:
 extends: .fallow
 variables:
 FALLOW_COMMAND: "audit"
 FALLOW_AUDIT_GATE: "new-only"
 FALLOW_FAIL_ON_ISSUES: "true"
Exits 0 on pass or warn, and 1 on fail.

When the GitHub or GitLab API returns a 5xx, a rate-limit response, or a partial-pagination failure, a CI integration can do less than it should without an error. Structured signals tell you when this happens:

The action sets three outputs on every run, also when nothing failed. Each output has a default value, so a later if: can match on a value (== 'false' or == 'none') and does not have to tell an absent output from false:

- uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3
 id: fallow

- name: Alert on degraded scoping
 if: steps.fallow.outputs.changed-files-unavailable == 'true'
 run: echo "::warning::Fallow ran unscoped; PR scoping disabled by API failure"

- name: Alert on dedup degradation
 if: steps.fallow.outputs.dedup-lookup-failed == 'true'
 run: echo "::warning::Fallow PR comments may be duplicated"

A 4xx response (auth, scope, or permission error) on the multi-comment review path causes exit 1 and fails the action step, because a new run cannot fix a configuration error. 5xx responses, 429s after all retries, and network errors return exit 0 with the warning, so a temporary problem does not break PRs.
comment.sh and review.sh write two sidecar artifacts with the same signals. The template lists both in artifacts: paths:, so later jobs can read them:

alert-degraded-fallow:
 stage: notify
 needs: [fallow]
 script: |
 if [ "$(cat fallow-skip-reason.txt)" = "pagination_failure" ]; then
 echo "WARNING: Fallow inline review skipped to avoid duplicates"
 fi
 if [ "$(cat fallow-dedup-lookup-failed.txt)" = "true" ]; then
 echo "WARNING: Fallow MR comments may be duplicated; re-run the fallow job"
 fi

A 4xx response on the multi-discussion review path returns exit 1, but the bash review.sh || echo "WARNING: ..." line in the template hides it. To fail CI on an auth misconfiguration, remove the || echo from your template, or gate on the sidecar files.

To gate on severity when your project uses the default combined run, add command: audit (FALLOW_COMMAND: audit). The PR comment, annotations, and review comments still work. The audit run adds a verdict banner at the top of the PR comment:
> :x: Audit failed · gate: `new-only` · 2 new findings introduced by this PR · 5 inherited (not gated)

To gate on every finding in changed files, inherited or introduced, use gate: all (FALLOW_AUDIT_GATE: "all"). This is the strict mode. No new finding gets in, but old findings in touched files block the merge until you clean them up.

The issue count of command: audit includes styling findings in both the GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template. Under gate: all, the count includes every entry of complexity.styling_findings. Under gate: new-only, it includes attribution.styling_introduced.

Under gate: new-only, an inherited complexity finding that got worse is worsened. For example, a function grew by 200 lines, or its cognitive complexity went up. The worsened input (FALLOW_AUDIT_WORSENED) selects the effect:
warn (default): the verdict is at least warn, and the job does not fail. A GitHub Check Run then reports neutral instead of success.
error: a worsened finding counts like an introduced finding. The issue count then also includes attribution.complexity_worsened, so a failed audit does not report 0 issues.
off: only growth of an exceeded metric is worsened, and the verdict is at least warn. Growth only in metrics that the finding does not exceed stays inherited.

- uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3
 with:
 command: audit
 worsened: error
The GitHub job summary marks each worsened finding. See Worsened complexity findings for the measured values and the line count minimum.

Audit needs a base ref. The action and the GitLab CI template detect the PR or MR base, so PR and MR pipelines need no extra configuration. On other pipelines (pushes, release branches, scheduled jobs), set changed-since (FALLOW_CHANGED_SINCE). Without it, fallow looks for a base itself: the upstream branch, then origin/HEAD, origin/main or origin/master, then a local main or master. When it finds none, the run stops with exit code 2. When the base it finds is the commit itself, for example on a push to main, audit has no changed files and returns pass without analyzing anything.
CI works best together with the agent and editor integrations:
Agent writes code and runs fallow --changed-since HEAD~1 to check its own work
Human reviews in VS Code and sees Code Lens annotations on new exports
CI runs the full analysis and catches what the first two steps missed

flowchart TB A["Agent
fallow --changed-since HEAD~1"] -->|generates + self-checks| B["Code"] B --> C["Human
VS Code Code Lens"] C -->|reviews| D["Pull Request"] D --> E["CI
Full fallow analysis + SARIF"] E -->|passes| F["main"]
Use fallow from AI agents through the CLI and MCP.
Configure severity levels and issue types.
Exclude test and dev files from analysis.
Add a health score badge to your README.
Render CI output from a saved result.

pages.title: Code health badge for your README
items: Code health badge for your README
Add a code health badge to your README. fallow shows the health score and letter grade of your project in a shields.io-compatible SVG badge.
A health badge shows readers your project's code health score in the README. One command writes the SVG.
The badge shows the letter grade and the numeric score in shields.io flat style:
Grades: A (≥85, green) · B (70–84, green) · C (55–69, yellow) · D (40–54, orange) · F (<40, red).
Your README needs a stable URL for the SVG. The three options below go from simplest to most reliable. Options 2 and 3 render only for public repositories. See Private repositories.
Generate the badge and commit it directly:

fallow health --format badge > .github/badges/health.svg
git add .github/badges/health.svg
git commit -m "chore: update health badge"
Then reference it in your README:
This is the simplest approach. The badge changes only when you regenerate it and commit it.
Add a CI step that generates the badge and publishes it to a badges branch:

- name: Generate health badge
 run: fallow health --format badge > badge.svg

- name: Publish badge
 uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v4
 with:
 github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
 publish_dir: .
 publish_branch: badges
 keep_files: true
 include_files: badge.svg
Then reference the badge from the badges branch:

health-badge:
 stage: deploy
 script:
 - fallow health --format badge > badge.svg
 artifacts:
 paths:
 - badge.svg
Use GitLab's badge API to link the artifact.
For a dynamic badge from shields.io, generate a JSON endpoint file:

fallow health --format json --score --quiet 2>/dev/null \
 | jq '{schemaVersion: 1, label: "fallow", message: "\(.health_score.grade) (\(.health_score.score | floor))", color: (if .health_score.score >= 85 then "brightgreen" elif .health_score.score >= 70 then "green" elif .health_score.score >= 55 then "yellow" elif .health_score.score >= 40 then "orange" else "red" end)}' \
 > health-badge.json
Host the JSON file, for example in a Gist or on the badges branch. Then use the shields.io endpoint badge:
The badge renders from the shields.io CDN and always shows the latest score.

raw.githubusercontent.com (Option 2) and the shields.io endpoint (Option 3) render only for public repositories. Neither host can read a private repo, so the badge shows as a broken image. Do not put a personal access token in the URL. That is insecure and against GitHub's terms.
For a private repo, commit the badge into the repository and reference it with a relative link. GitHub renders relative image links for any viewer with read access to the repo:
To update the badge from CI, regenerate it and commit it to a tracked path on your default branch. Do not publish it to a separate badges branch:

- name: Update health badge
 run: |
 fallow health --format badge > .github/badges/health.svg
 git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
 git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
 git add .github/badges/health.svg
 git diff --quiet --cached || git commit -m "chore: update health badge [skip ci]"
 git push

The job needs permissions: contents: write. A relative link resolves against the branch that the reader views the README on. The badge must be on that branch. A relative link cannot point to a separate orphan badges branch (Option 2), so a private repo commits the badge directly.
For workspace packages, scope the badge with --workspace:
Self-contained SVG with embedded Verdana font metrics. The badge makes no external requests
Each badge has unique element IDs, so you can inline more than one badge on a page
--format badge turns on --score, so you do not need to pass both
If fallow cannot compute the score, it prints an error and exits with code 2
You can also set the format with the FALLOW_FORMAT=badge environment variable
Health score, grades, and the other health report sections.
Run fallow on every push and pull request.
How fallow computes the health score and the grade.

pages.title: Fallow Node.js bindings: programmatic API
items: Call fallow from Node.js code with the NAPI bindings. Get typed results and the same JSON envelopes as the CLI, with no CLI subprocess and no JSON parsing.

With @fallow-cli/fallow-node, you call the main fallow analyses as async Node.js functions. You do not start a CLI subprocess or parse JSON. The functions use the same analysis layer as the CLI and return the same JSON report envelopes as --format json. The optional detectSimilarCode function verifies and starts its local model companion, which must be the exact matching version.
Use the bindings to embed fallow in code that would otherwise call the CLI:
The package is a native NAPI-RS addon. It has platform-specific optionalDependencies for these platforms:
Linux (gnu and musl on arm64 and x64)
The package requires Node 22 or newer.
Each function returns a promise. The promise resolves to the same JSON envelope that the CLI prints with --format json. The envelope has:
a top-level kind discriminator on typed roots
a _meta block with docs links, when explain: true

All nine functions are async and take an optional options object. The functions ignore unknown fields. Enum-like fields take lowercase CLI-style literals, such as "mild", "cyclomatic", "handle", and "low".

The --circular-deps and --boundary-violations flags of fallow dead-code are deprecated aliases. They select only one issue type, so they stay the exact CLI equivalents here. fallow architecture reports all import cycles, boundary violations and policy violations together. detectArchitecture is the binding for that command. detectCircularDependencies and detectBoundaryViolations continue to return the dead-code report (kind: "dead-code").

detectDeadCode, detectCircularDependencies, and detectBoundaryViolations take the same options type, DeadCodeOptions. When you set one or more filter booleans below, the report has only those issue types. When you set none, the report has every category, as the CLI does by default.
detectArchitecture takes ArchitectureOptions. It adds these fields to AnalysisOptions:
When you set no selector, the report has all architecture issue types.
DuplicationOptions adds these fields to AnalysisOptions:

Each returned clone group has spread. Near-miss groups also have similarity. ignoreSymlinks: true omits clone instances whose path is a symlink or lies under a symlinked directory. Otherwise, such an instance has is_symlink: true. Duplication stats can have clone_groups_ignored and near_candidates_skipped. The report leaves out these fields when the value is zero.

SimilarCodeOptions adds these fields for model-based search to
AnalysisOptions:

Before it reads any source, the loader finds the fallow-similar-code package
of the exact matching version and verifies its native binary.
detectSimilarCode never downloads the model. To get the model, run
fallow similar-code setup --local once through the CLI, after explicit user
approval. The results are unverified. Read
Semantic similar code before you use a score to plan
a refactor.
FeatureFlagsOptions adds one field to AnalysisOptions:
ComplexityOptions matches the fallow health flags:
A rejected promise throws a FallowNodeError. This is a plain Error with extra fields, and it has the same structured errors as the CLI:
The exit codes are the same as in the CLI, for example 0 for success, 2 for a generic or validation error, and 7 for a network error (license and cloud operations).
When to use bindings vs the CLI
The bindings and the CLI run the same analysis engine and return the same data.

The bindings cover the one-shot analyses only. They do not include commands that write to the filesystem: fix, init, hooks install, hooks uninstall, --save-baseline, license activate, and coverage setup.
detectSimilarCode is read-only and never does the first model download. For that, run fallow similar-code setup --local through the CLI after explicit approval.
There is no baseline or regression support yet. For those workflows, use the CLI flags --baseline and --save-baseline.
There is no watch mode. For incremental analysis, call the function again. The fallow per-file cache makes repeat runs fast.
The API is new. Until it is stable, a minor version can have breaking changes.
Look up the commands and flags that the bindings mirror.
Read the machine-readable contract of the result envelopes.
Give agents the same analyses as structured tool calls.

pages.title: Static analysis vs runtime coverage for dead code
items: Static analysis vs runtime coverage for dead code
Static analysis vs production data: static analysis shows what is connected, production data shows what ran. Know which findings need production data.
Use this page to decide when static analysis is enough and when you need runtime data. Fallow answers two questions about your codebase:
Static analysis answers "what is connected to what?".
You need both. One layer does not replace the other, and fallow health combines them.

Static analysis builds a module graph from your source. The graph has every file, import, export, and re-export chain, plus each dynamic import() that fallow can resolve. From that graph, fallow finds:
Reachability. Which files are reachable from an entry point, and which are not.
Exports with zero importers. Public API that no file uses.
Import cycles. Short and long cycles, with no depth cap.
Duplicated blocks. Structural clones across modules, also clones with renamed identifiers.
Complexity hotspots. Cyclomatic and cognitive complexity per function, maintainability scores, and correlation with churn.
Architecture boundaries. Layered, hexagonal, feature-sliced, or custom zones. Fallow follows re-export chains across zones.
Feature flag definitions. Where you declare flags, where the code branches on them, and which branches exist.
Static analysis reports these examples with confidence:
An export function computeTax that no file imports, directly or through a barrel.
A file at src/server/jobs/worker.ts that no entry point, script, or test reaches.
A tight cycle: a.ts -> b.ts -> c.ts -> a.ts.
A 60-LOC function with cyclomatic 28 and cognitive 34, in a file that changed 40 times in the last 90 days.
These results are deterministic. You can trace each finding back to a path through the graph.
The graph is a model of the code. It is not a recording of what the program did. Static analysis cannot see:
Dynamic dispatch. Handlers registered by string key, plugins loaded from an array, and methods called through obj[name]().
Conditional imports. if (process.env.FOO) { await import("./bar") } may or may not execute in production.
Feature flag branches. Static analysis sees both branches. It cannot tell you which branch users hit this month, and function-level runtime coverage cannot either.
Traffic-weighted importance. In the graph, a 5-line helper called 200 million times a day looks the same as a 5-line helper called once at startup.
Reachable but unused code. A function that is imported and could run, but had no calls in 30 days.
Static reachability tells you that code could run. It does not tell you that the code did run.
Production data adds evidence. It records which code executed, then merges that evidence into the analyses you already run:
Hot functions. The functions that handle production traffic. A change there needs extra review.
Cold functions. Reachable in the graph, but with no calls in production. These are high-confidence candidates for removal.
Runtime-weighted health. High complexity is a signal. High complexity on a hot path is an alarm.

Runtime coverage collects the production data. You pass it to the CLI with one flag: fallow health --runtime-coverage ./.fallow/runtime.json. To set up collection, see the runtime coverage analysis page.
fallow health merges static findings and runtime evidence into one result. Examples:

A file has cyclomatic complexity 24, a dead code ratio of 0.7, and zero runtime hits over 30 days. Static analysis alone calls it complex and partly unused. Runtime data alone calls it cold. With both, fallow calls it a confident deletion candidate.

In this PR, a function went from cognitive 12 to cognitive 26. It is on a hot path with 40M calls a day. Static analysis alone flags the complexity increase. Runtime data raises the priority of the review.

Runtime evidence refines static findings. It never overrides them. A function with zero runtime hits is only a candidate when static analysis says it is reachable. An unreferenced export is already dead, and runtime data does not change that.
Fallow, the open-source CLI, is free (MIT). You can run every static analysis on any project with npx fallow, with no license.
Fallow Cloud is the paid product: Fallow plus production data. Runtime coverage is the feature that collects the production data. These rules apply:
A single local capture is free and needs no license.
Continuous or multi-capture monitoring needs a license. A 30-day trial is available.
Runtime data from Fallow Cloud needs a FALLOW_API_KEY for an organization on the Pro or Enterprise plan, or in an active trial. It does not use the local license.
To start a trial or activate a license, see fallow license. For pricing and tiers, see fallow.tools/pricing.

Start with static analysis. It is free, and it already finds most of the dead code in a typical codebase. Add runtime data when you want hot-path review, runtime-weighted health, or deletion confidence from production evidence.

pages.title: Fallow vs ESLint, Biome, and oxlint
items: Fallow vs ESLint, Biome, and oxlint
Fallow vs ESLint, Biome, and oxlint: a linter checks one file at a time, and fallow checks the project graph. Find what a linter misses and run both in CI.

Linters check files. TypeScript checks types. Fallow checks the codebase, so it finds project-level issues that a linter misses. Use this page to see which tool finds which issue, and how to run them together in CI.
Each tool answers a different question:
Linter: "Does this file follow the rules?"

Fallow analyzes the module graph of the whole project. The analysis is static by default. Teams that want production evidence for dead code decisions can add Fallow Cloud, the optional paid product that adds production data (see static analysis vs production data).

oxfmt (recommended), or Prettier, Biome, dprint. Makes formatting consistent in all files, for example indentation, quotes, and trailing commas. Works on one file at a time and does not know about imports or project structure.

oxlint (recommended), or ESLint, Biome. Enforces coding rules and finds local code smells, for example undefined variables, missing dependencies in useEffect, and suspicious patterns. Works on one file at a time, with optional type context from tsc.

Fallow. Finds issues that exist only at the project level, for example unused files, orphaned exports, circular dependencies, and dependency graph violations. To find them, fallow builds and walks the full module graph.
Linters read files. Fallow builds the import graph of the whole project and checks the relationships between modules.

[1] Unused exports. eslint-plugin-import/no-unused-modules rebuilds the full import graph on every lint run. On projects with 20-30K LOC, this adds ~320 seconds to total lint time (#1487). The rule gives incorrect results with import { name as alias } (#1339), and it does not follow barrel file re-export chains. Biome and oxlint have no equivalent rule.

ESLint: eslint-plugin-import/no-cycle takes 45-305 seconds on large projects and has known OOM failures (#2348, #2076). Teams often set maxDepth: 1 to keep it fast, and then miss longer cycles. The rule covers only ES import, not require().
Biome v2: noImportCycles is written in Rust and is graph-aware, but Biome documents it as computationally expensive.
oxlint: no-cycle is written in Rust and is faster than the JS version.
Fallow: builds and caches the graph once, has no depth cap, and covers both import and require().

[3] Unused vs unlisted deps. no-extraneous-dependencies (ESLint) and noUndeclaredDependencies (Biome) find imports of packages that are missing from package.json. That is the opposite problem. No linter finds packages that package.json lists but no file imports. Fallow finds both.

ESLint: eslint-plugin-boundaries enforces import rules between element types with capture groups and templates. no-restricted-paths enforces directory-level restrictions, but you must list every forbidden pair. Neither rule follows re-export chains, so an import through a barrel file can bypass a boundary.
Biome: noRestrictedImports accepts plain string paths only. It has no globs or patterns.
Fallow: has zone presets (bulletproof, layered, hexagonal, feature-sliced) and follows re-export chains.
Fallow builds a persistent module graph, resolves re-export chains iteratively, and resolves TypeScript path aliases.

In a library, external code imports your public API exports on purpose. To stop fallow from flagging them, mark them with the /** @public */ JSDoc tag (or @internal, @beta, @alpha), or configure your entry points.

● Unused exports (3)
 src/utils/format.ts (2)
 :14 formatCurrency
 :28 formatDate
 src/components/Card/index.ts
 :1 CardFooter

no-unused-modules finds exports with no importers. It does not find files that no file imports. A file with no exports and no importers does not trigger any ESLint rule. Examples are an orphaned utility, or the leftover test file of a deleted component.

To find unreachable files, a tool must start from the entry points and walk the full import graph. ESLint has no concept of entry points. It lints files, and it does not walk a graph from its roots. Fallow reads entry points from package.json fields and framework conventions (Next.js pages, Vite entry, etc.). Then it marks every file that those roots do not reach.

Some cycles are not bugs. Dependency injection frameworks (NestJS, InversifyJS) create intentional cycles. To suppress one, use // fallow-ignore-next-line circular-dependency, the same way you use an ESLint disable comment. No tool automatically tells an intentional cycle from an accidental one.

Fallow follows re-export chains when it checks boundaries. If shared/index.ts re-exports a symbol from core/, fallow treats a named or default import of that symbol as an import from core/, not shared/. The finding names the barrel in via_path. Zone presets (bulletproof, layered, hexagonal, feature-sliced) cover common architecture patterns. Zones use glob patterns. You write rules as allowlists ("this zone can only import from these zones"), so you do not have to list every forbidden path.
With this config, a ui file can import from shared, and fallow reports an import from ui into api as a boundary violation.

Run the formatter, the linter, and fallow in parallel. The example uses oxfmt and oxlint, which we recommend. They are fast, and they use the same Oxc parser as fallow. Some linter plugins (no-cycle, no-unused-modules) find a subset of the issues that fallow finds. If you already use those plugins, fallow finds the same issues faster. It also finds the issues that linters cannot find: unused files, unused deps, duplication, and churn hotspots. If you do not use those plugins, fallow covers all of these in one pass:

jobs:
 format:
 runs-on: ubuntu-26.04
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - run: npx oxfmt --check .

 lint:
 runs-on: ubuntu-26.04
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - run: npx oxlint .

 analyze:
 runs-on: ubuntu-26.04
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - uses: fallow-rs/fallow@v3

With the sarif: true input and the security-events: write permission, the fallow GitHub Action uploads SARIF results to GitHub Code Scanning, so you get inline annotations on PR diffs. Linter results usually show up as separate status checks or linter-review actions. For GitLab CI and other runners, see CI integration.

If your codebase already has unused exports and files, use --save-baseline to save the current issues. Then run CI with --baseline so that it fails only on new issues. For incremental adoption, see the CI integration guide.
Add fallow to your project in under a minute.

pages.title: Dead code findings explained: what to fix first
items: Dead code findings explained: what to fix first
Dead code findings in fallow explained: what each issue type means, which to fix first, and which are safe to keep, including class members and cycles.

Use this page to decide which fallow dead-code findings to fix, in which order, and which ones you can keep. For each issue type, it explains what fallow reports, when to act, and the common false positives.

Each dead-code issue type has a default severity. An error finding makes the run exit with code 1. A warn finding shows in the output, but does not fail the run unless you pass --fail-on-issues or --ci. An off rule does not run, also when you pass its issue-type flag. Fallow then prints a note, and a zero count for the rule measures nothing. See Requested rules that are off. To change a severity, use rules.
Files that no entry point reaches. No module in the project imports them, and no framework plugin or entry point pattern matches them.
When to act: Almost always. Unused files make IDE indexing slower and add noise to search results.

Scripts run directly (e.g., node scripts/seed.ts): Call the script from a package.json script field (fallow parses those). If the script ships and runs in production, add it to entry. If it is a tool that does not ship, use a framework[] entry instead. See Dev dependencies in production.
Files loaded by tools that fallow does not know about: Add them to entry or to the relevant plugin config.
Exported symbols that no other module imports.

A TypeScript namespace without the export keyword is a local binding. This applies to namespace Foo { export const inner = 1 }, to declare namespace, and to the legacy module Foo {} form. The inner export declarations are members of that namespace, not exports of the file. Fallow never reports them here or under unused types. Only export namespace Foo { ... } adds a file-level export (Foo itself).

An exported namespace that holds only types emits no JavaScript, so Fallow treats it as a type export. This covers a body with only interfaces, type aliases, declare declarations, import type aliases and nested namespaces of the same kind, for example export namespace JSX { export interface Element {} }. When it is unused, it reports under unused types, and it is never an untested export in coverage gaps. A namespace with any other statement, or a namespace that merges with a function, class, enum or variable of the same name, stays a value export.
When to act: Remove most unused exports, or remove their export keyword. Unused exports make the public API larger and make it unclear what the module is for.

Library public API: External users import these exports, and fallow cannot see those users. Mark the exports with the /** @public */ JSDoc tag (or @internal, @beta, @alpha), add the library entry point to entry, or use ignoreExports for broad patterns.

Convention-based exports: Frameworks use these exports through naming conventions (e.g., Next.js getStaticProps). The fallow framework plugins handle most of them. If a plugin misses one, configure the plugin or add an ignore pattern.
Effect schemas as contracts: An exported Effect schema is also a type. To report unused schemas as unused types, set effect.schemaExportsAsTypes to true.
Type aliases and interfaces that no module references.
With effect.schemaExportsAsTypes, this issue type also includes unused Effect schema exports, such as export const User = Schema.Struct({...}).
When to act: Remove unused types. They add noise to auto-import suggestions and make the public type API larger.
Shared type packages: Types that you export for external users. Add the package entry point to entry.

Exported values, functions, classes, and types whose public TypeScript signature references a type that is declared in the same file but is NOT exported. Users can see the name of the private type in generated declarations or API docs, but they cannot import it. They must then type it again, or use workarounds such as Parameters<typeof X>[0] or ReturnType<typeof X>.

This is an opt-in API hygiene check. It is not a default dead-code finding. It is most useful for packages that publish TypeScript declarations or have a public API. For exports inside an app, private Props, Options, and State helper types are often intentional. Do not export them only to satisfy this rule.

type Props = { label: string; }; // private to the module

export function Component(p: Props): void {} // public, but Props leaks

When to act: Enable this check for packages that you publish or modules that emit declarations. To fix a finding, export the backing type together with the exported symbol. You can also change the public signature so that it does not reference the private type:

export type Props = { label: string; };
export function Component(p: Props): void {}

Interaction with unused types: when you export the backing type to fix a leak, fallow does not report the new export as unused-types, even if no other module imports it. If a public signature in the same file references a type by name, fallow treats that type as part of the public API. The unused-types check skips it.

ECMAScript #field private members and TypeScript private accessibility: these are not part of the public signature, so the types they reference do not leak. class Service { #state: InternalState; } does not flag InternalState.

Storybook story files: fallow skips *.stories.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,mts,cts,mjs,cjs} and the *.story.* variants. Without this, the canonical type Story = StoryObj<typeof X>; export const Default: Story = ... pattern gives one finding per story.

Framework routing conventions: route files where the framework forces several exports per file to share a private Props, Params, or LoaderArgs type. Fallow skips these files:

Next.js App Router: app/**/{page,layout,template,loading,error,not-found,route,default,global-error,forbidden,unauthorized}.{ts,tsx,js,jsx} plus the metadata files (opengraph-image, twitter-image, icon, apple-icon, manifest, sitemap, robots).
Next.js Pages Router: any file under pages/.

Remix v2 + TanStack Router: top-level files in app/routes/ and folder-route entries (route.tsx, _layout.tsx, _index.tsx, index.tsx, __root.tsx). Fallow still checks subdirectories under app/routes/<segment>/, because users put non-route helpers there.
The patterns match anywhere in the path, so fallow also skips monorepo subpackages (packages/web/src/app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx).
Enable: run fallow dead-code --private-type-leaks, or set private-type-leaks: "warn" / "error" in rules.
Suppression: add // fallow-ignore-next-line private-type-leak above the affected export, or keep private-type-leaks: "off" in rules.
Prior art: the Rust unreachable_pub lint, and the TypeScript TS4023 and TS4060 errors that --declaration emits. ESLint has no equivalent rule today.

An export whose leading JSDoc has a @deprecated tag, and that at least one reachable file still uses. The finding tells you who still uses a deprecated API, and which deprecated exports you can remove now.
This is an opt-in check. A deprecation window is a normal state, so the rule is off by default.

/** @deprecated Use `formatDate` instead. */
export function oldFormat(d: Date): string { /* ... */ }
consumer_count: the exact number of consumers.
consumers: a sample of up to 10 consumers, each with path, line, column, and reference kind. The sample is sorted by path and line.
deprecated_reason: the deprecation message as plain text, up to 200 characters. A bare @deprecated tag gives no deprecated_reason key.
public_api: true when the export is in an entry point, or when a re-export chain carries it to an entry point. Fallow cannot see external consumers, so it makes no removal claim for such an export.
For the full consumer list, run fallow dead-code --trace <file>:<export>. The next_steps array names this command for the deprecated export with the most consumers (id trace-deprecated-export).
A consumer in an unreachable file does not count. That file is dead code itself and has its own unused-file finding.
A deprecated export with no consumer stays an unused export. That finding then has deprecated: true and the deprecated_reason. The human and markdown output add (marked @deprecated).
A per-path override applies to the file that declares the export, not to the consumer. You cannot keep a deprecated API legal only for the consumers in legacy/**.
Under fallow audit with gate: new-only, the finding is new only when the file that declares the export changed. A change that only adds a consumer does not make the finding new.

When to act: Move each consumer to the replacement API. When the last consumer is gone, fallow reports the export as an unused export, and you can remove it. For a public_api export, keep your deprecation policy for external users.

Enable: run fallow dead-code --deprecated-exports-in-use to report only this issue type, or set deprecated-exports-in-use: "warn" / "error" in rules. The MCP analyze tool accepts issue_types: ["deprecated-exports-in-use"]. An overrides entry alone cannot turn the rule on: the base rule must not be off.
Suppression: add // fallow-ignore-next-line deprecated-export-in-use above the export.
There is no editor diagnostic for this finding, because TypeScript already strikes deprecated names through in the editor.
Packages in dependencies that no source file imports and that no package.json script uses as a binary.

When to act: If nothing imports the package, remove it from package.json. If the finding says that another workspace imports the package, move the dependency to that workspace. Unused dependencies slow down npm install, make node_modules larger, and increase the attack surface for supply chain vulnerabilities.

Internal workspace packages count too: in monorepos, fallow checks a workspace package name (e.g., @repo/ui) in the dependencies of another workspace the same way as an external npm package. If a workspace declares @repo/ui but never imports it, fallow reports the dependency as unused. A workspace package does not need to list its own name.

Uninstalled peer dependencies of other packages: Fallow counts a required peer as used when the package that requires it is installed under node_modules. The package that requires it must be in use: a file imports it, a package.json script runs it, or a plugin config names it. For example, a napi build script credits the peers of @napi-rs/cli. If only an environment outside the analyzed install tree requires the peer, check whether removing it breaks that runtime.
Runtime-only packages (polyfills, CSS frameworks loaded through @import): Add them to ignoreDependencies in config.
Same as unused dependencies, but for packages in devDependencies.
Same as unused dependencies, but for packages in optionalDependencies. Fallow reports these by default, and the --unused-deps filter includes them.
Enum values that no code references.
When to act: Remove the unused member. Unused enum members add to serialized values and make it unclear which values are valid.
Class methods and properties that no code outside the class body references.

What it detects: Public methods and properties that no module other than the class itself accesses. Fallow tracks internal this.member accesses in the class body separately. They do not count as external usage.

Inheritance awareness: Fallow builds an inheritance map from extends clauses and passes member accesses through the hierarchy. If a parent class method calls this.getArea(), the child class overrides (Circle.getArea(), Rectangle.getArea()) count as used. External member accesses on a parent type also count for the child implementations. This prevents false positives when a base class defines a contract that subclasses implement.

Decorator exclusion: Fallow automatically skips members with decorators (e.g., @Get(), @Column(), @Input(), @Inject()). A decorator means runtime wiring that static analysis cannot trace, so fallow never flags decorated members.

The one exception is a Lit @state() reactive property on a direct LitElement or ReactiveElement subclass, when lit is a declared dependency. @state is internal component state that no outside code can use. If no method or html template reads a @state field through this.<name>, fallow flags it as an unused class member. The public @property() decorator stays excluded. It is the attribute API of the element, and HTML, a parent binding, setAttribute, or CSS can set it.

Lifecycle method allowlists: Fallow never flags framework lifecycle methods. It has built-in allowlists for React (componentDidMount, render, shouldComponentUpdate, etc.) and Angular (ngOnInit, ngOnDestroy, canActivate, validate, etc.). For other frameworks (Web Components, ag-Grid, etc.), use the usedClassMembers config option to extend the allowlist.

Whole-object use heuristics: Some patterns mark all members as used, to be safe: Object.values(instance), Object.keys(instance), rest destructuring (const { foo, ...rest } = instance), and for (const key in obj).
When to act: Remove the member or mark it as private. An unreferenced public method is either dead functionality or wired at runtime. Investigate both cases.

Configuration: The usedClassMembers config option marks specific member names as always used. Use it for convention-based methods that DI frameworks or third-party libraries call reflectively (e.g., agInit, connectedCallback). Custom plugin definitions can also add names to this allowlist through their usedClassMembers field.
An exported member of an exported TypeScript namespace that no code reads.

What it detects: A member of export namespace N { ... } or of export declare namespace N { ... } in a .ts file that no code reads as N.member. A nested namespace member has a dotted name, for example Outer.Inner.x. When a nested namespace is unused, fallow reports the namespace and not each member in it. A namespace that merges with a class, a function, or an enum of the same name is checked too.

Usage it counts: A qualified read as a value or as a type (N.a, N.Inner.T, typeof N.a), destructuring (const { a } = N), an alias (import x = N.a), a read through a namespace import (ns.N.a), and a reference inside the namespace body (export const b = a). A re-export of N carries the reads of its consumers.

Abstain heuristics (false-positive safe): When the namespace object leaves its chain, every member counts as used: an argument (register(N)), an alias (const M = N), a spread, Object.keys(N), or keyof typeof N. The same rule applies to a nested namespace (register(N.Inner)). Fallow does not check declaration files (.d.ts), declare global, module augmentations (declare module "x"), namespaces without export, or a namespace that an entry point exports.

When to act: Remove the member. When only the namespace body uses the member, remove its export keyword. There is no auto-fix, because a member can be a function, a class, or a nested namespace over many lines. For generated code, turn the rule off for those files in overrides:
Suppress one member with // fallow-ignore-next-line unused-namespace-member.
A Pinia store member that no code in the project accesses. A store member is a state, getters, or actions key, or a key that a setup store returns.

What it detects: Code imports the store binding (so the module is reachable), but never reads a specific state property, getter, or action. Single-file linters (eslint-plugin-vue, eslint-plugin-svelte, eslint-plugin-pinia) and type-checkers (vue-tsc, svelte-check) cannot find members that no file uses, because that needs the project graph. The rule defaults to warn, not error like the class and enum member rules. Plugins and dynamic dispatch can add to a store, so the confidence is lower.
Activation: The rule runs only when pinia or @pinia/nuxt is a declared dependency. It never fires on an unrelated helper named defineStore in a non-Pinia project.

Usage it counts: const s = useStore(); s.member, destructures (const { count } = useStore(), const { count } = storeToRefs(store)), template store.member in .vue and .svelte files, this.member usage between getters and actions in the same store, a read through a parameter typed ReturnType<typeof useStore> (or a type alias of that form in the same file), and a read inside the setup function of a setup store, for example count.value in a computed. Pinia needs returned setup state for registration and hydration, so a returned ref that only the setup body reads is live. A plain write such as token.value = x is not a read.

Abstain heuristics (false-positive safe): Whole-object usage ({ ...store }, Object.keys(store), dynamic store[key]) marks the whole store as used, so fallow flags no member. The Options-API mapState, mapGetters, and mapActions helpers do the same. Fallow never reports the Pinia $-prefixed API ($patch, $reset, $subscribe, etc.). It skips a setup store completely when the returned object uses a spread (return { ...base, x }).

When to act: Remove the unused state property, getter, or action. There is no auto-fix, because a Pinia plugin or dynamic dispatch can access a store member reflectively. If code uses a member in a way that fallow cannot see, suppress it with // fallow-ignore-next-line unused-store-member.

Scope: Pinia only. The rule does not cover Svelte stores and Vuex yet. A Svelte writable is opaque and its value shape changes at runtime, so member-level detection would give false positives. The unused-export check already finds a store export that no code uses.
Import specifiers that fallow cannot resolve to a file on disk or a node_modules package.
When to act: Always investigate. An unresolved import usually means that the code will fail at runtime. Common causes:
Missing dependency (not installed or not in package.json)
Path alias not configured in tsconfig.json paths

A re-export through an unresolved import, such as export { iconsList } from '@scope/icons/index', still gives this finding. But the files that import iconsList credit the re-exported name, the same as a re-export from an npm package. So the name does not also report as an unused export. This happens for example with a workspace package whose main and types point to a dist directory that is not in the checkout. A re-exported name that no file imports still reports as an unused export.
Packages that source code imports but package.json does not declare.

When to act: Add the package to dependencies or devDependencies in the importing package. An undeclared import can resolve through hoisting or workspace links, but fail when the install excludes that package.

Fallow uses the nearest valid package.json inside the project, including a standalone nested package omitted from explicit workspace patterns. Its declarations count for files below that package. This does not change workspace membership.

Internal workspace packages count too: in monorepos, a workspace can import a workspace package (e.g., import { x } from '@repo/utils') while its own package.json does not list @repo/utils. Runtime source in a publishable package must declare that dependency itself. Private workspace packages and tooling files may use declarations from ancestor manifests. Self-references stay allowed, and a package does not need to depend on itself.

The result is the same for a direct import such as @repo/utils/format and for a package.json imports alias such as "#utils/*": "@repo/utils/*". It is also the same before and after an install that links the workspace packages into node_modules. One exception: when a tsconfig paths alias maps the workspace package to its source and no install link exists, fallow does not report the import.

The root package follows the same rule. A file that belongs to the root package, such as e2e/run.ts, needs the workspace packages that it imports listed in the root package.json. An npm workspace link makes the package resolvable without satisfying this declaration check. See workspace dependency declarations for a root manifest example.
Packages that a tool config needs: some configs name a package that a tool loads without an import. Fallow reports these packages too, and the finding points at the config value:
a tsconfig compilerOptions.plugins[].name, because TypeScript loads each language service plugin by name;
expo-system-ui, when an Expo app config sets userInterfaceStyle at the top level or under android. The Android build needs this package for the key.

The manifest that owns the config, each ancestor manifest, and the root manifest can list the package. A sibling manifest does not count. Fallow does not report a path, a Node.js builtin, a config in ignorePatterns, or a plugin that editor extensions ship, such as typescript-svelte-plugin. A --production run skips tsconfig plugins, because only the editor loads them.
If your project deliberately permits undeclared workspace imports, add those package names to ignoreDependencies. This suppresses dependency findings for the named packages.
Binaries that a package.json script or a process call in source runs, but that no installed or listed package provides.
When to act: Add the package that provides the binary to devDependencies. When the operating system or the CI image provides the binary, add its name to ignoreBinaries.
The scripts of the root package.json and of each workspace package. Fallow reads the command after environment, package-manager and wrapper prefixes, for each command of the script.

Process calls in source that run a literal command: spawn, spawnSync, exec, execSync, execFile and execFileSync of node:child_process, execa, execaSync, execaCommand, execaCommandSync and the $ template of execa, the $ template of zx, and Bun.spawn, Bun.spawnSync and Bun.$. A command that the code builds at runtime is not read.
A binary is provided when one of these is true:
A node_modules/.bin link with its name exists in the package directory or in a directory above it, up to the project root.
A declared dependency or a workspace package declares the name in its bin field.
The name maps to a declared dependency, for example tsc to typescript.
Fallow does not report these commands:
Shell builtins and core shell tools, such as echo, cp and grep.
Shell reserved words, such as for, do, then, fi and done. Fallow reads the commands inside a loop, a condition, a subshell ( ... ), a case branch and a function body.
Commands that npx, pnpx, bunx or pnpm dlx download.
Common operating-system tools, such as git, gh, ssh-keygen, curl, docker, ffmpeg, pgrep and xcrun, and the JavaScript runtimes and package managers.
The check needs installed dependencies. A project without a root node_modules reports no unlisted binaries, because fallow cannot tell a missing binary from one that an install links.

One finding covers one binary for the whole project. Each use site is in used_in. A script site points at the script line in package.json and carries script_name. A package.json file cannot hold a comment, so use ignoreBinaries instead of an inline suppression.
The same symbol name exported from more than one module. Auto-imports become ambiguous, and it is unclear which module is the canonical source.
When to act: Keep one canonical export. If more than one module must expose the symbol, re-export it from that one location.

Wrappers are duplicates: a module that imports the symbol under another local name and exports its own version of it is a wrapper. For example, import { configureAuth as core } from "../ci/auth" followed by export function configureAuth(). Importers see two configureAuth exports with different behavior, so fallow reports the pair. To keep a wrapper on purpose, add // fallow-ignore-next-line duplicate-export above its export, or add the name to ignoreExports.

Overlays are not duplicates: a module that also declares export * from the same source module is an overlay. It re-exports the full surface of the source module and replaces one binding. For example, export * from "../native.js" together with import { Engine as NativeEngine } from "../native.js" and export class Engine extends NativeEngine {}. Fallow does not report the overlay. A namespace re-export (export * as ns from) does not make a module an overlay. When a third module exports the same name independently, the finding stays between the source module and that module.

One module exports one binding under two or more names. For example, export const layer = createLayer() together with export default layer, or export { a, a as b }. Importers can import one value under several names, so the export surface of the module is larger than it needs to be.
Fallow groups the exports of each file by the binding that they export:
A local export groups by the local name. export { value as default } and export const value are one binding.
A named re-export groups by the source and the imported name. export { q, q as q2 } from "./source" is one binding.
Value exports and type-only exports are separate groups, because a value and a type can share one name.
Fallow does not report these cases:
Two bindings with the same value, such as export const one = shared and export const two = shared.
Function overloads, because they export one name.
export *, because it does not export one named binding.
A file with CommonJS exports (export = or module.exports).
This rule is different from duplicate exports, which reports one export name in several files.

When to act: Keep one export name and update the importers of the other names. There is no auto-fix, because code outside the project can import any of the names. When the names are an intentional public API, add them to ignoreExports. A * entry exempts the whole file, and a listed name exempts the binding that has that name. You can also add // fallow-ignore-next-line duplicate-export-alias above one of the names, or set the rule to off.
Modules that import each other, directly or transitively, and so form a cycle.

Circular dependencies, re-export cycles, package cycles, boundary violations, and policy violations are architecture findings. fallow architecture reports them. fallow dead-code also reports them until the next major version. To report only the cycles, run fallow architecture --cycles.

Detection during graph construction: Fallow finds circular dependencies while it builds the module graph, with Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm (O(V + E)). There is no separate analysis pass, so cycle detection adds almost no cost.
No depth limits: Fallow detects cycles of any length. The graph algorithm processes all strongly connected components of any size. Then it lists the individual elementary cycles in each component.

Type-only cycle filtering: Fallow automatically removes cycles where every edge is an import type import. The compiler erases type imports, so they cannot cause runtime initialization issues. Fallow tells these apart from runtime cycles with the is_type_only flag on each import symbol in the graph.

Lazy imports: By default, every runtime import edge takes part in cycle detection, also a dynamic import(). A top-level await import() loads eagerly, because the module waits for the target before it continues. To skip edges that load on demand or on another thread, set circularDependencies.ignoreLazyImports to true.
Cycle path reporting: Fallow reports the full path of each cycle, so you can see which files are part of it:
With the full path, you can find the weakest edge to break.
The module evaluation order becomes unpredictable. JavaScript evaluates modules depth-first, and a cycle forces at least one module to get an incomplete namespace object.
An export that you access before its module finishes evaluating returns undefined. This causes runtime errors that are hard to trace.
When bundlers cannot find a clean evaluation order, they can produce incorrect output or larger bundles.
Refactoring becomes dangerous. When you move code between modules in the cycle, you can break the initialization order, and you see the error only at runtime.
Type-only cycles: If the cycle uses only import type, there is no runtime initialization risk. Fallow automatically removes these from circular dependency reports.

Two or more barrel files that re-export from each other in a loop, or one barrel file that re-exports from itself. This is different from a circular dependency. A circular dependency is a runtime import loop. A re-export cycle is a declarative loop in the export * from graph, with no final module that declares the names.

Why this is its own category: Circular dependencies in the runtime import graph are sometimes intentional (mutual recursion between application modules). Re-export cycles are almost always bugs. Take src/api/index.ts with export * from './internal', and src/api/internal/index.ts with export * from '../index'. Neither file declares anything, so the chain has no source. An import { foo } from './api' cannot resolve foo, and the import silently gives undefined at runtime.
multi-node: a strongly connected component of two or more files in the re-export graph. Example: barrel-a.ts re-exports from barrel-b.ts, and barrel-b.ts re-exports back from barrel-a.ts.

self-loop: one file that re-exports from itself. This is almost always a leftover from a rename, where barrel.ts now has export * from './' or export * from './barrel'. It shows up under the same rule, with a different kind value so that tools can tell the two shapes apart.

Type-only cycles still fire: export type * from './b' together with export type * from './a' is also a re-export cycle. A type-only loop resolves no names, the same as a value loop, so fallow reports it too.

── Structure ─────────────────────────────────────

● Re-Export Cycles (2)
 src/api/index.ts
 Cycle (2 files):
 - src/api/index.ts
 - src/api/internal/index.ts
 To fix: remove one `export * from` statement on any member file.

 src/utils/index.ts
 Self-loop (1 file):
 - src/utils/index.ts
 To fix: remove the `export * from './'` (or equivalent) inside this file.
Pick any one file in the loop.
Remove the export * from (or export { ... } from) statement that points back into the cycle.
One removal breaks the cycle and makes the re-exports work again. You do not need to change every file in the loop.
For a self-loop, the fix is clear. Open the file and delete the stray export * from './' (or export * from './<this-file>' after a rename).
Suppression: the finding is file-scoped, because the cycle spans more than one file and has no single line. Suppress it with a file-level comment in any file of the loop:

Fallow accepts four spellings: re-export-cycle, re-export-cycles, reexport-cycle, and reexport-cycles. A per-file overrides.rules.re-export-cycle has no effect, because the severity of the rule is project-wide and the finding spans more than one file. Fallow reports the override as an override-rule-ineffective diagnostic. Configure the rule in the top-level rules block instead, or use the file-level fallow-ignore-file suppression above.

When to keep it as a warning: legacy projects with hand-written barrels from before ESM strictness can have harmless cycles that no code relies on. At warn, the diagnostic stays visible and CI does not break. Change the rule to error after you remove the cycles. After an upgrade, expect total_issues to go up on the first run. Cycles that existed before this rule shipped now show up as findings.

Workspace packages that import each other in a loop. Package a imports package b, and package b imports package a, directly or through other packages. A package cycle can exist when no file-level cycle exists: a/src/x.ts imports b/src/y.ts, and b/src/z.ts imports a/src/w.ts. The files do not form a loop, but the packages do.

Why it matters: packages in a cycle cannot be built, versioned, or published in dependency order. A build tool that builds dependencies first (for example with TypeScript project references or a task runner) has no valid order. One package must then use the build output of the other package from an earlier run.
How fallow builds the package graph:
Each workspace package is a node. A file belongs to the workspace package with the longest root that contains the file.
Each resolved import from a file in one package to a file in another package is an edge. A relative import that goes into another package counts the same as an import by package name.
Declared dependencies in package.json are not edges. Only imports in the code count.

Imports from test, spec, story, and fixture files and from tooling config files (for example vitest.config.ts) are not edges. A package often imports a sibling package only in its tests, and that import does not change the build order. Fallow matches these files by their path relative to the package root.
The check needs two or more workspace packages. A project without workspaces has no package cycles.

Type-only hops: a type-only import (import type) is an edge too. A type-only import has no runtime effect, but a declaration build can still need the other package first. Each hop in the finding has a type_only flag. The flag is true when every import on that hop is type-only. This is different from circular dependencies, which ignore type-only imports.

What the finding shows: the packages in cycle order, starting at the package with the lowest name, and one example import for each hop. The example import is the first runtime import of the hop by path and line. When the hop has only type-only imports, it is the first type-only import.

● Package cycles (1)
 @acme/core → @acme/utils → @acme/core
 packages/core/src/format.ts:3 → packages/utils/src/index.ts
 packages/utils/src/log.ts:1 → packages/core/src/index.ts (type-only)
In --format json, each finding in package_cycles has these fields:

Packages with the same name: a label is the package name. When two or more workspace packages have the same name, for example several examples/* packages named example, the label also shows the package root: example (examples/basic). The label is then unique in all output formats, in baseline keys, and in audit keys.

Limits: fallow lists the shortest cycles first, and at most 20 cycles for one group of packages that are connected in a loop. On a very dense package graph, fallow can also stop the search earlier. Fallow then sets group_truncated on each cycle of that group, and every output format shows the note "this package group has more cycles than listed". Break a listed cycle and run fallow again to see the other cycles.

Suppression: a suppression removes one import or re-export statement from the package graph. It does not hide the finding directly.
