A finding for each part alone would show less than the total complexity that a developer or agent must maintain. Two synthetic findings show the total:

Both findings use the same rule ids as function findings: fallow/high-cyclomatic-complexity, fallow/high-cognitive-complexity, and fallow/high-complexity. They use the same thresholds (max_cyclomatic, max_cognitive) and the same severity bands. Fallow reports each template above the configured threshold on its own. If a <template> and at least one class method in the same component file are both above the thresholds, fallow also adds a <component> rollup.
You act on these findings differently from function findings:
<template> findings: split the template into child components, move derived data into the class as computed signals (computed(...)), or replace nested control flow with a flatter structure.

<component> rollup findings: the class and the template together are above the budget. Fix the larger part first. The component_rollup.class_* and component_rollup.template_* fields show which part adds more.

A <template> finding gets its CRAP score from the component class that owns it. Because of the templateUrl edge, a template is reachable if and only if its class is reachable. Tests that run the class also run the template. The inherited_from field in the payload of a <template> finding names the .component.ts file whose coverage gave the score. So the increase-coverage action points at the class, which you can test, and not at the .html file, which you cannot test directly.
health.maxFileLines (or fallow health --max-file-lines <N>) sets a maximum file length. The default is 0, so the check is off. Set a limit, for example 500, to enable it.

Fallow counts physical lines, as an editor shows them. Blank lines and comment lines count. A final newline does not add a line. Fallow does not count only code lines, because blank and comment lines also make a file longer to read and to review.
A file with more lines than the limit is a complexity finding:

cyclomatic and cognitive are 0 on this finding. SARIF and CodeClimate use the rule id fallow/long-file. The JSON actions are split-file and suppress-file. The complexity-file-lines rule decides if the finding fails the run. It defaults to error.

To set a different limit for some files, add a health.thresholdOverrides[] entry with files and maxFileLines. Leave functions empty, because the limit applies to whole files. maxFileLines: 0 turns the check off for the matching files. To hide one file, put // fallow-ignore-file complexity at the top of the file. This comment also hides the function complexity findings of the file.

In fallow audit, the file finding follows the same rules as a function finding. A file that is new, or that crosses the limit in the change, is introduced. A long file that grew by 5 lines or more is worsened. A long file that did not grow by 5 lines stays inherited, so you can enable the limit on an existing project and stop further growth without a new failure.
Per-file scores from fallow health --file-scores. Fallow excludes files with zero functions (barrel files, re-export files).
Fallow uses a simplified Maintainability Index, adapted for JavaScript/TypeScript module graphs.

dampening = min(lines / 50, 1)
fan_out_penalty = min(ln(fan_out + 1) × 4, 15)
MI = 100 - (complexity_density × 30 × dampening) - (dead_code_ratio × 20) - fan_out_penalty

Fallow clamps the result to [0, 100]. Higher is better. The dampening factor lowers the density weight for files under 50 lines. A short file with a few branches has a high density, but it is still easy to read.

● File health scores (3 files) · sorted by triage concern

 57.5 src/helpers/errorUtil.ts structure
 48 LOC 1 fan-in 0 fan-out 100% dead 0.75 density 18.0 risk

 76.2 src/helpers/util.ts risk
 320 LOC 35 fan-in 0 fan-out 86% dead 0.22 density 42.0 risk

 90.5 src/types.ts structure
 154 LOC 42 fan-in 3 fan-out 0% dead 0.20 density 4.0 risk

 Sorted by triage concern: the larger of low-MI concern and CRAP risk. The risk
 / structure tag marks which one placed each file. MI reflects complexity,
 coupling, and dead code; risk reflects untested complexity (CRAP) and can
 diverge from MI. Risk: low <15, moderate 15-30, high >=30. CRAP scores are a
 static estimate from export references (85% direct, 40% indirect, 0%
 untested). Pass `--coverage <coverage-final.json>` for measured scores.
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/health/#file-health-scores
The original MI from Oman and Hagemeister (1992) combines Halstead Volume, cyclomatic complexity, lines of code, and comment percentage. Microsoft adapted it to a 0–100 scale for Visual Studio.
The fallow version makes three changes for the JS/TS ecosystem:

Replaces Halstead Volume with complexity density. Halstead metrics need full type resolution, and fallow does only syntactic analysis. Complexity density measures the same thing: how complex the code is per unit of code.
Adds dead code ratio. Unused exports are a maintenance cost specific to JS/TS, and the classic MI does not include them.

Adds fan-out coupling penalty. A high import count is a strong sign that a module is hard to maintain. The penalty uses logarithmic scaling (ln(fan_out + 1) × 4, capped at 15 points), because each extra import adds less risk than the one before.
Because the formula is different, you cannot directly compare fallow MI scores with Visual Studio or SonarQube MI scores.
Fan-in, fan-out, and dead code ratio
Fan-in: the number of files that import this file. With high fan-in, a change affects many files.
Fan-out: the number of files that this file imports. High fan-out means high coupling, and changes in other files are more likely to affect this file.
Dead code ratio: the fraction of value exports with zero references (0-1). Fallow excludes type-only exports (interfaces, type aliases).

Fan-in and fan-out coupling metrics come from Henry and Kafura (1981). The Chidamber & Kemerer OO metrics suite (1994) refined them later. Its Coupling Between Objects (CBO) metric applies the same idea to dependencies between classes.
Two vital signs metrics show coupling for the whole project:
The effective threshold is max(p95_fan_in, 10). The floor of 10 prevents false positives in small projects, where moderate fan-in is normal.
Risk profiles show the percentage of functions in each risk bin. Fallow reports two profiles as vital signs:
Unit size (function length in lines of code):
Both profiles appear as unit_size_profile and unit_interfacing_profile in the vital signs JSON. Each has the percentage values low_risk, medium_risk, high_risk, and very_high_risk.

When the unit size profile shows >= 3% of functions in the very-high-risk bin (> 60 LOC), the human output adds a Large functions list. The list shows each large function with file path, function name, line number, and LOC count. In JSON output, these functions are in a large_functions array on the health report.

You can change the 60-LOC threshold with health.maxUnitSize (for all files) or with a per-file health.thresholdOverrides[].maxUnitSize entry. When you raise it for a glob (e.g. **/*.test.*), fallow removes those functions from the Large functions list. The complexity, cognitive, and CRAP checks still run on the same files. This is the recommended way to keep test suites (long describe() / it() blocks) from filling the list. Like the other overrides, maxUnitSize filters only the reported list. The descriptive unit_size_profile and the unit-size score still use the raw sizes. To remove a file from the score completely, use health.ignore.

Risk profiles follow the SIG/TÜViT quality model. This model compares codebases by how their code spreads across risk categories, and not by averages. A codebase where 95% of functions are low-risk is healthier than one with the same average complexity and many very-high-risk functions.

Complex code without test coverage is the most likely source of production bugs. Fallow gives each function a risk score based on the CRAP metric (Change Risk Anti-Patterns). Alberto Savoia and Bob Evans developed CRAP at Agitar Labs in 2007.
The score appears in fallow health --file-scores output and JSON.
Fallow uses the canonical CRAP formula:
cov is the coverage of the function (0–100). Fallow gets that value in one of three ways:
To set up Vitest coverage for measured scores, see CRAP scores with Vitest.

For untested code, the quadratic term makes the score grow fast with complexity. With the default static_estimated model, a function that no test reaches, with cyclomatic complexity 5, scores 5^2 × 1 + 5 = 30. That is exactly the default threshold.

For evidence from real traffic (hot and cold paths, runtime-weighted dead-code results), see Runtime coverage. Runtime coverage is part of Fallow Cloud, the paid product, and a single local capture is free. It accepts V8 or Istanbul runtime data through --runtime-coverage, and adds that data on top of the active static coverage_model.
Default threshold: 30 (fallow flags functions with a score at or above this value)
A finding gets the highest severity of its cyclomatic, cognitive, and CRAP values.
The severity band does not decide if the finding fails the run. The complexity-cyclomatic, complexity-cognitive, and complexity-crap rules decide that. See Complexity rules.
To keep human output readable, fallow shows scores above 999 as >999. JSON output always has the exact value.

The risk column in --file-scores output uses different bands. It shows the highest CRAP score in the file: low below half of maxCrap, moderate up to maxCrap, and high at or above maxCrap. With the default maxCrap of 30, the bands are low <15, moderate 15-30, and high >=30.
Each file has two aggregated values:
The health summary shows the active model as coverage_model (static_estimated, istanbul, or the legacy static_binary). With measured coverage, coverage_input_format names the input: istanbul or v8.
To use the Node test runner without a conversion step:
Fallow reports the add_test_coverage refactoring target (label untested risk) when both conditions are true:
crap_above_threshold >= 2 (more than one risky function, not one outlier)
complexity_density > 0.3 (the file is complex, not only large)
These are the files where new tests remove the most risk for the effort.
To exclude a file from untested complexity risk reporting:
This comment suppresses all coverage findings for the file, also the CRAP-based scores.
To suppress complexity findings (cyclomatic and cognitive thresholds) for one function:
For all issue types that you can suppress, see Inline suppression.
A fully tested function (cov = 100) always scores exactly CC, at any complexity. A fully untested function (cov = 0) scores CC^2 + CC.
The default static_estimated model only estimates test coverage:
False negatives: When tests import a file but never run some of its functions, those functions score lower (look healthier) than they should.
False positives: When only non-test code references a file, but tests do cover it through indirect paths, the file can score worse than it should.

Alberto Savoia and Bob Evans introduced the CRAP metric at Agitar Labs. Original presentation: "CRAP4J" (2007). Complex code is not dangerous when tests cover it well, and simple code is low-risk even without tests. The risk is highest where code is complex and tests are missing.
A coverage gap is runtime code that no test reaches through the import graph. fallow health --coverage-gaps reports two finding types:

Only a value reference gives an export test reach. A test that imports a value export with import type does not run it, so the export stays an untested-export. At file level, an import type still makes the module test-reachable.
This is a static test dependency gap. It is not line coverage: a test can import a file and still skip most of its code. For measured coverage, use --coverage (see Untested complexity risk).
Use --coverage-gaps to show the gaps. The coverage-gaps rule sets their severity and is off by default. For the JSON shape and the mock rules, see With coverage gaps.

Runtime coverage adds production evidence to the health report. With --runtime-coverage, fallow merges V8 or Istanbul runtime data with the static analysis. Each runtime finding has a per-function verdict:
For the JSON fields, see With runtime coverage. For the concepts and the capture workflow, see Runtime coverage.

Coverage intelligence is an additive decision layer on top of runtime coverage. Fallow emits it when it can combine runtime evidence with static usage, test coverage, CRAP and complexity, ownership, or change scope. The JSON output has it as runtime_coverage.coverage_intelligence. Each finding has a stable fallow:coverage-intel:<hash> ID.
When fallow finds no combined finding, the output does not have the coverage_intelligence object.
Hotspots are files that are both complex and frequently changing. Bugs concentrate in these files, so a refactor there gives the highest return. Use fallow health --hotspots to see them.
Complex code that never changes is stable. You can manage simple code that changes often. Defects concentrate in complex code that changes often.

normalized_churn = weighted_commits / max_weighted_commits (0..1)
normalized_complexity = complexity_density / max_density (0..1)
score = normalized_churn × normalized_complexity × 100 (0..100)
Because the formula multiplies the two values, a file needs both high churn AND high complexity for a high score. One of the two alone gives a low score.

● Hotspots (3 files, since 6 months)

 72.1 ▲ src/types.ts
 47 commits 2739 churn 0.20 density 42 fan-in ▲ accelerating

 38.4 ─ src/helpers/util.ts
 23 commits 610 churn 0.22 density 35 fan-in ─ stable

 12.7 ▼ src/locales/en.ts
 8 commits 177 churn 0.35 density 2 fan-in ▼ cooling

 Files with high churn and high complexity
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/health/#hotspot-metrics
Fallow reports two different hotspot counts. Do not compare them directly.
vital_signs.hotspot_count counts the files with a hotspot score of 50 or more. It feeds the health score and the trend.
groups[].hotspot_count (with --group-by) counts the ranked hotspot entries of the group, before --top. It is the length of the ranked list, so it is larger than the first count on most projects.
The commit count, weighted by recency with exponential decay and a 90-day half-life:
A commit 90 days ago counts as ~0.5
A commit 180 days ago counts as ~0.25
Graves et al. (2000) introduced recency-weighted change metrics. Nagappan and Ball (2005) at Microsoft showed the empirical link between churn and defect density.
Compares the commit frequency in the first half and the second half of the analysis window:
Michael Feathers started this method, and Adam Tornhill made it systematic in Your Code as a Crime Scene (2015) and Software Design X-Rays (2018).

Change coupling finds two files that change together in most commits, while no import or re-export chain connects them. Fallow calls such a pair a hidden pair. An agent or a reviewer that follows the import graph does not find the second file. The change_coupling section of fallow health lists the hidden pairs. Use fallow health --hotspots to see them.
The section is advisory. It has no weight in the health score, and it never gates.
revisions_a and revisions_b are the commits that changed each file in the history window. shared_revisions are the commits that changed both files. Fallow rounds the degree to two decimals.
A pair is hidden when all of these conditions are true. The defaults are the Code Maat defaults:

A commit that changes more analyzed files than health.changeCoupling.maxFilesPerCommit (default 30, from 2 to 1000) is skipped. Bulk commits, such as renames and format passes, would make false pairs. The upper limit keeps the pair count of one commit small.
Fallow checks the ranges when it loads the config. maxFilesPerCommit must be from 2 to 1000, and minDegree must be from 0 to 1. A value out of range stops the run with exit code 2:

invalid config:
 - health.changeCoupling.maxFilesPerCommit must be from 2 to 1000, found 1
 - health.changeCoupling.minDegree must be from 0 to 1, found 1.5
An older fallow version rejects the changeCoupling key as unknown. When you commit the key, also set minimumVersion.
A pair with a degree of 0.5 or more is strong. A strong pair adds the hidden_coupling factor to the refactoring targets of both files.
Without --since, change coupling reads 12 months of git history. Hotspots keep their 6 month default. With --since, both read the same window. The since field shows the window that the section read.

A shallow clone, or a window with fewer analyzed commits than minRevisions, gives an empty pairs list. The workspace_diagnostics[] array then has the kind change-coupling-skipped, with cause shallow-clone or too-few-commits. This kind does not degrade the other sections, so degrades_analysis is absent. Fallow records the kind only when the run asks for the change coupling section, with the hotspot section. A run that reads the history only for the refactoring targets does not record it. See Debugging.

The section is present when the hotspot section ran and the run read git history. The sections list then has the token change-coupling. Fallow writes degree and the thresholds degrees as JSON numbers with a decimal point, for example 1.0 and 0.3. The commit counts are integers.
With --group-by, change_coupling stays at the root of the JSON envelope. No group has its own copy.
The markdown output adds a table after the hotspots table. Fallow leaves out the table when pairs is empty:

### Hidden Change Coupling (1 pair, since 12 months)

| File A | File B | Degree | Shared | Commits A | Commits B | Strong |
|:-------|:-------|:-------|:-------|:----------|:----------|:-------|
| `src/a.ts` | `src/b.ts` | 100% | 6 | 6 | 6 | **strong** |

*Files that change together in the commit history with no import between them.*
When --top cuts the list, a line under the table counts the pairs that are not shown.
The compact output has one line for each pair. degree has two decimals, and strong is true or false:
The VS Code extension shows the pairs in the Health view. The GitHub Action keeps a pair in a pull request when one of the two files changed.
Each hotspot entry has two change dispersion values. They show how far a change to the file usually spreads:
median_files_per_commit: the median number of analyzed files in the commits that changed this file.
median_lines_per_commit: the median number of added plus deleted lines, analyzed files only, in the commits that changed this file.

Both values use the change coupling window and skip the same bulk commits. The human hotspot row shows median_files_per_commit at the end, for example 3.0 files/commit. Both are absent when the history has no commit ids, for example a fallow-churn/v1 import without the commit field. In that import format, events with the same commit form one commit.

When to act: Look at the strong pairs first. If the two files must change together, make the dependency explicit with an import, or move the shared logic into one module. If the pair is a coincidence of the history, ignore it. The section never fails a run.

Refactoring targets are ranked recommendations that you can act on. fallow health --targets produces them. Fallow gives each file a priority score from the metrics above, and then sorts the targets by efficiency (priority divided by effort), highest first. Quick wins come first.

Quick start: Run fallow health --targets to get a prioritized refactoring list. For the fastest improvements, add --effort low. To block new regressions, save a baseline with --save-baseline and pass --baseline in CI. Update the baseline as you fix targets.
The other sections show measurements. Targets tell you what to do about those measurements.

priority = min(complexity_density, 1) × 30
 + hotspot_boost × 25 (hotspot_score / 100 if in hotspots, else 0)
 + dead_code_ratio × 20
 + min(fan_in / fan_in_p95, 1) × 15
 + min(fan_out / fan_out_p95, 1) × 10

fan_in_p95 and fan_out_p95 are the 95th percentiles of your project (floors 5 and 8), so the fan-in and fan-out terms adapt to the size of the codebase. Fallow normalizes all inputs to [0, 1], so each weight is a true percentage share. The formula does not use the Maintainability Index on purpose. MI already includes density and dead code, so they would count twice.
Every target has an effort estimate (low, medium, or high) based on three signals per file:

For "high", one criterion is enough (OR). For "low", all three must be true (AND). Fallow computes the fan-in percentiles from the file-score distribution of the project (P25 floor 2, P95 floor 5). A small file with fan-in at or above the P95 of the project is still "high", because a change to it affects many files.
Fallow divides the priority by the effort (low = 1, medium = 2, high = 3) to get efficiency. The default sort uses efficiency.
Every target also has a confidence level, based on the source of the data:
In human output, the second line of each target shows the category, the effort, and the confidence, separated by ·:

dead code · effort:low · confidence:high Remove 12 unused exports to reduce surface area (86% dead)
complexity · effort:high · confidence:high Extract parseRow (cognitive: 34) in 520-LOC file into smaller functions
Fallow adds structured evidence that links the target to specific analysis data. With this evidence, agents and scripts can act on a recommendation without a second tool call.
When no evidence field has data, fallow omits evidence from the JSON.
Evidence is for tools. In human output, the recommendation text already includes the key evidence (e.g., "Remove 12 unused exports" or "Extract processData (cognitive: 113)").
To track refactoring progress over time, use --save-baseline and --baseline with the health command. With an active baseline, fallow reports only new targets (targets that are not in the baseline).

# Save current targets as the baseline
fallow health --targets --save-baseline fallow-baselines/health.json

# On subsequent runs, only show new targets
fallow health --targets --baseline fallow-baselines/health.json

Baseline keys use the format relative_path:category_label (e.g., src/utils.ts:dead code). A target is "known" if the baseline has the same file and category, even when its priority score or effort level changed.
In CI, this blocks new tech debt, and you can fix the existing targets step by step.
Fallow checks the rules in priority order and gives each target the category of the first rule that matches:
A file can match more than one rule, but only the match with the highest priority sets the category. JSON output still shows all contributing factors.

The resolve_hidden_coupling rule runs last. It claims a file only when no other rule matches, so an existing target keeps its category and its baseline key. A health baseline that you saved before this rule existed has no resolve_hidden_coupling target. A run against that baseline reports these targets as new. Save the baseline again to accept them. A strong hidden pair still adds the hidden_coupling factor to the target of each file, whatever the category. The factor has the degree as value and 0.5 as threshold.

The resolve_hidden_coupling value moved the health schema_version to 12. Each envelope that embeds the health contract moved too: fallow audit to 13, the combined fallow report to 14, and the audit review brief to 13.

Later, the runtime coverage totals became nullable for a partial capture. That change moved the health schema_version to 13, fallow audit to 14, the combined fallow report to 15, the audit review brief to 14, and fallow coverage analyze to "3".

● Refactoring targets (5)
 1 low effort · 1 medium · 3 high
 score = quick-win ROI (higher = better) · pri = absolute priority

 55.8 pri:55.8 src/legacy/old-api.ts
 dead code · effort:low · confidence:high Remove 8 unused exports to reduce surface area (73% dead)

 30.8 pri:92.3 src/core/processor.ts
 churn+complexity · effort:high · confidence:low Actively-changing file with growing complexity, stabilize before adding features

 26.0 pri:52.0 src/graph/resolver.ts
 circular dependency · effort:medium · confidence:high Break import cycle, 8 files depend on this, changes cascade through the cycle

 23.7 pri:71.2 src/utils/helpers.ts
 high impact · effort:high · confidence:medium Split high-impact file (640 LOC), 15 dependents amplify every change

 13.9 pri:41.8 src/components/Dashboard.tsx
 complexity · effort:high · confidence:high Extract renderMetrics (cognitive: 45) and renderFilters (cognitive: 32) in 520-LOC file into smaller functions

 Prioritized refactoring recommendations based on complexity, churn, and
 coupling signals
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/health/#refactoring-targets
With --format json, each target has structured data for tools:

Each factor has the raw value and threshold. For categories that support it, the evidence field gives the details you need to act. AI agents can use evidence.unused_exports to create removal PRs without a second tool call. Categories without evidence do not have the field.

With fallow health --css, fallow reports first-class styling findings for CSS and CSS-in-JS. fallow audit also reports them when its CSS analysis is active. Each finding has a code, a sub_kind, an effective_severity, a location, an evidence value, and read-only actions. The JSON output has them in styling_findings.
The five styling rules default to warn. A finding with warn shows in the output but does not change the audit verdict. Set a rule to error to make it fail the verdict. See Rules.
These findings are different from the styling health grade. The grade is a descriptive score and never fails a run.
css-token-drift reports a styling value that bypasses the design token system. Examples:
A Tailwind arbitrary value in markup.
A hardcoded value that is near an existing design token.
A token that is almost a duplicate of another token.
Make sure that the value is not intentional, then replace it with an existing scale token where that is correct.
css-duplicate-block reports a declaration block that repeats across selectors or variant definitions. This usually shows copied styling that you can merge into one rule.
css-selector-complexity reports a rule that crosses a structural limit. The sub_kind gives the cause:
Reset rules, accessibility rules, and overrides of third-party generated markup can be intentional. Make sure that the rule is not necessary before you change it.
css-dead-surface reports styling that the analyzed project does not appear to use. Examples:
A scoped component class with no local use.
A class that no file references.
Dynamic class names and external consumers are not always visible to static analysis. Make sure that no dynamic consumer exists before you delete the styling.
css-broken-reference reports a styling reference that has no stylesheet definition in the analyzed project. Examples:
A class name in markup that is one edit from a defined class.
An animation that references a @keyframes name that no file defines.
The definition can come from an external stylesheet or from CSS-in-JS. Make sure that it does not exist before you fix the reference.
The health score is one 0–100 number for the overall quality of the codebase. Use fallow health --score to get it.
Fallow clamps the result to [0, 100]. Each penalty measures a different quality dimension:

health_score.formula_version identifies the formula. Version 3 keeps the density and tail metrics introduced in version 2. Its hotspot penalty counts files with a hotspot score of at least 50. Positive scores below that threshold contribute zero to this penalty. hotspot_top_pct_count remains a rank diagnostic.

Snapshots record score_formula_version. Fallow compares scores only when the saved and current formula versions are known and equal. Older snapshots remain readable, and their raw metric trends remain available. Fallow omits the score delta when the formula version is missing or different, so a formula update does not appear as a code improvement.
Letter grades: A (score >= 85), B (70–84), C (55–69), D (40–54), F (below 40).

A penalty field is absent from JSON when its analysis did not run. --score computes the score and automatically runs the duplication analysis. To include the churn-based hotspot penalty in the score, add --hotspots (or combine --score --targets).

An input that failed to load is a different case. It adds zeros, and a zero looks like a clean measurement. Before you trust a zero, look in workspace_diagnostics[] for an entry with degrades_analysis: true. See degraded inputs.
A metric is a signal. It does not prove that code is good or bad. Know these edge cases:
Generated files (GraphQL codegen, Prisma client, OpenAPI types) can have high complexity density, but you should not refactor them. Exclude them with health.ignore patterns.
Test files with many it()/test() blocks can have high cyclomatic complexity. This is usually fine, because test suites should cover many paths.
Config files (Webpack, ESLint) can show up as hotspots, because they change often during setup. Their churn usually goes down after the first configuration.
MI scores are not portable. The fallow formula is different from Visual Studio and SonarQube, so you cannot directly compare scores between these tools.
Hotspot scores are relative to your project. A score of 80 means "worst in your project," not "objectively bad." A well-maintained project can have a top score of 30.
Fan-in/out counts modules, not imports. import { a, b, c } from './utils' counts as 1 edge, not 3.
When you pass --explain, or run through MCP, the JSON output of each command includes a _meta object:
With _meta, AI agents and CI systems can interpret metric values without external documentation.
All flags for the health command.
Add production evidence to health results.
Read clone groups and families, and decide what to extract.
Get exact CRAP scores from Vitest coverage.

pages.title: Fallow telemetry and privacy
items: Fallow telemetry is opt-in and off by default. It sends no identifiers, and you can print the exact payload before you consent. Check what it sends.

Fallow telemetry is opt-in and off by default. This page lists what fallow sends when you turn it on, and what it never sends. The data helps improve agent, CI, JSON, MCP, and editor workflows. Fallow does not use it to track individuals or codebases. For the commands and environment controls, see fallow telemetry.
To keep telemetry off everywhere, set FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 or DO_NOT_TRACK=1. See Disabling everywhere.
repository, organization, project, branch, or git remote names
file paths, import specifiers, source snippets, or stack traces
package, dependency, workspace, or framework package names
raw errors, logs, or serialized exceptions
machine, user, project, or repository identifiers
Fallow does not send hashed versions of these values either.
The one exception is an anonymous install grouping token. With this token, aggregate dashboards can count distinct workflows per install instead of per run. The token has these properties:
It is a new random value. Fallow never derives it from your machine, user account, repository, project, file paths, or environment.
Fallow creates it only when you explicitly opt in: fallow telemetry enable, or the first upload after FALLOW_TELEMETRY=on.
Fallow sends it only as a private transport header (X-Fallow-Install) for server-side grouping. It is never a field inside the event.
fallow telemetry status reports only whether the token is present. It never shows the token.
You do not have to trust the list. To print the exact payload that a real command would send, without sending it, run:
Fallow prints the payload to stderr. The normal output of your command does not change.

When you enable telemetry, fallow records one small, high-level event per analysis run. A successful run gives a workflow_completed event. A failed run gives a workflow_failed event. To print this example, run fallow telemetry inspect --example:

{
 "schema_version": 2,
 "event": "workflow_completed",
 "fallow_version": "3.43.1",
 "workflow": "audit",
 "integration_surface": "mcp",
 "invocation_context": "agent",
 "agent_source": "codex",
 "output_format": "json",
 "quiet": true,
 "ci": false,
 "tty": false,
 "os": "macos",
 "arch": "aarch64",
 "duration_bucket_ms": "500-2000",
 "outcome": "issues_found",
 "exit_code_bucket": "1",
 "run_scope": "changed_only",
 "config_shape": "custom_rules",
 "output_destination": "stdout",
 "analysis_mode": "static",
 "file_count_bucket": "500-1999",
 "function_count_bucket": "1000-9999",
 "avg_fan_out_bucket": "1-2",
 "findings_present": true,
 "result_count_bucket": "1-9",
 "report_truncated": true,
 "truncation_reason": "comment_limit",
 "cache_state": "warm",
 "mcp_tool": "find_dupes",
 "has_parent_run": true,
 "run_role": "followup",
 "followup_kind": "audit"
}
Many fields are optional. Fallow omits a field when it does not apply to the run:
agent_source appears only on agent-driven runs.
failure_reason appears only on workflow_failed events.
mcp_tool appears only when a run came through the MCP server.
truncation_reason appears only when report_truncated is true.
The scale buckets, findings_present, result_count_bucket, report_truncated, and cache_state appear only when the workflow computes that value.
Two values travel as private HTTP headers, never as fields in the event:
X-Fallow-Parent-Run: a sanitized correlation token for follow-up runs. Fallow sends it only when a run is explicitly linked to a previous one.
X-Fallow-Install: the anonymous install grouping token described above.

When fallow runs through the MCP server, the server tags the CLI process that it starts. The one event from that run then counts toward the mcp surface and the specific tool, instead of a plain cli_json run. Code Mode snippets can make several read-only host calls. Fallow attributes the CLI events from those calls to code_execute, not to free-form code text or nested helper names. This tagging sends no extra event and does not change what fallow collects.
The LSP server, editor extension, and library embeddings run in-process and currently emit no telemetry.
The schema_version field increments if the collected fields change. The fallow team updates this page before any new field ships.
When telemetry is enabled and fallow classifies a run as agent-driven, fallow may send one normalized agent_source value from a fixed allowlist:

none codex claude_code cursor copilot opencode aider roo
windsurf gemini cline continue zed goose other_known unknown

Fallow never sends none. It is the internal default before fallow classifies a run, and fallow sends agent_source only for agent-driven runs. Fallow groups agents that are not on the list, for example enterprise IDE assistants, under other_known. Fallow also normalizes aliases: hyphen aliases such as claude-code, and CLI aliases such as gemini_cli and antigravity (both map to gemini).
Fallow does not upload any of these:
process names or parent process paths

If you write an agent wrapper, set FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE=<allowlisted-value>. Fallow ignores a value that is not on the allowlist, and then sends no agent_source. If your wrapper cannot name the agent, set FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE=unknown. Setting FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE never enables telemetry by itself and uploads no codebase content. When more than one agent environment is present, attribution is best-effort and can depend on check order. To name the agent yourself, set FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE.
Fallow sends each request as an HTTPS POST with a JSON body to https://api.fallow.cloud/v1/telemetry/events (override the host with FALLOW_API_URL)
Fallow uses no cookies and sends no authentication token
At exit, fallow writes the event to a local spool file (telemetry-spool.jsonl, next to the user-level telemetry config). It does not upload the event during the run that produced it
At the start of the next telemetry-enabled run, a background thread uploads the spooled events. The upload does not slow down your command
Delivery is best-effort. The spool keeps at most the 64 newest events, so a machine that stays offline drops its oldest events. The counts are a rough sample, not an exact usage count
Fallow ignores network errors, and they never affect command output or the exit code
Fallow never writes telemetry to stdout
The server does not add customer, repository, organization, git, package-registry, or license data to telemetry
The server drops or truncates IP addresses as early as practical
The server keeps raw events for a short window only, then deletes them
Public reporting uses only coarse aggregate trends after privacy review.

The DO_NOT_TRACK and FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED environment variables are kill switches with top precedence. When either is truthy, telemetry stays off and fallow refuses fallow telemetry enable. In managed and CI environments, use FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 as the fleet-wide switch.
Commands and environment controls for telemetry.

pages.title: React and Next.js static analysis with fallow
items: React and Next.js static analysis with fallow
React and Next.js static analysis that finds wrong client and server directives, colliding routes, dead server actions, and unused or drilled props.

Fallow finds React and Next.js problems that per-file tools (eslint-plugin-react, eslint-plugin-next) cannot see, often before the build fails. It builds a module graph of the whole project, so it can find:
A "use client" file that exports a server-only name.
Two route files that resolve to the same URL.
A prop drilled through three components.
A server action that no code uses.
React is the largest ecosystem that fallow supports, and Next.js is the framework that fallow parses in the most depth.
This page is the index of the React and Next.js rules. The dead-code explanation page has the full definition of each rule, with severities, suppression syntax, and the cases where the rule abstains.

The Next.js and React rules are gated on dependencies. Each rule runs only when the relevant package (next, or react, react-dom, or preact) is a declared dependency. They never fire on an unrelated project.

These four rules check the boundary between "use client" and "use server" across the whole project. They run in the same pass as the rest of dead-code analysis, before a build runs, and only when next is a declared dependency.

A file with "use client" that also exports a server-only or route-segment-config name. Examples are metadata, generateMetadata, viewport, generateStaticParams, dynamic, revalidate, runtime, the Pages Router data functions, a route HTTP method handler, and the rest of the reserved set.
Next.js rejects these files at build time. Fallow finds them statically and never flags the default export of the component. Default warn.

A barrel file (a file with at least one export ... from re-export) that re-exports both a "use client" module and a server-only module. An import of one name from this barrel can pull the directive context of the other module across the React Server Components boundary. The result is a confusing build or hydration error far from the barrel. A single-file linter cannot detect this pattern, because it spans files.

The check classifies only direct re-export origins and skips type-only re-exports. It also skips a re-export through a webpack inline loader (export * from 'raw-loader!./server'), because the loader forwards its own output, not the module and its directive. It never flags a barrel that only mixes a client module with an ordinary utility. Default warn.

A "use client" or "use server" directive below an import (or any other statement), not in the prologue at the top of the file. When a statement comes before the directive, the bundler treats the string as an ordinary expression and ignores it without a message. A file that you wrote as a client component then becomes a server module, and nothing reports an error. To fix it, move the directive above every import. Default warn.

A Next.js Server Action (an export of a "use server" file) that no code in the project references. There is no import-and-call, no action={fn} binding, and no <form action={fn}>. Dead actions of this kind build up when you refactor a page. eslint-plugin-next checks one file at a time, so it cannot see them.

The rule is a more specific version of unused-export for "use server" files. It uses the fallow reference graph for the whole project, so prop forwarding and wrapped action factories (withAuditLogging(...)) count as real uses. Default warn.

This rule moves some findings from unused-export (default error) to unused-server-action (default warn). A dead action that failed CI as unused-export before is now a warning. To keep CI failing on it, set unused-server-action: "error", and save any baseline snapshot again once.
Both route rules only compute paths over your App Router tree, so no heuristic can misfire. They run only when next is a declared dependency.
The rules check each app root separately, based on your workspace package roots. A monorepo with several independent Next apps that share a path is not flagged. Fallow treats the tree as follows:
Route groups (name) do not change the URL.
Intercepting markers and private _folders are excluded.

Two or more App Router route files (a page or a route handler) that resolve to the same URL in one app root. Route groups and parallel slots do not change the URL, so app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx and app/(shop)/about/page.tsx both own /about.

Next.js fails the build here, but it names only one colliding file and stops. Fallow lists every colliding file at once, before the build. Default error, because the rule matches a next build failure: a project with this problem already fails.

Two or more sibling dynamic route segments at the same tree position with different param names ([id] vs [slug], or a catch-all [...x] vs an optional catch-all [[...x]]). When a request reaches that position, Next.js throws "You cannot use different slug names for the same dynamic path" at runtime.
next build does NOT catch this. The build succeeds and CI passes, and then the route crashes on the first request. The fallow static check is the only gate that fails on it, so it defaults to error.

The component-health signals treat React and Preact components as a graph. They show how many places render a component, whether a live component has a dead prop, and whether a component only adds a layer with no function. Three signals are opt-in and default to off. The prop and fan-in signals are on by default.
Fan-in is the number of files that import a given file. For a component, it also measures blast radius. A component that many places render has high fan-in, so a change to it affects many files.
The fallow health analysis computes fan-in for every file. It shows fan-in in the hotspot and refactoring-target output, and adds high fan-in to the coupling penalty in the health score.
The health page explains how fallow computes fan-in / fan-out and where the effective threshold comes from.
A prop that the component destructures from its first parameter and never reads in its body. The component is live and rendered, but it does not use one of its declared props.

unused-component-prop is one rule key for all frameworks. The React and Preact part runs only when react, react-dom, next, or preact is a dependency. It covers inline-destructured literal props. To avoid false positives, it abstains on:
Props passed as a whole object to a hook.
A forwardRef or memo component whose props come from an imported interface.

A prop that passes unused through two or more intermediate components before a component uses it. "Passes unused" means that an intermediate component reads the prop only as the root of a child JSX attribute value, and never uses it in another way. For example, <Child userName={user.name} /> passes user straight through. Per-file linters cannot see this signal, because it spans files.

When you enable the rule, it reports one chain for each drilled prop. The chain has the owning source, each pass-through hop, and the consumer, each with file, line, and component name. The rule abstains when it cannot prove a clean pass-through:
A component passed as a prop, a render prop, or function-as-children.
A matching context *.Provider in the subtree.

Set prop-drilling: "warn" under rules for advisory findings, or "error" to make findings fail CI. A warn finding stays advisory even with --fail-on-issues. The enabled rule also adds a small penalty to the health score: one point for each chain, with a maximum of five. When the rule is off, the health score does not change.

A component whose entire body is return <Child {...props} />. It renders a single child, forwards all props through a spread, and adds no markup, hooks, or logic of its own. Every call site could render the child directly.
The rule abstains on intentional wrappers:
A wrapper whose body is more than the single spread-forwarded child.
Off by default. To enable it, set thin-wrapper: "warn" (or "error") under rules.
Three or more components, in two or more files, that declare an identical set of prop names. This suggests that you extract a shared Props type (or a base component).
To avoid noise, the rule requires all of these:
An exact match of the full set.
At least four significant prop names, after it removes common DOM-passthrough names (id, className, children, style, ...).
At least three components in at least two files.
Two buttons that only share {label, onClick} are never grouped. Off by default. To enable it, set duplicate-prop-shape: "warn" (or "error") under rules.
prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, and duplicate-prop-shape all default to off. Enable the ones you want under rules:
Fallow never flags a component or server action that is used correctly. The fallow framework plugins know the conventions that each router uses to reach code, and count them as uses. They cover:
Next.js App Router: convention exports (page, layout, loading, error, route, and the metadata files), route segment config, middleware, proxy, and instrumentation count as entry points.
Next.js Pages Router: any file under pages/, and the data functions that Next calls by name (getStaticProps, getServerSideProps, getStaticPaths).
Server-action bindings: action={fn}, <form action={fn}>, plain import-and-call, component-prop forwarding, and wrapped action factories all count as real uses of a "use server" export.

React Router (@react-router/dev), Remix (@remix-run/node, @remix-run/react, and the other @remix-run/ runtime packages), and TanStack Router (@tanstack/react-router, @tanstack/start, @tanstack/react-start): fallow recognizes their route conventions, so it does not flag route modules as unused.

Fallow counts these conventions automatically, so the component and server-action rules fire only on code that nothing uses. Built-in plugins lists the enabler packages and what each plugin extracts. To see the active plugins in your project, run fallow list --plugins.
If fallow does not count a convention, add the file to entry or write a custom plugin. Before you act on a finding, verify it with fallow dead-code --trace <file>:<symbol>.
Definitions, severities, and suppression syntax for every rule on this page.
Set each rule to error, warn, or off, and enable the opt-in component signals.
Auto-detected enabler packages for Next.js, React Router, Remix, and TanStack Router.
Fan-in, blast radius, and the coupling penalty in the health score.

pages.title: Built-in fallow plugins for Next.js, Vite and Jest
items: Built-in fallow plugins for Next.js, Vite and Jest
Built-in fallow plugins detect Next.js, Vite, Jest, Tailwind, ESLint, and many other tools, so fallow knows the files and exports that each tool uses.
Built-in plugins give you accurate results without configuration. Without a plugin, fallow can report a route file, a config file, or a tool dependency as unused, because no import reaches it.

Fallow has built-in plugins for popular TypeScript and JavaScript tools. Each plugin tells fallow the conventions of one framework or tool: entry points, config files, used exports, and tooling dependencies.

Most plugins activate automatically when the relevant package is in your package.json. Some plugins (ESLint, Vitest) also activate when a config file is present in the workspace root, even without the package. This covers a monorepo that installs the tool at the root and gives the workspace packages their own config files.
These plugins do more than detect a package. They parse your config files with the Oxc AST parser and extract entry points, dependencies, aliases, and other settings automatically:
Run fallow list --plugins to see which plugins are active in your project.

Active plugins:
 - nextjs
 - vite
 - vitest
 - playwright
 - storybook
 - oxlint
 - typescript
 - tailwind
 - drizzle
If your framework is not in the list, write a custom plugin. Custom plugins support any internal or third-party tool, with declarative JSON or TOML.
The Jest plugin reads every Jest config in a package:
Each config adds its own test patterns. A config with its own testMatch or testRegex does not remove the default test patterns of the other configs.
Fallow converts a simple testRegex to a glob:
When fallow cannot convert a regex, add the test files to entry.
A --config file that a script passes to jest is also an entry point, for example jest --config ./jest-integration.config.ts.

Fallow reads the command and commands of each nx:run-commands target in a project.json file as a script. For example, tsx scripts/seed.ts makes scripts/seed.ts an entry point, and jest --config ./jest-integration.config.ts makes the Jest config an entry point.
Fallow also reads a command in the configurations of the target.
A command that calls another target of the same project, such as nx ts-node -- src/run.ts, uses the command of that target.

Fallow reads a target only when it runs in the project directory, for example with cwd set to {projectRoot}. A target without cwd in a nested project runs from the workspace root, so Fallow skips it. Fallow also skips a target with a cwd that points to a different directory, because its relative paths can point to the wrong files.

Fallow reads the migrations option of a DataSource config in data-source.{ts,js}, *.data-source.{ts,js}, *.datasource.{ts,js}, and ormconfig.{ts,js,json}. Each glob becomes an entry pattern, because TypeORM loads the migration files at runtime without an import.
When a template selects between two paths, fallow uses the path that starts with src/. When no path starts with src/, fallow changes a dist/ path to the same path under src/.

Fallow does not read the entities and subscribers options. TypeORM uses only the decorated classes of these files. An entry point for each file would also hide the other unused exports and members of the file.
Classes and enums that a library reads by reflection
Some libraries read every member of a class or an enum. Project code does not name these members, so fallow counts them as used in these cases:

ORM entities. An entity class that you pass to getRepository, getCustomRepository, getTreeRepository, getMongoRepository, or createQueryBuilder uses all of its members. The type argument of a repository getter, as in getRepository<Order>(), counts too.

ORM find calls. An entity class that you pass to find, findBy, findOne, findOneBy, findOneOrFail, findOneByOrFail, findAndCount, or findAndCountBy uses all of its members. This applies only when the file imports from typeorm, @nestjs/typeorm, or a @mikro-orm/ package.
GraphQL enums. An enum that you pass to registerEnumType from @nestjs/graphql or type-graphql uses all of its values.
An entity class that code uses only as a type can still have unused properties. See Entity properties that code uses only as a type.
The OpenTelemetry SDK calls the methods of the samplers, processors, exporters and propagators that you register. Your code does not call these methods, so fallow counts them as used in these cases:
Other members of these classes stay reportable as unused-class-members.

Alchemy reads a stack from alchemy.run.ts, or from the file that a script passes to the CLI (alchemy deploy ./stacks/app.ts). No project code imports a stack file, so fallow uses these files as entry points:
Each alchemy.run.ts, .mts, .cts, .js, .mjs or .cjs file, at any depth.
Each stack file that a package.json script passes to alchemy deploy, dev, destroy or plan, also with --config.
The bundle entry that a resource names in its main property, for example main: "./src/worker.ts" or main: new URL("./src/index.ts", import.meta.url).pathname.
A stack runs at deploy time, so a stack file is a support entry, not a production entry. The Worker code that a stack imports stays reachable with --production.
The Alchemy CLI loads @effect/platform-node or @effect/platform-bun with a dynamic import(), so fallow does not report these packages as unused dependencies.
Fallow also reads a webpack config that lives under config/, build/ or webpack/ instead of the package root. Rspack and rsbuild configs stay at the package root; they do not have this directory rule.

A file under config/ or webpack/ counts as a webpack config when it exports a webpack configuration: an object with a webpack config key other than name or dependencies (also returned from a function), an array of configurations, or a webpack-merge call (merge, mergeWithCustomize, mergeWithRules, or the imported package). A helper file such as config/webpack.paths.js does not export a configuration, so fallow still reports it as unused when nothing imports it.

build/ also holds build output, so fallow reads a narrower name there: only webpack.<target>.{ts,js,mjs,cjs}, such as build/webpack.prod.js, and only when it passes the same export check. Fallow never reads build/webpack.config.*, because that name is more likely to be a compiled or stale copy.
Fallow probes these directories beside a root config, so build/webpack.prod.js is read together with a root webpack.config.js.
Entries resolve like the bundler resolves them:
Rspack reads context, and rsbuild reads root. A relative entry, and a Module Federation exposes target, resolve against that directory.
An entry without an extension, such as ./lib or ./src/app, matches the source file (./lib.ts) or the directory index (./lib/index.ts). This also applies when context or root is set.
A Module Federation exposes target and the remotes scope of a webpack config in config/, build/ or webpack/ resolve against the package root, the same as webpack does without context.
An import can name its loaders inline, such as require('!raw-loader?esModule=false!./shim.js'). Fallow reads these requests in every project, also when the webpack plugin is not active:
The request resolves to its resource, the last segment (./shim.js). The !, !! and -! prefixes and the ?options of each loader do not change the target.
Each loader package, such as raw-loader, counts as a used dependency. A loader in devDependencies is not reported as a dev dependency that production code uses.

A loader replaces the exports of its resource. A loader import therefore uses every value export of the resource, default included, and fallow does not report these exports as unused. A type export of the resource (a type alias or an interface) follows the same rule as a type export of a file that a dynamic import pattern matches: only an import that names it uses it.

A text loader returns the text, the bytes or a URL of the file: raw-loader, file-loader, url-loader, text-loader and similar. The resource counts as used, but its own imports do not. They do not keep other files in use, and they are not production imports. A loader that runs the file, such as worker-loader, css-loader or babel-loader, keeps the imports of the resource.

A text loader import does not run the resource, so it does not cross an architecture boundary, it does not carry server code into a "use client" file for client-server-leak, and a re-export through a loader is not a client or server origin of a mixed client/server barrel. A package file behind a text loader (raw-loader!pkg/notes.txt) is read at build time: the package is a used dependency, but not a dev dependency that production code imports.

A worker loader runs the resource in another thread: worker-loader, sharedworker-loader, worklet-loader, workerize-loader, comlink-loader, service-worker-loader and similar. The import loads the same way as new Worker(new URL('./work.js', import.meta.url)). A cycle through the import is reported by default, and circularDependencies.ignoreLazyImports skips it. fallow list --entry-weight counts the resource as out-of-thread code, not as startup code.

A ! is also valid in a file name. A request without a prefix, such as ./we!rd.js or pkg/a!b.js, resolves as a plain path first when that file exists, also an installed package file. When the file does not exist, for example in a clone without installed packages, fallow reads the request the way webpack does: webpack splits every request on !, so pkg/a!b.js is the loader pkg/a for b.js.

Only inline loaders change an import. A loader that a rule in module.rules of a webpack config applies, such as { test: /\.worker\.js$/, use: 'worker-loader' }, gives no worker or text loader semantics. The rule conditions (test, include, exclude, issuer, resourceQuery, the oneOf order) use JavaScript regular expressions and computed paths, and many projects build the rules in code, for example with webpack-merge, in the webpack function of next.config.js, or in Storybook webpackFinal. A static read would miss or misapply rules, and a misapplied text loader rule would hide the imports of every file that it matches. The configured loader packages still count as used dependencies.
When the resource does not resolve, the unresolved import shows the full request, so an ignoreUnresolvedImports entry must use the full request.
Vite+ keeps the config of each tool that it bundles in vite.config.*, and runs the tools through the vp command. Fallow reads each block of the config with the rules for the same tool:
In this example, src/index.ts and src/cli.ts are entry points, and @e18e/eslint-plugin is a used dependency.

Fallow reads the staged and run.tasks blocks from the root vite.config.* of the project and of each workspace package. A config in a nested fixture directory gives no command. The scripts in .vite-hooks/ are read like Git hook scripts.
The vp, vpr and vpx binaries credit vite-plus. The bundled tool decides how fallow reads the arguments of a vp subcommand:
vp lint, vp fmt and vp check take file targets that are not entry points. See Formatter and linter targets.
vp test -c <file> reads the file as a Vitest config.
vp pack <file> makes the file an entry point.
vp run <task> and vpr <task> call a declared script, also with the -r, -w and --filter selection of pnpm.
vp exec, vp dlx and vpx run their child command, as npx does. A vp exec with -r or --filter makes no entry point.
vp config, vp install and the other subcommands take no file arguments.
A vi.mock call through vite-plus/test counts as a Vitest mock.
The Egg loader loads the files of an app, a framework or a plugin by directory convention, so no source file imports them. Fallow marks these files as entry points:
the files in app/controller, app/service, app/middleware and app/schedule, also in subdirectories

The same rules apply to a nested app, such as an example app or a test fixture app. Fallow finds a nested app through its config/config.default.* or config/plugin.* file. Each pattern also matches the .cjs, .mjs, .ts, .cts and .mts extensions.

tegg loads every source file of a directory whose package.json has an eggModule key, or that config/module.json lists. Fallow marks these files as entry points too. Like tegg, it skips hidden directories, node_modules, test, coverage, declaration files and vitest.config.*.
A package value in config/plugin.* counts as a used dependency:

Fallow credits the package to the package.json that owns the app: the nearest manifest with a dependency section outside a test or fixtures directory. A test fixture app therefore credits the workspace package that runs its tests. A package that only another workspace names stays reported.

With Module Federation, fallow keeps exposed modules out of the unused-file report, does not report remote imports as unlisted dependencies, and does not report shared packages as unused dependencies.

Fallow reads exposes, remotes, and shared from module-federation.config.{ts,js,mjs,cjs,mts,cts}. It also reads them from a Federation plugin call in a webpack, rspack, rsbuild, vite or next.config.* file. Fallow recognizes these plugin calls: ModuleFederationPlugin, NextFederationPlugin, moduleFederationPlugin, pluginModuleFederation and federation. Fallow reads such a call wherever it is in the config program. A call counts only when its first argument is an object that declares exposes, remotes, or shared.

exposes: each target becomes a runtime entry point. The exposed module, and everything it reaches, stays out of unused-file. Its exports follow includeEntryExports, like the exports of any other entry point. A target that names a bare module request instead of a local path ("./utils": "shared-utils") credits that dependency, but only in the package that owns the config.

remotes: fallow treats each alias and its subpaths as provided by the remote container, so it does not report import("checkout/Button") as an unlisted dependency. The alias holds only under the directory of the config that declared it. A sibling workspace package that declares no remote still reports the dependency.

shared: each package that the option names counts as used, so it does not report as an unused dependency. Fallow reads the object form (shared: { react: { singleton: true } }), the array form (shared: ['react', 'react-dom']), an object element in the array form, and the import and packageName fields of an entry descriptor. A key with a trailing / credits the same package. A relative key shares a project module and credits no package. The credit applies only to the package that owns the config (the nearest package.json at or above the config), so a sibling workspace that declares the same package and does not use it still reports it. A shared entry for a package that package.json does not declare creates no finding. A shared value that fallow cannot read gives no credit and records no diagnostic.
Fallow reads a plugin call in these positions:
A nested plugin array, and a plugin list that a variable holds.
A tool-specific key such as tools.rspack.plugins.
A hook body, such as an rsbuild appendPlugins hook or a Next.js webpack(config) hook.

A helper module that the bundler config imports with a relative import or require, such as config/module-federation.js. Fallow reads the helper one import deep, inside the project root, as if the call was in the config. The diagnostics and the trace sources name the helper file.
Fallow also reads the plugin options through one step of indirection:

An export const in the same file (export const mfConfig = { ... }), and a plain const (const mfConfig = { ... }). The program must have one binding of that name, and no code may write to the binding or to one of its members.
A TypeScript non-null assertion on the binding, such as new ModuleFederationPlugin(mfConfig!).
A computed callee, such as new container['ModuleFederationPlugin']({ ... }).
A relative import of a sibling config file, including a default import and a named import.
A relative require of a sibling config file, one step deep. A require of a package stays silent.
An object spread over a same-file binding ({ ...base }) and Object.assign({}, base).
The array form of exposes. A string element is both the public name and the module request. An object element uses the object reader.
exposes targets and the remotes scope of a webpack config under config/, build/ or webpack/, resolved against the package root, as webpack does without context. See config directories.
Every config reader that resolves an options object, not only Module Federation, follows export const config = { ... }; export default config the same way.
The array form of remotes. A bundler derives the request scope of an element from the whole container location, so the alias is not a bare specifier.
A value that is not a static object literal, an unreadable require of a package, and an array element that holds glob syntax, a nested array, or a value that is not a string.

A spread over a binding fallow cannot resolve. This records a plugin-config-unreadable diagnostic with the spread reason for each Federation key the readable part does not declare. When the options declare no Federation key at all, a bare federation(...) call records nothing, because other libraries use that name too.

A remote can also come from a call to the Federation runtime. Fallow reads these calls in a file that imports them from @module-federation/runtime or @module-federation/enhanced/runtime, by name, by a renamed import, or through a namespace import. A local function with the same name registers nothing.
registerRemotes([{ name: 'checkout', entry }]) registers checkout, and a literal alias when the object has one.
loadRemote('checkout/Button') registers checkout. A scoped name keeps two segments (@scope/remote).
init({ remotes }) and createInstance({ remotes }) register the remotes that their remotes option names. Fallow also reads the registerRemotes and loadRemote methods of the instance that they return.

A remote from a runtime call follows the same rule as a remotes entry: the alias and its subpaths are provided only inside the workspace that holds the file. Fallow also reads these calls in the <script> blocks of a .vue or .svelte file. The blocks count as one file, so an import in one block covers a call in another.

Fallow reads only a static literal argument. A call whose argument is not a static literal, such as loadRemote(`${scope}/${module}`), records a plugin-config-unreadable diagnostic on the source file, with the function name as key and the reason dynamic-argument.
--trace-file and --trace-dependency name the Federation config when it is the reason for the result:
--trace-file on a file that an exposes entry makes an entry point lists each config that exposes it.
--trace-dependency on a remotes alias lists each config that declares the alias, and says that a remote container provides the name, not an npm package.

The human output adds one Source: line for each config. The JSON output has a sources array with { kind, plugin, config, key } entries, for example { "kind": "module-federation", "plugin": "webpack", "config": "packages/cart/webpack.config.js", "key": "exposes" }. For a remote that only a runtime call names, config is the source file and key is the function name. A trace with no Federation involvement has no sources array. The MCP trace_file and trace_dependency tools have the same field.

Fallow reads the config syntactically. It fetches no remote container and validates nothing about the remote. Fallow does not check the availability of the remote, its exports, its versions, or its shared singletons.

When fallow cannot read a declaration in full, it adds a plugin-config-unreadable entry to workspace_diagnostics[] and prints a warning on stderr. The entry names the plugin, the key, and the reason, with the config file in path. For a runtime call, path is the source file.

reason is not-object-literal, array-form, spread, unreadable-entries or dynamic-argument. For a runtime call, key is registerRemotes, loadRemote, init or createInstance. More values can come later, so do not treat this list as closed.
The plugin is module-federation for a standalone config file and for a runtime call. It is webpack, rspack, rsbuild, vite or nextjs when fallow read the options from the config of that plugin.
Two unreadable keys in one file give two entries.
The entry has degrades_analysis, so both CI integrations that fallow ships report it under degraded inputs.

fallow: Plugin 'module-federation': `exposes` in 'module-federation.config.ts' is not a static object literal, so the targets are not registered as entry points. Name the exposed files in `dynamicallyLoaded`.
fallow: Plugin 'webpack': `remotes` in 'webpack.config.js' uses the array form, which is not read yet, so the aliases are not treated as provided by a remote container. Name the aliases in `ignoreDependencies`, or declare them as the keys of an object literal, whose values may be computed.

For an exposed file that fallow cannot see, use dynamicallyLoaded. For a file that is a project entry point of its own, use entry. Put a remote alias in ignoreDependencies. Note that ignoreDependencies also hides unused-dependency findings for that name.

Fallow scans plugins/, middleware/ and modules/ the same way Nuxt does: one level deep. A file is an entry point when it is a direct child of the directory, or the index file of a direct child directory. For example, plugins/bar.ts and plugins/foo/index.ts are entry points. plugins/foo/helper.ts and plugins/foo/deep/index.ts are not, so they report as unused when nothing imports them.
A file in the plugins list of nuxt.config is an entry point at any depth.
The files in modules/<name>/runtime/ stay entry points, because a module registers them through resolver.resolve() strings that fallow does not follow.
The same rules apply under app/ and in each local layer. Under a configured srcDir, they apply to plugins/ and middleware/.

A string value of dir.pages, dir.layouts, dir.middleware or dir.plugins in nuxt.config sets that convention directory, relative to srcDir. A string value of dir.modules is relative to the project root, as in Nuxt.
Nuxt lets a project extend other Nuxt codebases, called layers. Fallow scans a local layer the same way it scans the project root.
A directory is a local layer when it holds a nuxt.config file (ts, js, mjs, cjs, mts or cts), and either:

A nuxt.config names it in extends, as a relative path. This includes the project root config and the config of any local layer already found, so a layer chain (a layer that itself extends another local layer) resolves too.
It sits under layers/<name>, beside the root config. Fallow scans every layers/<name> directory that has a nuxt.config, without an extends entry.
A local layer without a nuxt.config is not a layer, so its files keep reporting as unused when nothing references them.
Its convention files (pages, layouts, components, composables, utils, server, plugins) are entry points, the same as the project root.
Its root files (app.vue, app.config.*) are always used.
With autoImports on, its components and composables are auto-import sources. An unreferenced layer component then reports as unused-file.

Its own nuxt.config takes part in the autoImports surface classification, alongside the root config. The advisory that fallow prints for a custom components: or imports: shape names the config file that decided that surface.
#layers/<name>/ resolves to a local layer by its $meta.name:
A layers/<name> directory without a $meta.name resolves by its directory name.
An extends layer without a $meta.name gets no alias, so an import through #layers/<name>/ stays unresolved.
A remote layer (a github: or gh: reference) or a package layer (an npm name) stays a dependency reference only. Fallow does not scan its files.

Fallow reads the modules of a package layer, so a module that the layer registers is active for the app. For example, with extends: ['docus'], or another package layer that lists @nuxt/content in its own modules, the components/content/ files and the content.config.* file of the app stay entry points. Fallow reads the nuxt.config of the layer from the nearest node_modules/<name>. docus activates @nuxt/content also when it is not installed. Fallow does not follow the extends of a package layer. A local layer that registers @nuxt/content also marks the content.config.* file of the app as used.

With autoImports on, an auto-import name marks as used only the files of the app that renders or calls it, and of the layers that this app extends. In a monorepo, a <Card /> in one app does not keep the unused Card.vue of another app. A run with autoImports on can therefore report more unused files than before.

A layer that an app extends by a relative path outside the app, or by the package name of a workspace, shares its names with that app in both directions. The app uses the components and Pinia stores of the layer. A layer layout can render a component that the app overrides.
Two apps that extend the same layer do not see the names of each other.
These component files stay entry points, because fallow cannot see how they render:
Files in components/global/ and *.global.vue files. A string reference such as resolveComponent('Name') can render a global component.
Files in components/content/ of the project and of each local layer, when @nuxt/content is in modules. Markdown content renders these components, and fallow does not read Markdown.

nuxt-og-image renders the template that a string names, so no import or template tag reaches the file. A defineOgImage('Docs.takumi') or defineOgImageComponent('Docs') call marks the matching file as used, under an OgImage/, og-image/, OgImageCommunity/, or OgImageTemplate/ components directory. The name match is the one that nuxt-og-image uses: dot segments join in PascalCase, and the renderer suffix (.satori, .browser, .takumi) and the directory prefix do not count. A template that no call names with a static string still reports as unused.

Storybook reads each stories pattern in .storybook/main relative to the directory of that config file. Fallow does the same, so a pattern such as ../src/**/*.mdx matches the story files that Storybook loads.

A pattern can point into another workspace of the project. For example, a central docs app with apps/docs/.storybook and stories: ["../../../packages/ui/src/**/*.docs.tsx"] marks the matching files in packages/ui as used.
Fallow drops a pattern that leaves the project root.
Storybook reads a leading / as an absolute filesystem path. A pattern such as /src/** outside the project therefore marks nothing as used.

A pattern can use the extglob groups @(..), ?(..), +(..), *(..) and !(..). A @(ts|tsx) group, as in the Storybook config template, matches like {ts,tsx}. A negated group excludes files: ../src/**/!(*.dev).stories.@(js|ts) does not match button.dev.stories.ts. See Extglob groups in tool globs.

Fallow reads the object form { directory, files, titlePrefix }. directory resolves against the .storybook/ directory, and files applies under it. Without files, the Storybook default **/*.@(mdx|stories.@(js|jsx|mjs|ts|tsx)) applies.
Fallow also reads the .storybook/main config of a workspace when the root package uses Storybook too.
Fallow reads the extglob groups @(..), ?(..), +(..), *(..) and !(..) in these tool globs:
import.meta.glob patterns, see Dynamic import resolution
The glob matcher cannot repeat a group, so fallow changes each group into a glob that it can match:
A negated group !(..) in an include glob excludes the files that match its alternatives.

A +(..) group in an include glob matches one or more repetitions. Fallow reads +(ts|js) as {ts,js}*. Thus *.test.+(ts|js) also matches a.test.jsx and a.test.tsx, so a few more files can become entry points.
An exclude glob matches a +(..) group once and a *(..) group zero times or once. An exclude glob with a !(..) group removes no file. Thus an exclude never removes a file that the tool keeps.
A Playwright testMatch glob with a group makes only the matching files entry points. The match ignores case, as before.
A Vitest plain (a|b) group matches one of its alternatives.
Support internal frameworks with external plugin files.
Inspect active plugins, entry points, and project metadata.

pages.title: Write a custom fallow plugin in JSON or TOML
items: Write a custom fallow plugin in JSON or TOML
A custom fallow plugin stops false positives from an internal framework or unknown tool. Declare entry points, config files, and used exports in JSON or TOML.

When fallow does not know an internal framework or tool, it can report the files and exports that the framework uses as unused. A custom plugin fixes this. It is a declarative JSON or TOML file that tells fallow the conventions of your framework.
Start with the JSONC format. It supports $schema and IDE autocomplete.

2Configure the fieldsSet the plugin fields for your framework. Only name is required. Add the fields that you need.RequiredFieldTypeDescriptionnamestringUnique plugin name (shown in fallow list --plugins)OptionalFieldTypeDescriptionenablersstring[]Package names that activate this plugin. A plugin with neither enablers nor detection never activatesentryPointsstring[]Glob patterns for entry point filesentryPointRolestringCoverage role of the entry points: runtime, test, or support. Defaults to supportconfigPatternsstring[]Glob patterns for config files (always used). Under includeEntryExports, the default export of a matching file counts as usedconfigDefaultExportOptOutstring[]Entries of configPatterns whose default export does not count as used under includeEntryExports. Write each entry exactly as in configPatterns. Use it when the pattern also matches ordinary source filesalwaysUsedstring[]Files that fallow always treats as usedtoolingDependenciesstring[]Packages that you use through a CLI, not through importsdetectionobjectActivation logic with conditions (see below)usedExportsobject[]Exports that fallow always treats as usedusedClassMembers(string | object)[]Class method or property names that the framework calls at runtime. A scoped object { extends?, implements?, members } matches only classes with matching heritagemanifestEntriesobject[]Entry points that come from framework manifest files (see Manifest-derived entries)

3Verify the pluginMake sure that fallow loads your plugin. For manifestEntries, also see what the plugin matched and seeded:fallow list --plugins # is the plugin active?
fallow plugin-check --format json # what did each rule match, seed, and warn about?fallow plugin-check is a read-only dry run. It always exits 0. It reports whether each plugin activated, and the unmet requirement when a plugin did not. For manifestEntries rules, it also reports:
The manifests that matched.
The when-gate result for each manifest.
The entries seeded, with a path_exists flag.
A plugin activates through simple enablers, or through detection logic with boolean combinators.

A plugin with neither enablers nor detection never activates. Fallow prints a warning on stderr when it loads the config. The findings and the exit code do not change. Run fallow plugin-check to see why a plugin is inactive.
This is the simplest way to activate a plugin. Fallow checks each package name against package.json. The plugin activates if any enabler matches:
A trailing / turns on prefix matching, so @myorg/ matches any package in the @myorg scope.
Activate a plugin when specific config files exist in the project:
Combine conditions with all (AND) or any (OR). There is no not condition:
This plugin activates only when @my-org/core is installed and a my-org.config.* file exists.
