In a framework that works by convention, the framework uses some exports by name at runtime. Mark these exports as always used:

List the class method or property names that the framework calls at runtime through an interface or contract. Fallow adds these names to its built-in Angular and React lifecycle allowlist. It then never flags members that implement these contracts as unused class members.
Each entry is one of these:
A plain member name, which suppresses the name everywhere.
A scoped object, which matches only classes whose heritage clause includes the configured extends or implements identifier.

A plain name like agInit is unique enough to suppress everywhere. A common name like refresh or execute would cause false negatives on unrelated classes, so scope it with implements or extends. A scoped rule needs at least one of extends or implements. Fallow rejects an object rule without either at load time.
Use usedClassMembers for libraries that call methods on your classes through reflection. Examples:
Any strategy or plugin pattern in which the library calls your methods, and your own code does not.
The allowlist applies only to class methods and properties. Fallow still checks enum members with the same names.
For a project-wide allowlist that applies whatever packages are installed, use the top-level usedClassMembers field in your fallow config. See Configuration overview.

Some frameworks declare their entry points in a manifest file in each package, not in package.json main/exports or a single app entry. A large monorepo can have hundreds of these manifests, and the fields of each manifest decide its entry file. Static entryPoints globs cannot read those fields. With manifestEntries, a plugin gets its entries from the manifests.
Finds manifest files with a recursive glob.

For every manifest that passes the when gate of the rule, resolves each entries[].path relative to the directory of that manifest into an entry point. The entry point gets the entryPointRole of the plugin.
Kibana uses this manifest shape, and fallow has a built-in kibana plugin for it. You do not need a custom plugin for Kibana.

entries[].path is a glob relative to the directory of the manifest. It must include its own extension (public/index.{ts,tsx}). Fallow matches entry-point globs literally against discovered files and does not try other source extensions.
The path can contain ${dotted.field} interpolation, which expands over the named manifest field:
A string field gives one entry.
An array field gives one entry for each element.
A missing or empty field gives no entry.
Each entry can have its own when gate.

when matching uses strict equality. { "plugin.browser": true } matches a manifest whose plugin.browser is literally true. Fallow skips that entry for a manifest with plugin.browser: false. To test only that a field is present, use { "plugin.browser": { "exists": true } }. A path can go through an array of objects with [*], and it then matches when any value matches.
Manifest discovery respects .gitignore and skips node_modules. Fallow does not see manifests in ignored directories, and it would not analyze their entries anyway.
Fallow emits a warning when a manifests glob matches nothing, when a when gate excludes every manifest, or when a field path resolves in none of the matched manifests (probably a typo).

To debug a rule that seeds nothing, run fallow plugin-check --format json. For each rule, it shows which manifests matched, which passed the when gate, the entries seeded (with path_exists), and any warnings. The warnings are manifests-matched-none, when-excluded-all, field-path-unresolved, entries-empty, manifest-parse-failed, field-values-limit-exceeded, entry-expansion-limit-exceeded, entry-outside-root, and seeded-paths-missing.
Fallow searches for plugin files in this order:
Explicit paths from the plugins config field
Repo tooling that does not ship

Use a plugin with the support role for scripts that you run by hand and do not ship. In a normal run, their files stay reachable. Their imports do not count as production imports. Set "entryPointRole": "support" explicitly: then a --production run also leaves these files out, like test files, and their imports keep nothing in use.
External plugins cover most use cases. To parse config files with an AST, as the built-in ESLint and Vite plugins do, you need a built-in Rust plugin.

For IDE autocomplete, generate the schema locally with fallow plugin-schema. The local file matches the fallow version that you installed. The npm package does not include it. The fallow repository also has the schema at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/plugin-schema.json.
Then reference it in your plugin file:
The built-in framework and tooling plugins.
Check the active plugins and inspect project metadata.
Check why a custom plugin does not activate.

pages.title: fallow dead-code: find unused exports and dependencies
items: fallow dead-code: find unused exports and dependencies
Find unused files, exports, dependencies, and types in TypeScript and JavaScript. fallow dead-code traces code from your entry points and reports the rest.

fallow dead-code finds the code that nothing uses, so you can delete it and keep the codebase smaller. Fallow starts at your entry points, traces all reachable exports, and reports each file, export, dependency, and type that is not used.

Bare fallow runs all analyses (dead code, architecture, duplication, and health). To run only the dead code analysis, use fallow dead-code. For import cycles, boundaries, and policy rules, use fallow architecture. fallow check is still a hidden alias for fallow dead-code.

fallow dead-code
fallow check # Hidden alias for fallow dead-code
The five deprecated aliases continue to work in version 3.

When a filter flag asks for a rule that the config sets to off, fallow does not run that check. It prints a note on stderr, for example Note: unused-dependencies is off in config, so --unused-deps did not check it. The JSON output adds a requested-rule-off entry. The findings and the exit code do not change. See Requested rules that are off.

fallow dead-code continues to report circular dependencies, re-export cycles, package cycles, boundary violations, and policy violations by default until the next major version. When the human output reports such a finding, fallow prints one hint on stderr:
Tip: run `fallow architecture` for import cycles, boundaries and policy rules. A future major version removes them from `fallow dead-code`.
--quiet and the machine formats do not print the hint. The JSON, SARIF, CodeClimate, compact, and markdown output do not change. Use fallow architecture for these findings.

Type-aware TypeScript analysis describes the safety
contract, and what fallow checks compared with tsc and Oxlint.

When a quarter or more of the saved baseline entries match no current issue, the run prints a partial-staleness warning on stderr with the command to save the baseline again. health --baseline works the same way. Some runs print no warning, because they cannot judge the loaded baseline. These are runs narrowed by --file, --changed-since, --diff-file, --workspace, --changed-workspaces or a positional path. A run also cannot judge a baseline that was saved in another mode. The file records --production and --include-entry-exports, and fallow compares them with the run. A --production run judges a baseline saved with --production. It does not judge a baseline saved without it. An --unused-* filter judges the baseline only when the run reports every category that the file holds. --fail-on-stale-baseline turns each stale entry into exit 1.

When the run loaded a baseline, the JSON output of the analysis run has a baseline_staleness object. fallow report --from renders a saved envelope again, and includes the object only if that envelope already had it. The object contains:
gate_trips, which applies the rule of --fail-on-stale-baseline, so a CI integration reads one boolean and does not need to repeat the rule
Read change_scoped before you divide the counts: a narrowed run can report matched_entries: 0 on a healthy baseline.

scope_reasons names what stops the run from judging the file, so you do not have to guess which input caused it. It is present and not empty exactly when change_scoped is true. dead-code reads the flags and reports diff, changed-since, workspace, changed-workspaces, scope, file, issue-type-filter, production and include-entry-exports. production and include-entry-exports appear when the run and the file differ on that mode, so production can appear on a run without --production. issue-type-filter appears when the file holds a category that the active --unused-* filter does not report. Each command reports what it can see, so the names differ per command. Expect new names in the set.

Use scope_reasons to see if a repeat run can remove the scope. production, include-entry-exports, workspace and changed-workspaces describe what you consider the project to be, so a repeat run keeps them. To clear production or include-entry-exports, use the same flag as the file, or save the file again.

A run can load a baseline with entries and use only the inputs that a repeat run can remove: diff, changed-since, scope, file and issue-type-filter. Such a run also adds a recheck-baseline entry to next_steps[] with the unscoped command. That command reads the baseline again and reports. It never saves the baseline again.

A run in production mode, or a run scoped to workspaces, adds no entry. These settings can come from the config and the environment as well as from a flag, so the command in the entry would be just as narrow.
For the same reason, a diff-scoped run adds no entry while you export FALLOW_DIFF_FILE.
A bare fallow run follows the same rule and adds the same entry.

Each command writes its own baseline format, and a saved baseline names that format. Every file that --save-baseline writes has a top-level kind of dead-code, dupes or health. A baseline from an earlier release has no kind and still loads. For such a file, its keys decide the format.

A dead-code baseline also names its key form. --save-baseline writes a top-level "identity": "dc1" and one canonical key for each finding, for example unused-export:src/utils.ts:helper. A canonical key holds the rule, the root-relative path and the names. It never holds a line, a column or a suppression reason, so a line shift does not change the file. The file repeats a key once for each occurrence: N saved occurrences hide at most N current findings with that key.

A dead-code baseline from an earlier release has no identity and still loads. Each old entry matches only its exact old form. Some old forms hold a line, for example the keys of stale suppressions, so these entries can go stale after a line shift. A run that loads an old baseline prints a note on stderr in human output, and sets baseline_staleness.format to legacy in JSON. Neither fails the run. Run --save-baseline once to rewrite the file in the new form. An older fallow version reads a dc1 file without an error, but matches nothing in it, so save the baseline again if you downgrade. A baseline with an identity value that this version does not know exits 2.

fallow dead-code --baseline loads a baseline of another kind as zero entries, so no entry stays unmatched. Such a run prints a warning on stderr, with or without --quiet, that names both kinds and the path. It reports baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format: true and suppresses nothing. Next to it, saved_by names the command that saved the file: dead-code, dupes, or health. The saved_by field is absent for an empty file, for a baseline saved before files named their writer, and for a writer that this version does not know. The field is present only when it is true. An absent field means false. Read this field and not baseline_entries == 0, because a baseline from a project with nothing to record is correctly empty. The baseline gate trips on such a file, so --fail-on-stale-baseline exits 1. A run with no gate turned on keeps its exit code. Invalid JSON still exits 2. A dead-code baseline that has only some of its own keys also exits 2.

# Why is formatDate reported as unused?
fallow dead-code --trace src/utils.ts:formatDate

# What imports/exports does this file have?
fallow dead-code --trace-file src/utils.ts

# Where is lodash used?
fallow dead-code --trace-dependency lodash

# Pipeline performance breakdown
fallow dead-code --performance

A whole-word text search for an export name (grep -w) does not find every consumer. The module graph finds all of them. The JSON output of --trace FILE:NAME tells you which consumers the text search does not find. Each entry in direct_references[] and in direct_references_by_namespace[].references[] has these fields:
import-alias: the consumer imports the export under another name (import { foo as bar }).
default-import: the consumer imports a default export under another name.
re-export-alias: a barrel re-exports the export under another name, and the consumer imports that name.
namespace-use: the consumer imports the whole namespace (import * as ns) and does not name the export.
dynamic-import: the consumer loads the module with import() and does not name the export.

pass-through: the consumer only forwards the export and does not use it. The consumer is a barrel (export * from, export { foo } from), or a file that imports the export and only exports it again (import { foo } from './x'; export { foo }, import bar from './x'; export { bar }, import bar from './x'; export default bar, import bar from './x'; export = bar, or a renamed re-export such as import { foo as baz } from './x'; export { baz }). The importers of the forwarding file show in the trace.

A pass-through consumer is found, and it is never a gap. A change of the export needs no edit there. Fallow checks the files that import through it on their own. A file that also uses the binding in another place stays a normal consumer. A .vue, .svelte, .astro, or .mdx file that imports the export also stays a normal consumer, because a template can use the binding.
Example: a consumer has import { formatNumber as utilFormatNumber } from "./utils". A trace of src/utils.ts:formatNumber gives this entry:

For a class member trace, each entry in owner_direct_references[] has the same fields. There the check uses the owner export name, not the member name, because a search for the class name finds the users of the class.

The --impact-closure output adds search_visibility, reason, and search_as to each coordination_gap[] entry. The check uses the consumed symbol names. When a consumer uses more than one symbol, the worst level applies: missed, then renamed, then found.

Each such entry also has search_symbol. It names the entry of consumed_symbols that search_visibility, reason, and search_as describe. For a default export, the value is default. The field is present when search_visibility is present. When the consumer uses more than one symbol, the human hint names the symbol, for example [default: name search misses it, search Widget].

Example: src/lib.ts has export default function Thing() and a formatDate export. The consumer src/multi.ts has import Widget, { formatDate } from './lib'. A search for Thing does not find the local name Widget. The --impact-closure src/lib.ts gap for that consumer has these fields (note is left out):

Fallow reads the consumer sources when the trace runs. A match in a comment or a string counts as found, because a text search finds it too. The fields are absent when no check applies, for example when fallow cannot read the consumer source. The human output marks missed and renamed references with a short hint. The MCP trace_export and impact_closure tools return the same fields. fallow audit --brief collects the gaps of the changed exports in impact_closure.search_gap. For a .vue, .svelte, .astro, or .mdx file, the declaration ranges come from the script blocks: the SFC <script> blocks, the Astro frontmatter, and the MDX statements. So a change inside a declaration body in such a file counts.

A framework calls some exports by convention, so no file imports them. Examples are the default export of a Next.js page and the export that a Serverless handler names. A framework plugin marks these exports as used. The JSON output of --trace FILE:NAME lists these credits in plugin_credits. --trace-file lists them on each entry of exports[].

plugin is the plugin that gives the rule. pattern is the project-relative file pattern of the rule. When the file is reachable, a credited export traces as is_used: true, and reason names the plugin. Some credits are for the exports that a tool reads from its config files or from the files that a config names, such as a Serverless handler. These credits count only with --include-entry-exports, the same as in the analysis. The field is absent when no plugin credits the export. The MCP trace_export and trace_file tools return the same field.

--unused-deps selects six kinds. Three kinds are unused packages: unused-dependencies, unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies. Three kinds are used packages in the wrong section: type-only-dependencies, test-only-dependencies and dev-dependencies-in-production. Only the unused packages are removal candidates.
Fail only when a package is unused
Run the filter without --ci. The exit code counts only rules at error.
A project with only used packages exits 0, also when a used package is in the wrong section.
A project with an unused package in dependencies exits 1.
unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies are warn by default. They exit 0 until you set them to error:

--ci sets --fail-on-issues, so a rule at warn also fails the run. A used package in the wrong section then exits 1. To keep these findings out of the gate, pass a second config with -c. This config extends the main config and sets the placement rules to off:
This command exits 0 on a project with only used packages and 1 on a project with an unused package. Set only the placement rules that you want out of the gate to off.

This recipe gives no requested-rule-off note. For --unused-deps, the note is only for unused-dependencies, unused-dev-dependencies and unused-optional-dependencies. A placement rule at off is the way to remove it from the selection.
To stop the issue count from growing, save a regression baseline on your main branch. Then compare later runs against it, for example in PR checks.

Save a regression baseline on main:
fallow dead-code --save-regression-baseline
This writes the issue counts to .fallow/regression-baseline.json (or a custom path).

On each PR, compare against the baseline:
fallow dead-code --fail-on-regression
fallow exits with code 1 if the total issue count is more than the baseline plus the configured tolerance.

Optional: set a tolerance to allow small changes:
fallow dead-code --fail-on-regression --tolerance 2% # percentage
fallow dead-code --fail-on-regression --tolerance 5 # absolute
With --fail-on-regression and --format json, the output can include a regression object:

A regression baseline that an older version saved counts the findings in unused files. Fallow now hides these findings, so the baseline allows more new findings than before. Save the regression baseline again with --save-regression-baseline.
These flags also work with fallow dupes and bare fallow (all analyses). The regression check compares the total issue counts of all enabled analyses.
In --format json, re-export cycles have their own field, with the shape of each cycle:

files is sorted lexicographically. The multi-node shape has two or more entries, and the self-loop shape has exactly one. explanations/dead-code#re-export-cycles explains why the cycles have these shapes.
With --format json, each issue has an actions array with fix and suppress hints that a script or agent can apply.

Re-export findings include a warning note about the effect on the public API. Dependency issues use an add-to-config suppress action (not an inline comment) with the package name and config_key: "ignoreDependencies".
With --format json, the output can include these top-level objects:
Counts the resolved entry point files, in total and per source. The module graph starts from these files:

The number of findings that fallow hid because their file is an unused file. These are unused exports, types, class members, and enum members. Fallow omits the field when the count is 0. With --group-by, the field is at the root of the grouped output, and no group has it. SARIF has the same count in runs[0].properties.cascadeHidden.
Pass --show-cascade to list these findings. See Findings in unused files.
The JSON output always includes a summary counts object, with a count for each issue type. This excerpt shows some of the keys:

private_type_leaks is always in the JSON output, so the schema stays stable, but the rule is off by default. Fallow fills it only when you enable it with --private-type-leaks, or set private-type-leaks to warn or error in the configuration.

deprecated_exports_in_use works the same way: the array and the summary.deprecated_exports_in_use count are always in the JSON output. Fallow fills the array only when you enable the rule with --deprecated-exports-in-use or in rules. An unused_exports entry for an export with a @deprecated tag has deprecated: true and, when the tag has a message, deprecated_reason. Both keys are absent when the export is not deprecated.

absent_component_props contains optional props that their component reads but no inspected reachable caller supplies. Fallow omits this array when it is empty; summary.absent_component_props still reports its count. The rule is off by default. Enable it with --absent-component-props, or set absent-component-props to warn or error in rules. These are manual review candidates. See Absent component props for supported syntax and exclusions.

Each entry has component_name, prop_name, and framework to identify the prop. has_default records whether the declaration has a default. path, line, and col point to the declaration. Each entry in inspected_call_sites has path, line, and col for a reachable caller that fallow inspected. Review those callers and the default before proposing a change.

constant_parameters contains function parameters that each visible call passes in the same way. Fallow omits this array and summary.constant_parameters when no finding exists. The rule is off by default. Enable it with --constant-parameters, or set constant-parameters to warn or error in rules. These are manual review candidates. See Constant parameters for the conditions that prevent a finding.

Each entry has function_name, parameter_name, and parameter_index to identify the parameter, and path, line, and col to point to it. reason is identical-argument or never-passed. For identical-argument, value has the kind and the text of the value. kind is boolean, null, undefined, number, string, or binding for a const with a literal initializer or an enum member. A finding about one key of an object-pattern parameter has option_key, the property key, and parameter_name is the local binding of the key. line and col then point to that binding. optional and has_default describe the declaration. condition_reads counts the conditions that test the parameter. call_site_count is the exact count of calls, and inspected_call_sites lists up to 20 of them with path, line, and col.
Each finding has an optional effective_severity field (error or warn) with its rule severity, after overrides[].rules. The CI formats read it. See Levels in CI formats.
An unused dependency finding can include used_in_workspaces. This happens when the workspace that declares the package does not use it, but another workspace in the monorepo imports it:

In human, markdown, GitHub, and GitLab output, this shows as "imported in" or as an "Imported elsewhere" column. The dependency is in the wrong workspace. Move it to the workspace that imports it, and do not remove it automatically.

Each dead-code finding has an optional finding_id, stale suppressions included. Use it to track one finding across runs, or to join a finding to its SARIF result, editor diagnostic or CI review thread.

The form is dc1:<rule>:<16 hex digits>. Fallow computes the id from the rule and the subject of the finding: the root-relative path and the symbol name. The line and the column are not inputs, so these changes keep the id:
you add lines above the finding

A rename of the file or the symbol gives a new id. Another issue type also gives a new id. When two findings of one type have the same subject, for example a static and an instance member with one name, the first keeps the base id and the next one gets the suffix ~1.

Fallow computes the ids on the full result set, before the filters run. Workspace scope, --changed-since, ignoreFindings and baselines therefore never change the id of a finding that stays in the report. A finding that is absent from a scoped run, or from a run with other config, is unknown in that run. It is not resolved. To ask if a finding still exists, use --finding-id.
The field is optional in the JSON schema, so schema_version does not change. Security findings keep their own finding_id form. See fallow security.
--finding-id reports only the findings that you ask for. Repeat the flag or pass a comma-separated list:

fallow dead-code --finding-id dc1:unused-export:81a349a3b9ea3b15 --format json --quiet
fallow dead-code --finding-id dc1:unused-file:0123456789abcdef,dc1:unused-export:81a349a3b9ea3b15 --format json --quiet
The filter runs after every other filter and after the baseline, and it does not change the ids. The JSON output then has a finding_id_query object:

A missing id means "resolved" only when conclusive is true. The finding is then fixed, suppressed with an inline comment, or ignored by config such as ignoreFindings. When conclusive is false, the state of a missing id is unknown. These options make the answer not conclusive, because each one can hide a finding that still exists:
a diff, --changed-since, --workspace, --changed-workspaces, a positional path or --file
production mode or includeEntryExports, from the flag or from the config
a rule set to off for the rule of a missing id, in rules or overrides[].rules (rule-off)
inconclusive_reasons is an open set of kebab-case names. Read a name that you do not know as "not conclusive". A project with production mode in its config never gets a conclusive answer.

analysis_fingerprint hashes the fallow version, the merged config, the loaded plugins and rule packs, the detection options, the ignore files, the package.json, tsconfig and jsconfig files and the plugin config files (for example vite.config.ts). Store it with your verdict. When a later query gives another fingerprint, treat a missing id as unknown, also when conclusive is true. An edit to a manifest or a tsconfig changes the fingerprint, also when the edit fixes a dependency finding.

The exit code follows the normal rule for the filtered report: 1 when a reported finding has error severity, 0 when every requested id is missing. A malformed id exits 2, so a typo never reads as "resolved". Regression detection and --save-baseline see the findings before the id filter. In human output, a note on stderr gives the counts and says if the answer is conclusive.
The MCP analyze tool (finding_ids) and the Node bindings (findingIds on detectDeadCode) take the same option and return the same finding_id_query.
With --baseline, a baseline object shows how many entries the baseline file has, and how many of them matched a current issue and were filtered out:
The baseline_staleness object has the details. See Incremental.
When an ignoreDependencies glob matches no declared dependency, or an ignoreFindings pattern matches no finding, workspace_diagnostics[] has one entry for each such pattern:

The other output formats name the same patterns: SARIF as toolConfigurationNotifications, Markdown, the job summary, the PR comment and the review summary body as a section, and the other formats as a note on stderr. See Unmatched config patterns.

The list also names config entries that match but change nothing: an entry pattern for files that are entry points anyway (entry-pattern-redundant), an ignoreDependencies entry that hid no finding (ignore-dependencies-entry-redundant) and an ignorePatterns glob that excluded no file that fallow would otherwise analyze (ignore-patterns-entry-redundant). See Redundant config entries.
The list also names each rule that a filter flag asks for and that the config sets to off (requested-rule-off). See Requested rules that are off.
When you fix an issue, its suppression comment can stay behind. Fallow finds // fallow-ignore comments and /** @expected-unused */ JSDoc tags that no longer match an issue, so you can remove them.

# Only report stale suppressions
fallow dead-code --stale-suppressions

# JSON output includes stale_suppressions array
fallow dead-code --format json --stale-suppressions
Fallow detects two types of stale suppressions:
The stale-suppressions rule defaults to warn. To enforce it in CI, set it to error:
With --format json, stale suppressions are in the stale_suppressions array:

Use /** @expected-unused */ and not // fallow-ignore-next-line when you want fallow to tell you if a suppressed export becomes used later. Fallow checks both for staleness, but @expected-unused shows your intent more clearly.

fallow dead-code exits 1 when at least one finding has a rule at error, in every output format. A rule at warn reports the finding and does not fail the run. --fail-on-issues and --ci raise warn to error. Invalid input exits 2.
Bare fallow runs the same dead code analysis, but its exit code depends on the format:

The bare run in a machine format reports and does not gate, because the GitHub Action and the GitLab template read its output and not its exit code. Its gate_outcomes entry error-severity-findings then has status: "fail" and enforced: false. Fallow also prints one line on stderr, also under --quiet:
[W] Exit code 0: gate error-severity-findings (2 at or above error) failed, but bare fallow does not enforce it in --format json. To exit 1 on it, pass --fail-on-issues.
To fail a CI job on a bare machine run, pass --fail-on-issues or --ci. To gate only on dead code, run fallow dead-code.
Configure severity and thresholds per rule.
Run dead code analysis on every save.

pages.title: fallow type-aware: check the TypeScript companion
items: fallow type-aware: check the TypeScript companion
Check that the optional fallow-type-aware companion is installed and compatible before you use --type-aware. The status command does not analyze the project.

fallow type-aware inspects the optional TypeScript semantic companion, fallow-type-aware. The --type-aware flag of dead-code, fix, health, and other commands uses this companion. For what type-aware mode does, see Type-aware TypeScript analysis.
The command has one subcommand, status.
Reports if the companion is available and compatible with this fallow build. It does not load or analyze the project, and it does not read the config file.

fallow type-aware status
fallow type-aware status --format json --quiet
The human output is one line:
When the companion is not available, the output says so and gives an Action: line with the fix, for example the npm install command for the matching companion version.
Run the command in the same environment as the surface that you check, for example the CI job or the MCP server process. The backend and the companion path come from environment variables.
type-aware status exits 0 also when the companion is not available. Read available to decide. It accepts only human and json output. Other formats exit with code 2.
fallow type-aware status has no flags of its own. It accepts the global flags, for example --root, --format, and --quiet.
Learn what the semantic pass adds and how to install it.
Refine cleanup findings with --type-aware and run symbol queries.
Check the project readiness before the first analysis.

pages.title: fallow guard: architecture rules for a file before you edit
items: fallow guard: architecture rules for a file before you edit
Check the architecture rules for a file before you edit it. fallow guard reports the boundary zone, allowed imports, forbidden calls, and rule-pack policies.

Before you write code in a file, fallow guard tells you what the file is allowed to do. You can then choose an allowed import from the start, and you do not have to fix a violation later. For each file, guard reports:
the boundary zone of the file
the zones that the file can import from
the calls that are forbidden in that zone
each rule-pack policy in scope, with the token that suppresses it
guard reads the configuration and runs no analysis. It is fast enough to call on every edit, and it works on files that do not exist yet.

fallow guard src/ui/App.ts
fallow guard src/ui/App.ts src/db/query.ts --format json

guard shows the rules before an edit. For violations that already exist in the code, run fallow architecture after the edit. fallow audit also reports boundary-violation and policy-violation findings in the changed files.

src/ui/App.ts (zone: ui)
 note: Same-zone imports are always allowed.
 may import zones: shared, ui (same zone) type-only: db
 forbidden calls in zone: child_process.*, eval
 policy rules:
 warn house-rules/no-child-process banned-call: child_process.*
 suppress: // fallow-ignore-next-line policy-violation:house-rules/no-child-process -- <reason>
 severities: boundary-violation=error policy-violation=warn
Files that do not exist yet
guard matches the path against the zone patterns and does not read the file. You can call it for a file that you are about to create:
The JSON has "exists": false, and the human output adds an exists: false line. guard fills every rule field as usual.
For a path that matches no configured zone, guard returns "zone": null and an empty rule set. This is a normal answer and not an error: import rules do not restrict files outside every zone.

src/orphan/thing.ts (zone: none)
 note: Files outside every zone are unrestricted for import and call checks.
 may import zones: none type-only: none
 forbidden calls in zone: none
 policy rules:
 warn house-rules/no-moment banned-import: moment
 suppress: // fallow-ignore-next-line policy-violation:house-rules/no-moment -- <reason>
 severities: boundary-violation=error policy-violation=warn

A file outside every zone has no import rules, but the policy rules still apply. A rule-pack rule that declares no zones applies everywhere, so it still appears in the output. A banned-import rule with allowNames adds the list to its line, for example banned-import: three (allowed names: Vector3, Quaternion).

Some projects set boundaries.coverage.requireAllFiles. If the path does not match an allowUnmatched glob, the JSON has "coverage_required": true. An analysis run then reports the file as a boundary-coverage-violation because it belongs to no zone. The human output adds a second note that says boundaries.coverage.requireAllFiles is enabled. In scripts, read coverage_required from the JSON.

--help also lists the analysis flags. They have no effect on guard because it runs no analysis. This includes the scoping, baseline, and severity-gate flags. Any format other than human or json exits 2 with guard supports --format json or human.
guard reports no findings, so it never exits 1.
allowed_zones always contains the zone of the file itself, because same-zone imports are never restricted.
unrestricted is true when no import rule applies to the file. This happens when boundaries are not configured, or when the path is outside every zone.
policy_rules contains only the rules in scope for that file. A rule that declares zones appears only for files in those zones. The array is empty when rules.policy-violation is off.

For a gdp-proof-producer policy, allowed_files lists the globs where proof factories are permitted. proof_kinds, when present, lists the exact label filter. An absent filter checks every recognized factory call, including dynamic labels. The human output also shows the allowed producers and proof kinds. These fields describe permission; the rule's scope still comes from files, exclude, and zones.
Each policy rule reports the exact token that suppresses it. You can copy the comment directly from the output:

// fallow-ignore-next-line policy-violation:house-rules/no-moment -- vendored, migrating in Q3
import moment from "moment";
The token is policy-violation:<pack>/<rule-id>. Rule ids are unique in a pack, so the pair identifies one rule in all places.

Call guard on the files you are about to change, while you can still choose what to write. An agent that reads the rules first can pick an allowed import. An agent that runs an analysis after the edit can only fix the violation it already wrote.
After the edit, run fallow architecture to find the violations in the code:
The guard MCP tool gives the same output as fallow guard. The MCP integration guide describes it.

How fallow detects imports that cross zone boundaries.
Define zones, import rules, and forbidden calls.

pages.title: fallow architecture: cycles, boundaries and shared state
items: fallow architecture: cycles, boundaries and shared state
Find import cycles and boundary violations, or inspect an opt-in shared-state inventory in TypeScript and JavaScript projects.
fallow architecture reports the findings that break the structure of your code:
package cycles (workspace packages that import each other in a loop)
boundary violations, which include boundary coverage and forbidden calls

fallow architecture
fallow architecture --cycles
fallow architecture --boundaries --changed-since main

By default, the command runs the same analysis as fallow dead-code with only these issue types selected. The JSON output has kind: "architecture" and its own schema_version (2). With --group-by, the kind is architecture-grouped. The arrays, the finding ids, the actions, the exit codes, the gate outcomes, and the baselines are the same as on dead-code.
Run fallow guard before an edit to see the rules that apply to a file. Run fallow architecture after the edit to find the violations in the code.
Without a selection flag, the command reports all architecture issue types. You can combine the flags, for example --cycles --policy.

When a selection flag asks for a rule that the config sets to off, fallow does not run that check. It prints a note on stderr and adds a requested-rule-off entry to workspace_diagnostics[]. The findings and the exit code do not change. A run without a selection flag gives no note. See Requested rules that are off.
The global flags work as on dead-code. These include --format, --quiet, --changed-since, --workspace, --baseline, and --save-baseline.
The first command selects only the inventory. Add --cycles, --boundaries or --policy to include those findings. Ordinary runs do not collect the inventory.

Imported writes identify direct property assignments, updates and deletions through imported values, with their resolved declarations. For custom properties of window, globalThis, self or global, each group lists reads and writes to the same property in different non-test files. These sites do not establish a shared runtime or execution order.

The inventory uses static property keys. Aliases, dynamic keys, inferred mutator calls, Object.assign, destructuring targets and iteration targets are excluded. Review observations against the source before changing ownership or initialization.

Observations do not enter finding totals, health scores, baselines or automatic fixes. Parse and completeness gates still apply. In JSON, inspect shared_state.complete and shared_state.truncated. Completeness covers supported syntax; it does not imply that every runtime interaction was found.
Human, JSON and Markdown output support the inventory. Saved JSON can render as Markdown. Other formats, SARIF sidecars, --group-by and --finding-id are refused, even for an empty inventory.

Suppress intentional sites with fallow-ignore-next-line shared-state or fallow-ignore-file shared-state. Use sharedStateAllowlist in your config to exclude an exact global name and property pair. For example, [["window", "analyticsQueue"]] excludes window.analyticsQueue.
When any site matches a file, workspace or diff filter, the output keeps all reads and writes in that global group.

fallow architecture and dead-code with the matching filter flags find the same issues, with the same finding ids and exit codes. The JSON root kind, the schema_version, and the human headings are different:

These five dead-code flags are deprecated aliases. They continue to work in version 3. fallow dead-code also continues to report the architecture findings by default until the next major version. In human output, dead-code prints a hint on stderr that points to fallow architecture when it reports such a finding.

── Architecture ─────────────────────────────────────

● Circular dependencies (1)
 src/static/a.ts
 → b.ts → a.ts

● Boundary violations (1)
 src/ui/App.ts:5 → src/db/query.ts (ui → db)
The output has one "Architecture" category. The sections in it are the same as in dead-code output. With --group-by, each group has its own "Architecture" heading.
In --format json, the findings are in the same arrays as in dead-code output, for example circular_dependencies, re_export_cycles, boundary_violations, and policy_violations:

The exit codes are the same as on dead-code. A circular dependency and a boundary violation have error severity by default. A re-export cycle, a package cycle and a policy violation have warn severity by default. A rule in a rule pack can set its own severity. Change the severity in rules.

fallow architecture reads and writes the same baseline format as dead-code. You can use a baseline from fallow dead-code --save-baseline with fallow architecture --baseline. The baseline file keeps kind: "dead-code", because it is a dead-code baseline.

A fallow architecture run reports only part of the issue types. For this reason, --fail-on-stale-baseline does not gate on fallow architecture, with any baseline. A baseline that fallow architecture --save-baseline writes lists only the architecture findings. When fallow dead-code reads such a baseline, fallow shows a warning.
Save the JSON output of a run to a file. Then render the file in another format with fallow report, without a new analysis:

fallow architecture --format json -o results.json
fallow report --from results.json --format github-summary
fallow report reads the architecture and architecture-grouped kinds. Results without an inventory support every report format. A result containing shared_state supports Markdown only:

fallow architecture --shared-state --format json -o inventory.json
fallow report --from inventory.json --format markdown

# Before an edit: the rules that apply to the file
fallow guard src/ui/App.ts --format json --quiet

# After an edit: cycles, boundaries, and policy rules
fallow architecture --format json --quiet

# Only import cycles in the files that changed since main
fallow architecture --cycles --changed-since main --format json --quiet

# Only boundary findings in one workspace
fallow architecture --boundaries --workspace web

# Adopt the check on an existing codebase
fallow architecture --save-baseline fallow-architecture-baseline.json
fallow architecture --baseline fallow-architecture-baseline.json

Bare fallow also reports these findings. In human output, they show in an "Architecture" category inside the Dead Code section, after the other dead code categories. This is the same with --quiet. The JSON and the other machine formats do not change: the findings stay in the dead code part of the output.
To run only this section, pass --only architecture. To leave it out, pass --skip architecture. See global flags.
See the architecture rules for a file before you edit it.
Define zones and the imports that each zone allows.

pages.title: fallow dupes: find duplicate and copy-pasted code
items: fallow dupes: find duplicate and copy-pasted code
Find duplicate code in TypeScript and JavaScript projects. fallow dupes detects copy-pasted code blocks with suffix-array analysis and configurable thresholds.

fallow dupes finds copy-pasted code blocks across your whole codebase. Each clone group shows you code that you can extract into one shared function. You can also fail CI when duplication is more than a threshold. Fallow uses suffix-array analysis to find the clones.

When a quarter or more of the saved entries match no current clone group, the run prints a warning on stderr with the command to save the baseline again. A run narrowed by --changed-since or --production prints no warning, because it cannot judge a whole-project baseline. --workspace, --changed-workspaces, --diff-file and a positional path narrow only the rendered report. The comparison, and a new save, still cover the whole project.
When the run loaded a baseline, the JSON output of an analysis run has a baseline_staleness object. It contains:
gate_trips, which applies the rule of --fail-on-stale-baseline, so a CI integration reads one boolean and does not need to know the rule

fallow report --from renders a saved envelope again, and it includes the object only when that envelope already had it. Read change_scoped before you divide the counts: a narrowed run can report matched_entries: 0 on a healthy baseline.

scope_reasons names what narrowed the run, so you do not have to guess which input caused it. It is present and not empty exactly when change_scoped is true. dupes compares before the report filters run, so it reports only the inputs that narrow the analysis: changed-files for a resolved changed-file set, and production. Each command reports what it can see, so the names differ per command. Expect new names in the set.

A run can load a baseline with entries and use only --changed-since. Such a run also adds a recheck-baseline entry to next_steps[] with the unscoped command. That command reads the baseline again and reports. It never saves the baseline again. A run in production mode adds no entry. Production mode can come from the config and the environment as well as from a flag, so the command in the entry would be just as narrow.

Each command writes its own baseline format, and a saved baseline names that format. Every file that --save-baseline writes has a top-level kind of dead-code, dupes or health. A baseline from an earlier release has no kind and still loads. For such a file, its keys decide the format.

fallow dupes --baseline loads a baseline of another kind as zero clone groups, so no entry stays unmatched. Such a run prints a warning on stderr, with or without --quiet, that names both kinds and the path. It reports baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format: true and suppresses nothing. Next to it, saved_by names the command that saved the file: dead-code, dupes, or health. The saved_by field is absent for an empty file, for a baseline saved before files named their writer, and for a writer that this version does not know. The field is present only when it is true. An absent field means false. Read this field and not baseline_entries == 0, because a baseline from a project with no duplication is correctly empty. The baseline gate trips on such a file, so --fail-on-stale-baseline exits 1. A run with no gate turned on keeps its exit code.

On large projects, fallow dupes caches tokenized source, so later runs do not tokenize unchanged files again. The cache is on for projects with at least duplicates.minCorpusSizeForTokenCache source files (default 5000). It is stored per project under <root>/.fallow/cache/dupes-tokens-vN/. On the first save, the cache writes a .gitignore file with * next to it, so git status does not show its contents.
To disable the cache for one run, pass --no-cache.
To keep the cache off on larger projects, set a higher minCorpusSizeForTokenCache.
Below the threshold, the cache stays off: on small projects, loading and saving the cache costs more time than it saves.

With --changed-since, on a project with at least duplicates.minCorpusSizeForShingleFilter files (default 1024), fallow also drops some unchanged files before it builds the suffix array. It drops each unchanged file whose k-token shingles do not overlap any changed file. You set both options in the [duplicates] section of .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, or .fallow.toml.

By default, fallow dupes skips common framework output: .next, .nuxt, .svelte-kit, .turbo, .parcel-cache, .vite, .cache, out, and storybook-static. Fallow adds these defaults to duplicates.ignore. They do not replace your configured ignores.

By default, fallow also skips test and mock files: *.test.*, *.spec.*, __tests__/, and __mocks__/ paths. Test setup is often repetitive on purpose, and it causes much noise on the first run of a hand-coded project. These patterns are part of the same ignoreDefaults set as the generated-output ignores.
To opt out and use only your duplicates.ignore list, set ignoreDefaults to false.
To accept one clone group and keep all other duplication findings, add the group to duplicates.ignoredClones:

The key is <fingerprint>:<instance_count>. Copy the fingerprint from the human listing or from clone_groups[].fingerprint in JSON. When the tokens change or a new occurrence appears, fallow reports the group again. An edit that changes only the formatting keeps the same fingerprint.
Collision handles use dup:<16hex>-rN. Ordinary short and widened handles do not change. Older dup:<16hex>-N handles no longer select or suppress a group.
To replace a saved key, run fallow dupes again and review the reported group. Do not insert r into the old handle.
Upgrade all runners before you add -rN keys to a shared ignoredClones configuration.
For the baseline behavior, see migrating collision handles.

Both flags keep only the clone groups with at least one instance under a selected workspace root. Fallow still builds the full cross-workspace index. It then computes the reported groups and the duplication_percentage stat again from the scoped part.
Each mode normalizes more syntax than the previous one before it compares code. You find more clones, with less precision.
From strict to semantic, you find more clones and also more possible false positives. Start with mild, and increase the sensitivity when you need to.

The default report and --top rank clone groups by duplicated token count times occurrence count, with a spread boost. spread is the maximum directory-tree distance between instances. In a same-file group, each 250 lines between instances count as one spread step. The boost is at most 15%.
Each JSON clone_groups[] entry has these fields:
spread: maximum directory or same-file line distance
similarity: lowest all-pairs similarity for near-miss groups, omitted for exact groups
Each entry in clone_groups[].instances[] can also have is_symlink: true. See Symlinked files.

start_line and end_line of an instance are 1-based. start_col and end_col are 0-based byte column offsets, the same as the column fields of the other analyses. On a line with non-ASCII text before the column, a byte column is larger than a character count.
stats always describes the corpus that the run measured. A presentation cap such as --top shortens the arrays and does not change stats. Four counters on the envelope report the split:

clone_groups_shown + clone_groups_omitted always equals stats.clone_groups. In the same way, the family counters add up to stats.clone_families. Read clone_groups_shown for the number of groups in the array. Read stats.clone_groups for the number of groups in the project.

Scope filters work differently from presentation caps. --changed-since, --workspace, and a duplication baseline narrow the corpus itself. Fallow computes stats again for the narrowed corpus, and reports nothing as omitted.
The human output gives the same information in words. A capped run ends the listing with the counts that it withheld:

... and 63 more clone groups
 ... and 52 more clone families withheld by the same display limit
With --summary, the counts block shows the corpus totals next to the shown counts. This makes it clear that the numbers cover two scopes:

2 Clone families
 2 Clone groups
 2,605 Duplicated lines
 9.5% Duplication rate
 ... and 63 more clone groups and 52 more clone families withheld by a display limit
 Corpus totals: 65 clone groups, 54 clone families; duplicated lines and rate cover all of it
The stats object can also include these fields. Fallow omits them when they are zero.
near_candidates_skipped, when bounded-work limits skip near-miss comparisons

A clone instance can come from a file whose path is a symlink, or lies under a symlinked directory, inside the project root. Such a clone can be one file under two paths, not copied code. Fallow marks these instances in each output format:
JSON: is_symlink: true on the instance. Fallow omits the field when it is false.
Human: a (symlink) marker after the location.

By default, the report keeps symlinked instances. To report only duplication between real files, pass --ignore-symlinks or set duplicates.ignoreSymlinks: true in the config. Fallow then removes the symlinked files from the duplication corpus. A clone group with fewer than two remaining instances is not reported. The file and line totals in stats and the duplication percentage that --threshold checks count only real files. --no-ignore-symlinks overrides a config value of true.
Without a gate flag, fallow dupes exits 0, also when it finds clone groups. These flags turn on a gate:

The duplication-findings entry is present only when you pass --fail-on-issues or --ci. It is always enforced. observed is the number of clone groups and threshold is 0. The bare run with --only dupes --fail-on-issues uses the same gate. Invalid input exits 2. For the parse error gate, see global flags.

Before fallow 3.32.0, fallow dupes --fail-on-issues and fallow dupes --ci exited 0 when they found clone groups. A CI job that runs fallow dupes --ci now fails when the project has clone groups. To keep a job that only reports, use --format sarif --quiet in place of --ci, or gate with --threshold. The GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template already failed such a job, so their result does not change.

● Duplicates (3 clone groups)

 5,433 lines 2 instances
 deno/lib/types.ts:45-5477
 src/types.ts:45-5477

 914 lines 2 instances
 deno/lib/__tests__/string.test.ts:8-921
 src/__tests__/string.test.ts:7-920

 42 lines 3 instances
 src/features/forecasting/server/procedures/analytics.ts:141-181
 src/features/forecasting/server/procedures/cashflow.ts:153-194
 src/features/forecasting/server/procedures/income.ts:590-631

 Identical code blocks detected via suffix-array analysis, https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/duplication/#clone-groups

✓ 27,255 lines (19.4%) duplicated across 398 files (0.23s)

● Duplicates (3 clone groups)
 ...

✗ 27,255 lines (19.4%) duplicated across 398 files (0.23s)
Duplication (19.4%) exceeds threshold (15%)
When fallow detects two directories that are mostly duplicates (for example, a deno/ mirror of src/), the JSON output includes a mirrored_directories array:
Each entry names the two directories, the shared filenames, and the total duplicated lines in those files.
Set default modes and thresholds in your config.

How to read clone groups and families.

pages.title: fallow similar-code: find semantically similar functions
items: fallow similar-code: find semantically similar functions
Reference for fallow similar-code: flags, subcommands, and exit codes. Find functions that may do the same job with a pinned local model, then inspect and review them.

fallow similar-code finds pairs of functions that may do the same kind of work, also when their code looks different. A pinned local model compares complete functions. Every result is an unverified candidate. A person or an agent inspects it and decides.
The command is opt-in. It does not run in bare fallow, audit, dupes, CI gates, SARIF, LSP, or auto-fix. For the full workflow, see Semantic similar code.

fallow similar-code status
fallow similar-code setup --local
fallow similar-code --format json --quiet > similar-code.json
fallow similar-code inspect <CANDIDATE_ID> --candidates similar-code.json
fallow similar-code review --candidates similar-code.json --verdicts verdicts.json
Without a subcommand, fallow similar-code runs discovery and prints the candidates.
The scope flags select which functions fallow compares first. Fallow compares only pairs where at least one function is fully in scope.
Use --yes on setup only when a person already approved the download. Project config and agents cannot approve the download.
status exits 0 also when the model is not ready. Read model_ready in its JSON output to decide.
Follow the discovery, inspect, and verdict workflow.
Find exact and near-miss copies of code first.
Use the read-only find_similar_code and inspect_similar_code tools.
Set the similarCode threshold, minimum lines, and ignore globs.

pages.title: fallow health: find complex code and refactoring targets
items: fallow health: find complex code and refactoring targets
Find complex functions and files and the best places to refactor first. fallow health combines cyclomatic and cognitive complexity, git churn, and coverage.
fallow health shows where your codebase is hard to maintain and where a refactor pays off first. It measures function complexity and file-level health, and combines them with git churn and coverage.
By default, fallow reports all standard health sections:
The coverage layers are opt-in: static reachability with --coverage-gaps, exact CRAP scores with --coverage, and runtime production evidence with --runtime-coverage.

Fallow also scans Angular templates, together with JavaScript and TypeScript functions. External templateUrl files and inline @Component({ template }) literals produce synthetic <template> findings. When the class and the template of a component both score, fallow adds a <component> rollup. The totals of the rollup drive the ranking and --targets.
To suppress inline-template findings and the rollup, put // fallow-ignore-next-line complexity above the decorator or above the worst class method.
To suppress external-template findings, put <!-- fallow-ignore-file complexity --> at the top of the template.
See Complexity metrics for what each shape counts and how to act on it.
To give known legacy functions a documented local ceiling, use health.thresholdOverrides[] in config. An override:
matches files globs and, optionally, exact functions
can set maxCyclomatic, maxCognitive, maxCrap, maxUnitSize, and maxFileLines (maxFileLines applies to whole files, so an entry that sets it must leave functions empty)
Overrides keep the exceptions visible in the output. Suppression comments hide them.

The thresholds decide which functions have a finding. The rules complexity-cyclomatic, complexity-cognitive, complexity-crap, and complexity-file-lines decide if a finding fails the run. They default to error. With warn, the finding stays in the output and fallow health exits 0. With off, fallow does not report it. overrides[].rules can set these rules for some files. See Complexity rules.

For every --sort mode, fallow orders tied complexity findings by file path, line, column, and then function name. The order and the --top selection then stay the same across checkout locations and thread settings. The metric keeps its priority.
By default, fallow includes all standard sections. To select individual sections, use these flags:
You can combine section flags (for example --complexity --hotspots).

To see how public signatures couple modules through types, add
--type-aware --type-coupling. The output is advisory. It reports exact type
edges and cycles, and does not change the health score.

When automatic project selection misses a consumer project, add repeatable
--type-aware-project <PATH> flags. To fail CI when checker evidence is
partial or unavailable, use --type-aware-require complete. See
Type-aware TypeScript analysis.

A coupling report is one report for the whole project. It carries up to
10,000 type edges. Above that limit, the report is partial, and
--type-aware-require complete fails the run. Use best-effort for a larger
project.

--mutation-report <FILE> reads a saved fallow mutation report and shows the mutation score of each complexity finding under its CRAP score. The file is the saved report of the last run (.fallow/mutation/last-report.json) or the -o file of a run. Health reads the file only. It runs no test.

 74% mutation score (17 killed, 6 survived, 1 no coverage)

 Mutation report: 3 of 4 findings matched; 1 stale file has no score. The score does not change CRAP or the health score.
The killed count in the line includes the timeout mutants, because both count as detected.
A finding matches a function of the report when the path, the first line, and the name are the same.
A function whose file changed since the run is stale. It shows mutation score: stale (file changed since the run) and no score, so a changed function never shows an old value.
The mutation score never changes CRAP, the health score, the vital signs, or a gate.
Only complexity findings get a score. A function under each threshold has no finding, so its score stays in the mutation report.
The SARIF, CodeClimate, markdown, and compact formats do not show the score.
A --plan document, a missing file, or an invalid file exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_REPORT_INVALID.
The JSON fields are in With a mutation report.
--score, --trend, and --save-snapshot also work on bare fallow (all analyses combined). See global flags for details.

When a quarter or more of the saved entries match no current finding, the run prints a warning on stderr with the command to save the baseline again. A run narrowed by --changed-since, --diff-file, --workspace, --changed-workspaces or --production prints no warning, because it cannot judge a whole-project baseline.

On an analysis run, summary.baseline_staleness reports how much of the baseline still matches. fallow report --from renders a saved envelope again, and includes this object only if that envelope already had it. The object has:
gate_trips, which follows the rule of the --fail-on-stale-baseline flag
Read change_scoped before you divide the counts. A narrowed run can report matched_entries: 0 on a healthy baseline.

scope_reasons names what narrowed the run, so you can see which input is responsible. It is present and not empty exactly when change_scoped is true. health compares after the flags resolve. It reports diff, changed-files for a resolved changed-file set, workspace for both --workspace and --changed-workspaces, and production. Each command reports what it can see, so the names differ per command. Treat the set as open.

When a run loads a baseline with entries and is narrowed only by a diff or --changed-since, it adds a recheck-baseline entry to next_steps[] with the unscoped command. That command reads the baseline again and reports. It never saves the baseline again. A run in production mode, or a run scoped to workspaces, gets no entry. Those scopes also come from config and from the environment, not only from a flag, so the command in the entry would be just as narrow. For the same reason, a diff-scoped run gets no entry while you export FALLOW_DIFF_FILE.

Each command writes its own baseline format, and a saved baseline names that format. Every file that --save-baseline writes has a top-level kind of dead-code, dupes or health. A baseline from an earlier release has no kind and still loads. For such a file, its keys decide the format.

fallow health --baseline loads a baseline of another kind as zero entries, so no entry stays unmatched. Such a run prints a warning on stderr, with or without --quiet, that names both kinds and the path. It reports summary.baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format: true and suppresses nothing. Next to it, saved_by names the command that saved the file: dead-code, dupes, or health. The saved_by field is absent for an empty file, for a baseline saved before files named their writer, and for a writer that this version does not know. The field is present only when it is true. An absent field means false. Read this field, not baseline_entries == 0, because a baseline from a project with nothing above the threshold is correctly empty. The baseline gate trips on such a file, so --fail-on-stale-baseline exits 1. A run without a gate keeps its exit code.

Plain fallow health (no gate flag) exits 1 on any finding whose complexity-* rule is error, which is the default. A finding with rule warn shows in the output and does not fail the run. To show health without a failure, use --report-only. When a run exits 1 under --quiet or in a machine format, fallow prints one stderr line that names the failed gate, for example [X] Exit code 1: gate health-findings (3 at or above error) failed. A workspace warning such as node-modules-missing never changes the exit code. The gate flags change what sets the exit code:

--report-only cannot be combined with --min-score or --min-severity (exit code 2). A --mutation-report file that is a plan, is missing, or does not parse also exits with code 2. With --fail-on-issues (or --ci, which sets it), a warn complexity finding becomes error: the JSON effective_severity and the CI levels of the finding are then error too.

With --fail-on-parse-error or failOnParseError, the run also exits 1 when fallow cannot parse a source file. --report-only shows this verdict and does not fail. With or without the gate, fallow health names each file that did not parse cleanly in the report body, below the health score. The score does not change.

The human summary line shows a yellow ⚠ when the run passes with findings, for example with only warn findings or with --report-only. A red ✗ shows only when a gate fails the run. A run with no finding and no failing gate shows ✓. The runtime-coverage gate (--runtime-coverage) and the coverage-gap gate stay independent, explicit opt-ins. --min-score does not demote them. To gate only on complexity that a change introduces, use fallow audit --gate new-only.

Fallow orders file scores by risk-aware triage concern: the larger of low-MI concern and CRAP risk. Files with very high untested complexity then stay near the top, even when their Maintainability Index is not the lowest. File health scores documents the formula and its components.
Each file score reports these metrics (informational, not in the formula):
The hotspot score finds files that are complex and also change often. Hotspot metrics documents the formula, the recency weighting, and the trend rules.
The hotspot summary in the JSON output gives context about the analysis:

Ownership analysis shows where knowledge can get lost, which high-churn files have no owner, and who should review a change. Pass --ownership (with or instead of --hotspots) to add ownership signals to each hotspot entry. Fallow derives the signals from git author history and the CODEOWNERS file of the repository.

fallow health --hotspots --ownership
fallow health --hotspots --ownership --ownership-emails anonymized --format json
Human output adds a summary line above the hotspot list. It shows how many hotspots depend on a single recent contributor, and the top authors across the set:

The color of the bus= marker follows the actual risk:
bus=1 (sole author): red + bold when share is 100% (one person, no co-authors)
bus=1 (at risk): red + bold when bus=1 AND trend is accelerating (active, high-concentration file)
bus=1: yellow for the common case (bus=1 without extreme share or acceleration)
Red is only for the strongest signals. It keeps its meaning on repos where most hotspots have a single contributor.

Fallow keeps test files in the hotspot ranking on purpose, because test maintenance IS real work. It tags them with [test], so you can tell them apart from production code. In JSON, these files have an is_test_path: true field.
A file is a test file when one of these conditions is true:
A directory in its path is test, tests, __tests__, __test__, spec, specs, __mocks__, __fixtures__, fixtures, __snapshots__ or e2e. A directory at the project root also counts.
The match ignores ASCII case. fallow audit and fallow similar-code inspect use the same definition for test files.
With --ownership, the actions array on hotspot entries can have up to three more action types. AI agents can use them to act on ownership signals:

By default, fallow shows only the local part of an author email (for example alice@example.com shows as alice). Fallow also removes GitHub-style noreply prefixes (12345+alice@users.noreply.github.com shows as alice). To change this, use --ownership-emails:

The anonymized and hash modes use xxh3 for pseudonyms that stay the same across runs. xxh3 is not a cryptographic hash. Anyone with a list of the email addresses in an organization can brute-force a rainbow table. These modes keep raw PII out of CI artifacts (SARIF, code-scanning uploads). They do not give strong privacy.

botPatterns are glob patterns that fallow matches against the raw author email. The default list covers *\[bot\]* (with escaped brackets, because [abc] is a glob character class), dependabot*, renovate*, github-actions*, svc-*, and *-service-account*.

*noreply* is NOT a default, on purpose. Most human GitHub contributors commit from <id>+<handle>@users.noreply.github.com (the GitHub privacy default). A noreply filter would silently exclude most real authors. The actual bot accounts already match \[bot\].

fallow computes ownership signals only when --hotspots runs and a file passes the min_commits threshold (default 3). The analysis then runs only on files with enough history. Squash-merged commits make single authors look more dominant, and shallow clones distort the result more. Fallow warns about both when --ownership is active.
Importing churn from a non-git VCS
Use --churn-file to get hotspots, ownership, and refactoring targets on a project that does not use git.

--hotspots, --ownership, and --targets read change history from git log. On a project with no git repository (Yandex Arc, Mercurial, Perforce), they print note: hotspot analysis skipped: no git repository found and exit 0.

--churn-file <PATH> reads the history from a normalized JSON file instead. A small wrapper translates your VCS log into the contract. Fallow then runs the same recency weighting, trend, and ownership logic on the imported events. Fallow resolves the file relative to --root. When a git repository is also present, the file wins.
Add one entry per (commit, file) pair, the same shape as the output of <vcs> log --numstat.
Fallow ignores extra fields, so a wrapper can add metadata (a commit id, a timezone) safely.
For git, fallow runs git log --numstat --no-merges --no-renames --use-mailmap. A wrapper should copy these four behaviors. If it does not, hotspots and ownership are skewed:
Omit merge commits. Otherwise the merge author looks like a contributor to every merged file. That makes the bus-factor too high and skews the trend.
Omit binary-file rows entirely (do not emit 0/0). git skips binary -/- numstat rows.

Renames: emit under the new path only, with the real add/delete count. Do not emit a row that deletes the old path. (Perforce models a move as a full-size delete of the old file and a full-size add of the new file, which would create fake hotspots.)
One row per (commit, file), with timestamp in UTC seconds.

Author identity is an opaque key. fallow does NOT apply mailmap to imported authors, so emit one canonical form per person (preferably the email). If your VCS records commits under a merge or CI bot identity, add that identity to health.ownership.botPatterns in config. Otherwise the bus-factor drops to 1 everywhere.

Validation is strict where the math depends on it. fallow rejects a timestamp more than a year in the future with exit 2. Such a value is almost always milliseconds instead of seconds. An empty events array is valid (no hotspots), not an error. A malformed file stops the run with a clear error, and fallow never skips it silently.
This Mercurial example reads the last six months, excludes merges, and emits one event per file per commit:

# hg-churn.sh: emit fallow-churn/v1 for the last 6 months (no merges).
hg log --no-merges --rev 'date(">6 months ago")' \
 --template '{date|hgdate}\t{author|email}\t{join(files, "\t")}\n' \
| python3 -c '
import json, sys
events = []
for line in sys.stdin:
 cols = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
 if len(cols) < 3:
 continue
 ts = int(cols[0].split()[0]) # hgdate is "epoch tzoffset"; take the epoch
 author = cols[1]
 for path in cols[2:]:
 events.append({"path": path, "timestamp": ts, "author": author,
 "added": 0, "deleted": 0})
print(json.dumps({"schema": "fallow-churn/v1", "events": events}))
' > churn.json

The hg template separates fields with tabs (\t), which never appear in paths or emails. The script sets the per-file added/deleted to 0. Fill them in if your VCS gives line counts at low cost. The hotspot score uses the number of commit events, not line totals, so the ranking is correct either way. For Yandex Arc, build the same shape from arc log. For Perforce, build it from p4 changes + p4 describe.

--churn-file feeds only the churn-backed health signals: --hotspots, --ownership, and --targets. The diff-based commands need git, because they need the tree of the base revision, not only the history:
For the line and file filters of --changed-since, use the file-based equivalent: --diff-file / --diff-stdin accept a unified diff. If your VCS can emit a git-format patch, pass that patch.
fallow audit and fallow impact check out the base revision into a temporary git worktree and analyze it again. That needs the real contents of the base tree, so they require git.

Vital signs give you a few top-level numbers for the health of the codebase. When file scores are on (with --file-scores, or implicitly with --save-snapshot), the JSON output has a vital_signs object.
Snapshots let you track the health of your codebase across builds, sprints, or releases. Use --save-snapshot to record the vital signs at one point in time.

Score trends require a known formula version that matches the current score. If the baseline formula is missing or different, the report explains why it omitted the score delta. Stored scores and grades remain historical values. Raw metric trends still compare normally.

With --group-by, --trend and --trend-from also compare each group against the same group key in the baseline snapshot. The baseline must be saved with the same --group-by mode. Each group gets trend_status:
compared: the group has a trend object with the same shape as health_trend.
new_group: the baseline holds no group with this key.
no_group_baseline: the baseline holds no group data for this mode. The run also records a trend-group-baseline-unavailable entry in workspace_diagnostics. The project trend still works.
To build a history of codebase health, store snapshots as CI artifacts or commit them to your repo.

The fields of a section appear only when that section is on. A section that is off is absent from the envelope, not empty.

A health input that failed to load gives zeros, and such a zero looks like a clean measurement. To tell a measured zero from a missing measurement, read the number together with workspace_diagnostics[]. A diagnostic with degrades_analysis: true next to a zero means that fallow measured nothing.
These inputs report in this way:
A project with no git repository.
A --since window fallow could not read.
A --churn-file that became unreadable after validation.

The inputs that stop churn share one kind, hotspots-skipped. Its cause names the input: not-a-repository, invalid-since or churn-file-unreadable. coverage-auto-detected is an exception. It names the coverage file that fed the CRAP scores, so it reports the source of an input that did load. It leaves degrades_analysis unset. A shallow clone, or a history window with too few analyzed commits, also gives an empty change_coupling.pairs list and the kind change-coupling-skipped, with cause shallow-clone or too-few-commits. That kind does not degrade the analysis, because the other sections still measure, so it leaves degrades_analysis unset. Debugging lists every kind, and which numbers each kind leaves at zero.
Select on degrades_analysis, not on a list of kinds. A kind that fallow adds later then reaches your tool without a change:
Fallow writes every entry with or without --quiet, so a CI job that drops stderr still reads it.

A complexity finding that fallow evaluated with a local ceiling includes effective_thresholds and threshold_source: "override". When configured threshold overrides affect a run, JSON also includes a top-level threshold_overrides[] array. See Threshold overrides below.

Each complexity finding has an optional effective_severity field (error or warn) with the result of its complexity-* rule. The severity field keeps the band (moderate, high, or critical). The CI formats take their level from effective_severity. See Levels in CI formats.

With --css, JSON also includes css_analytics for descriptive CSS evidence and styling_findings for first-class styling issues. Each styling finding has code, sub_kind, effective_severity, location, evidence value, and read-only actions. You configure styling findings through the styling rules.

Use threshold_overrides[] to find overrides that no longer do anything or do not go far enough. When configured health.thresholdOverrides[] entries affect a run, JSON includes this array. It has one row per entry per threshold dimension that the entry uses:
complexity covers the maxCyclomatic, maxCognitive, maxUnitSize, and maxFileLines ceilings. A maxFileLines row names the file-level unit <file>.
An entry that configures a structural ceiling and also maxCrap produces two rows with the same override_index. To count configured entries and not rows, group on override_index.

In this row, the first configured entry raised the CRAP ceiling to 40. legacyFlow scores 56, so the CRAP finding stays. outstanding shows that the unit also still breaches the complexity dimension. An insufficient row means that the override applied but did not resolve the finding. Raise the ceiling more or fix the function.
With --file-scores, the JSON output has more fields:

--file-scores adds the file_scores array and the summary.files_scored / summary.average_maintainability / summary.coverage_model fields. The coverage_model field shows how fallow got the CRAP coverage:
static_estimated (default): a per-function estimate from export references (85% direct, 40% indirect, 0% untested).

istanbul: real per-function statement coverage from the --coverage flag or an auto-detected coverage-final.json. summary.coverage_input_format tells which input the coverage came from: istanbul or v8.
CRAP findings have a coverage_source field. When the output has such findings, summary.coverage_source_consistency reports uniform or mixed, even when summary.coverage_model is absent.
