Each metric has a direction (improving, declining, or stable) that shows if the change is good. Percentage metrics have previous_count and current_count with the raw numerator and denominator. overall_direction is the majority vote across all metrics.
--trend requires at least one saved snapshot in .fallow/snapshots/. Create snapshots first with --save-snapshot. Without snapshots, the output has no health_trend object.

Coverage gaps show the runtime code that no test reaches. With --coverage-gaps, the JSON output has a coverage_gaps object. It lists the runtime files and exports that no test dependency path reaches.

The analysis is mock-aware. Some tests replace a module with vi.mock / jest.mock and a statically closed factory. Such a factory provably never loads the original: it has no vi.importActual / jest.requireActual, and no outer imports of the mocked module. Such a test does not count as reaching that module. A module that tests import only behind such a mock can therefore show up as a gap.
When fallow cannot prove that a mock replaces the module, the module keeps its coverage credit:
Automock (vi.mock / jest.mock without a factory) never removes credit, because the runner can still evaluate the original module.
vi.doMock / jest.doMock never remove credit, because they are not hoisted and depend on order.

doMock also gives credit to its target. For path-shaped static specifiers like ./services/api, it also gives credit to the __mocks__ sibling. Bare package specifiers (vi.doMock('axios')) give credit to the package, but not to a root __mocks__ file. Templated specifiers give credit to nothing.

The bare fallow run applies the same rule. At warn or error, its health section reports the coverage gaps. At error, a project with gaps fails the human, compact and markdown formats. The json, sarif and codeclimate formats fail only with --fail-on-issues or --ci. The gate_outcomes object of the bare run carries the verdict as health-coverage-gaps.
Set the severity of the coverage-gaps rule to error, warn, or off in your config (default off):
The files array lists runtime files where no test dependency path reaches any export. The exports array lists single exports that no test reaches, in files that tests otherwise cover.
With --mutation-report, each matched complexity finding gets a mutation object. The findings in groups[].findings[] get the same object. The sections list then has the token mutation.
The top-level mutation object summarizes the join:
The mutation fields never change crap, the health score, the vital signs, or a gate.
Runtime coverage shows which code production actually runs. With --runtime-coverage, the JSON output has a runtime_coverage object that merges runtime evidence into the standard health report.
The runtime_coverage object gets additive fields as the fallow-cov protocol changes. summary.capture_quality is optional. HotPath.end_line lets a tool check line-range overlap against a --diff-file.

For first-run capture instructions, use fallow coverage setup. A single local capture is free. For continuous or multi-capture monitoring, start a trial with fallow license. For the concepts and trade-offs, see Runtime coverage.

The function above then has the value 2 for the gates. A chain qualifies only when all of these are true:
Every operator in the chain is ||. Parentheses do not change the chain.
Every operand is a === check between a plain identifier and a string, number, bigint, boolean, or null literal. The literal can be on either side.
Every operand checks the same identifier.

Member access (obj.kind === "a"), calls, ==, !==, template literals, and a chain that also contains another condition keep the standard count. A chain inside a wider condition, such as flag && (kind === "a" || kind === "b"), counts as one predicate, and the && still adds 1.
the cyclomatic value that maxCyclomatic and thresholdOverrides[].maxCyclomatic compare against;
the cyclomatic value in every CRAP score, so maxCrap does not fail the same chain;
the CRAP values in the file scores (crap_max, crap_above_threshold).
The health score, the complexity density, the vital signs, and the hotspots keep the standard count, so grades stay comparable across projects. The cognitive metric does not change.

In JSON output, summary.cyclomatic_policy names the policy. A finding has the policy value in cyclomatic, and the standard value in standard_cyclomatic when the two differ. With --complexity-breakdown, each || contribution of a recognized chain has "literal_membership": true.
To remove a single function from the complexity findings, add an inline comment:

The comment suppresses the cyclomatic and the cognitive metric together. File scores and vital signs do not change, because they show the actual complexity and do not raise alerts. To suppress all functions in a file, use // fallow-ignore-file complexity.
To exclude a file from the coverage-gap report, use // fallow-ignore-file coverage-gaps.
In the JSON output, each health finding has an actions array with hints that a tool can act on (refactor, add coverage, suppress). Fallow omits the suppress-line hint automatically when:

--baseline or --save-baseline is active. The baseline file already suppresses existing findings. Extra // fallow-ignore-next-line comments would become dead annotations when you regenerate the baseline.

health.suggestInlineSuppression is false in config. Use this when your team manages suppressions only through hand-written // fallow-ignore-* comments, and does not want inline suppression hints from CI in the JSON output.

When fallow omits the hint, it adds a top-level actions_meta: { "suppression_hints_omitted": true, "reason": "baseline-active" | "config-disabled" } field to the health JSON envelope. A tool can use it to see why the hint is missing.
For a finding that CRAP triggers, a rule based on the CRAP formula selects the primary action. The coverage_tier field selects the description:

Coverage CAN clear CRAP (cyclomatic < maxCrap): more coverage can bring the CRAP score of the function below maxCrap, because CRAP = CC^2 * (1 - cov/100)^3 + CC drops to CC at 100% coverage. The tier selects the description:

none (no test reaches the file, or Istanbul reports 0%): emits add-tests with a "start from scratch" description.
partial (some coverage exists, Istanbul (0, 70), or estimated 40% band): emits increase-coverage with a "targeted branch coverage" description, because the file already has a test path.

high (Istanbul >= 70, or estimated 85% band): emits increase-coverage (NOT refactor), because more coverage can still bring CRAP below the threshold when the cyclomatic complexity of the function is small enough.

Coverage CANNOT clear CRAP (cyclomatic >= maxCrap): no amount of coverage brings CRAP below the threshold. Fallow emits refactor-function instead, for every tier. The only remaining fix is lower cyclomatic complexity.

For a CRAP-only finding whose cyclomatic count is within health.crapRefactorBand of maxCyclomatic, fallow also emits a secondary refactor-function action next to the coverage action. It does so only when cognitive complexity is at or above maxCognitive / 2. The default band is 5. Set it to 0 to add the secondary refactor only when cyclomatic already reaches maxCyclomatic.

The cognitive floor suppresses the secondary refactor on flat type-tag dispatchers and JSX render maps. In those functions, the high cyclomatic count comes from a single switch with almost no cognitive load, so a refactor is the wrong advice.
See Inline suppression for all suppressible issue types.
The CRAP metric, maintainability index, hotspot scoring, and coverage model.
Find unused code next to complexity hotspots.
Set default thresholds in your config file.
Enforce complexity limits in your pipeline.
Get exact CRAP scores from Vitest coverage.

pages.title: fallow flags: find feature flags in your codebase
items: fallow flags: find feature flags in your codebase
Find feature flags in TypeScript and JavaScript code to review and retire them. fallow flags detects environment variable gates, SDK calls, and config toggles.

fallow flags finds the feature flags in your codebase, so you know where each flag is and which ones to review. For each feature flag, fallow reports the location and the detection confidence, and links it to dead code findings.
The regression options work on fallow flags only together with --retirement:

A run with --changed-since or --workspace skips the gate and saves no baseline, because its counts do not compare with a whole-project baseline. The verdict is in retirement.regression in the JSON output. The verdict of each gate also prints on stderr in every output format, so a run that exits 1 always tells you why.

# On main: record the flag counts
fallow flags --retirement --flag-age off --save-regression-baseline .fallow/flags-baseline.json

# In a pull request: fail when the PR adds a flag, or a new test-only flag
fallow flags --retirement --flag-age off --fail-on-regression \
 --regression-baseline .fallow/flags-baseline.json --reason test-only

Without --retirement, the regression options have no effect on fallow flags, write no file, and the exit code stays 0. The command prints a warning in that case. --baseline, --save-baseline, --summary, --group-by, and --performance have no effect on this command.
Fallow detects three categories of feature flag patterns:
Each detected feature flag has a confidence level. It shows how sure fallow is that the pattern is a feature flag.

A flag SDK or a flag module is an import or a top-level require() where one path segment names a flag provider or flags. Examples are @unleash/proxy-client-react, flags/next, @/lib/flags, ./featureFlags and ./flags.server. A source such as country-flag-icons, @/features/checkout/api or ./ThemeToggle is not a flag module. When the file has a flag import, a generic name has high confidence. To keep high confidence for your own isEnabled() in every file, add the name to sdkPatterns.

Fallow does not report a call to a generic name that the file declares, or that the file imports from a module of the project, such as getVariant('oak-30x40') from ./product. This applies only when the file has no flag import. A module of the project with a name such as ./featureGate, @/lib/features or ./experiments can be a flag module, so a call from it stays a flag with medium confidence.

An SDK call can name its flag through a registry of keys, such as useFlag(FLAGS.NewCheckout) or useFlag(FLAGS['NewCheckout']). Fallow reports the key that the registry member holds. The registry must be one of these:
A module-level as const object with string values: const FLAGS = { NewCheckout: 'new-checkout' } as const.
An enum with string values: enum FLAGS { NewCheckout = 'new-checkout' }.

The registry can be local or imported. A relative import names the file that declares the registry. An import through a path alias or a barrel file resolves when exactly one registry in the project has the imported name. Fallow does not report a call that it cannot resolve.
A flag read that controls a block of code is a guard. Fallow uses the guarded lines to find unused exports inside them, and reports the match in dead_code_overlap. These shapes are guards:
The test of an if statement or a ternary, for example if (useFlag('beta')).
if (!flag) return. This guards the rest of the enclosing block.
A const binding that holds one flag read, such as const enabled = useFlag('beta'). The first if, ternary, or JSX && that tests the binding is its guard.

fallow flags --retirement groups the sites of each flag into one row and lists the reasons that the flag can be retired. The report is advisory. Fallow does not remove code, and every action has auto_fixable: false. You decide which flags to remove.
The identity of a flag is its detection kind, its SDK provider and its name. In a monorepo, the workspace root is also part of the identity, so each workspace gets its own row.
single-read-site, test-only and defined-never-read count every read of the flag in the project. Reads in other workspaces and reads outside --changed-since or --workspace also count.

These reasons come from the code only. They do not tell you that a flag is on or off in production. Use --flag-state to add the state from your flag provider, or check the state in the provider before you remove the flag.
With --flag-state, these reasons are also available:

A literal const flag gets the kind constant. It shows in the retirement report only, not in feature_flags[]. The binding must be the value of the test, as in if (FEATURE_X) or if (FEATURE_X === 'on').
Each row also gives the age of the flag from git.
blame (default) runs git blame on the lines of the flag sites. The age counts from the oldest line that still holds the flag. A rewrite of a line resets its date, so this age is a lower bound.
pickaxe runs git log -S<name> for each flag name and sets first_seen to the first commit that added the name. This mode is slower on a long history.
off measures no age and starts no git process.

Ages count days to the analysis clock: the commit time of HEAD, or FALLOW_CLOCK_EPOCH when you set it. Two runs on the same commit give the same ages. Fallow keeps the results in its cache directory for the current HEAD, so a second run starts no git blame.

In a shallow clone, the age is null and workspace_diagnostics[] has a flag-age-shallow-clone entry. Run git fetch --unshallow for the full history. Outside a git repository, or on a branch without commits, the entry is flag-age-unavailable. In these cases generated_at_clock is also null.

Without git history, --max-flag-age cannot check a flag. The gate then has the status skipped in retirement.max_flag_age.status, the command prints Flag age check skipped on stderr, and the run does not fail. The default checkout of GitHub Actions is a shallow clone with depth 1, so set fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout for this gate:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
 with:
 fetch-depth: 0
- run: npx fallow flags --retirement --max-flag-age 180
retirement.max_flag_age.unmeasured counts the flags in scope without an age. The gate does not check these flags.

--flag-state <FILE> reads a local JSON file with the state of each flag in your flag provider. Fallow reads the file offline. It uses no credentials, makes no network calls and has no vendor clients. You make the file from the export of your vendor, for example with one of the jq recipes below.
The file has one vendor-neutral schema:
Fallow rejects an unknown field, an unknown state, a duplicate key and a file larger than 16 MiB. The command then exits 2 with the error code FALLOW_FLAG_STATE_INVALID.
How the export matches the code:
Only SDK flags match the export. Environment variables and config objects do not.
When source names an SDK in the project, such as launchdarkly for LaunchDarkly, only the flags of that SDK match. Thus a LaunchDarkly export does not mark your Statsig flags as missing-in-vendor.
The flags.vendorKeyPrefix config key removes a prefix from each vendor key before the match. For example, "web." makes web.new-checkout match the code flag new-checkout.
The SDK check reads every SDK site of the project. Thus a run with --changed-since or --workspace gives a flag the same vendor reasons as a full run.

vendor-only rows need a whole-project run. A run with --changed-since or --workspace adds none. These rows do not count in summary.distinct_flags, so a key that exists only in the vendor does not change the flag count of the code, and it does not trip the regression gate.

When the export file is outside the project root, for example in a CI temp directory, the evidence and the SARIF and CodeClimate locations show its file name only. All output paths stay relative to the project root.
The human output warns when the export is more than 30 days old. The JSON output gives the age in retirement.vendor_state.export_age_days.

Each recipe turns the JSON of the vendor REST API into the schema above. The field names follow the vendor APIs at the time of writing, so compare them with your export. Set state to rolled_out or serves_single_variation to true when your vendor data shows that a flag serves one variation, because that gives the strongest reason.

The list endpoints of most vendors return one page of flags per request. An export with only the first page marks every flag on the other pages as missing-in-vendor, and it adds no vendor-only row for those keys. Get every page before you run a recipe:
LaunchDarkly returns 20 flags per page by default. Set limit, and follow _links.next until it is absent. totalCount gives the number of flags.
GrowthBook pages with limit and offset. Request pages until hasMore is false.
PostHog returns about 100 flags per page. Follow the next URL until it is null.
For another vendor, read its API docs for pagination.
Then merge the pages into one file with the same shape as one page, and give that file to the recipe. For example, for LaunchDarkly pages saved as page-1.json, page-2.json and so on:
For GrowthBook use .features instead of .items, and for PostHog use .results. Compare the number of keys in flag-state.json with the flag count in your vendor before you trust missing-in-vendor.
For another vendor, or for an in-house flag service, write the same schema from its data. Set source to a name that is not an SDK label, such as in-house, to match every SDK flag.
Every format of fallow flags supports --retirement. The per-site output does not change, and the candidates come after it. A row without a reason is not a candidate and is not in these formats.
Fallow has built-in detectors for the common providers and env-var conventions, so most projects need no configuration.

If fallow flags reports No feature flags detected but your project uses feature flags, your SDK or env prefix is probably not in the defaults. Add it in the flags section of .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, or .fallow.toml.
When you run fallow flags with all defaults and fallow finds nothing, the CLI lists the built-in env prefixes and SDKs that it checked. Use this list to tell a true negative from a missing detector.

The configuration reference documents the flags fields (sdkPatterns, envPrefixes, configObjectHeuristics, vendorKeyPrefix). Fallow merges custom sdkPatterns and envPrefixes with the built-in sets. They never replace the built-in sets.
Fallow applies the custom patterns when it parses a file, and the parse cache keys on them. After a change to the flags section, the next run parses every file again.

# Detect all feature flags
fallow flags

# Show only the top 10 flags
fallow flags --top 10
With --retirement, the output also has a top-level retirement object. Without the option, the key is not there and the output does not change.
With --changed-since, the output also has a root request_outcomes object with the changed-since entry. When fallow cannot resolve the ref, the entry says so, and the report covers the whole project.
The feature_flags MCP tool wraps fallow flags --format json --quiet --explain:

Set retirement: true to add the retirement object. flag_state is the path of a vendor export (a relative path resolves against root), and flag_age is blame, pickaxe or off. The regression gates are CLI only.
The tool returns the same JSON envelope as the CLI. For setup instructions, see MCP integration.
Links feature flags to dead code findings.
Flags available on every fallow command.
Use fallow tools from AI coding agents.

pages.title: fallow security: find secret leaks and unsafe sinks
items: fallow security: find secret leaks and unsafe sinks
Find security candidates in TypeScript and JavaScript: server secrets that reach client code, and untrusted values that reach dangerous sinks. Opt-in and local.
fallow security finds local security candidates for you or a coding agent to verify. Each candidate comes with a structural trace that shows the reviewer where to look. Two rule families ship:
client-server-leak (graph-structural): a "use client" file reads a non-public process.env secret, directly or through a module that it imports transitively.
tainted-sink (a data-driven catalogue): syntactic candidates for dangerous sinks, across a catalogue of CWE categories.
Both families default to off. They run only under fallow security, never under bare fallow or the audit gate.

Findings are candidates, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Fallow reports a structural trace, so an agent or a human can verify if a secret can actually reach client-bundled code, or if untrusted input can actually reach the reported sink.
fallow security accepts these two runtime coverage flags. For the coverage formats, the capture steps and the hot-path rules, see fallow coverage.
A refactor that only touches a file with an existing sink passes. A change fails when, on a changed line, it adds a new sink or connects a new untrusted source to an existing sink.
The human output says REVIEW REQUIRED, not FAIL.
SARIF keeps every result at level: note and puts the verdict in run.properties.fallowGate.
--format json adds a gate block (mode / verdict / new_count).

newly-reachable ignores candidates that are unreachable in both trees. In this mode, diff-only inputs (--diff-file / --diff-stdin) exit 2. When newly-reachable cannot map the analysis root into the temporary base worktree, it prints a warning on stderr and analyzes the whole worktree.
8: the change adds a new candidate on the changed lines.
0: clean (or a docs-only or empty diff).
2: the gate could not compute the diff, for example because of an unfetched ref on a shallow clone, a bad ref, or a directory that is not a git repo. The gate fails loudly and never passes silently.
Exit 8 is dedicated and stable. A pipeline can soft-gate it without allow-listing real errors (GitLab allow_failure: exit_codes: [8]).

On a shallow clone, the merge-base can be missing. In GitHub Actions, set
fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout. In GitLab CI, set GIT_DEPTH: 0.

# GitHub Action / generic CI: gate the PR's committed range
fallow security --gate new --changed-since "$BASE_SHA"

# Gate existing sinks that became entry-point reachable
fallow security --gate newly-reachable --changed-since "$BASE_SHA"

# Pre-commit hook: gate the STAGED content (not committed HEAD)
git diff --cached --unified=0 | fallow security --gate new --diff-stdin

This rule finds server secrets that can end up in client code. The detector starts at each file with a top-level "use client" directive and follows static imports. It reports a candidate when the client boundary can reach a module that reads a non-public process.env value.
Two kinds of import do not extend the client cone:

An import of a Server Action module. This is a "use server" module whose value exports are all async functions. The bundler replaces the import with an action reference, so the module and its imports stay on the server. A "use server" module with a different value export, such as a top-level const, a re-export, or a default value, stays in the cone, because that export ships to the client.

An import that names only type exports. import { Props } from "./x", where x exports interface Props, is erased at build time, the same as import type. An import that also names a runtime value stays in the cone.
Fallow excludes env values that are public by convention:
The output counts dynamic import() edges that the graph cannot follow as unresolved edge files. An empty finding list with a non-zero unresolved count does not mean that the code is clean.

The rule needs at least one "use client" file as a starting point. Some projects mark no client code with this directive, for example a React Router Framework Mode app or a Vite SPA. In such a project the rule checks nothing. Fallow then adds a client-server-leak-no-client-roots entry to workspace_diagnostics, and the human output prints a blind-spot line.

A zero leak count in that run does not mean that no secret reaches client code. fallow security always runs the rule, so the entry appears in each such project. Other commands add the entry only when the config sets the rule to warn or error.

Fallow checks the same client cone (the modules that "use client" files reach) against a second sink set. It reports these findings as the server-only-import category: a "use client" file that transitively reaches a server-only module. A module counts as server-only when one of these is true:
It has a "use server" directive and a value export that is not an async function. The cone stops at a Server Action module, so its directive alone does not produce a finding.
It imports the server-only package, next/server, node:fs / node:fs/promises, or node:child_process (the node: and bare forms both count).
It imports a server-only next/headers API (cookies, headers, draftMode).

The sink set is narrow on purpose, to avoid false positives. Fallow excludes a module that comes in only through next/dynamic(() => import('./x'), { ssr: false }), the sanctioned client-only escape hatch. An import that does not run its target is not followed either: require.resolve('./x') gives only a path, and a webpack asset loader request (raw-loader!./x.js) gives the text, the bytes or a URL of the file. The human output gives this category its own label, and SARIF uses the rule id security/server-only-import.
The secret-leak check and the server-only check are independent. A client cone that reads a secret and also reaches server-only code produces one finding for each check.

tainted-sink is a data-driven catalogue of syntactic sink candidates. It finds values that go into known dangerous APIs. client-server-leak is a graph-reachability rule. tainted-sink instead flags a call, a member assignment, or a tagged template that reaches a known dangerous sink.

Most catalogue rows require a non-literal argument. A few narrow rows check literals, and flag deterministic unsafe values such as wildcard postMessage origins, weak crypto algorithms, disabled TLS validation, and JWT algorithm issues.
Each catalogue finding has kind: "tainted-sink", a category (the catalogue id), and a cwe number. The catalogue ships these categories:

The catalogue is deliberately conservative. A non-literal argument is a signal to verify, not proof of a vulnerability. Fallow does not prove that the value is attacker-controlled or that it reaches the sink unsanitized. The agent does the verification.

The output counts sink-shaped nodes whose callee fallow cannot resolve to a static path (dynamic dispatch, computed members, aliased bindings) as unresolved_callee_sites. When present, unresolved_callee_diagnostics adds bounded sample locations, top files, and reason counts for follow-up review. As with client-server-leak, an empty finding list with a non-zero count does not mean that the code is clean.
Fallow does not report flows through trusted local sanitizers. The detector recognizes:
local HTML escape helpers that the syntax proves safe
renderer helpers whose dynamic HTML fragments all go through a sanitizer
SQL identifier quoting helpers in identifier positions
Mixed HTML or SQL templates with unsanitized dynamic fragments still report as candidates. SQL identifier quoting does not count as value parameterization.
To choose which catalogue categories run, set security.categories in the config:

When both lists are empty, the ordinary catalogue categories run. hardcoded-secret and secret-to-network are include-required on purpose. They run only when you list them in security.categories.include.

secret-to-network is opt-in because legitimate auth also sends a secret in a network call, for example a bearer token to its own provider. Each candidate has the destination in candidate.network.destination. It holds the request URL when the URL is a literal, and is absent when the URL is dynamic. Use it to tell exfiltration from intended auth. Fallow never treats public-by-convention env vars (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, REACT_APP_, ...) as secrets.
To suppress a known false positive, add a file-level comment. Each rule has its own token:

One security-sink token covers every catalogue category. Suppress a finding only after you verify that the value cannot reach the sink unsanitized. For example, the input is a trusted constant, is server-only, or is sanitized upstream.

fallow security raises a top-level off for security-sink and security-client-server-leak to warn, so the command always reports candidates. To set another severity for some files, use overrides[].rules:

Each candidate takes the severity of its rule for its own path. Overrides match in the same way as for dead-code findings. An override matches the file that the candidate is anchored on: the sink site for security-sink, or the "use client" file for security-client-server-leak.
off removes the candidates in matching files. This also applies when fallow security raises the top-level off to warn.
error makes fallow security exit 1 when a candidate in a matching file stays.
A candidate fails the run only when its own rule is error. An error on one security rule does not fail the run for candidates of the other rule.
The editor diagnostics and fallow viz show the same result. The bare fallow run and fallow audit do not report security candidates, so overrides do not change them.
--format json returns a typed root envelope with kind: "security".

The configured and effective severities in config.rules are the values of the top-level rules only. An overrides[].rules entry can set another severity for a path. Such an override can drop candidates or fail the run, also when effective is warn. See Per-path severity.

When a run writes the --sarif-file document, the output has a root request_outcomes object. Its sarif-file entry is applied and names the path that the run wrote. This tells a run that wrote the document apart from a run that did not request one. A failed write makes the run exit 2 with an error document, so no envelope reports that entry as unapplied.
fallow security --summary --format json --quiet returns the same kind, schema_version, version, elapsed_ms, and config metadata. It replaces the candidate arrays with aggregate counts in summary:
attack_surface is present only when you pass --surface. Use it when an agent verifier needs the source-to-sink path context and the defensive-boundary prompts.
Each finding has kind, path, line, col, evidence, trace, actions, severity, and an optional reachability.

severity is a review-priority tier (high, medium, or low). Fallow derives it from reachability, boundary, source-backed, and runtime-hot signals. It is not a verified vulnerability verdict, and it does not change the gate or the exit codes. SARIF maps high and medium candidates to warning, and low candidates to note.

Every finding has a category. A tainted-sink finding has the catalogue id, for example "dangerous-html", and cwe (the CWE number of the category). A client-server-leak finding has category: "client-server-leak" for a secret read, or "server-only-import" for a server-only module, and no cwe. You can group candidates on category alone.

tainted-sink findings can also include reachability.untrusted_source_trace when a module with a known untrusted source imports the sink module. This trace is context for ranking and triage only. It does not prove that a specific value reaches the sink.
When reachability.reachable_from_untrusted_source is set, reachability.taint_confidence gives the strength of the association:

"arg-level" (the stronger candidate): the sink argument traces back to a source read in the same module, directly or through up to three chained local bindings. The first hop of the trace points at the line of the actual source read.
"module-level" (the weaker candidate): the sink is only in a module that a source reaches over the import graph. The source hops use the role "module-source" and never imply a proven value path.
Rank candidates with this field. Do not parse the evidence text.
When present, unresolved_callee_diagnostics adds bounded metadata about unresolved callees for follow-up review:
sampled[] rows with path, line, col, reason, and expression_kind
the sample and top-file limits that fallow applied
This is blind-spot metadata, not a finding list. It follows the same --file, --workspace, --changed-since, and --gate new scoping as the security candidates.

Each finding also has a candidate record, an optional taint_flow triple, a location-based finding_id, and a line-independent stable_finding_id. An agent can act on these fields without parsing the evidence string.
The candidate record has three slots:

source_kind: the kind of untrusted input that reaches the sink, as a stable catalogue source id such as "http-request-input", "process-env", "process-argv", "message-event-data", or "location-input". Absent when no untrusted source matched (always absent for client-server-leak). Treat an unknown id as an untrusted source of unknown kind. Never drop a candidate because its id is unknown.

sink: a complete description of the sink site (path, line, col, category, cwe, and the captured callee). You can act on candidate.sink without reading the rest of the finding. For a named import or a destructured require() binding of node:child_process, node:fs, node:fs/promises or node:vm, the callee names the module: const { execSync } = require("child_process"); execSync(cmd) gives node:child_process.execSync. A default or namespace import keeps its written callee, such as fs.readFile. URL-category sinks (SSRF, open redirect) can add url_shape when the shape is statically visible: "fixed-origin-dynamic-path" (a fixed origin with a dynamic path or query, the less alarming shape) or "dynamic-origin" (the origin itself is dynamic). The static prefix must complete the authority. A dynamic value directly after the host, in the port, or after userinfo makes the shape "dynamic-origin". A /, ?, or # after the host completes it. A relative URL counts as fixed-origin only when a path segment comes before the dynamic value: `/path/${id}` is fixed-origin, `/${id}` is "dynamic-origin".

boundary: whether the flow crosses a client_server boundary (a "use client" file in the trace) or a cross_module boundary (the source reaches the sink across one or more import hops). It also has an architecture_zone (from/to) when the anchor is part of a declared architecture-boundary violation.
There is no impact field. The verifying agent decides exploitability. Fallow flags candidates with structural evidence and a review-priority tier from severity.

taint_flow is present only when an untrusted source reaches the sink through imports. It has the { source, sink, path } shape that agent SAST tools expect. path is a compact summary (intra_module and cross_module_hops). The full ordered hop list is in reachability.untrusted_source_trace, and taint_flow does not duplicate it.

candidate.network is present only on secret-to-network candidates. Its destination field holds the URL of the network call when the URL is a static string literal. That case is usually intended auth to the credential's own provider. destination is absent when the destination is dynamic, which is the stronger exfiltration signal. Use this field to tell exfiltration from intended auth without reading the code again.

finding_id is a stable correlation id. It is identical across runs for the same rule, path, line, and column, and it matches the SARIF partialFingerprints["fallowSecurity/v2"] value of the finding. The CLI, the MCP security_candidates tool, and the language server report the same id. An editor diagnostic has it in data.findingId. Two sinks on the same line get different IDs. Use it to join JSON and SARIF output. An edit above the sink moves its line, so the finding_id changes. IDs from earlier fallow versions hash only the rule, path, and line, so every ID changes when you upgrade. See Finding identity migration.

stable_finding_id does not change when an edit moves the sink to another line. It hashes the rule, the project-relative path, and the exact source text of the full sink expression: the full assignment for an assignment sink, and the full call with all arguments for a call sink. Whitespace, comments, line endings, and trailing commas do not count. The text of a string literal counts as it is, so a new quote style gives a new ID. Identical sinks in one file get the suffix ~1, ~2, and so on, in source order. A change to the sink text or a file rename gives a new ID. Use it to track a candidate across runs (for example after a rebase) and to key stored verdicts. The field is absent when fallow does not know the exact sink text, for example for a sink in Vue, Svelte, or Angular template markup. Then key the verdict by finding_id. See Finding identity migration for the hash input of each finding kind.
Two read-only subcommands support the agent verification loop. Neither one feeds analysis assumptions back into the candidate output:
survivors joins existing candidates with the verdicts of an external verifier.
blind-spots reshapes the unresolved-callee diagnostics that fallow already produces.
See Security agent verification for the full recipe and the fallow-security-verdict/v1 verdict schema.

Show only the candidates that a verifier kept. survivors joins the raw candidate output of fallow security --format json with the verdict file of the verifier, and renders the survivors. It does not rewrite the original candidate fields.

fallow security --format json --quiet > candidates.json
# (run your verifier, writing verdicts.json keyed by stable_finding_id)
fallow security survivors --candidates candidates.json --verdicts verdicts.json

The output reports summary.unverdicted, so you can tell reviewed candidates from unreviewed ones. The human output separates verifier dispositions from candidates that still need review. Without --require-verdict-for-each-candidate, an incomplete verdict file does not fail the run. The gap shows in summary.unverdicted.

survivors exits 2 when the candidate file has a duplicate finding_id, or when the verdict file has two verdicts for one finding_id. It also exits 2 when a verdict names a finding_id that is not in the candidate file.

The finding_id of a verdict can hold the finding_id or the stable_finding_id of the candidate. A verdict keyed by stable_finding_id keeps its candidate after edits that move the sink. A verdict keyed by finding_id fails after such an edit. Two verdicts for one candidate are a duplicate, also when each verdict uses a different ID. The output stays keyed by the finding_id of the candidate.

Show a verifier where the structural trace stops. blind-spots groups the security callees that fallow could not resolve (dynamic dispatch, unmodeled framework entry points) into blind-spot output that you can act on. You can pass --file before or after the subcommand.
Hand candidates to a verifier and render the survivors.
Scoping, output, and performance flags shared by every command.
Use fallow tools from AI coding agents.

pages.title: Mutation testing with fallow mutation
items: Mutation testing for JavaScript and TypeScript. fallow mutation changes your code, runs Vitest, node:test, or bun test, and reports changes no test detects.

fallow mutation runs mutation testing on JavaScript and TypeScript code. It measures whether your tests fail when the changed code is wrong. It makes small changes to the code (mutants), runs your project tests against each mutant, and reports the mutants that no test detects.

A mutant changes one thing, for example <= to <, + to -, or true to false. When a test fails, the test detected the change and the mutant is killed. When every test passes, the mutant survived. A survivor shows a place where the code can be wrong and your tests still pass.
Fallow reports evidence. It does not write tests and it does not propose code changes. You decide what a survivor means.

Mutation testing is opt-in. Bare fallow, fallow audit, fallow health, the CI gates, SARIF, CodeClimate, and LSP never run it. The GitHub Action and the GitLab template run it only when you turn it on. See Mutation testing in CI. fallow health can read a saved report. See Mutation score in fallow health.
Only fallow mutation without --plan and inspect --replay run code. Project config cannot start a run, and the MCP server cannot start a run.
By default, fallow mutates only the changed code against the base ref. It finds the base ref in the same way as fallow audit.

The changed-code scope, --all, and paths are exclusive. --workspace and --changed-workspaces exit with code 2, because the plan cannot narrow to a workspace yet. To mutate one package, pass its directory as a path:

For changed-code scope, --diff-file, --diff-stdin, and --diff-file - use the supplied patch. An empty patch selects no mutants. If fallow cannot resolve the patch paths against the project or repository root, it exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_DIFF_NOT_APPLIED before running tests. Regenerate the patch from the project or repository root and try again.
This refusal applies to explicitly supplied patches. Inherited FALLOW_DIFF_FILE behavior is unchanged.
When fallow generates the changed-code diff, it asks Git to detect renames and copies with -M -C. Unchanged lines in a detected copy receive no mutants. Edits within the copy remain in scope.

Ordinary copy detection considers modified source files and keeps Git's configured rename limit. Copies from unchanged sources or from outside the selected package root can still appear as additions. Untracked files also remain additions.

With --diff-file, fallow uses the supplied hunks as written. A patch that describes a file as a new addition selects all its added lines. Generate the patch with git diff -M -C to include copy detection. Add --find-copies-harder to that Git command if you need to search unchanged source files too; this can take longer in large repositories.

The changed-code scope mutates only the added lines of the diff. A change to a parameter or a signature line holds no mutant, so the default scope can select nothing for it. --function-scope, or mutation.functionScope: true in the config, widens the scope:
Each added line selects all mutants of the innermost function that holds it. A parameter line, a signature line, and a body line select the same function.

When no function holds the line, the largest function that starts on the line counts, for example export function f() {. A line outside each function, for example a top-level const, selects only its own mutants.
A mutant of a nested function is part of the outer function.
The ranking still puts the mutants on added lines first.
--all and paths do not use the option, and the flag is an error with them. --recheck does not accept the flag. No flag turns the config key off.
The plan, the run, and inspect cover these files:

Vue, Svelte, and Astro components (.vue, .svelte, .astro). Only the script blocks get mutants: the Vue <script> and <script setup> blocks, the Svelte instance and module scripts, and the Astro frontmatter. The template and the styles do not change, so the framework plugin of your project compiles the mutated component.
The mutant line, column, and span in a component are positions in the whole file, not in the script block. An edit of the template does not change the mutant ids.
The framework compiler moves some code out of the script block. These positions give no mutant:

A call of a Vue compiler macro (defineProps, defineEmits, defineExpose, defineModel, defineOptions, defineSlots, withDefaults) in a <script setup> block, its arguments, and the destructure defaults of a declaration such as const { size = 1 } = defineProps().
An expression that holds a Svelte rune call, for example $state(0) or $derived(a + b). The arguments of the rune still get mutants.
An exported declaration in the Astro frontmatter.
--plan selects, maps, and ranks the mutants. It runs no code.
The plan shows each mutant with its location, function, operator, and id:

Mutation plan (no code runs)
Scope: all source files
Mutants: 8 planned, 0 pending, 0 no coverage, 0 pruned
Files: 1 instrumented, 1 test file reaches them

● Planned (8)
 #1 src/pricing.ts:2:7 applyDiscount relational-operator c65def5cd9bd279a
 #2 src/pricing.ts:2:15 applyDiscount relational-operator 72487a15b6adc213
 ...
Use the plan to see the size of a run before you start it. When the changed-code scope is empty, the output suggests fallow mutation --plan --all.
When a mutant is no_coverage and the project has test files, the plan prints one line with the test reach counts, for example No coverage by test reach: 2 mocked-only, 1 none-file.

The plan reads the package.json of the installed Vitest and runs no code. A run stops with FALLOW_MUTATION_RUNNER_UNSUPPORTED when the version is outside the supported range. The plan shows this before the run:

Runner: vitest 3.2.4 is not supported; the supported range is >=4.1.0 <6.0.0. A run stops before the first mutant.
 hint: install vitest 4.1.0 or a later version below 6.0.0; a vitest 4.x release from 4.1.0 is in the range
The plan prints these lines only when the run starts a runner, that is when the plan has a test file and a mutant. The plan still exits with code 0, because a plan is not a run.
The JSON plan has a runner object:
fallow doctor gives the same verdict in its mutation-runner check.
fallow mutation without --plan runs your project tests against each mutant.
Vitest 4.0 is not supported. Fallow stops with an error for Vitest 4.0, because that version ignores the test-id filter and each mutant looks killed.

Bun 1.3 is not supported. Fallow stops with an error for Bun 1.3, because that version gives no test results for a run that stops at the first failure, and it reports each runtime error as an assertion failure.
The default value auto selects the runner from the project, in this order:
A vitest dependency in the root package.json selects Vitest.
Otherwise, the test module that most test files import: vitest, bun:test, or node:test.
Otherwise, a bunfig.toml, bun.lock, or bun.lockb file at the root selects bun test.
Otherwise a node --test or borp command in a package.json script selects node:test.

borp is a test runner that runs node:test. Fallow reads the test files of a borp command in this order. First, it reads the positional arguments. Fallow ignores a glob that starts with !, so it does not exclude those files. Second, it reads the glob of -p or --pattern. Third, it uses the default glob **/*.test.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,mts,cts}. These files are test entry points, so the plan finds the test files of the project. Fallow does not read a .borp.yaml file.

Fallow finds Vitest in the project node_modules. For node:test and bun test, each test file runs in its own process. The test files are the files that the default patterns of the runner find. These patterns do not go into a hidden directory, such as .github/. A test file in a hidden directory also runs when the plan maps it statically and its path matches a default pattern of the runner. A mapped test file that no default pattern matches does not run, and the run is partial with the reason test-files-not-discovered.

With Vitest, a test that loads a source file with a native require, for example through createRequire(import.meta.url), also gets the mutated file. This needs Node.js 22.15 or later. On an older Node.js version, the test runs the original file, and the report lists the file in unloaded_paths. Load the file with a static import instead.

The node:test runner reads the node --test command in your package.json scripts. It reads the test script first, then the other scripts in name order. Each test process gets the module loading flags of that command:

Fallow ignores the other flags of the command. A relative --import, --require or loader path resolves against the project root. Example: a project that uses a TypeScript enum runs its tests with node --experimental-transform-types --test. fallow mutation then uses the same flag, and you do not need to set it.
NODE_OPTIONS of the fallow mutation process also reaches each test process. Use it for a Node flag that is not in the list above.

With node-test, a Node process that a test starts (for example with execFileSync(process.execPath, [...]) or fork()) also loads the mutated files. A test that checks the output of your CLI can then kill a mutant. Fallow adds its preload to NODE_OPTIONS of the test process for this. With Vitest and node:test, the code that a Node child process of a test runs counts as coverage of that test. So fallow selects a test that checks only the output of a child for the mutants that the child reaches. A child that a signal ends, or that still runs after its test ends, adds no coverage. A child process that is not Node, or that gets an environment without NODE_OPTIONS, loads the original files.
When a test file does not load, the baseline failure message starts with the error line. Example: SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode.

Node.js and Bun cannot load a Vue, Svelte, or Astro component file. With node-test or bun-test, the plan leaves each component file out. The report lists the file in skipped_files with the reason runner-cannot-load, and the human output prints one Skipped files: line. The mutants of these files do not count in the coverage. To test component files, use Vitest with the framework plugin of your project.

--runtime takes a name or a file path. A bare name such as node or bun, without a path separator, is a PATH lookup, as in a shell. On Unix, the lookup skips a file without an execute bit. A path with a separator, such as ./bin/node, is a file path relative to the current directory.

--runtime must name a runtime of the correct kind for the runner. A Bun runtime for node-test, or a Node.js runtime for bun-test, exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_RUNTIME_NOT_FOUND. For bun-test, install Bun.

--runner-config <path>, or the mutation.runnerConfig config key, selects the config file of the test runner. Use it when your project keeps its integration, UI, or browser tests in a separate Vitest config:
The flag wins over the config key. --config is a different flag: it selects the Fallow config.
A relative flag path resolves against the project root, then against the current directory. A relative config key path resolves against the project root.
The file must exist inside the project root. Otherwise the run exits with code 2, FALLOW_INVALID_MUTATION_OPTIONS, and the context mutation.runnerConfig.
Only the Vitest runner reads a config file. With node-test or bun-test, a selected config exits with code 2.
Without a selection, Vitest finds its config the usual way.

Fallow starts Vitest from the project root, as vitest run does there. The root and test.root of the selected config stay in effect, and a relative root resolves against the project root. Test files, test ids and report paths stay relative to the project root, also when the Vitest root is a subdirectory.

The selected config sets the test files that Vitest lists. When the selected config does not include a static test file of the plan, the run is partial with the reason test-files-not-discovered. See Completion.
A change to the selected config file changes the result cache key. The key does not include the files that the selected config imports.

Mutation testing (ran the project tests)
Scope: all source files
Score 71.4% killed 5 survived 2 timeout 0 complete
Coverage 87.5% no coverage 1

● Survived (2)
 src/pricing.ts
 #2 2:15 applyDiscount relational-operator if (percent <= 0) return total; -> if (percent < 0) return total;
 id 72487a15b6adc213
 covered by 1 test: src/pricing.test.ts::discount
 #3 2:15 applyDiscount relational-operator if (percent <= 0) return total; -> if (percent == 0) return total;
 id 77ac825e81517e35
 covered by 1 test: src/pricing.test.ts::discount

● No coverage (1): no test reaches these mutants
 src/pricing.ts 1 mutant test reach: 1 none-file

Next
 Inspect a survivor (runs no code): fallow mutation inspect 72487a15b6adc213
The human output shows the 10 best-ranked survivors, grouped by file. The JSON report lists all survivors and all covering tests.
The output can add these lines:
The score line adds compile error N when the survivor type check found N mutants that do not type-check.

Survivor type check: 2 checked, 1 does not type-check, 1 not checked (no-project 1) after a run with --typecheck. The line adds , N have an equivalence hint when the check hints N survivors. Each hinted survivor has a dim hint: note under it. When the check fails, the line says that the survivors keep the status survived.
Cache: 2 results came from an earlier run. Pass --no-cache to run each mutant. when the result cache gave at least one result.
A run with human output prints phase lines on stderr, so a long run does not look stalled. Each line starts with fallow: mutation: and ends with the run time:
The phases are the runner setup, the baseline run, the mutant runs with done and total counts, the retries of survivors and timeouts, and the final worktree check and report.
A run with no covered mutant and no test file prints only the final phase.
The start of each phase prints at once. A mutant count prints at most once in each interval and at the end of its phase.
A phase that prints nothing for one interval prints a line that says it continues. The interval is 5 seconds on a terminal and 15 seconds in captured output, for example a CI log.
--quiet and --format json print no progress lines. Stdout never gets a progress line, so the JSON report does not change.
The global flag --no-cache turns off the result cache for one run.

The operators are in two sets. A run that names no operator uses the default set. The opt-in operators run only when --operators, mutation.operators, or the MCP operators parameter names them. A list that names an operator replaces the default set, so --operators regex-literal,regex-assertion runs only those two. To add an opt-in operator to the defaults, name each default operator and the opt-in operator.

Most opt-in operators follow the StrykerJS mutator set. nullish-fallback is not in that set. The opt-in operators make many more mutants, and many of them are equivalent or killed by any test that runs the code. These rules apply to them:

block-statement: the directive prologue of a function body stays, so the body keeps its strictness. In a constructor, a body or block with a super(...) call keeps its statements, because each instance creation would throw. A class static block gives no mutant.

block-statement and switch-case: the range gives no mutant when it holds a declaration at its own top level (let, const, class, function, var, or a TypeScript declaration), or a var or function declaration at any depth outside a nested function. Such a declaration would change its scope in the instrumented code.
array-literal and object-literal: a destructuring pattern and an assignment target give no mutant.

method-expression: startsWith and endsWith, every and some, toLowerCase and toUpperCase, toLocaleLowerCase and toLocaleUpperCase, trimEnd and trimStart, and min and max swap. The date setters setDate and setTime, setFullYear and setMonth, setHours and setMinutes, setSeconds and setMilliseconds, and their UTC forms swap. charAt, filter, reverse, slice, sort, substr, substring, and trim are removed with their call: s.trim() becomes s. A call in an optional chain and a call on super give no mutant.
switch-case: the clause falls through to the next clause.

call-expression: a call statement, a returned call, and a concise arrow call body give no mutant, because removed-call or return-value gives the same result. This is also true when the run does not select those two operators. A call in an optional chain, a super(...) call, a require(...) call, and a logging call give no mutant. The replacement is always (void 0), so f() + 1 becomes (void 0) + 1.
throw-statement: only a throw of a new expression is removed.
regex-constructor: the pattern must be a string literal, and the flags a string literal or absent. The callee is RegExp, with or without new.
regex-assertion: \b in a character class is a backspace, so it gives no mutant.

nullish-fallback: the ?? token and the right operand are removed. The mutant survives when no test gives a null or undefined left operand. logical-operator changes ?? to &&, which does not remove the fallback. a ??= b gives no mutant. With --typecheck, a survivor can get the hint type-non-nullish.
The regex-literal operator gives one mutant for each of these tokens:
A ^ anchor at the start of an alternative is removed: at the start of the pattern, or right after (, (?:, or |. A ^ in a lookbehind stays.
A $ anchor at the end of an alternative is removed: at the end of the pattern, or right before ) or |.

A +, *, or ? quantifier is removed, together with its lazy ?, for example /\/+$/ to /\/$/. When the removal joins two tokens into another token, an empty group takes the place of the quantifier: /(a)\1?2/ becomes /(a)\1(?:)2/.
A character class is negated, for example [a-z] to [^a-z], and the reverse. A pattern with the v flag gets no negation.
A class escape gets the opposite case: \d to \D, \w to \W, and \s to \S, and the reverse.
The flags of the regular expression do not change. A mutated literal that does not parse is dropped.
These rules apply to the other operators:

negate-condition: a loop test that is a comparison or a logical expression becomes false only, because true gives an endless loop. A plain loop test such as while (x) keeps both mutants. for (init;; update) gets the test false.
negate-condition: only an operand of && or || that is a comparison or a !x gets a mutant. For dir === "." && !path.includes("/"), the mutants are true && !path.includes("/") and dir === "." && true.
relational-operator: an == or === loop test gets no true constant.
arithmetic-operator: an expression with a string or template operand gets no mutant. This applies to *, /, and %, and also to + and -.
unary-operator: -x becomes +x only when x is not a number literal.
return-value: a concise body that is already undefined, a void expression, or a boolean literal gets no mutant. A call body gets the removed-call mutant.
string-literal: a tagged template gets no mutant, because the tag reads the raw parts. A template in a type position gets no mutant.
When two rules give the same text at the same place, the result is one mutant. An existing mutant keeps its id.

The removed-chain-link operator removes one link of a fluent call chain. For export const quantitySchema = z.number().int().positive(); it gives one mutant without .int() and one mutant without .positive(), so a validation schema without a literal or an operator still gets mutants. A link is a call r.m(args) with a static member .m and a receiver r that is also a call, so the root call z.number() is not a link. The call must be in the initializer of a const declaration that no function encloses. A let or var declaration, a const in a function body, and a chain with an optional link (?.) get no mutant. A link that only adds metadata, such as .describe() in zod, gives an equivalent mutant: mark it with an equivalent verdict.

A case label of a switch gets no string-literal or boolean-literal mutant when its clause body is the same as the default body. The original label and the changed label then select the same code for each input, so no test can detect the mutant. Fallow skips the label only when all labels are string, number, boolean, or null literals, both bodies end in return, throw, break, or continue, and no other label has the original or the changed value. The mutants in the clause body still run.

The test of a counted for loop gets no != mutant from relational-operator. For a loop such as for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++), the counter takes each integer from the start to the bound, so i < 12 and i != 12 select the same iterations and no test can detect the mutant. Fallow skips it only when the counter is one let variable with an integer literal start, the bound is an integer literal that the start does not pass, the update is i++, ++i, or i += 1 (or the decrement for >), and the loop body has no other write to the counter and no eval call. The <= mutant and the constant mutant of the test still run.

A zero comparison on the length of a known array gets no equivalent mutant from relational-operator. An array length is never negative, so items.length > 0 and items.length != 0 give the same result, and no test can detect that mutant. For the same reason, Fallow skips the == mutant of items.length <= 0, the constant false of items.length < 0, and the constant true of items.length >= 0, and also the reversed forms such as 0 < items.length. The receiver must be an array literal, or a name that resolves by scope to an array binding: a const with an array literal, Array.from(...), or Array.of(...) value, a variable or parameter with the type T[], readonly T[], Array<T>, ReadonlyArray<T>, or a tuple type, or a rest parameter (...items) with no assignment to it. An object with a length property, items?.length, and items["length"] keep each mutant. A reference to a global with the same name, a redeclared binding, a with statement, a direct eval call, or a local Array binding also keeps each mutant.

A conditional lookup in an array before .filter(Boolean) gets no true mutant from negate-condition. In ["base", align ? alignment[align] : ""].filter(Boolean), a truthy align takes the same branch in the mutant. For a falsy align, the mutant reads alignment[align], which is undefined, and filter(Boolean) drops it as it drops "", so no test can detect the mutant. Fallow skips it only when the conditional is a direct element of an array literal with a .filter(Boolean) call that is not optional, the test is a local name, the consequent is obj[test] or obj?.[test] with the same name as key, and the alternate is "", an empty template, null, undefined, false, 0, or 0n. The object must be a local const object literal that is not exported, with plain properties only and no key that a falsy value converts to (undefined, null, false, 0, NaN, or the empty string), and each use of it must be a member read. The false mutant still runs. A template literal, a .join without .filter(Boolean), a .filter((v) => v) callback, a spread, getter, or __proto__ key, a write to the object, a local Boolean binding, a with statement, and a direct eval call keep the true mutant.

Fallow has no absolute-value operator (x to -x). Without type information, that operator applies to each operand of each arithmetic or relational expression. These expressions already get mutants, so the extra mutants add run time and little new information.
--mutants-per-line <N>, or mutation.mutantsPerLine in the config, keeps at most N planned mutants on each source line. The flag wins over the config key. N must be at least 1.
The plan makes the choice, before the dry run and before --max-mutants. The result cache does not change it.

A line keeps its mutants in this operator order: relational-operator, negate-condition, arithmetic-operator, logical-operator, unary-operator, update-operator, return-value, removed-call, optional-chaining, boolean-literal, string-literal, regex-literal, and removed-chain-link, then the opt-in operators method-expression, call-expression, throw-statement, switch-case, nullish-fallback, regex-assertion, regex-constructor, array-literal, object-literal, and block-statement. A stable hash of the mutant id orders the mutants of one operator, so a second run on the same code keeps the same mutants.
Each mutant that the limit leaves out is pending with pending_reason: "sampled-out". The run does not execute it. --plan shows the same status and reason.
A left-out mutant that no test covers is no_coverage, so the coverage does not depend on the limit.
summary.sampled_out and plan.counts.sampled_out give the number of left-out mutants. They are part of the pending count.
The completion is partial with the reason sampled-out when a left-out mutant stays pending.
--recheck does not accept the flag. A run of selected mutant ids never samples.
A run executes your project tests, so fallow applies these rules:

Clean worktree. A run refuses a git worktree with uncommitted changes and exits with code 2. Commit or stash your changes, or pass --allow-dirty. After the run, fallow compares the worktree with the start state and reports each path that changed.

What the check sees. The check covers tracked and untracked files. It also covers the ignored files that git lists at the start, such as .env, so a write to one of them or a delete is a change. Git lists an ignored directory such as node_modules/ or coverage/ as one entry, so the check does not see the files below it. A new ignored file is not a change, because test runs make such files. The check leaves out mutation/ in the fallow cache directory and the output files of the run.

Safe cache directory. A run refuses a cache directory that is the project root or a directory above it, or that holds a planned source or test file. It exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_UNSAFE_CACHE_DIR. Such a directory would hide the writes of your tests from the check.

Side effects. Fallow skips the mutants in a function whose own body calls a file system, process, network, or database API. A mutant in top-level code is skipped when the module makes such a call at the top level. These mutants have the status pruned with the reason side-effect-sink. A mutant there can remove a guard of a real side effect. The rule does not follow calls: a mutant in a function that calls a helper, which then makes the call, still runs. A database write through an ORM or a query builder, such as db.insert(table), db.insertInto("person") or prisma.user.create(...), counts as such a call. Fallow finds it by the method name (insert, update, delete, create, upsert, save, transaction and similar). SQL text that starts with a write verb also counts, such as sql`insert into ...` or pool.query("DELETE ..."). A prepared statement run also counts, such as stmt.run(value) after const stmt = db.prepare("INSERT ..."), unless its SQL text starts with select. The statement can be in a name or in a property that the same module sets: a declaration, an assignment, a class field (also a static or a #private field) or an object literal property. Examples are this.insert.run(value), this.#insert.run(value), Repository.insert.run(value) and statements.insert.run(value) after const statements = { insert: db.prepare("INSERT ...") }. A property matches by its name only, whatever object holds it. A statement that a function gets as a parameter, or that the module imports, does not count. A route registration such as app.delete("/items/:id", handler) does not count. The module must import a database client package (drizzle-orm, @prisma/client, kysely, pg, better-sqlite3, mongodb and similar), or import a project module that imports one. An ES import, a require() call and an impor

Project files never change. Fallow does not write to your project files. The changed copies of your files live in a run directory in the fallow cache. Two runs of the same plan share one directory, and a run never reads a partly written one. Fallow keeps the 5 most recently used run directories. It removes older ones that no run used in the last hour. The report lists any path that your tests changed.

No test process outlives fallow. The test processes run in their own process group on Unix and in a Job Object on Windows. Fallow ends them when the run ends, on SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, or SIGQUIT, and on a crash. When fallow starts with SIGHUP ignored, as under nohup, a hangup does not end the run.

No temp files stay behind. Each test runner gets its own temp directory, named fallow-mt-<id> in the system temp directory. Fallow sets TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP to it, so your tests and their child processes write their temp files there. Fallow deletes the directory when the runner ends. It also deletes it when it stops a test run after a timeout, because the teardown of your suite does not run then. On Ctrl+C or another signal, fallow deletes it before it exits. After a crash, the next run deletes it. On Unix, only your user can read the directory.

Do not redirect the report with > mutation.json. The shell creates the file before fallow starts, so the clean-worktree check refuses the run. Use -o .fallow/mutation.json or the saved report instead.
The report gives two separate values. In JSON, both are fractions from 0 to 1.

The score covers only the mutants that ran. A mutant that no test reaches is no_coverage, and it never enters the score. The coverage reports these mutants apart. A run of 200 mutants in a large project therefore gets a score that describes the 200 tested mutants.

Before the mutants run, fallow runs your tests once with no active mutant (the dry run). The dry run decides the coverage of every planned mutant, also of the mutants after the --max-mutants limit. A run that --max-mutants limits therefore reports the coverage of the full plan. A planned mutant that no test covers is no_coverage and does not use a place in the limit. The next covered pending mutant in rank order runs in its place. A cached result uses a place in the limit, so a run with the result cache can execute fewer than N mutants. The --plan output comes before the dry run, so a run can execute a mutant that the plan shows as pending.

The dry run executes the instrumented code, which is slower than your original code. So the dry run gives each test three times the test timeout of your project: the testTimeout and hookTimeout of each Vitest project, or the default timeout of bun test. A timeout that a test sets in its own code, for example test("name", fn, 1000), stays as it is.
A run with no executed mutant has no score (null in JSON).
--min-score and mutation.minScore use percent, not a fraction.
A pruned mutant has a reason. One of the reasons:

framework-config: the mutant changes framework or tool config, not tested logic. Framework config is an export that an active plugin reads, for example export const revalidate = 60 in a Next.js page. It is also the default export of a tool config file, such as vite.config.ts, vitest.config.ts, eslint.config.js, .eslintrc.js or docs/.vitepress/config.ts. A top-level module.exports = ... statement counts as the default export. When no test and no application code imports a tool config file, each mutant of the file is pruned, also a mutant in an inline Vite plugin hook or in a middleware callback. That code runs only in the build tool. When a test or application code imports the tool config file, only the config object is pruned, because that code can call its functions. An example is an Angular src/app/app.config.ts that src/main.ts imports. These mutants do not lower the coverage.

build-tool-only: only tool config files reach the file, for example a Vite plugin module that only vite.config.ts imports, and the modules that it imports. The code runs in the dev server or in the build, and no test or application code loads it. A file that a test, a setup file or application code also imports keeps its normal status. The --plan JSON counts these mutants in counts.pruned_build_tool_only. The field is absent when it is 0.
no-target-coverage: a --kill-matrix-for run skipped the mutant, because no target test covers it. See Check named tests.

A survived or timeout mutant runs a second time in a new runner process. Host load can make a test time out, so one timeout is not proof that your tests detect the mutant. The second run of a timeout gets twice the time. A mutant with "retried": true in JSON got both runs. A survived or timeout mutant without the field got no second run, because the time budget ended first, or because it is a loop timeout of short tests (see below). With --time-budget, the mutant runs keep time free for these second runs, so the result cache stores the confirmed survivors. A repeat run with the same budget then continues with the next mutants. A survivor without a second run is not stored, so a repeat run does it again.
A killed result gets no retry. A failed test is a fact about the mutant.

With Vitest, a mutant that keeps a test in an endless loop stops in under a second. The test stops when it uses more CPU time than a loop budget: 1.5 times the time of its covering tests in the baseline run, plus 500 ms. The check runs when the loop passes through code of your source files. Waiting time and other processes on the host do not count, because the budget counts the CPU time of the test thread. A loop timeout of covering tests that take 200 ms or less in the baseline run gets no second run, because the budget is then at least four times the work of the tests. Each other timeout gets the second run. On a Node.js version without process.threadCpuUsage (before 22.19 and 23.9), the budget counts wall time, and each loop timeout gets the second run.
A loop budget can also stop a mutant that only makes a test do much more work. Its status is then timeout in place of killed or survived.
A survived result with a timeout second run stays survived. The first run finished all tests with the mutant active, and host load alone can make the second run time out.

The second run of a survivor runs each test of the files of its covering tests. The first run uses only the tests that executed the mutated code in the baseline run. A test can read a value that an earlier test of its file computed and cached, so it does not execute that code itself. A kill by such a test is killed when the same tests pass in a run with no active mutant. When they do not pass, the mutant stays survived and the failed tests are baseline failures. covering_tests stays the tests that reached the mutant in the baseline run, so killed_by can name a test that is not in that list.
The second run of a survivor stops at the first test that fails, and that test decides the result. The tests of each file run in file order.

A retried mutant has an attempts array in JSON: the first run, then the second run. Each entry has the status and the duration_ms of that run alone. A killed entry has killed_by and a failure_kind (assertion, error or timeout). A timeout entry has the failure_kind timeout. A runtime_error entry has a detail with the first line of the reason. A timeout then survived result and a survived then killed result are both flaky, and attempts shows which history each one has.
A mutant without a retry, and a reused result, have no attempts.
timings.retry_ms is the time of the retries, for the survived and the timed-out mutants.

completion.status is complete or partial. Only a complete run makes an empty survivor list conclusive. A partial run lists its reasons, for example mutant-limit, time-budget, sampled-out, runtime-error, baseline-failure, typecheck-failed, or test-files-not-discovered.

The reason test-files-not-discovered means that the runner did not list a test file that the plan maps statically. For example, the test file is included only by a second Vitest config. The tests of that file never run. The errors entry with the same code names each such file. A survivor or a no_coverage mutant that such a file reaches is then not proof of a test gap. To include the file, select its config with --runner-config.

Two tests with the same full name, for example from test.each without unique titles, get one test ID each: the runner adds a number such as (2) to the second one, in report order. The kills and survivors of these IDs can belong to the other test, so they are not reliable. The errors entry duplicate-test-ids names each such ID, and the human output shows it as a warning. Only tests that ran count, so a skipped or todo twin makes no duplicate. The run does not stop, and the results of the other tests stay valid. To remove the warning, give each test a unique title.

A skipped or todo test, for example it.skip, runs no assertion, so it cannot kill a mutant. The changed-code scope warns about these tests in each runner test file that the diff adds, changes, or removes a line in:
A scan of the syntax tree finds the tests, so a change to the tests alone starts no runner.

The scan finds it, test, describe, and suite with .skip or .todo, the xit, xtest, and xdescribe aliases, and the node:test options { skip: true } and { todo: true }. A condition that the run decides, such as it.skipIf(flag) or { skip: process.env.CI }, is not a skipped test.
The errors entry skipped-tests names up to ten of these tests with file, line, and name. The human output shows it as a warning.
The run does not stop, and the completion and the exit code do not change. A run with --all or paths gives no such warning, and --plan does not show it.
A partial run does not change the exit code. The run exits with 0, with 1 when the score is lower than --min-score, or with 2 when baseline failures leave no mutant with a test result.

A test that fails in the dry run is a baseline failure. Fallow lists it in baseline_failures, and its result decides no mutant status. The message keeps the first error of the test: the error name and message, then the stack frames of your project. This also applies to the dry run of a restarted runner process, where a test can fail because it depends on state outside the test, such as the process id. Fix the failing test, then run again.

Parallel runner processes use the same project root and can share files or a database. Vitest's fileParallelism: false serializes tests within each process, but fallow can still run several processes at once.

During a parallel phase, fallow suggests --concurrency 1 or mutation.concurrency: 1 when a restarted process fails during startup or its dry run. The hint also covers a restarted process that cannot find a covering test from the baseline. Shared state is a possible cause; the report preserves the original error. Retry with one worker to check whether the failure depends on parallel execution. Serial phases and the first process's setup do not receive this hint.

When your Vitest config enables the type-check pass (typecheck.enabled), the run does not execute it. A mutant that only a type test detects is not counted as killed. The report adds typecheck-not-run to runner.notes, and the human output prints one line for it. The survivor type check does not run these type tests either.

A type test file (*.test-d.ts, *.spec-d.ts, or a TypeScript file below a test-d/ directory) is not a test file of the mutation plan. No runner executes it. A project whose only test files are type tests has no_test_files: true, and a file that only type tests reach has no coverage.

The --kill-matrix mode runs all covering tests with bail disabled. It can increase execution time.
Read the matrix evidence status before you review candidates. Normal mode reports kill-matrix-disabled and no candidates.
With --kill-matrix, incomplete evidence produces no candidates. With --kill-matrix-for, only the tests of complete targets can be candidates.

kills and unique_kills are arrays of mutant IDs.
Individual subsumers cover a candidate's full kill set. Other tests can also cover that set collectively.
Review each candidate separately, including equal kill sets. Removing equal candidates together can remove their shared protection.
A candidate does not prove safe removal. Baseline-failing tests cannot become candidates or subsumers.
