Tests with runtime coverage and no observed kills appear separately. Zero kills do not prove that a test has no assertions.
Sole-file notes use observed instrumented-file coverage. Public-export notes use static test-file reach, without per-test export coverage claims.
The mutation and mutation-inspect JSON envelopes use schema version "2". The mutation-plan envelope and verdict document keep schema version "1".
The kill_matrix object has these fields:
Each mutant and attempt records killing_tests and kill_matrix_complete. The existing killed_by field keeps the first observed killer. Outside matrix mode, killing_tests is empty.
Survivors and timeouts do not count as kills. Matrix mode uses separate cache keys and journal inputs from normal mode.

Matrix mode does not add the other tests of the covering test files to the retry of a survivor. A survivor that normal mode kills in that retry can stay survived in matrix mode, so the two modes can give different scores.

fallow mutation --all --kill-matrix-for src/cart.test.ts --format json --quiet
fallow mutation --all --kill-matrix-for "src/cart.test.ts::adds an item" --format json --quiet

--kill-matrix-for checks whether the named tests are redundant, without the cost of a full kill matrix. A target is a test file (each test in it) or a test ID (file::name). Repeat the flag for each target.
Only the mutants that a target test covers run. The other mutants are pruned with prune_reason: "no-target-coverage".
Each mutant runs its target tests with bail disabled. Then it runs its other covering tests with bail enabled, up to the first failure.
kill_matrix.tests has only the target tests. subsuming_tests is empty, because bail hides the other killers.

Each target test has the field target_only_kills. It lists the kills that only other targets share, each as { mutant_id, targets }. The test stays redundant only while one of those targets stays in the suite.
kill_matrix.targets lists each target as { target, test_ids, status, reasons }. test_ids are the dry-run test IDs that the target selects. The field is absent outside target mode.

Each target has its own evidence status: complete or incomplete. A target is incomplete with the reason incomplete-mutant-results when one of its tests covers a mutant with incomplete evidence. missing-test-file-metadata makes each target incomplete.

A baseline failure (a test that fails with no active mutant) gives a target the reason baseline-failure only when the failure can affect the target. This is true when the failing test is a test of the target or is in a test file of the target. It is also true when a test that passed the first dry run and failed a later rerun with no active mutant covers, kills, or ran without a mutant that a test of the target covers or kills. The other targets can stay complete. Shared state across test files, for example a global or a database, is outside this rule. The human report names the failures under the line of each affected target.

When baseline failures are the only cause of a partial run, only the targets with baseline-failure also get partial-mutation-run. Each other cause of a partial run, for example time-budget, gives each target partial-mutation-run.

A failing test gives no kill evidence. A passing test in the test file of a baseline failure can share state with the failure. Neither test makes the kill of a target test shared, also when it is a test of another target. Such a kill stays in unique_kills, so the target test is not a candidate.
Only the tests of a complete target can be candidates. One incomplete mutant removes only the candidates of the targets that cover it.

The top-level kill_matrix.status is incomplete when any evidence is incomplete. Thus candidates can have entries while the top-level status is incomplete. The human report shows the status and the reasons of each target.

A target that selects no test of the dry run does not stop the command. The other targets run. The entry of the target in kill_matrix.targets has empty test_ids, the status incomplete and the reason unmatched-target. One more reason tells why:
With only unmatched-target, the dry run ran the file, but no test of the file has the target ID, or each test of the file has a duplicate ID.

When no target selects a test, the command stops with exit code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_TARGET_UNMATCHED. A command with one target stops in the same way. The message names each target and its reason. When the dry run runs the file of no target, the command stops before the dry run. This is also true when no test file reaches the planned code. The same error applies when the runner cannot run single tests.

A test ID target that names a duplicate test ID stops the command with exit code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_TARGET_DUPLICATE_TEST_ID. A test file target drops its duplicate test IDs and keeps its other tests. --kill-matrix-for and --kill-matrix cannot be used together.

Each no_coverage mutant has a test_reach object in the run report and in the plan. It gives the static reason why no test covers the mutant. Mutants with other statuses do not have the object. The object never changes the score or the coverage.
none-file: no test loads the file. A project without test files gives none-file to each mutant.
mocked-only: tests reach the code only through a mock.
none: a test loads the file, but no test reaches this code.
direct or transitive on a no_coverage mutant is not a conflict. A test refers to the export, but no test ran the code of the mutant.
In the human output, each file line in the no-coverage section adds the counts by class, for example test reach: 2 mocked-only, 1 none-file.

--typecheck, or mutation.typecheck: true in the config, type-checks each survived mutant after the tests. The check uses the same TypeScript companion as --type-aware. Other mutants are not checked, so the cost grows only with the number of survivors.
The companion applies one mutant at a time to a copy of the file in memory. It never writes a project file.
It compares the type errors of the mutated file with the type errors of the original file. An error that the original file already has does not count.
A survivor with a new type error gets the status compile_error. type_error_codes lists the TypeScript error codes, sorted, at most 8. The mutant leaves the score, and it counts as covered.
The check reads only the mutated file. A mutant that breaks only another file stays survived.

A survivor that removes an optional-chaining link (a?.b to a.b, a?.() to a(), a?.[k] to a[k]) or a nullish fallback (a ?? b to a) can get an advisory hint. For a ?? b, the hint does not apply when a is an optional chain, such as o?.items.map(f) ?? []. When the declared type of a excludes null and undefined, and the mutated file type-checks, the survivor gets equivalence_hint: "type-non-nullish". The status stays survived, and the score does not change. The human report and fallow mutation tasks show one line under the survivor.

The hint needs strictNullChecks (or strict) and noUncheckedIndexedAccess in the tsconfig.json of the file, and a TypeScript file. It reads the declared type, not the narrowed type. It does not apply to any, unknown, a type parameter, a union with null or undefined, an assertion (as, <T>x, x!), an element access, or a binding that code assigns after its declaration. A declare variable, a variable in a .d.ts file, and a class property without an initializer get no hint either.

The hint is not a verdict, and it can be wrong. For example, a method that a caller detaches loses its this, so this?.value returns undefined and this.value throws. Also, a function can declare the return type { b: number } but return the result of JSON.parse("null"). Then parse(s)?.b returns undefined and parse(s).b throws. Read the code, then record an equivalent mutant with a verdict. A verdict removes the hint.

A survivor that the check cannot check stays survived. The reasons are no-project (no tsconfig.json includes the file), not-type-checked (// @ts-nocheck, or a JavaScript file without checkJs), source-changed, file-missing, and unsupported-file (a Vue, Svelte or Astro component, which the checker cannot read).

The run looks for the companion before the tests start. When no trusted companion exists, the run exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_TYPECHECK_UNAVAILABLE. Fallow finds the companion in the same way as for --type-aware: FALLOW_TYPE_AWARE_BIN, the npm wrapper, or the companion next to the fallow executable.

When the companion fails after the tests, the survivors keep the status survived. The report then has an error with the code typecheck-failed, and the completion is partial with the reason typecheck-failed.
--plan --typecheck exits with code 2, because a plan has no survivors. The config key has no effect on a plan.
With the option on, the report has a typecheck object:
The report also has summary.counts.compile_error, functions[].counts.compile_error, and timings.typecheck_ms. Without the option, the typecheck object is absent and no mutant gets compile_error.
A negate-condition survivor can get the advisory hint equivalence_hint: "constant-parameter". The hint needs no option.

Each visible call passes true for strict, so !strict is always false. The mutant if (false) changes nothing for these calls, and no test can kill it through a real caller. The mutant if (true) changes the result, so it gets no hint.
The test of the condition must be a parameter p, !p or !!p: the test of an if, a ?: or a loop. A test such as p && q gets no hint.

Each visible call must pass the same literal for the parameter. The hint uses the call evidence and the closed-world gate of the constant-parameter rule, also when the rule is off. A function that the gate blocks gets no hint, for example a function with a value reference, an export of an entry point, or a public API export. A module that only tests reach gets no hint. A test call counts as a call.
An inline or file suppression of constant-parameter removes the hint. A severity in rules or overrides does not change it.

The literal decides the test value as JavaScript does: false, null, undefined, 0, -0, NaN and "" are falsy. When each call passes undefined for a parameter with a default value, the default applies, and the survivor gets no hint.

The hint is advisory. The status stays survived, and the score does not change. A caller outside the project can still pass another value. Read the callers, then record an equivalent mutant with a verdict. A verdict removes the hint.

A run stores the result of each killed mutant and of each survived mutant that a retry confirmed. A later run uses a stored result when the key is the same, and does not run that mutant again. The dry run always runs.

The key covers the mutant, the content of its source file, its covering tests, the content of the covering test files and the files that they import, the runner setup files, the lockfile, the runner config files at the root and the files that they import, the configs that the root tsconfig.json extends, the runner and runtime versions, and the fallow version. A change to one of them runs the mutant again.

Some inputs are not in the key: dynamic imports that the module graph does not resolve, and files that your tests or the runner config read. Runner configs and tsconfig.json files below the root, for example in a workspace package, are also not in the key. A change to them does not run the mutant again. Pass --no-cache when such a change can affect your tests.
A timeout, flaky, runtime_error, or pending result is never stored.
A reused survived result also has "retried": true, because only a survivor that a retry confirmed is stored.
A reused result has "cached": true on its entry in mutants[]. Without a reused result, the key is absent. A reused result counts in the score and the coverage in the same way as a new result.

The report has a cache object: hits (the reused results), stored (the stored results), and not_keyed (["dynamic-imports", "file-reads"]). The object is absent with --no-cache, and when no test process started.
The cache file is mutation/results.json in the fallow cache directory. The cache directory has its own .gitignore.
A failed write of the cache file adds a cache-write-failed entry to errors[]. The run result stays.
The global --no-cache flag turns off the result cache. The run then reads and writes no entry.

Each run writes its final results to mutation/journal.jsonl in the fallow cache directory, by default .fallow/mutation/journal.jsonl. A result is final when the mutant is killed, or when a retry confirmed that it survived. The run writes each result when it is final. An interrupted run, for example after Ctrl-C, therefore keeps its finished results. The run writes the journal also with --no-cache.
fallow mutation --resume reuses the results in the journal and runs only the other mutants:
The dry run always runs, because it finds the covering tests.

The journal must come from a run with the same inputs. These inputs include the fallow version, the runner, the runtime, the planned files, the runner config, the scope, the operators, and --allow-side-effects. A journal of other inputs exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_RESUME_MISMATCH. The message names each input that differs.
--max-mutants, --mutants-per-line, --time-budget, and --concurrency are not inputs. You can continue a run with other limits.
--function-scope can add mutants, so a resume that changes the option can exit with code 2.
When a covering test file changed, the run does not reuse the journal result of that mutant. The mutant runs again, or its result comes from the result cache.
When no journal exists, the run starts from the beginning and does not exit. The report says why.
--plan --resume exits with code 2, because a plan runs no mutant.
A reused result has "resumed": true on its entry in mutants[]. It counts in the score and the coverage in the same way as a new result.
The report has a resume object: journal (the path), reused, rejected, and note when the run did not read a journal. The object is absent without --resume. The human output prints one Resumed: line.
A timeout, flaky, runtime_error, no_coverage, or pending result is never in the journal. These mutants run again in a resumed run.

A complete run removes the journal. A partial run keeps it, so that a later --resume can continue it. An interrupted run and a run that exits with code 2 also keep the journal. A run without --resume replaces the journal.

Each run saves its full JSON report to .fallow/mutation/last-report.json in the fallow cache directory. The cache directory has its own .gitignore, so the saved report does not make the worktree dirty. Each run replaces the saved report.
For a report file that you keep, use -o with a path in the cache directory:
A report file in another project directory is an uncommitted path. The next run then refuses the worktree and exits with code 2, unless you add the file to .gitignore or pass --allow-dirty.
Each mutant in the JSON report and in the --plan document has a change object. It shows the edit without the code of the project:
A side is an operator token, a fixed literal such as true, undefined, "", "fallow" or void 0, or a regular expression token such as ^, $, [^ or \d.

A side that is project code is a placeholder: <condition> for a negate-condition test, <call> for a removed-call statement or a removed-chain-link link (with an empty to), <expression> for a return-value argument or a comparison that becomes true or false, and <string> for a non-empty string.
An empty side means that the edit removes the token, for example { "from": "!", "to": "" }.
To see the code of a mutant, use fallow mutation inspect.
fallow health --mutation-report <FILE> reads a saved run report and shows the mutation score of each complexity finding under its CRAP score. It reads files only. It runs no test.
The mutation score never changes CRAP, the health score, or a gate. A function whose file changed since the run gets no score. See fallow health.
fallow mutation inspect shows one mutant against the current file. It runs no code.

Without --report, inspect reads the report that the last run saved. Pass --report <file> to read another saved mutation report or --plan document. Pass the same --root and --config as the run, because the config can move the cache directory. From a subdirectory, inspect finds the report of a run at the project root.
The report holds no source text. Inspect reads the current file and finds the mutant again:
fresh: the file matches the report. The output shows the original and the mutated line, the covering tests, and the killing test.
stale: the file changed or is missing. The output shows no code, so a changed file never gives a wrong answer. Run fallow mutation again.
Inspect exits with code 2 when no run saved a report, or when the id is not in the report.

fallow mutation inspect <mutant_id> --replay calls the export that holds the mutated function with one input on the current code and on the mutant, and shows the results side by side. It runs project code: the module of the file and the modules that it imports, but no test.

Replay shout("hey")
 call original mutant
 1 'HEY!' 'HEY'
 2 'HEY!' 'HEY'
 3 'HEY!' 'HEY'
Witness: each side gave the same result on each call, and the sides differ. A test with this input can kill the mutant.
Replay contract 1: the clock starts at 1767225600000 ms and moves 1 ms at each read, Math.random seed 1, a new worker for each call, 5000 ms call limit.
--args <json> gives the arguments as a JSON array. Without --args, the replay uses up to 3 inputs that a --record-args values run recorded (see Argument recording), and stops at the first witness.
--export <name> calls another export of the file, for example the export that calls a local function, or the export that reads a value of top-level code.
--call-timeout <duration> sets the limit of one call (default 5s, at most 10m).

The replay calls each side three times, in turns. Each call runs in a new worker with new modules, so module state never reaches the next call. The clock starts at a fixed time and moves 1 ms at each read, and Math.random has a fixed seed, so a value from the clock is the same on each call.
The Vitest and node:test runners replay. bun test does not.

The JSON output adds the replay object to the mutation-inspect envelope, with each call (side, index, outcome, value and text). Arguments and results use JSON, plus objects with a $replay tag for values that JSON cannot hold, for example {"$replay": "undefined"}, {"$replay": "bigint", "value": "12"} and {"$replay": "error", "name": "RangeError", "message": "..."}.
fallow mutation --record-args values records the arguments of the changed exported functions, so a replay and the open tasks can use them. Recording is off by default.

After the mutant runs, a separate pass runs your tests once more with the exported functions wrapped. Only this pass sees the wraps, and its test results count for nothing, so recording never changes a result of the run.
A function keeps up to 8 distinct inputs. A function, a class instance, a proxy, a cyclic value and similar values are "not replayable", with a reason.

The inputs stay in .fallow/mutation/recorded-args.json for 7 days, in a file that only you can read. The redaction removes each input with a value under a secret key name (token, password, authorization and similar) or a string that looks like a secret. The redaction is a heuristic: do not record in a project whose tests pass real credentials.
--record-args shapes keeps only the argument types. A replay needs values.
The report gets a recording summary with counts and reasons. It never holds an argument value.

fallow mutation tasks lists the open tasks of a saved report as one batch. A task is a survived or no_coverage mutant: a small change to the code that made no test fail. Give the batch to a coding agent, or use it yourself, to write the missing tests. It runs no code.
Without --report, the command reads the report of the last run, as inspect does. A --plan document has no test results, so the command refuses it.
Each task holds the source lines before and after the change, and no other source text. The lines come from the current file. When the file changed after the run, the task is stale and shows no code.

--format markdown puts the lines in a fenced block. --format json gives the mutation-tasks envelope: each task has mutant_id, file, line, column, operator, function, status, original_lines, mutated_lines and covering_test_files. A task of a survivor with an equivalence_hint also has that field, and the text and Markdown output add the hint: line to it.

After a --record-args values run, a task can have witness: a recorded input (args) with the result of the current code (original) and of the changed code (mutant), and replay_command. Only the verdict witness has these values. A test with these arguments that asserts the original value should kill the mutant; run it on the current code to confirm, because the replay ran with a fixed clock and seed. A stale task shows no values. The text output shows the input and both results:
 witness: input ["hey"] gives 'HEY!' on the current code and 'HEY' on the changed code (fallow mutation inspect 784f69d6646408c8 --replay)
The Markdown output can go into a PR comment, so it shows only that a recorded input shows a difference, and the command.
The command exits with code 0, also when the batch has tasks. To gate a run, use --min-score.

fallow mutation export writes a saved report in the open mutation-testing-report-schema format, schema version 2. Mutation dashboards and HTML report viewers read this format, so you can keep the dashboard that your team uses. It runs no code.

fallow mutation src/utils.ts # run, and save the report
fallow mutation export -o mutation-report.json # the report in the schema format
Without --report, the command reads the report of the last run, as inspect does. A --plan document has no test results, so the command refuses it with exit code 2.
The format holds the full source of each mutated file. Each mutated file must be as the run saw it. When a file changed after the run, the command exits with code 2 and names each file and the cause.
The output is JSON with --format human and with --format json.
Lines and columns are 1-based. A column counts UTF-16 code units, the unit of a source string in a browser.
The schema has fewer statuses than fallow. The export maps each status so that a mutant counts as killed or survived only when the run showed it:

A partial run can miss kills. In a partial run, each Survived and NoCoverage mutant gets a statusReason that names the reasons and says that the result is not conclusive. config.completion holds the completion of the report. A dashboard counts NoCoverage in its score, and fallow does not, so the dashboard score can be lower than summary.score.

fallow mutation --recheck reruns the open tasks of a saved report against the current tests. With tasks, it gives a loop: list the tasks, write tests, recheck, and the mutants that still survive are the next batch.

fallow mutation src/utils.ts # run, and save the report
fallow mutation tasks # the open tasks as one batch
# write or change tests
fallow mutation --recheck # rerun the open tasks
fallow mutation tasks # what is still open
--mutant <ID> rechecks only these ids, with any status. Without it, the recheck runs each survived and no_coverage mutant of the report.

A recheck proves a change of the tests only. When a selected file changed after the report, the recheck exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_SOURCE_CHANGED. An uncommitted change to a file that is not a test file exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_NON_TEST_CHANGE. A change that you committed after the report to another file, for example a module that a selected file imports or the runner config, is not detected. Run fallow mutation again after such a commit.

The run tests only the selected mutants. Each other mutant of the earlier report keeps its earlier status and evidence, and gets carried: true. The summary, the score and the function results count the full set. The kill matrix gives only the evidence of this run.

An earlier result applies only while its file is unchanged since the earlier report. An earlier kill also needs each test file of its killing tests. When a file that the recheck did not select loses an earlier result, the report leaves out its mutants, and recheck.stale_files names the file. Run fallow mutation on that file for new results.

The recheck does not run a carried mutant again. When you remove a test from a test file that still exists, or make a test weaker, a carried kill stays. After such a change, run fallow mutation without --recheck.
The report gets a recheck object. It gives carried, the number of mutants with an earlier result. For each rechecked mutant, it gives the earlier status, the new status and an outcome:

A recheck without --mutant replaces the saved report. With --report <PATH>, it also replaces that file. Then tasks and tasks --report <PATH> list the mutants that are still open. A recheck with --mutant keeps both reports as they are.
A --mutant id that the report does not have exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_UNKNOWN_MUTANT. A report without an open task exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_NOTHING_TO_RECHECK.
--recheck cannot be combined with a scope flag, --plan, --resume, --allow-dirty, --max-mutants or --min-score. The mutation.minScore gate does not apply to a recheck.
fallow mutation --compare <PATH> compares the run with a saved report. It shows if a change of the tests weakens the detection of mutants: a mutant that a test killed before and that survives now.

fallow mutation src/utils.ts --format json -o .fallow/before.json # save a report
# change, move or remove tests, then commit
fallow mutation src/utils.ts --compare .fallow/before.json

The saved report is a fallow mutation --format json report. Keep it in a file of its own, because each run replaces the saved report of the last run. Keep the file in the cache directory, so that it does not make the worktree dirty for the second run.

The compare matches the mutants of the two runs by mutant_id. A mutant id stays the same until its enclosing function changes, so an edit of a test file keeps the ids. Run the two runs over the same files.

The saved report and the run must have completion.status: complete. A saved report that is not complete exits with code 2 and FALLOW_MUTATION_COMPARE_INCOMPLETE before the run starts. A run that is not complete writes its report without a compare object, then exits with code 2 and the same code.
A regression does not change the exit code. To fail a CI job on a regression, read compare.regressed of the JSON output.
--compare cannot be combined with --plan or --recheck. A verdict document applies before the compare, so an equivalent mutant is not a regression.
The report gets a compare object with these fields:

Each entry of mutants has mutant_id, file, line, change, previous_status (absent for added), status (absent for removed) and previous_killing_tests. previous_killing_tests holds the killing_tests of the saved report, else its killed_by.

The human output adds a compare section after the run report. Each regressed mutant names the test that killed it in the saved report. When no mutant id is in both runs, the section says so, because the compare checked no mutant.
Some mutants do not change the behavior of the code. No test can detect them. You can mark them in a verdict document:
The review_key is the mutant_id. The id stays the same until the enclosing function changes, so one verdict document can serve many runs.

The JSON report lists each group under verdicts, together with a digest of the document. A malformed document, an empty or duplicate review_key, or an unknown field stops the command with exit code 2 before any test runs.
The flag wins over the config key. A run with no score exits with 0, also when every mutant is no_coverage.
Set project defaults in the mutation config section:
A CLI flag wins over the config. No config key starts a run or keeps side-effect mutants.
The MCP server has three read-only tools. No tool runs tests.
mutation_plan returns the plan envelope: each mutant's id, location, operator, disposition, and static test files. It takes changed_since, all, paths, max_mutants, and operators.
mutation_inspect shows one mutant of a saved report. It takes mutant_id and an optional report. Without report, it reads the report of the last run.
mutation_tasks returns the open tasks of a saved report, the same JSON as fallow mutation tasks --format json, with witness after a --record-args values run. It takes an optional report.
A run needs the CLI command fallow mutation, which executes your tests. An agent should ask you before it starts a run.
The output formats are human and json, plus markdown for tasks. There is no SARIF, CodeClimate, LSP, or CI gate output.
--workspace and --changed-workspaces are not supported. Pass a package directory as a path.
A run executes the mutants that a verdict marks. Fallow applies the verdicts after the run.
The in-process mode of node:test (isolation: "none") is not supported.

With node:test and bun test, fallow can match the code that a test ran to that test only when the tests of a file run in a fixed order. When tests overlap (concurrency in node:test, test.concurrent in Bun) or randomize = true is set in bunfig.toml, each test of the file shares the code that the file ran. A mutant then runs against each test of the file that can kill it.
Get a verdict for the files that a PR changes.
Set the runner, operators, minimum score, concurrency, and type check.
Show the mutation score next to the CRAP score.

pages.title: fallow audit: quality gate for pull requests
items: fallow audit: quality gate for pull requests
Quality gate for pull requests. fallow audit gives one pass, warn, or fail verdict for the changed files from dead code, complexity, and duplication checks.

fallow audit tells you if a PR passes your quality gate. It checks the changed files for dead code, complexity, duplication, and styling, and returns a pass, warn, or fail verdict from the severity of the issues it finds.

Audit checks only the changed files, which keeps the signal-to-noise ratio high. By default, only issues that the current PR or commit introduces fail the gate. Inherited findings in touched files show as context.
Audit also runs diff-risk rules. These rules report risky facts about the change itself, such as a skipped test or a new suppression comment.

Dependency findings (unused, misplaced, type-only or test-only dependencies, overrides and catalog entries) are in the audit only when the change touches the package.json or catalog file that declares them. Unlisted dependencies follow their import sites. fallow dead-code reports all of them.

fallow audit is the gate for pull requests. For the first full-repo cleanup of an existing codebase, start with Adopt Fallow in an existing repo. That guide walks through fallow, fallow dead-code, fallow dupes, and fallow health, and hands the actual cleanup to an AI agent before you turn on audit in CI.
You can set the gate in three places. All three accept the same values (new-only, all). Precedence: the CLI flag or the MCP gate parameter, then the config, then the default (new-only).

Under new-only, an inherited complexity finding must not get worse. A finding is worsened when it matches a base finding, it is not introduced, and a measured value is higher than in the base finding. The measured values are:

the CRAP score, at any growth. Fallow compares CRAP only when the base finding and the head finding both have a score. A CRAP score from estimated coverage can make a finding worsened, but never introduced. See Estimated CRAP under new-only.
the line count of the function, when it grows by at least 5 lines. The line count includes comments and blank lines. The minimum keeps a finding inherited after a short comment or a formatter rewrap.
For example, a function that grows from 80 to 300 lines with the same complexity values is worsened, not inherited.

Growth of a metric that the finding already exceeded is also worsened when the finding stays in its severity tier (moderate, high or critical). For example, a function that already exceeded the cyclomatic threshold grows from cyclomatic 100 to 103 and stays critical. The finding is introduced in two cases:
The growth of an exceeded metric moves the finding to a higher severity tier.
The finding now exceeds a metric that the base finding did not exceed, and that metric grew.

The tiers are the fixed severity bands of fallow health, not your configured thresholds. The exceeded flags and the tier of the base finding come from the base run. A threshold change in the same pull request, for example in health.thresholdOverrides, therefore does not make an old finding introduced.
--worsened selects the effect on the verdict:
You can set the mode in three places. Precedence: the CLI flag or the MCP worsened parameter, then the config key audit.worsened, then the default (warn).

The human, compact, and markdown output add a "Worse than base" section. It lists each complexity finding with a grown value, with the base value and the head value. The section also lists an introduced finding whose exceeded metric grew. A compact line has this shape:

SARIF results put attribution and worsened_metrics in the property bag. CodeClimate descriptions name the grown values. The fingerprints do not change. In JSON, read attribution and worsened_metrics on each complexity finding. See Key fields.
To keep the earlier gate, in which growth of an exceeded metric fails the run, set --worsened error or audit.worsened: "error".

Without coverage data, fallow estimates the CRAP score from static test reachability. The estimate does not measure the change. Under --gate new-only, a CRAP score from estimated coverage therefore does not fail the audit:

A complexity finding that exceeds only the CRAP threshold, with coverage_source estimated or estimated_component_inherited, has effective_severity: "warn". The finding stays in the report. It makes the verdict at least warn, and the exit code stays 0.
A finding that also exceeds the cyclomatic or cognitive threshold keeps the severity of its complexity-* rule, so it still gates.
A CRAP score from estimated coverage never makes a matched finding introduced. When the score grows, the finding is worsened.
A CRAP score that the base finding does not have is not growth.

SARIF reports such a finding at level warning. A CRAP score from measured coverage still gates: --coverage, health.coverage, FALLOW_COVERAGE or runtime coverage. --gate all does not change. To give the gate measured coverage, pass a coverage map with --coverage, as described for fallow health.
Classes that the base cannot prove

The base snapshot holds committed files only. A file that git ignores, for example a workspace member that CI clones into the repository, is not in the base snapshot. The base run then cannot prove some dead-code classes, and it skips them. Today this applies to unused-catalog-entries: fallow does not report them while a workspace pattern points to a missing directory.

The head run can see these files, so it reports the class. Under --gate new-only, audit reads each finding of a class that the base run could not prove as inherited. The verdict, the attribution counts and the introduced flags agree. The human output counts these findings in the line audit gate excluded N inherited findings.

In such a run, a really new finding of that class is inherited too, because audit cannot tell it apart from a finding that the base did not measure. To gate every finding of the class, use --gate all.

A complexity finding in a test file does not fail the audit, under both gates. A long it(...) or describe(...) callback often exceeds the cognitive threshold, and the gate is for production code. Test files include these paths:
a file below a test directory: __tests__/, test/, tests/, e2e/
a mock or a fixture: __mocks__/, fixtures/, *.fixture.*

The finding stays in the report with its attribution. In JSON, it has effective_severity: "warn" and gate_exemption: "test-file". It makes the verdict at least warn, and the exit code stays 0. SARIF reports it at level warning with gate_exemption in the property bag. The human, compact, and markdown output list it under "Test files, not gated". A compact line has this shape:
fallow health does not change. It still reports these findings at the severity of their complexity-* rule.

Under --gate new-only, audit normally runs every analysis twice: once on the current tree, and once on a temporary worktree at the base ref. The second run tells audit if each finding is introduced or inherited.
audit skips the second run when every changed file is one of these:
a .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.mjs/.mts/.cjs/.cts source file that is token-equivalent at the base ref (a comment-only or whitespace-only edit)

In that case, audit reuses the findings of the current run as the base snapshot and classifies all of them as inherited. Docs-only PRs and formatter sweeps then take about one analysis pass instead of two.

To check if the fast path fired, run fallow audit --base main --gate new-only --performance. The JSON output has base_snapshot_skipped: true|false, and the human output prints the same value on stderr. The fast path turns on automatically when every entry in the diff qualifies. No flag turns it on or off.

Under --gate new-only, clone-group attribution has one exception. When no instance of an introduced clone group overlaps an added line in the diff of the run, audit demotes the group to inherited. This happens when a change removes duplication elsewhere and so gives a remaining clone group a new structural key. The group is new to the report, but the change wrote no duplicated line, so the group does not fail the gate.
You can see every demotion. The stderr note about findings that the gate excluded gets an extra line with the demoted count and the diff that decided it:

audit gate excluded 3 inherited findings (run with --gate all to enforce)
 of which 1 clone group was reclassified as pre-existing: no duplicated line was added by this change (diff source: merge-base worktree diff vs main)
With --explain, the duplication section adds one line per demoted group, with the same cap as the clone listing. Each line shows:
the group's dup:<fingerprint> id (matching the listing and fallow dupes --trace)

A closing line names the diff source. In JSON, each demoted entry in duplication.clone_groups[] has a demotion_reason field, and the attribution block counts demotions in duplication_demoted. See Key fields.

The decision uses the same diff precedence as diff scoping. A diff from --diff-file, --diff-stdin, or FALLOW_DIFF_FILE wins over the merge-base worktree diff. A supplied diff with a narrower base than the merge base can demote duplication that the branch really introduced. An example is a diff of only the last commit on a branch with several commits. Compute a supplied diff from the same base that the audit compares against. When no diff is available, audit skips this check and every introduced clone group still gates.

In review-github and review-gitlab output, the comment of an audit finding names its attribution after the severity label: introduced, worsened or inherited. This applies to complexity, dead-code, stale-suppression, duplication and styling findings. When the gate does not count the finding, the label says why, for example **error** · inherited · not gated (`--gate new-only`). The other reasons are --worsened warn, --worsened off and a test file. A live audit run and fallow report --from on a saved audit give the same text. Under --gate all, the audit has no attribution, so the label has only the severity.

The comment of an inherited complexity finding also names each exceeded metric with its base and head values, for example (inherited from the base: cyclomatic 23 -> 19, cognitive 22 -> 18). This text is also in the codeclimate output. The JSON output does not store the base values, so fallow report --from on a saved audit shows the comment without them. The CodeClimate fingerprints do not change.
fallow audit accepts these two runtime coverage flags. For the coverage formats, the capture steps and the hot-path rules, see fallow coverage.

audit rejects the global --baseline / --save-baseline flags (exit 2), because audit runs three analyses with incompatible baseline formats. Use the per-analysis flags above, or set defaults in .fallowrc.json:
Store committed baselines outside .fallow/. fallow init adds that directory to .gitignore for the machine-local cache.
CLI flags override config. An unset baseline has no effect. You can set any subset (for example dead-code only).

An audit analyzes only the files that changed against its base. A whole-project baseline therefore matches less of the run. The narrow scope causes this, not a stale baseline. An audit loads the baselines that you pass, but it does not judge them.
Each loaded baseline has its own baseline_staleness object in the envelope:

All three report change_scoped: true. Their scope_reasons names what narrowed that sub-pass: changed-since for dead_code, and changed-files for duplication and complexity. All three report gate_trips: false. A section that loaded a baseline it cannot read as its own reports true. Do not build a gate on these values.

To judge a baseline, run the command that owns it over the whole project. The section label is not the command name: duplication belongs to fallow dupes, complexity to fallow health, and dead_code to fallow dead-code.

An audit that loaded a baseline also has gate_outcomes["stale-baseline"] set to {"status": "skipped", "enforced": false}. There is one entry for any number of loaded baselines. The entry puts this fact on the gate outcomes line, which the pull-request comment and the merge-request note render. The entry also stays skipped for a baseline of another kind. See CI for what the shipped integrations report per baseline.

An audit checks the kind of every baseline that it loads, and reports every mismatch. Each mismatch prints a warning on stderr that names the flag with the path: --dead-code-baseline, --dupes-baseline or --health-baseline. That section has baseline_staleness.unrecognised_format: true. Next to it, saved_by names the command that saved the file: dead-code, dupes, or health. The saved_by field is absent for an empty file, for a baseline saved before files named their writer, and for a writer that this version does not know. To fix it, point that flag at a baseline from the command that owns it.
audit accepts --fail-on-stale-baseline, but in audit this gate never runs. A run that sets the flag with a baseline prints one warning on stderr, which names the commands that can run the gate.

--fail-on-baseline-growth does run in audit. It does not judge the findings of the run. It compares each file of --dead-code-baseline, --dupes-baseline and --health-baseline with the same file at the base ref, so a scoped run can judge it. See Baseline growth gate.

Dead code issues use the severity from your rules configuration (error/warn/off). Diff-risk rules use their rule severity in the same way. Complexity findings above the configured thresholds use the complexity rules. They default to error. With warn, a complexity finding gives a warn verdict. The thresholds come from your fallow health config (defaults: cyclomatic 20, cognitive 15). Duplication is a warning unless you configure a --threshold. With the default new-only gate, the report can show inherited error-severity findings while the audit exits 0. A worsened complexity finding makes the verdict at least warn, or counts like an introduced finding with --worsened error. A complexity finding in a test file makes the verdict at least warn and does not fail it. The audit ignores --fail-on-issues and keeps its own verdict.

The parse error gate (--fail-on-parse-error or failOnParseError) checks every file that the audit parsed, not only the changed files. The verdict does not include this gate. Read gate_outcomes for the exit reason.
Inline suppression comments (// fallow-ignore-next-line) work in audit. They suppress findings in changed files in the same way as in fallow dead-code.
JSON contract: which fields are severity-aware
Audit reports three counts that look alike but answer different questions. A CI integration or other tool that reads the output must gate on the right one:

Rule of thumb for CI gating: branch on verdict == "fail", or check the exit code, which follows the verdict. Do not count introduced findings. A count brings back the bug that command: audit was built to fix: a project with unused-exports: warn would fail CI on every PR that adds a warn-tier finding, although the verdict correctly says warn ("do not fail"). The official GitHub Action and GitLab CI template already gate on the verdict. Third-party wrappers should follow the same contract.

Rule of thumb for AI agents: read verdict first to see if the run passed or failed. Then read attribution for the new and inherited counts, and walk the finding arrays per category for the details. To keep only the findings that the current PR introduced, filter on introduced: true.

# Auto-detect base branch
fallow audit

# Explicit base ref
fallow audit --base main

# Audit last 3 commits
fallow audit --base HEAD~3

# Strict mode: fail on inherited findings too
fallow audit --gate all

✓ dead code: 0 issues · complexity: 2 findings (warn) · 8 changed files (1.18s)
The ■ summary line appears only on warn verdicts, before any detail sections. --quiet hides it.

Audit scope: 12 changed files vs main (d4a2f91..HEAD)

── Dead Code ──────────────────────────────────────

● Unused exports (2)

✗ dead code: 2 issues · complexity: 1 finding · duplication: 1 clone group · 12 changed files (2.14s)

Resolve base ref: audit uses --base if you set it, then FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE. Otherwise it auto-detects the git merge-base (fork point) with the branch's upstream (@{upstream}) or the remote default (origin/HEAD → origin/main → origin/master). Because audit uses the merge-base and not a bare branch name, a feature branch compares against the point where it forked, not against a local main that can be stale. Repositories with no origin remote fall back to the local main / master branch. If audit cannot find a base, it stops with an error.
Find changed files: runs git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD (three-dot diff, showing changes since the merge base).
Run three analyses scoped to changed files: dead code, complexity, duplication.

Compute attribution: with new-only, audit runs the same analyses at the base ref and compares structural issue keys. A dead-code key is the line-free canonical key of the finding: the rule, the root-relative path and the names, the same input as the finding_id. A line shift above a finding therefore keeps it inherited. The keys compare by count, so a new second finding with the key of an inherited finding is introduced. An unlisted dependency is keyed by the package, so a new import site of a package that the base already reports stays inherited.
A dead-code finding of a class that the base run could not prove is inherited. See Classes that the base cannot prove.
A complexity finding matches its base finding by the root-relative path and the function name. The line and the exceeded category do not affect the match, and a renamed file keeps its match. The finding is introduced when no base finding matches it, when the growth of an exceeded metric moves it to a higher severity tier, or when it now exceeds a metric that the base finding did not exceed and that metric grew. An unchanged or lower metric keeps the finding inherited, also when the exceeded category changes (for example from both to cyclomatic). When a file has more than one finding with the same function name, each base finding matches at most one head finding. Findings with unchanged values and an unchanged line count match first. Findings with unchanged values match next. The other findings then match in line order.
A matched finding that is not introduced is worsened when a measured value grew. This includes growth of an exceeded metric in the same severity tier. See Worsened complexity findings.
A merge of the default branch brings in code that the default branch already has. When audit auto-detects the ba
Compute verdict: new-only gates only introduced findings. --worsened decides the effect of worsened findings. all gates every finding in changed files and skips the extra base-snapshot analysis.

The diff-risk rules report a fact about the change itself. Audit compares the base text and the head text of each changed file. The base text comes from the merge base of the base ref and HEAD. Each finding is new in the change, so each finding has introduced: true. Only fallow audit and the MCP audit tool run these rules.
A finding is not a proof of a defect. It shows a change that a reviewer must look at, for example a skipped test or a new suppression comment.
The rule severity sets the effect on the verdict:
An error finding fails the audit.
A warn finding changes a pass verdict to warn.
An off rule does not run.

Each finding has only suppression actions. Fallow never applies a fix for a diff-risk finding. A file that cannot hold a comment, such as a package.json or a JSON config file, gets only a suppress-in-config action. The same is true for a deleted file. A rename source is skipped. A rename target reads its base text at the old path.
The change makes the tests weaker. The kind field tells how:

The test kinds read JavaScript-family test files only, such as .test.ts or .spec.js files. A test file in another language, such as a Rust integration test, can hold it.skip text in a string, so the rule does not read it.
A test or an assertion that moved to another changed test file does not report, because the total did not drop.
These drops do not report either:

The lost test lines name code that the same change removed, such as a deleted function, error code, or fixture directory. The tests went with that code. A name of a deleted file that a changed file still holds, a name that a deleted file only imports, a directory that still exists, and a reserved word such as import do not count. A deleted directory or file name matches only a whole path segment.
An assertion drop where assertions are less than half of the code lines that the test file lost. A test rewrite that moves setup checks into a shared helper does not report.

coverage-threshold reads test-runner, coverage, and Fallow config files, such as vitest.config.*, jest.config.*, .nycrc, .c8rc, package.json, and .fallowrc.json. A lower lines, branches, functions, statements, minScore, or minCoverage value reports. A higher maxCrap, maxCyclomatic, or maxCognitive value reports too.
Example: a change turns it('charges tax', ...) into it.skip('charges tax', ...), or lowers coverage.thresholds.lines from 90 to 70.

When to act: Always look at the finding before you merge. If the weaker test or threshold is intended, suppress the finding with // fallow-ignore-next-line weakened-tests. Use // fallow-ignore-file weakened-tests for a finding about the whole file.

The change adds a comment line with a suppression. Audit reports these markers: eslint-disable, oxlint-disable, biome-ignore, deno-lint-ignore, @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error, @ts-nocheck, istanbul ignore, c8 ignore, v8 ignore, and fallow-ignore.
A moved comment is not added, so it does not report.
A marker inside a string literal does not report.
A fallow-ignore comment that names only diff-risk rules does not report.

A file below a fixture or generated directory (fixture, fixtures, __fixtures__, __snapshots__, generated, __generated__) does not report, because a tool writes it or a test reads it as data. The match uses the directory name only.
Only a suppression that names added-suppression hides this finding. A new blanket fallow-ignore comment cannot hide itself.
A finding for a fallow-ignore comment has a suppression object with kinds, reason, and security_without_reason. Write the reason after --. Every kind accepts this syntax:

// fallow-ignore-next-line security-sink -- the HTML is a constant template
el.innerHTML = html;

When the comment hides security-sink or security-client-server-leak and gives no reason, security_without_reason is true, and the message says so. The review brief evidence then reads fallow-ignore added (security-sink, no reason). A blanket comment without a kind does not set the flag. The signal is advisory: the severity, the verdict, and the exit code do not change. To find existing security suppressions without a reason, run fallow suppressions --format json and select the markers with reason_present: false.
Example: a change adds // @ts-expect-error above a call, where a correct type is the better fix.
When to act: Make sure that the suppression is necessary. If it is, keep it and add // fallow-ignore-next-line added-suppression, or set the rule to off for the path in overrides.
The change adds a line to a non-test source file that checks the test environment. Audit reports these checks:

Such a branch lets the tests take a path that production does not take. import.meta.vitest does not report, because Vitest in-source tests use it on purpose. Test files, type-test files, and tool config files (such as vite.config.ts or .eslintrc.js) are skipped. A token inside a string literal does not report. A check that only keeps console output quiet in tests, such as if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'test') console.warn(...), does not report. A check that picks an env file, such as '.env.test', does not report.
Example: a change adds if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') return cached; to src/pricing.ts.
When to act: Use a seam that the tests can inject, such as a parameter or a module mock. If the branch is intended, suppress it with // fallow-ignore-next-line test-only-branch.

The change edits exactly one copy of a base clone group, the edit breaks the clone, and all other copies keep their text. The other copies can need the same change. The related field lists the unchanged copies.
A cosmetic edit that keeps the clone.
A change that removes a copy.
A change that edits every copy.
An edit to a test copy or a story copy (*.stories.*, *.story.*).
The rule needs the base snapshot of --gate new-only. With --gate all, or when audit skips the base pass, the rule does not run.

This rule is off by default. Copies often differ on purpose, for example an input and an output type, a legacy copy, or one component that gets a new feature. Set the rule to warn or error to review every diverged copy.
Example: src/a/total.ts and src/b/total.ts held the same function. The change fixes a bug in the first copy only.

When to act: Look at the copies in related. Apply the same change there, or extract a shared function. If the copies must be different, suppress the finding with // fallow-ignore-next-line diverged-clone-sibling.
The change adds a dependency to a package.json. A new dependency is often correct, so this rule is off by default. Set it to warn or error to review each new package.
An invented package name already fails as an unresolved import or an unlisted dependency, so this rule is not necessary to catch it.
Example: a change adds "left-pad": "^1.3.0" to dependencies.

When to act: Make sure that the package exists, is maintained, and does not repeat a dependency that the project already has. You cannot suppress this finding with a comment, because a package.json cannot hold a comment. Add an overrides entry that sets added-dependency to off for the path, or set the rule to off.
Set each rule in the rules object. overrides[].rules sets a rule for some paths only.

Fallow also accepts the plural keys added-suppressions, test-only-branches, diverged-clone-siblings, and added-dependencies. The suppression token of a rule is its rule name, for example // fallow-ignore-next-line test-only-branch. added-dependency has no suppression comment. Use an overrides entry for it.
Every output format of fallow audit shows the diff-risk findings:
The human output adds a Diff risk section with one line for each finding. The status line names the number of diff-risk findings.

--format compact prints one record for each finding: <rule>:<path>:<line>:<evidence>,severity=<severity>[,kind=<kind>]. The line is 0 for a finding about the whole file. Only weakened-tests records have kind.
--format markdown adds a ## Fallow: N diff-risk findings table with the location, the rule, the severity, and the evidence of each finding.
--format json and the MCP audit tool put them in the diff_risk section. See Key fields.
--format sarif adds a run with automationDetails.id fallow/audit/diff-risk. The rule ids are fallow/<rule>, and helpUri links to this section. The unchanged clone copies are relatedLocations.
--format codeclimate adds issues with the check name fallow/<rule> and the category Bug Risk.
--format github-annotations writes one annotation for each finding. An error finding gives ::error, and a warn finding gives ::warning.

--format github-summary adds a Diff Risk table to the audit summary, with the rule, the location, the evidence, and the severity of each finding. The table shows 15 findings at most, and a note gives the number of other findings.
The GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template add the diff-risk findings to the issue count of command: audit, under both gates.
The VS Code extension adds the diff-risk findings to the gating-candidate count of the audit status bar, and shows a diff-risk row in the tooltip.
For example, a change that skips a test and adds a @ts-ignore comment gives this output:

── Diff risk ──────────────────────────────────────
 src/index.test.ts:3 weakened-tests (skip-only) [warn] it.skip
 src/index.ts:2 added-suppression [warn] @ts-ignore
⚠ diff risk: 2 findings (warn) · 2 changed files (0.14s)

## Fallow: 2 diff-risk findings

| Location | Rule | Severity | Evidence |
|:---------|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| `src/index.test.ts:3` | `weakened-tests` / `skip-only` | warn | `it.skip` |
| `src/index.ts:2` | `added-suppression` | warn | `@ts-ignore` |
The audit schema_version is 14. Version 14 follows the embedded health contract, where the runtime coverage totals are null for a partial capture.

The dead_code, complexity, and duplication sub-objects hold full results in the same format as fallow dead-code, fallow health, and fallow dupes. audit omits them when no files changed. By default, the complexity sub-object can also include the css_analytics and styling_findings blocks of the health report. When you pass --runtime-coverage, it can also include runtime_coverage and additive coverage_intelligence blocks.
The audit MCP tool wraps fallow audit --format json --quiet --explain:

When you omit base, the tool resolves it as described under How it works. To pin it, set FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE in the server environment. Set gate to all for strict mode. Set worsened to warn, error, or off to select the effect of a worsened complexity finding. When you omit it, the tool uses audit.worsened. Set skip (for example ["dead-code"]) or only to choose the sub-analyses, with the values and rules of --skip and --only. The tool includes styling findings by default. Set css_deep to false to skip project-wide styling reachability, or to true to force it back on when config turns it off. The tool returns the same JSON envelope as the CLI.

The audit tool description is a short summary. Read the fallow://tools/audit tool guide for the detail. The guide names the five diff-risk rules and holds the styling, coverage, complexity unit, group_by, baseline, runtime-coverage and FALLOW_DIFF_FILE detail.
See MCP integration for setup instructions.
Under --gate new-only, audit creates a temporary base snapshot (a git worktree checkout) to compare against the base ref.
When the current checkout has node_modules, audit links it into the snapshot. tsconfig extends chains into installed packages and path aliases then resolve as in the working tree.
audit unregisters the snapshot from git right after it creates it. The snapshot never appears in git worktree list, IDE repo views, or .git/worktrees/, even if the process is force-killed.
The next audit deregisters entries that earlier fallow versions registered, and keeps their warm caches.

Each project root keeps one base-snapshot cache that the root owns. audit rebuilds it in place when the resolved base SHA changes. audit holds the reuse lock for the whole run, so cleanup can never remove files under a running audit.

audit also saves the result of each base pass as a snapshot file in the fallow cache directory, below .fallow/cache/audit-base-v<N>/ by default. The key of a file includes the base SHA, the changed files, and --brief. A later audit with the same key reads the file and does not run the base pass again.

Every audit runs an automatic age-based garbage collection (GC). The default age is 30 days. To change it, set the FALLOW_AUDIT_CACHE_MAX_AGE_DAYS env var or the audit.cacheMaxAgeDays config field. 0 turns off the age-based sweep. For the snapshot files, the age counts from the last use. After each save, audit also keeps only the newest 32 snapshot files. This cap applies also when the age is 0. Two subcommands clean the caches on demand.
To remove all caches of one project, warm or not, run fallow audit-cache remove --root <PATH>:

fallow audit-cache remove --root ./my-project --dry-run # preview what would be removed
fallow audit-cache remove --root ./my-project --yes # remove (required in non-interactive shells)

--dry-run reports what the command would remove and does not touch the filesystem. Removal in a non-interactive shell requires --yes. The command leaves lock-contended entries (an audit is in the middle of a rebuild) in place, reports them, and exits 2.

Use fallow audit-cache prune when audit caches from deleted checkouts or old branches take disk space. It cleans up now, with a visible decision per entry, and you do not wait for the silent sweep of the next audit.
prune applies the same GC policy that every fallow audit run applies silently:
age-based reclaim under the resolved threshold
reclaim of abandoned entries whose recorded owner root no longer exists
the age threshold and the newest-32 cap for the base-snapshot files in the fallow cache directory of --root

It reports every cache entry that it considered, with sizes and ages. It never touches entries that other live projects own. In the fallow cache directory, it removes only files with the name pattern that audit writes.

fallow audit-cache prune --dry-run # preview every decision without touching the filesystem
fallow audit-cache prune # apply the GC policy now
fallow audit-cache prune --max-age-days 7 # tighter age threshold for this run
--root is optional for prune and defaults to the current directory. The command measures sizes with a full recursive walk of each cache entry, which can take a few seconds on large caches.

Human output prints one row per considered entry, sorted by path, with the decision, reason, size, and age. An entry that stays because another live project owns it gets a hint: run audit-cache remove to clear the cache of that project. The closing line gives the total of reclaimed bytes.

prune exits 0 whenever it ran, unlike remove. This includes runs that skip entries because of lock contention (an audit is in the middle of a rebuild) and runs with per-entry failures. On a shared runner, the command reports entries of other users as kept and does not fail. Exit code 2 is only for validation errors and an unreadable scan root. Scripts gate on the complete field of the JSON envelope, not on the exit code.
With --format json, prune returns its own maintenance envelope. It is separate from the audit envelope, and sits next to the audit-cache-remove envelope:

A normal audit run does its GC silently. To see the per-entry decisions, set RUST_LOG=fallow=debug. fallow audit and audit-cache prune then log one diagnostic line per considered entry, with its decision, reason, age, and threshold. With RUST_LOG unset, the audit output does not change.

fallow review shows a reviewer where to look in a change. It is an alias for fallow audit --brief. It produces a deterministic review brief from the module graph and always exits 0. The output includes the verdict for information only. fallow audit is the command that gates (exits non-zero on a fail verdict). --format is independent of --brief, so the brief renders in human or json like any other audit output.
The brief answers "where do I look?", not "will CI block this?". It runs the same analysis as the gating audit and organizes the result around four jobs:
Each focus unit has a score object. The score is a sum of named components, and total is that sum. A component that is zero is not in the JSON, so read an absent component as zero.

Each component has a cap, so one signal cannot hide the others. The components only add to the total. No component multiplies another, so you can see which component moved a file up. The reason text names each present component, for example changed often (23 recent commits), makes 1 function more complex.
Without --mutation-report, Fallow does not measure surviving mutants. An absent mutation component then does not mean that each mutant was killed.
The focus score does not change triage.risk_class. That class depends only on the size of the change.

The decision surface is the ranked set of coupling-boundary, public-api-contract, and dependency decisions in the change, capped by --max-decisions. Each decision is a framed judgment question anchored to a signal_id. fallow decision-surface prints the decision surface alone. That page documents the categories, the fields of each decision, and suppression.

fallow review --format json returns decisions, focus, deltas, impact_closure, partition, and graph_facts. When the project has a CODEOWNERS file, it also returns ownership. When the diff changes a value export, it also returns test_reach. The brief schema_version is 14. Consumers can use it to detect contract changes.

deltas also has the dependency keys that the decision surface reads: dependency_added (<manifest>::<name>) and dependency_major_bumped (<manifest>::<name>@<from>-><to>). The envelope names what changed even when the cap collapses the decision. Both keys are always present, as empty arrays when nothing changed.
weakening lists the guardrails that the change makes weaker. Each entry has kind, file, and evidence. The signals are advisory and never gate. The kind values are:

The first three kinds come from the diff_risk findings of the same run, so the brief and the diff_risk section agree. They follow the rule severities and the suppressions: when you set weakened-tests or added-suppression to off, or suppress a finding with a fallow-ignore comment, the brief drops the signal. They also follow the diff-risk scope. A test that moves to another changed test file is not a removed test. A threshold signal comes only from a test-runner, coverage, or Fallow config file. A suppression signal comes only from a source or style file. Only files under the analysis root (--root) give these signals. The security-check-removed scan stays local to the brief.

A sink substitution matters because a rule that flags one sink does not flag the other. A rule that flags new Function does not flag vm.runInNewContext, so the swap silences the rule and keeps the risk. The sink classes are:
code execution: eval, new Function, vm.runIn*, vm.compileFunction, and new vm.Script;
HTML: innerHTML, outerHTML, srcdoc, srcDoc, insertAdjacentHTML, setHTMLUnsafe, createContextualFragment, document.write, and dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

A sink that moves into an object key under a JSX spread, a computed member such as globalThis['eval'], or an alias gives evidence such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML sink moved into an object key. A sink that only moves in the file, or that goes away, gives no signal. Test files do not take part. The JSON keys and the kind values are the same as before. The evidence text is a free string that follows the diff-risk evidence, so do not parse it.
impact_closure reports the blast radius as a magnitude, a sample, and a distribution instead of one long list:
affected_count is the exact number of files outside the diff that the change reaches, computed before any cap.

affected_not_shown is a path-sorted sample of at most ten of those files. It is a prefix of the sorted set, so it clusters in the directory that sorts first. Use it to open representative files. Do not use it to list the full reach or to infer its shape.

affected_by_dir gives the shape as { dir, count } rows: heaviest directory first, the directory path as tie-breaker, at most twenty-five rows. affected_by_dir_omitted counts the lighter directories that did not fit. The count in every row is exact.
coordination_gap is separate and has no cap. It is not a subset of the sample. It skips, on purpose, the story and test consumers that the affected set counts.

search_gap lists the consumers that a text search for a changed export name does not find (missed) or finds only under another name (renamed). Only exports whose declaration the diff changes count, and only consumers outside the diff. For a .vue, .svelte, .astro, or .mdx file, fallow reads the declaration ranges from the script blocks (SFC <script> blocks, Astro frontmatter, and MDX statements). So a change inside a declaration body in such a file counts. exports[] has one entry per export (file, export_name, line, total) with at most 10 consumers[] (consumer_file, line, search_visibility, reason, search_as), missed first. total is the sum of the per-export totals before the cap. A pass-through consumer (a barrel, or a file that imports the export and only exports it again) is never a gap. When no such consumer exists, the key is absent. See Search visibility in traces for the field values.

co_change_gap lists the changed files that have a hidden change-coupling partner outside the diff. The two files changed together in most commits of the history window, but no import or re-export chain connects them, so the graph facts cannot point at the partner. Each entry has changed_file, partner_file, shared_revisions (the commits that changed both files), degree (the coupling degree, from 0 to 1), and note. The fact is advisory. It is history evidence, not a proof that the partner must change, and it never gates. The list has at most ten entries, highest degree first, then the most shared_revisions. co_change_gap_count gives the full number of gaps before the cap. The gaps apply health.ignore and the workspace filter (--workspace, --changed-workspaces), the same as the change_coupling health section. Fallow omits both fields when there is no gap.

partition has independent_slices only when there are two or more slices. A slice is a connected component of the dependency graph between units, given as a sorted list of module directories. Two or more slices mean that the change splits along a seam that the graph proves, into pieces that you can review and merge separately. A single slice would only repeat order, so fallow leaves the field out. The field helps you orient. It never asks you to split the change.
ownership shows how many CODEOWNERS owner groups the change reaches:
group_count counts the owner groups of the changed files and of the impact closure. (unowned) counts as one group.
transitive_only_count counts the groups that own no changed file and that the change reaches only through the impact closure.
unowned_direct_count counts the changed files that no CODEOWNERS rule owns.

groups is a capped list of { owner, direct_count, affected_count } rows, sorted by direct_count (highest first), then affected_count (highest first), then owner. groups_omitted counts the groups that did not fit.
slices is present only when partition.independent_slices is present, with the same order. Each entry is { module_dirs, owners, separable }. separable is true when the slice has one owner.

Each file maps to its primary owner: the last matching rule, and the first owner of that rule. The section reads only the CODEOWNERS file (the configured codeowners path, else the standard locations), so it does not need git history. routing reads the same configured path. Without a readable CODEOWNERS file, the ownership key is absent. A configured path that fallow cannot read prints a warning. The human output lists the owner groups, and names each slice that has one owner. Fallow does not split the change: the reviewer decides.

test_reach states how tests reach each value export that the diff changes. An export counts when its declaring statement overlaps an added line. Type-only exports, re-exports and exports of test files do not count. Fallow reads the reach from the module graph, so it needs no coverage run. Each export gets one reach class:
status is measured, or no-tests when the project has no test files. With no-tests, every export counts as none-file and exports is empty.

masking is active when a test uses a closed mock factory, no-mocks when no test does, and capped when the tests use more than 1024 distinct mock sets. With capped, mock detection is off and a mocked module counts as reached.
total is the number of changed value exports, and counts has one key per reach value.

exports lists at most 25 exports that need attention: mocked-only, none, none-file and transitive, in that order. Inside a class, changed declarations (modified) come before new ones (new), then the order is file, line and name. Each row has file, export_name, line, reach and change. change is new when the file did not export the name at the base of the diff: a new export, a renamed export, or an export of a new file. An edited, rewritten or moved declaration is modified. A mocked-only row adds tests (the mocking test files, at most three), tests_total, test_changed (one of those tests changed in the diff) and mocked_targets (the mocked modules, which can be a barrel in front of the declaring file). exports_omitted counts the rows past the cap.

e2e_runner is true when the project uses Playwright or Cypress. End-to-end tests drive the running app and do not import source files, so the reach classes do not count them. The key is absent when no such runner is present.

Treat reach as an open set: a later version can add a class. Read an unknown value as "needs attention". The section is advisory and never changes the verdict or the exit code. The human brief prints the counts and the first three rows.

Some limits apply. A change inside a non-exported helper is not attributed to the exports that call it. An automock without a factory (vi.mock('./x')) counts as reach. Code that only a setup file imports, and pages that only end-to-end tests visit, get none-file. A test that imports a file only with import type does not load the file, so that file also gets none-file.

The walkthrough guide turns the brief into a strict contract with a coding agent. The graph checks the agent, not a second model. Fallow validates every judgment that the agent returns against the live graph. Fallow fences the free-text framing of the agent as non-deterministic, and that framing never gates.

Save the guide and the judgment outside the project tree, for example in the temporary folder. A new file in the project tree changes the snapshot hash, and fallow then refuses the judgment as stale. Do not create .fallow/ for these files, because a folder that you create has no ignore file.

The response has digest (brief + decision surface), direction, graph_snapshot_hash, agent_schema, injection_note, emitted_signal_ids, and change_anchors. Fallow builds the digest from the graph only and never adds PR prose, so the digest resists injection. The snapshot hash is pinned into the digest.
none: no test file imports the changed unit directly.
untouched: a test imports the unit, and none of those tests is in the diff.
changed: at least one importing test changed together with the unit.

The field is absent when the graph was not retained or the unit is itself a test file. It is a graph fact about direct importers, not a coverage claim. Mocks, fixtures and snapshots help tests but are not tests, so an importer under __mocks__/, fixtures/, __fixtures__/ or __snapshots__/, or a *.fixture.* file, does not count. An importer inside a test directory, such as test/fixtures/, still counts.
action_vocabulary (block, address, consider, fyi): the closed set of values for the action of a judgment.

a recommended concern_vocabulary with the thirteen trade-off lenses: abstraction, coupling, data-model, error-handling, control-flow, performance, dependencies, api-ergonomics, compatibility, state-ownership, extensibility, testability, trust-boundary.
concern stays free text in the JSON. A value from the list lets a review tool group judgments by lens.

change_anchors has one stable chg: id per changed region (hunk), derived from the same diff source that the run used. The id is content-addressed (file path + normalized added text, without line numbers). It survives an edit above the hunk and a whitespace-only change, and it survives a rename through previous_change_anchor. With a change anchor, an agent can anchor a judgment about a changed REGION that has no graph finding (a trade-off with no signal_id). Fallow can then validate that broader trade-off, so the agent cannot invent it.

2. The agent returns judgment JSON. Each judgment cites a signal_id OR a change_anchor that fallow emitted. The agent echoes the hash. The agent writes the judgment to $review/fallow-judgment.json, next to the guide.

action tells the author of the change what to do with the judgment. block and address are required actions, consider is optional, and fyi needs nothing. It is the instruction of the reviewer. Fallow fences it together with the framing, and it never gates.
3. Post-validate the judgment against the live graph.
Fallow sorts each judgment into one of these outcomes:
An accepted judgment echoes action next to agent_framing when the agent set one.
Full dead code analysis with issue-type filters.
Complexity metrics, file scores, hotspots, and targets.
Use fallow tools from AI coding agents.
