pages.title: fallow watch: dead code analysis on every save
items: fallow watch: dead code analysis on every save
Get dead code results each time you save a file. fallow watch re-runs dead code analysis in your TypeScript and JavaScript project when files change.
Keep fallow watch open while you edit, and see new dead code as you save. Watch mode re-runs dead code analysis when files change. Fallow debounces saves. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Watch mode supports the global flags, for example --format, --production, --fail-on-issues, --include-entry-exports, --type-aware, and the --dupes-* flags. The dead-code issue-type filters, such as --unused-exports, are not available.

# Production mode
fallow watch --production

# Compact output
fallow watch --format compact

# Silent, only show results
fallow watch --quiet
Fallow runs the analysis one time at start. Then it runs the analysis again after each change:

✓ No issues found (0.03s)

Watching for changes... (press Ctrl+C to stop)
Changed: src/db.ts

── Unused Code ─────────────────────────────────────

● Unused exports (1)
 src/db.ts
 :2 unusedThing
 Exported symbols with no known consumers
 https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#unused-exports

✗ 1 export (0.02s)

Watching for changes... (press Ctrl+C to stop)
Run the same analysis one time.

pages.title: fallow fix: remove unused exports and dependencies
items: fallow fix: remove unused exports and dependencies
Remove unused exports and dependencies automatically. fallow fix edits your TypeScript and JavaScript files in place, with a dry-run preview and JSON output.
fallow fix removes unused exports and dependencies for you, so you do not clean them up by hand. Fallow edits your source files in place, so use it as you would use a refactoring tool.
Always commit your changes before you run fallow fix. Then you can roll back if a change is wrong.
fallow fix does not fix unused files. Without type-aware analysis, it does not fix unused class members. Use fallow dead-code to find them.
Fallow deletes catalog entries from pnpm-workspace.yaml line by line and keeps the rest of the file intact.
Fallow removes an object-form entry, such as react:\n specifier: ^18.2.0, as one block.

When fallow removes the last entry of a catalog group, it rewrites the header to catalog: {} (or <name>: {}). This keeps the file installable: a bare catalog: with no value parses as null, and pnpm then fails at install time.
Fallow keeps the other comments and the formatting of the file.
After a catalog edit, fallow reminds you to run pnpm install, so pnpm-lock.yaml stays in sync.

By default, fallow also removes a contiguous YAML comment block directly above the entry when the block clearly belongs to that entry. To change this, set fix.catalog.deletePrecedingComments to "auto", "always", or "never". Two exceptions keep your comments safe:
A # fallow-keep marker on any line in the block keeps the block, for all policies. This is the same convention as inline suppression.
The auto policy also keeps section-banner blocks. These are comments whose body starts with three or more =, -, *, _, ~, +, or # characters (for example, # === React 18 production pins ===).
When fallow removes at least one comment line, the human summary adds (+M catalog comment lines) to the count of fixed issues.

Fallow skips entries with a non-empty hardcoded_consumers, so the next pnpm install does not break. In that case, a workspace package still pins a hardcoded version of the same package. Fallow reports the skip on stderr and in the JSON output ({"type": "remove_catalog_entry", "applied": false, "skipped": true, "skip_reason": "hardcoded_consumers", "consumers": [...]}).
The JSON action has two line fields, so CI annotators can pick the anchor they need:
line is the first deleted line. When the policy removes a leading comment, this is the comment line.
entry_line is the original 1-based line of the catalog entry.
The JSON envelope has a top-level "skipped" count next to "total_fixed". CI can use it to gate on partial fixes.

When fallow fix finds duplicate-export issues and no fallow config exists, it creates .fallowrc.json. The next fallow dead-code run then does not show new findings. Fallow builds the file the same way as fallow init (framework and test-runner detection, $schema, entry, ignorePatterns) and adds the ignoreExports rules. Fallow reports the new file on stderr:
Created .fallowrc.json with 2 ignoreExports rule(s). Add it to git.

In a monorepo subpackage, fallow fix does not create a config file, so your config does not split across N sub-packages. Fallow treats a directory as a subpackage when one of pnpm-workspace.yaml, package.json#workspaces, turbo.json, lerna.json, or rush.json is above it. Instead, fallow tells you to use the workspace root:

Skipped duplicate-export config fix: no fallow config file at packages/ui and the
directory is inside a monorepo (workspace root: /repo). Run `fallow init` at the
workspace root, or invoke `fallow fix` from /repo instead of from a subpackage.
In pre-commit hooks, CI bots, and fallow watch, a new top-level file can be a surprise. To prevent it, pass --no-create-config:

# Pre-commit hook
fallow fix --yes --no-create-config

# CI: never create configs as a side effect
fallow fix --yes --no-create-config --format json
Fallow then skips the config change for duplicate exports and prints a message that tells you why. The source-file edits (unused exports, dependencies, enum members, catalog entries) run as usual.

A source file can change between the analysis and the write, for example from an editor save, a CI rebase, or another tool. fallow fix then skips that file, so it does not apply out-of-date line offsets. Fallow reports the skip on stderr (Skipping <path>: file content changed since fallow dead-code ran. Re-run fallow fix to refresh the analysis first.) and in the JSON output ({"type": "skipped", "path": "...", "skipped": true, "skip_reason": "content_changed"}).

A run with a content-changed skip exits with code 2, so CI does not treat the partial run as a clean no-op. The JSON envelope always has a top-level skipped_content_changed: number with the count. This count is separate from skipped, which counts only the catalog and YAML guard skips.
Fallow writes each file change to a temporary file next to the target first. It moves the temporary files to their final paths only after all of them are written.
If a write fails (read-only directory, full disk), all target files keep their original content.
If a rename fails in the middle of the batch, fallow reports it per path, so you can safely run fallow fix again. This is rare: each rename is atomic, but POSIX cannot rename many files atomically.
Fallow reads package.json and pnpm-workspace.yaml again at fix time. If a dependency or catalog entry is already gone, nothing happens.
It is safe to remove an export keyword only when fallow can see every consumer of that symbol. Static analysis cannot see some consumers:
Vitest mock aliases (test.alias that points at a __mocks__ file)
end-to-end suites outside the workspace that import shared helpers
fixture or golden harnesses that a build step connects
If fallow removes an export that one of these uses, a false positive becomes a tsc error and a broken build. For this reason, fallow fix does not remove exports in two low-confidence cases:

Off-graph consumer directories. The file is under one of __mocks__, __fixtures__, fixtures, e2e, e2e-tests, cypress, playwright, examples, evals, or golden (matched on any path segment). Plain test directories (test, tests, __tests__) are not on the list on purpose. Dead test helpers are common, and fallow fix still removes them.
Files with an unresolved import. The file imports something that fallow could not resolve. Its local usage graph is incomplete, so fallow is less sure that the export is unused.

In both cases, fallow writes the per-file entry as {"type": "skipped", "path": "...", "skipped": true, "skip_reason": "low_confidence_off_graph"} (or "low_confidence_unresolved_imports"). The JSON envelope always has a top-level skipped_low_confidence_exports: number with the combined count, separate from skipped.

This skip does not change the exit code. The drift and encoding skips are recoverable failures, but this skip is a deliberate, conservative choice. fallow dead-code still reports the export, so you can confirm that it is unused and remove it by hand. Fallow still removes high-confidence exports in normal source files.

Fallow still reports findings with nonempty reachability_caveats, but fallow fix does not remove them. A caveat can come from a parse error, an unreadable file, or a skipped source file, because each of these can hide a reference. workspace_diagnostics shows where the incomplete evidence comes from. Type-aware approval of a class method does not override this guard.

The fix entry has skipped: true and skip_reason: "low_confidence_incomplete_analysis". The JSON envelope has separate counters for skipped_low_confidence_exports, skipped_low_confidence_dependencies, and skipped_low_confidence_members. They are separate from the general skipped counter. These skips do not change the exit code, so check them even when the command succeeds.
fallow fix supports UTF-8 only. It handles two encoding cases explicitly:

UTF-8 BOM round-trip. Some files start with a UTF-8 byte-order mark (EF BB BF). This is common in TypeScript written on Windows with Notepad, older VS settings, or some IDE plugins. Fallow removes the BOM before it parses the file and computes line offsets, so the reported line numbers do not shift. On write, fallow puts the BOM back, so the file keeps its encoding. Fallow never adds or removes a BOM: if your input has one, the output has one.

Mixed CRLF / LF rejection. Some files contain both \r\n and bare-LF line endings. This is common after cross-platform edits without core.autocrlf. Fallow skips these files, so it does not write changes at the wrong offsets. The stderr message tells you how to fix the file:
Skipping src/mixed.ts: file has mixed CRLF/LF line endings.
Normalize with `dos2unix` or set `git config core.autocrlf input`, then re-run `fallow fix`.
The JSON envelope has a per-file entry ({"type": "skipped", "path": "...", "skipped": true, "skip_reason": "mixed_line_endings"}). It always has a top-level counter skipped_mixed_line_endings: number, separate from skipped_content_changed. If this count is not zero, the run exits with code 2.
The skip does not fix itself. When you run fallow fix again on the same file, you get the same skip. You, your CI, or your AI agent must normalize the line endings of the file first. When one file has findings for more than one fixer (an unused export AND an unused enum member), fallow reports the skip once per file, not once per fixer.

For duplicate-export findings, fallow fix --dry-run prints the proposed config change as a unified diff. You can check the exact bytes before you pass --yes. When fallow would create a new config file, the diff shows the full proposed file (BEFORE is empty):

Would create .fallowrc.json with 2 ignoreExports rule(s):
--- .fallowrc.json (does not exist)
+++ .fallowrc.json (proposed)
@@ -0,0 +1,35 @@
+{
+ "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/schema.json",
+ "entry": ["src/index.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}", "src/main.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}"],
+ "ignorePatterns": [".storybook/**"],
+ ...
+ "ignoreExports": [
+ { "file": "src/components/Button/index.ts", "exports": ["*"] },
+ { "file": "src/components/Card/index.ts", "exports": ["*"] }
+ ]
+}

When a config file already exists, the diff shows context lines around the proposed additions. The JSON output (--dry-run --format json) has the same diff in a proposed_diff field on the fix entry. When fallow would create a config file, the JSON also has a created_files: [".fallowrc.json"] array, so agents can detect that a new file will appear.

# See what would be removed
fallow fix --dry-run

# JSON output for scripting
fallow fix --dry-run --format json

pages.title: fallow list: show files, entry points and plugins
items: fallow list: show files, entry points and plugins
Debug your fallow setup. fallow list shows the discovered files, entry points, active plugins, boundary zones, workspaces, and the import weight of each entry.

When a result looks wrong, first check what fallow found in your project. fallow list shows the files, entry points, plugins, and boundary zones that fallow uses. Use it to debug the configuration, or to confirm that fallow sees the correct project setup.

fallow list --entry-points shows the entry points that the analysis uses. The listing runs the same framework plugins and the same entry-point discovery as fallow dead-code, so the two agree. For example, on a Nuxt project with autoImports on, a component that nothing renders is not an entry point in the listing, and fallow dead-code reports it as an unused file. The MCP project_info tool gives the same list.

When a framework plugin cannot use a config, the listing records it in workspace_diagnostics[], with the same plugin-config-unreadable and plugin-effect-not-modeled entries as the analysis. A --plugins or --entry-points listing has the array only when the plugin stage recorded an entry. See Debugging for the diagnostic kinds.
fallow list --entry-weight shows how much code each runtime entry point loads before it runs. Use it to find the imports that make startup slow, and to keep that number from growing.
For each runtime entry point, fallow walks the import graph and puts every project module that the entry reaches into one of three groups:

import type loads nothing, so fallow does not follow it. A declaration file (.d.ts) loads nothing, so it is not an entry and fallow does not count it when a value import reaches it. Test and config entry points are not runtime entries, so they are not in the report.

Startup import weight of 1 runtime entry (source bytes on disk, not bundle size)
src/main.ts (package.json main)
 eager 9 modules, 4.7 KiB (24 B CSS)
 deferred 4 modules, 209 B
 out of thread 3 modules, 141 B
 eager packages 2: lodash, react
 imports that keep the most bytes eager:
 src/main.ts:5 -> src/heavy/view.ts 3.7 KiB, 3 modules
 src/heavy/view.ts:1 -> src/heavy/chart-data.ts 2.7 KiB, 1 module

Every byte count is the size of the source file on disk. Types, comments, and code that tree shaking removes all count, and bundler chunks do not apply. The value is therefore not a bundle size. It is a repeatable count: the same tree gives the same number, and the number goes down when you move an import behind import(). Package code is not measured: eager_packages lists the packages on the eager path with the specifiers as written, for example lodash/debounce. Platform built-ins such as node:fs are not listed.
Imports that keep the most bytes eager

dominating_imports lists single imports, heaviest first. For each import, exclusive_bytes is the number of bytes that leave the eager group if that one import becomes an import(). An import only counts when it is the only way into its target, so a module that two eager files import is never in the list. line is absent for an edge without a binding, such as export ... from or an eager glob match.

Treat this list as evidence for a review, not as a fix. A lazy load of code that the first screen needs can make startup slower. To see why one module is eager, run fallow trace --path <entry> <module> --eager-only. See Import path between two modules.
The report does not change the health score.
Gate the startup weight in CI
The gate is opt-in. Save a baseline file on your main branch:

The file stores eager_bytes, eager_modules, and the eager package names of each entry. When the file already holds issue counts from fallow dead-code --save-regression-baseline, those counts stay, and the reverse is also true.
Compare a later run with the baseline:

# Report the change of each entry, exit 0
fallow list --entry-weight --regression-baseline .fallow/regression-baseline.json

# Exit 1 when an entry grew by more than 5%
fallow list --entry-weight --regression-baseline .fallow/regression-baseline.json \
 --fail-on-regression --tolerance 5%

The comparison adds entry_weight.regression to the JSON output. Each row has baseline_eager_bytes, current_eager_bytes, new_eager_packages, and exceeded. --tolerance takes a byte count, such as 1024, or a percentage, such as 5%. The default is 0. A new entry has nothing to grow from, so it never fails the gate. --save-regression-baseline needs a file path here, and a run with a [PATH] scope cannot save a baseline.

# Show active plugins
fallow list --plugins

# JSON output for scripting
fallow list --plugins --format json
Fallow reports workspace-discovery problems as workspace_diagnostics[] entries. The kind field tells you the type of problem:
A malformed ROOT package.json is a hard config-load error, and fallow exits 2. For all other problems, fallow prints a warning and continues, so the analysis still runs on the remaining workspaces.

The JSON output of fallow dead-code, fallow dupes, and fallow health also contains these workspace-discovery diagnostics (omitted when empty). A CI job can fail on discovery problems without a separate command. The same JSON output can also include source-discovery skip diagnostics:
skipped-large-file and skipped-minified-file, each with size_bytes
excluded-by-default-ignore, for files that a built-in ignore pattern removed

Other kinds report problems with source reads and parsing, a missing node_modules directory, and checks that did not run. New kinds can appear in later releases. Treat an unknown kind as a new diagnostic, not as an error.

pages.title: fallow inspect: all context for one file or export
items: fallow inspect: all context for one file or export
Get all context for one file or export before you edit it: trace, dead code, duplication, complexity, security, and optional Fallow Cloud production data.

Before you edit a file or exported symbol, get all its evidence in one bundle with fallow inspect. The command is for agents that need the same context as the MCP inspect_target tool, without an MCP session.

fallow inspect --file src/api.ts --format json --quiet
fallow inspect --symbol src/api.ts:fetchUser --format json --quiet

Each evidence section has a status and a scope. The status is ok, partial (the type-aware backend reported incomplete coverage), unavailable (the analysis cannot run in this environment), or error. When one analysis in the bundle fails, and the failure is not fatal, fallow reports an error in that section and adds a warning. You can still use the rest of the bundle.

impact_closure uses the target file as the seed. It lists the files that a change to the target can affect. For a symbol target in type-aware mode, the bundle also has the semantic_trace, api_surface, symbol_impact, and targeted_tests sections.
inspect accepts the project and performance flags: --root, --config, --workspace, --production, --no-cache, and --threads. For the full list, see global flags.
With --cloud, fallow reads the production data of the file from Fallow Cloud and pairs it with the functions of the local file:
The key comes from $FALLOW_API_KEY, else from the key that fallow cloud login stored. The cloud section has its own status:
A status other than ok never fails the run. The static evidence stays complete.
Fallow pairs each local function with a deployed function in two steps:
The stable_id: a hash of the file path, the function name, and the start line.

Else the name plus the position among the functions with the same name in the file. This step pairs a function that moved to another line. When the count of functions with that name changed, fallow does not pair them.

A local function without a pair goes to unpaired_local. It is new, or it moved in a way that fallow cannot follow. Fallow never pairs by name alone, because that gives the numbers of another function.

state is the state in the current deployment. period_state covers the whole period, earlier deployments included. A function with state: "never_called" and period_state: "called" did not run in this deployment, but it ran in an earlier one.

When the data of the file is not actionable yet, for example during the warm-up of a new deployment, Fallow Cloud withholds the never_called rows. The section message then says so, and each local function without a pair gets a note that it can still be deployed and tracked.
A null count means "not measured", never zero. For example, errors is null when error capture did not cover the function, and cpu_ms_per_hour is null without a CPU profile.
Each paired function also has these fields:
--format compact prints one line per item, with or without --cloud:

fallow src/services/user.ts
finding unused-export src/services/user.ts:42 `formatUser` is never imported
finding complexity src/services/user.ts:14 loadUser cyclomatic 21 cognitive 30
prod loadUser:14 called 4120 calls, 1 error group (7 events), 812.5 ms CPU/h, 2 never-run branches, 3 static callers, prod callers getUser (src/routes/user.ts)
prod parseRow:60 never_called in 30 days
prod formatRow:72 not called in this deployment, called earlier in 30 days
prod newHelper:80 no production data (new or moved since deploy)

The MCP inspect_target tool uses the same CLI flow and returns the same JSON shape. When you already work in a shell or an editor command, use the CLI. When an agent is already connected to the MCP server, use MCP. Set cloud: true on a file target to add the cloud section. Set format: "compact" to get the compact text.
See the call-chain data that --symbol-chain adds.
Use the inspect_target tool from AI coding agents.

pages.title: fallow trace: find callers and import paths
items: fallow trace: find callers and import paths
See what calls an exported symbol and what it calls before you change it, or how one module comes to import another. fallow trace uses the module graph.
Before you change an exported symbol, use fallow trace to see how it connects to the rest of the codebase. The command walks the call chain of one symbol in two directions, up to --depth:
Callers, up: the modules that import the symbol.
Callees, down: the import-symbol edges, plus the call sites in the same module.

fallow trace src/api.ts:fetchUser --format json --quiet
fallow trace src/api.ts:fetchUser --callers --depth 2
fallow trace --path src/app.ts src/db.ts
fallow trace --dependency date-fns --format json --quiet

--path answers a different question: which chain of imports connects one module to another. See Import path between two modules. --dependency reports how the code uses each imported name of a package. See Usage of a package.

fallow trace is a standalone, best-effort command. Its results are not part of the ranked review brief, and they never change the focus map or its ranking. Use trace to see how a symbol connects. For a prioritized review, use the review brief.
fallow trace takes one positional argument in FILE:SYMBOL form:
FILE is a project-relative path, and SYMBOL is the exported symbol name. When you pass --path or --dependency, omit this argument. --path takes two file paths. --dependency takes a package name.

When a file exists at the exact path from the project root, fallow takes that file. src/api.ts then never selects packages/x/src/api.ts. When no file has the exact path, fallow accepts a path suffix. A short path that matches more than one file takes the first match, so use the full project-relative path in a monorepo.

Without --callers or --callees, fallow walks both directions. trace also accepts the project, output, and performance global flags: --root, --config, --format with human or json, --quiet, --no-cache, --threads, and --changed-since.

The walk is best-effort and syntactic. Fallow reports resolved and unresolved callees. An unresolved callee, for example a dynamic call that fallow cannot resolve statically, stays in the output as unresolved. The chain thus shows what fallow could follow and what it could not.

When code references the same export in type space and in value space, the JSON output adds direct_references_by_namespace. This field has separate evidence for each namespace. For compatibility, namespace and direct_references keep their earlier meaning: they describe only the winning namespace. When only one namespace has references, fallow omits direct_references_by_namespace. Read a missing field as the usual case of one namespace.
Each reference entry also tells you if a text search for the export name finds the consumer. See Search visibility in traces.

When two export * sources both give the requested name, the barrel exports
nothing under that name. The JSON output reports symbol_found: false and adds a
star_export_ambiguity object:

sources lists the files that declare the name, sorted, as project-relative paths.
namespaces tells you if the collision is in type space, value space,
or both, with type before value. With this object, you can tell a barrel
collision from an unknown or misspelled symbol. To fix the collision, keep one
origin and rename the others, or replace the star exports with explicit re-exports.
You can also get the same best-effort call-chain data as opt-in evidence from fallow inspect --symbol-chain and from the symbol_chain option of the inspect_target MCP tool.
--dependency <PACKAGE> reports how the code uses each imported name of a package. Use it before a library migration or an API change, when you must know which names the code uses and where.

fallow trace --dependency date-fns --format json --quiet
fallow trace --dependency date-fns --specifier format --format json --quiet
fallow trace --dependency date-fns --callers --depth 1 --format json --quiet
The JSON output is the --trace-dependency result of fallow dead-code plus one usage object:
specifiers has one entry for each imported name: file_count, type_only_file_count, and call_site_count.

wrappers lists the project exports that wrap the name, for example export const useAppSelector = useSelector.withTypes<RootState>(). Each wrapper has its consumer files and calls. The trace follows one wrapper step.

unresolved counts each use that the trace cannot resolve, for each name: value_alias, non_call_reference, jsx_element, re_export, nested_wrapper, and binding_without_site. The top-level unresolved counts the file-level forms: dynamic_import, require, side_effect_import, star_re_export, and unattributed_file. A use that the trace cannot resolve is counted. It is not dropped.

sites is a page of usage sites, sorted by file, line, and column. Each site has a kind. When more sites exist, pass the next_cursor value to --cursor. Fallow adds the page when you pass --sites, --specifier, --limit, or --cursor.
closure lists the files that import the users, up to --depth, when you pass --callers.
The trace is syntactic (confidence: "syntactic"). It does not use the TypeScript compiler. fallow dead-code --trace-dependency keeps its own output without the usage object.
Use --path to find out why a module depends on another module. fallow trace --path <FROM> <TO> reports the shortest chain of imports from FROM to TO. Both are project-relative file paths.

An exact project-relative or absolute path wins over a suffix match. Fallow accepts an abbreviation only when it identifies one module. A missing or ambiguous endpoint exits with code 2. To remove the ambiguity, use the full project-relative path.

Shortest import path (syntactic; OFF the ranked path)

 from: pages/report.tsx
 to: components/Box.tsx
 hops: 3

 [1] pages/report.tsx:20 -> lib/related.transform.ts
 [2] lib/related.transform.ts:1 -> components/RelatedContent.tsx
 [3] components/RelatedContent.tsx:3 -> components/Box.tsx
The JSON output has the same walk under kind: "trace", with its own schema_version:

{
 "kind": "trace",
 "schema_version": "1",
 "from": "pages/report.tsx",
 "to": "components/Box.tsx",
 "reachable": true,
 "hops": 3,
 "path": [
 {
 "from": "pages/report.tsx",
 "to": "lib/related.transform.ts",
 "type_only": false,
 "dynamic": false,
 "import_line": 20
 },
 {
 "from": "lib/related.transform.ts",
 "to": "components/RelatedContent.tsx",
 "type_only": false,
 "dynamic": false,
 "import_line": 1
 },
 {
 "from": "components/RelatedContent.tsx",
 "to": "components/Box.tsx",
 "type_only": false,
 "dynamic": false,
 "import_line": 3
 }
 ],
 "reason": "pages/report.tsx reaches components/Box.tsx in 3 hops"
}
You can rely on these behaviors:
Fallow reports a type-only hop with type_only: true and does not skip it. A path that exists only in type space is thus visible.
Fallow reports a lazy hop with dynamic: true. The target of such a hop loads only on demand (import(), a lazy glob) or on another thread (a worker, a fork). The human output tags the hop [dynamic].

With --eager-only, the walk follows only static imports that carry a runtime value. import(), lazy globs, worker loads, and import type do not qualify. The route explains why a module is in the eager group of fallow list --entry-weight. When no such route exists, reachable is false.
An unreachable pair is a result, and not an error. reachable is false, path is empty, hops is 0, and reason says that fallow found no import path. The command still exits 0.
A trace from a module to itself returns reachable: true with hops: 0. The hop count is 0 in both cases, so branch on reachable.
Get one evidence bundle for a file or exported symbol, with opt-in --symbol-chain.
Get a verdict on changed files, plus the graph-derived review brief and decision surface.

Use fallow tools from AI coding agents.

pages.title: fallow trace-error: map a stack trace to your code
items: fallow trace-error: map a stack trace to your code
Map a runtime stack trace to the definitions in your code. fallow trace-error resolves each frame against the module graph, without reading source maps.
Give fallow trace-error a runtime stack trace, and it tells you which definitions in your project the frames name. First, it sorts each reported frame into one of three origins:
Then it resolves the in-project frames against the definitions that fallow already extracted.

fallow trace-error crash.txt
cat crash.txt | fallow trace-error
fallow trace-error - --format json --quiet

Fallow reads the trace from a file argument, from -, or from stdin when you give no argument. Fallow resolves a relative path against the project root, the same as --diff-file. Fallow supports V8, Node, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore traces.
trace-error is a standalone, best-effort command. Its results are not part of the ranked review brief, and they never change the focus map or its ranking.
When the command cannot answer, it says so, and it does not guess.
A frame that matches several definitions reports ambiguous. It lists a limited number of candidates, and candidates_omitted counts the other matches.
A frame that matches nothing reports not_found. It stays in the output.
A frame that fallow did not try to resolve reports not_attempted, with the reason.
Reported frames stay in frames[] in input order. counts has the total for each outcome. frames_omitted counts the frames beyond the report limit.
An exact project-relative or absolute file path wins over an abbreviated suffix match. If an abbreviated path matches more than one module, the result reports that ambiguity.

Fallow does not read source maps. It reports a frame inside generated build output as generated output. A stale source map can point to the wrong line without a warning, and a wrong line is worse than no line.
trace-error takes the project, output, and performance global flags: --root, --config, --format with human or json, --pretty, --quiet, --no-cache, and --threads.
The input limit is 1 MiB. The report includes up to 256 frames, and up to 10 candidate definitions for each frame. The report always counts what it omits. Input over the limit exits with code 2.

Stack-trace frames (syntactic; OFF the ranked path)

 source: crash.txt
 error: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title')

 [0] Box components/Box.tsx:12 [in-project/not-found]
 no definition named 'Box' is exported from the module this frame points at; a module-local function is not in the graph's definition set
 [1] renderWithHooks node_modules/react-dom/cjs/react-dom.development.js:14985 [node-modules/not-attempted]
 frame is in an installed dependency, not in project source
 [2] Object.<anonymous> /opt/build/generated/chunk-4f2a.js:1 [out-of-corpus/not-attempted]
 '/opt/build/generated/chunk-4f2a.js' is generated build output; resolving it back to source needs a source map, which this command does not read

 frames 3 | resolved 0 | ambiguous 0 | not found 1 | not attempted 2
Each frame shows its origin and resolution as an [origin/resolution] pair. The indented line below gives the reason.

{
 "kind": "trace-error",
 "schema_version": "1",
 "source": "crash.txt",
 "header": "TypeError: boom",
 "frames": [
 {
 "index": 0,
 "raw": "at transformCard (lib/card.transform.ts:22:9)",
 "function": "transformCard",
 "file": "lib/card.transform.ts",
 "line": 22,
 "column": 9,
 "origin": "in_project",
 "resolution": "resolved",
 "candidates": [
 {
 "file": "lib/card.transform.ts",
 "symbol": "transformCard",
 "kind": "export",
 "line": 20
 }
 ],
 "candidates_omitted": 0,
 "reason": "'transformCard' names lib/card.transform.ts:transformCard (export)"
 }
 ],
 "counts": {
 "frames": 1,
 "frames_omitted": 0,
 "in_project": 1,
 "node_modules": 0,
 "out_of_corpus": 0,
 "resolved": 1,
 "ambiguous": 0,
 "not_found": 0,
 "not_attempted": 0,
 "unparsed_lines": 0
 },
 "reason": "1 frame: 1 resolved, 0 ambiguous, 0 not found, 0 not attempted"
}

counts.frames is the number of reported frames. resolved + ambiguous + not_found + not_attempted equals that number, and so does in_project + node_modules + out_of_corpus. To get the total number of recognized input frames, add counts.frames_omitted. If fallow recognizes no line in a trace, it reports zero frames and a non-zero unparsed_lines. You can thus tell it apart from an empty trace.

The trace_error MCP tool runs this command. Give it the stack trace from a failing test or a production error. Then read frames[].candidates[] to find the files to open. A not_found result on an in-project frame means that fallow could not match the frame name to a definition. The function may be module-local, or the runtime name may differ from the extracted definition.
Walk a symbol's call chain, or find the shortest import path between two modules.
Get one evidence bundle for a file or exported symbol.

pages.title: fallow decision-surface: find the decisions to review
items: fallow decision-surface: find the decisions to review
Find the structural decisions in a code change that need a human judgment call. fallow decision-surface prints each one as a question with the expert to ask.
A large diff often contains only one or two choices that are expensive to undo. fallow decision-surface finds those structural decisions and gives you each one as a question for the right reviewer.
a signal_id, a deterministic anchor from the module graph
decision-surface prints the top layer of the review brief without the rest of the brief.

fallow decision-surface --base main
fallow decision-surface --base main --format json --quiet
fallow decision-surface --base main --max-decisions 5

fallow decision-surface always exits 0 when the analysis runs. It never blocks CI, and its output has no verdict. A runtime error, such as a base ref that does not exist, exits 2. fallow audit is the command that exits non-zero on a fail verdict. Use decision-surface to find the one or two things that need a human judgment call. Use audit to find out if CI blocks the change.
Three commands inspect changed code. Each one answers a different question.

fallow decision-surface runs the same changed-code analysis as fallow review, but prints only the decisions. It drops the rest of the brief: the subtract list, the weighted focus map, and the walkthrough contract. Use it when you want only the few structural choices in the diff.

A change can touch hundreds of lines and still contain only one or two choices that are expensive to undo. The decision surface isolates those choices. Each entry is a framed judgment question with the context that a reviewer or coding agent needs to answer it. It is not a recommendation. Fallow never tells you which option to choose.
The decision surface has exactly three categories:
Fallow never reports these changes as dependency decisions:

The importer count is a union over the batched packages, so a module that imports two bumped packages counts once. For entries outside dependencies, the question names the section (dev, optional, peer). When a package is in several sections, the decision uses its dependencies range and anchor line.

Fallow ranks the decisions by consequence (blast radius x reversibility) and caps the list at 3 to 5 decisions. The default is 4. Set the cap with --max-decisions. There is no pagination. The cap is deliberate: a reviewer can keep a few structural questions in mind, but not a long list of findings.
The human output shows the question and the trade-off. Read reversibility from the consumer count. Fallow never labels a decision as a one-way or two-way door.

To suppress a coupling-boundary or public-api-contract decision, add // fallow-ignore-next-line decision-surface <category> above the decision's anchor. The suppress action holds the exact comment. A dependency decision anchors on package.json, which cannot hold a comment. It has no suppress action, but ask-expert still applies. Suppression removes a decision from the output. It does not change the verdict.
Fallow builds the decision surface for coding agents. Request JSON output:
For each decision, show the question and the expert list to the human, not the raw diff.

Use internal_consumer_count to choose how strongly to flag the decision. 0 means a cheap choice that is easy to undo. A high count means many modules depend on the anchor, so the choice is expensive to undo.
Quote the tradeoff text word for word. It is a fact, so the agent can pass it on without comment.
Attach each comment to signal_id. If the run reports a previous_signal_id, move the earlier comment across the rename. Do not post a duplicate.
fallow builds the decisions from the module graph only. It never adds PR prose to them. The decisions show the actual structural change, not a description of it.
decision-surface scopes to changed code in the same way as fallow audit. Use --base (or its alias --changed-since) to set the ref that "changed" compares against.

# Against the merge-base with the default branch (auto-detected)
fallow decision-surface

# Explicit base ref
fallow decision-surface --base main

# Decisions embedded in the last 5 commits
fallow decision-surface --base HEAD~5
See global flags for the full list.

# Auto-detect base; render the decisions for a human
fallow decision-surface

# Explicit base ref
fallow decision-surface --base main

# Raise the cap
fallow decision-surface --base main --max-decisions 5

Decisions to make (2):
 1. [dependency] `package.json` adds 1 third-party dependency (`left-pad`),
 imported by 1 in-repo module. What does each replace, and who owns the
 new surface?
 trade-off: Takes on 1 new maintenance and supply-chain surface; 0 in-repo
 modules outside this diff already import the added packages.
 ask: alice (bus-factor 1)
 2. [public-api-contract] This change adds 2 exports to the public API surface.
 Intended as maintained contracts, or should they stay internal?
 trade-off: Adds 2 maintained contracts; 0 in-repo modules already consume
 this surface, and any external consumers become a contract you cannot
 remove without a breaking change.
 ask: alice (bus-factor 1)
When the change has no structural decision, the output is Decisions: none (no consequential structural decision in this change).

fallow decision-surface --format json returns the decisions[] array. Each entry has the fields in What each decision carries. signal_count is the number of signal IDs that fallow emitted, including decisions below the cap. truncated is present when fallow collapsed decisions below the cap. fallow review --format json returns the same decisions in decisions.decisions[], without actions.

{
 "kind": "decision-surface",
 "schema_version": 1,
 "version": "3.43.1",
 "command": "decision-surface",
 "decisions": [
 {
 "signal_id": "sig:efab2fe6cef7b663",
 "category": "public-api-contract",
 "question": "This change adds 2 exports to the public API surface. Intended as maintained contracts, or should they stay internal?",
 "anchor_file": "src/index.ts",
 "anchor_line": 1,
 "signal_key": "src/index.ts::y|src/index.ts::z",
 "blast": 0,
 "consequence": 0,
 "expert": ["alice"],
 "bus_factor_one": true,
 "internal_consumer_count": 0,
 "tradeoff": "Adds 2 maintained contracts; 0 in-repo modules already consume this surface, and any external consumers become a contract you cannot remove without a breaking change.",
 "actions": [
 { "type": "ask-expert", "description": "Ask alice to make this call", "auto_fixable": false },
 {
 "type": "suppress",
 "description": "Suppress this decision if it is settled",
 "command": "// fallow-ignore-next-line decision-surface public-api-contract",
 "auto_fixable": false
 }
 ]
 }
 ],
 "signal_count": 1
}
The decision_surface MCP tool gives an agent the same decisions through a structured tool call:

base and max_decisions map to the CLI flags with the same names. The MCP tool also returns dependency decisions, because both routes use the same manifest diff. See MCP integration for the full tool list and setup.
The audit that gates CI, and the full review brief that includes these decisions.

pages.title: fallow workspaces: inspect monorepo workspace discovery
items: fallow workspaces: inspect monorepo workspace discovery
List the monorepo workspaces that fallow discovers, with diagnostics for malformed package.json files, unmatched globs, and missing tsconfig references.

fallow workspaces shows the workspace packages that fallow discovers in a monorepo. It also shows the workspace-discovery diagnostics, for example a malformed package.json, a glob that matches no package, or a missing tsconfig reference.
The command is equal to fallow list --workspaces. Use it when you need only the workspace topology. The other list sections stay hidden.
The human output gives one line for each workspace, with its package name and its project-relative path:
A malformed root package.json stops the config load, and fallow exits with code 2. For all other problems, fallow prints a warning and continues with the remaining workspaces.
fallow workspaces has no flags of its own. It accepts the global flags, for example --root, --config, --format (human or json), and --quiet.
To scope an analysis to some workspaces, pass --workspace <glob> or --changed-workspaces <ref> to the analysis command. See Workspaces.
Show files, entry points, plugins, boundaries, and workspaces together.
Configure workspace discovery and scope analyses to packages.
Check the project readiness before the first analysis.
See the flags that every command accepts.

pages.title: fallow explain: what a finding means and how to fix it
items: fallow explain: what a finding means and how to fix it
Learn what a fallow finding means and how to fix it. fallow explain prints the rationale, an example, fix guidance, and a docs link for one issue type.
Get a short rule guide for one issue type before you decide to fix, suppress, or configure a finding. fallow explain does not run analysis. Agents and CI bots use it to read the rule before they act.

fallow explain unused-export
fallow explain fallow/code-duplication --format json --quiet

{
 "kind": "explain",
 "id": "fallow/unused-export",
 "name": "Unused Exports",
 "summary": "Export is never imported",
 "rationale": "Named exports that are never imported by any other module in the project. Includes both direct exports and re-exports through barrel files. The export may still be used locally within the same file.",
 "example": "export const formatPrice = ... exists in src/money.ts, but no module imports formatPrice.",
 "how_to_fix": "Remove the export or make it file-local. If it is public API, import it from an entry point or add an intentional suppression with context.",
 "docs": "https://fallow.tools/docs/explanations/dead-code/#unused-exports"
}
The fallow_explain MCP tool runs fallow explain <issue-type> --format json --quiet:
An agent can call it to read the rule before it applies a fix or a suppression.
An unknown issue type exits with code 2. The error message gives examples of valid values.
Set the severity of each issue type.
Suppress a finding with a comment or config.
Call fallow_explain and other tools from an agent.
Read what each dead code finding means.

pages.title: fallow suppressions: list every fallow-ignore comment
items: fallow suppressions: list every fallow-ignore comment
List every finding that your team chose to ignore, and why. fallow suppressions lists each fallow-ignore marker by file with its reason and a stale count.

Use fallow suppressions to review what your project ignores, and to find markers that have no reason. The command lists every active fallow-ignore-next-line and fallow-ignore-file marker in the analyzed files. It groups the markers by file, with line, kind, level, and reason. It also prints project totals and a stale count, which comes from the stale-suppression findings of this run.
The command is for review and governance. It does not detect issues, and it always exits 0.

● Suppression inventory (1)
 src/util.ts
 :1 unused-export (file-wide) reason: legacy surface for the v2 SDK migration window

● Totals by kind
 unused-export: 1
A marker gives its reason after a -- separator. The inventory reports markers without a reason, so you can require a reason on each marker:
// fallow-ignore-file unused-export -- legacy surface for the v2 SDK migration window
--format json prints the suppression-inventory envelope (schema version 1). A blanket marker has no kind and suppresses everything. Its JSON has kind: null, and the human output shows "blanket".
The stale count is not a new detection. Fallow takes it from the stale-suppression findings of this run. A marker is stale when it no longer matches any issue.
A run with --changed-since also has a root request_outcomes object with the changed-since entry. When fallow cannot resolve the ref, the entry says so, and the inventory covers the whole project.

Agents that use MCP get the same inventory from the list_suppressions tool. The tool returns this envelope unchanged. It runs a full analysis, so on large repositories, raise FALLOW_TIMEOUT_SECS. See MCP integration.
Rule severities, including stale-suppressions and require-suppression-reason

pages.title: fallow impact: a local report of fallow results
items: fallow impact: a local report of fallow results
See what fallow has done in a project. fallow impact is a local-only report of current findings, the trend, commits stopped at the gate, and resolved findings.
See what fallow has done for you in this project. fallow impact reports:
how many issues fallow reports now
the trend since the last recorded run
how many commits the pre-commit or agent gate contained (blocked, then cleared after a fix)
how many findings were truly resolved over time
Impact is opt-in and local-only. The history is in your user config dir (see Storage and cleanup):
fallow never writes anything into the repo: no .fallow/ directory, and no .gitignore change.
Recording never changes exit codes or analysis output.
Fallow does not record in CI, or for a project in a system temp folder (for example /tmp or $TMPDIR). Such a folder holds test fixtures and throwaway clones.

fallow impact enable # track this project (overrides the global default)
fallow impact # render the value report (also prints the store path)
fallow impact status # tracking state and history size
fallow impact statusline # print one stable line for a status bar
fallow impact disable # stop tracking this project (history is retained)
fallow impact default on # track every project by default (one global opt-in)
fallow impact reset # delete this project's history (--all wipes every project)
fallow impact --all # roll up every project: impact across all your repos

To turn on Impact for every project at once, run fallow impact default on. A per-project fallow impact enable or disable always wins over the global default. You can thus opt one repo out and keep Impact on everywhere else.

fallow impact statusline prints exactly one plain-text line for shell and editor status bars. The line contains no paths. The command reads only the local Impact store. It starts no analysis, never turns on recording, and writes nothing to stderr on success.

The command ignores --format on purpose. Do not parse its output as JSON. The trend uses only whole-project scans that fallow can compare. Fallow labels older changed-file history and shows it without a trend.

To see what fallow has done for you in all your projects at once, run fallow impact --all. It combines the per-project histories in your config dir into one ranked table, plus grand totals. It reads only the stored histories and runs no analysis, so it works from any directory, also outside a repo.

fallow impact --all # ranked table + grand totals (sorted by most recent)
fallow impact --all --sort resolved # rank by lifetime findings resolved
fallow impact --all --limit 10 # cap printed rows (totals still cover every project)

To sort, use --sort {recent,resolved,contained,name} (default recent). Fallow summarizes projects with no recorded history yet, and does not list them. Each repo has its folder name as its label. A history from an older fallow version shows a short key until its next recorded run.

The --format json output has a separate impact-cross-repo shape. Each entry contains the same per-project report as fallow impact, plus a stable project_key. Like the single-project report, it never includes a filesystem path. As with all of Impact, the report shows local developer work, and it is empty in CI.

Fallow adds to the history when fallow audit runs with a gate marker. Two gates pass that marker: the Git pre-commit hook from fallow init --hooks, and the Claude Code agent gate from fallow hooks install --target agent. Local bare fallow runs update the whole-project Surfacing and Trend signals.
When tracking is on and the results are not zero, fallow shows the headline numbers at most once a week:
The JSON output has an impact-report entry in the next_steps[] array, also on runs that are otherwise clean.
Bare fallow prints a one-line Impact: summary next to the failure summary.

Fallow stores the time of the last digest in the impact store. The digest thus stays weekly across agents, sessions, and surfaces. Fallow never shows a digest with zero results, and CI never gets the digest.
Each project keeps one small history file in your user config dir:

Fallow keys each file by repository. When you run fallow impact from any subdirectory or git worktree of a repo, you see the history of that repo. An advisory lock puts concurrent recordings in sequence, for example a pre-commit gate that runs in two worktrees at once. Neither run thus loses the data of the other.

When you delete a repo from disk, its store stays until you remove it. Set FALLOW_IMPACT_STORE_MAX_AGE_DAYS to a number of days. A recorded run then removes each store that nobody touched for longer than that. When the variable is unset (the default), fallow keeps every store forever. You can also delete history with fallow impact reset (this project) or fallow impact reset --all (every project).

A newer fallow can write a store with a higher schema_version than your fallow supports. This can happen when a project pins an older fallow and you also run a newer global fallow. An older fallow does not change such a store, because it can lose the data of the fields that it does not know:
fallow impact enable, fallow impact disable, and fallow init --decline exit with code 2. The error names the store schema and the fallow version of the newest record.
Audit and combined runs do not record into the store, and they log the same message. The weekly digest does not appear.
Reads stay available: fallow impact, fallow impact status, and fallow impact statusline.
To fix this, upgrade the fallow that the project uses to the version that wrote the store, or a later one.
fallow impact --format json and fallow impact status --format json print the report shape from the published output schema:
Three fields help an agent that asks the user about the opt-in in a conversation:
enabled_source says why tracking is on or off. The values are project (an explicit per-repo enable or disable), user (the global default), or default (off).

explicit_decision is set only by an explicit impact enable or impact disable. An agent can thus tell "asked and declined" (enabled: false, explicit_decision: true) from "never asked" (enabled: false, explicit_decision: false), and offer the opt-in exactly once.
onboarding_declined is set by fallow init --decline. It stops the first-contact setup pointer of fallow for this project.
Install the pre-commit hook. It passes the gate marker that Impact records.
Install the agent gate. It adds to the containment count.
FALLOW_IMPACT_STORE_MAX_AGE_DAYS and the other Impact settings.

pages.title: fallow viz: visualize your codebase as an HTML map
items: fallow viz: visualize your codebase as an HTML map
Visualize dead code, duplication, boundary violations, and complexity in your codebase. fallow viz writes one HTML map with a treemap and an import graph.

Use fallow viz to see where the findings sit in your codebase, and to click from a finding to the evidence behind it. The command runs one project analysis and writes one self-contained HTML file. The file needs no server and no external assets, and it has the same style as the rest of fallow. fallow viz is read-only.

fallow viz # writes fallow-viz.html and opens it in your browser
fallow viz --out map.html --no-open
fallow viz --viz-format dot # emit the import graph as Graphviz DOT
fallow viz --viz-format mermaid # emit the import graph as a Mermaid diagram
The HTML map has two views of the same project:
Treemap of files sized by bytes, nested by directory.

Force-directed import graph, with clusters by directory and by import community. When you focus a file, an import that loads its target only on demand (import(), a lazy glob, a worker) has a dashed line.
Each lens gives the map different colors. The two views share the four lenses:
Click a file to open a detail panel. The panel shows the evidence behind each finding:
clone groups and their other locations
importers and imports, as links to click through
a fallow ... --trace command that you can run to verify the finding

The map also has search, breadcrumb drill-down, keyboard shortcuts, shareable URL deep links, and dark and light themes. Findings have a hatch texture and an [E] or [W] prefix, so color is never the only signal. All motion follows prefers-reduced-motion.
Global flags such as --root, --config, --production, --no-cache, --changed-since, --workspace, and --threads also apply.
To pipe the import graph into other tools, use --viz-format dot or --viz-format mermaid. Fallow then writes the graph as text, and does not write the HTML map:

fallow viz --viz-format dot | dot -Tsvg -o graph.svg
fallow viz --viz-format mermaid > graph.mmd
Find the unused code that the dead code lens shows.
Find the duplication that the duplication lens shows.
Find the complexity hotspots that the complexity lens shows.
Verify one finding from the command line, with the same --trace command that each detail panel shows.

pages.title: fallow doctor: check your project setup
items: fallow doctor: check your project setup
Check if fallow sees your project correctly before you trust its results. fallow doctor runs read-only checks on config, workspaces, plugins, and caches.

A misconfigured project can give output that looks clean but is wrong. fallow doctor checks your setup without running an analysis, so you know if you can trust the results of other commands. It checks:
that the project root is readable
that workspace discovery found the packages you expect
that the optional type-aware companion is present
that the persisted caches are compatible with the project
that the installed Vitest is a version that fallow mutation supports
Each check is a local read. You can safely run doctor as the first command on a repository that you have never analyzed. It is also fast enough for a CI preflight step.
doctor only tells you if fallow can see your project correctly. It does not analyze your code. When it reports ready, run fallow dead-code and fallow health to analyze the code.
When a check that is not required cannot run, it reports skipped. A skipped check never fails the command. The type-aware check is skipped when type-aware analysis is off, which is the default.
The last four checks can only warn. They cannot fail, so they never change the exit code.

dependencies warns when the project has no node_modules directory and needs one. Until you install the dependencies, fallow gives less accurate results for package exports, plugin activation, and dependency classification.

cache and graph-cache warn when a persisted blob exists but a run would discard it. The warning gives the reason and the size on disk. A project with no cache yet passes, because a first run has no cache.

mutation-runner warns when the installed Vitest is outside the supported range of fallow mutation, or when Vitest is not installed. The message gives the supported range and the install step, and the remediation is the install command. The check reads the package.json of the installed Vitest and runs no code. It passes for a supported version. It is skipped for the node-test and bun-test runners. It is also skipped when mutation.runner does not select Vitest, the root package.json declares no Vitest, and the root node_modules holds no Vitest. A workspace package can declare a Vitest that the package manager installs at the root, so the check counts the root install.
A project with one of these warnings reports the aggregate warn and still exits 0.

There are two cache checks because a run reuses the two blobs independently. The extraction cache can be reusable while fallow rebuilds the module graph on every run. graph-cache checks that the blob loads and belongs to this project root. A pass does not prove that a run will reuse the blob. The reuse decision also compares resolver options, entry points, and per-file content hashes. To compute those, fallow must run discovery and extraction, and doctor does not do that.

When FALLOW_CACHE_DIR is nonempty, it sets the cache location and takes priority over the configured cache directory. Fallow resolves relative paths against the project root, the same as during analysis.
An absent cache is normal on a first run.
An unreadable cache gets a separate report with a hint about the path and permissions.
A decoding failure can mean an older cache format or damaged data. It does not prove corruption. When you rebuild the cache, it uses the current format.

doctor reads and never writes, so it rejects --output-file. The report goes to stdout, and the files that doctor checks do not change. doctor runs no analysis, so it also rejects analysis and gate flags such as --production and --fail-on-issues. It does not ignore them silently.
doctor never exits 1. That code means error-severity findings. doctor checks your setup and not your code, so it has no findings.

Fallow doctor (.)
[OK] root: Project root is an accessible directory.
[OK] config: Configuration resolved from .fallowrc.json.
[OK] workspaces: Workspace discovery completed (30 workspace packages).
[OK] plugins: No external plugins are configured; built-in detection remains available.
[-] type-aware: Type-aware analysis is not enabled.
[OK] dependencies: Dependencies are installed, or the project runs without a node_modules directory.
[W] cache: Extraction cache (0.9 MB) would not be reused: cache format version changed. The next run parses every file.
 Action (from project root): fallow dead-code --quiet
[OK] graph-cache: Module-graph cache (0.5 MB) loads; a run reuses it when the analysed files and options are unchanged.
[OK] mutation-runner: vitest 4.1.12 is in the supported mutation runner range >=4.1.0 <6.0.0.
Status: ready with warnings
The last line gives the status: ready, ready with warnings, or not ready. When a check has a remediation, it prints the remediation on an indented Action line under the message.

 },

 },

 "id": "mutation-runner",
 "category": "companion",
 "status": "pass",
 "required": false,
 "message": "vitest 4.1.12 is in the supported mutation runn
The top-level status is pass, warn, or fail. The status of a single check can also be skipped.
A check can have a remediation object with command, cwd, and mutating:
cwd is always the project root.
mutating tells you if the command writes anything. An agent can run the read-only commands without asking.

An install remediation uses the package manager of the project: pnpm install, yarn install or bun install instead of npm install. The type-aware companion install follows the same rule. The packageManager field of package.json wins, then the lockfile. A workspace package uses the signal of its monorepo root. Without either signal, the command uses npm.

If you pass --config with a project-relative path that is safe to render, the remediation command repeats it. For an external config path, or a path that is not safe to render, fallow omits the command. The message then tells the caller to use the same --config value again.

Run fallow doctor --format json --quiet before the first analysis on an unfamiliar repository. A clean project and a misconfigured project can both give empty results, and doctor is the fastest way to tell them apart. Branch on the top-level status. Then read checks[].message to tell the user what to fix.
Config file discovery and the available options.
How fallow discovers the packages in a monorepo.
Set up the optional type-aware companion.
Variables such as FALLOW_CACHE_DIR that change fallow behavior.

pages.title: fallow init: create a fallow config file
items: fallow init: create a fallow config file
Create a fallow config file with editor autocomplete and validation. fallow init generates a .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml file with schema support.
Use fallow init to create a configuration file for your project. The generated config has a $schema field, so your editor gives autocomplete and validation.
Most projects do not need a config file. Fallow detects entry points and frameworks automatically. Create a config file only if you need custom entry points, rules, or ignore patterns.
fallow init detects your project setup and adapts the generated config to it:
TypeScript: finds tsconfig.json and turns on TypeScript-aware defaults.
Monorepo: finds workspace configurations (npm, yarn, pnpm) and adds the workspace patterns.
Frameworks: finds installed frameworks (Next.js, Remix, Vite, and others) and adds the matching entry point patterns.

After fallow init writes the config, it names the next step: run fallow for a first report, and run fallow agent install --dry-run to see the setup for coding agents. When the config root is not the current directory, both commands include --root. --quiet removes this line.

A bare fallow run on a project without a config shows a one-line setup hint. The hint names fallow init for a config and fallow agent install --dry-run for the agent guide, the skills, the MCP server, and the commit gate. The JSON setup next step makes the same offer. To hide the hint, run fallow init --decline.

fallow init --agents gives coding agents a starting guide for your project. It writes a short starter AGENTS.md with prompts for these sections: project overview, architecture, commands, fallow workflow, and agent rules.

The file also has a task-to-command matrix. The matrix sends common agent tasks to the right fallow command, for example: delete "unused" code, commit, prioritize refactors, and consolidate duplication. It is the same matrix as task_matrix in fallow schema.
The command does not overwrite an existing AGENTS.md. The file is guidance for agents. It is not a readiness score.
When fallow can reliably detect the project shape, it prefills these lines:
Install from the packageManager field in package.json, or pnpm install when pnpm-workspace.yaml is present
Test with the detected test framework (Vitest, Jest, or Playwright), but only when exactly one is present
Typecheck or lint with tsc --noEmit when tsconfig.json exists
Module boundaries with the workspace patterns for monorepos
Fallow leaves an ambiguous line blank and does not guess:
It never infers a package manager from lockfiles.
It leaves the test line empty when more than one test framework is installed.
It names the workspace tool only when the packageManager field or pnpm-workspace.yaml proves it.
Each prefilled command line has an HTML comment that shows where the value came from. Confirm these lines before you rely on them.
fallow agent install writes the same guide. It also writes the skill, the MCP registration, and the commit and push gate for each harness that it detects.
To check each commit before it lands, install a git hook. The hook runs fallow audit against the base branch before each commit:
fallow init --hooks does the same, as a shortcut during project setup.
Fallow detects your hook manager and writes to the matching location:
Lefthook: writes no file, and prints the pre-commit command to add to lefthook.yml
Has a binary guard (command -v fallow), so commits still work when fallow is not installed.

Finds the base ref at commit time. When an upstream is set, it uses git merge-base @{upstream} HEAD. Otherwise it uses the --branch value, else the default branch of origin, else main. A feature branch from a non-default integration branch (next-release, hotfix, or LTS) thus compares against the correct base, and not against its own remote tracking branch.
Runs fallow audit --base "$BASE" --quiet, which combines dead-code, complexity, and duplication analysis.

Uses gate=new-only by default. Only findings that the changeset introduces fail the gate. Older findings in touched files do not block the commit. To fail on every finding in changed files, set [audit] gate = "all" in fallow.toml.
Returns exit code 1 on verdict: "fail", as audit does by default. You do not need --fail-on-issues.
Prints git commit --no-verify as the bypass option in the success message.

To gate commits from Claude Code or Codex agents too, use fallow hooks install --target agent. The two hooks work together. fallow hooks install --target git checks human commits, and fallow hooks install --target agent checks agent commits.

To remove the baseline entries of fixed findings before the audit, pass --prune-baselines. The hook then runs fallow baselines prune and stages the pruned baseline files. It skips the prune when the working tree has unstaged or untracked changes, and for a commit with paths.
To change the fallback base branch that the hook uses when no upstream is set, pass --branch:
fallow init adds .fallow/ to the .gitignore of your project. The .fallow/ directory holds machine-local data (parse cache, regression baselines, snapshots). Do not commit this data.
If .gitignore exists and already contains .fallow/, nothing changes.
If .gitignore exists without the entry, fallow appends it.
If .gitignore does not exist, fallow creates it.
By default, fallow init creates .fallowrc.json. The file content is JSONC, with comments. For a plain JavaScript project, the file looks like this:
The detected entry patterns change with your project setup. The real file also has commented-out duplicates.ignore examples.
With --toml, it creates fallow.toml. To get editor highlighting for JSON with comments, rename the file to .fallowrc.jsonc. Fallow finds both names.
If .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, or .fallow.toml already exists, fallow init changes nothing and exits with code 2.

fallow init also exits with code 2 when the config file or the hook file, or a directory on the way to it, is a symlink that resolves outside the project root, or a dangling link. When .gitignore is such a link, fallow prints a warning and does not update the file. A link that stays inside the project still works.
Get started with fallow in under a minute.
Get a proposed config before you write one.

pages.title: fallow agent: set up Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
items: fallow agent: set up Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
Set up fallow for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor with one command. It installs AGENTS.md, the skill, the MCP server, and a commit and push gate.
Set up fallow for each coding-agent harness in a project with one command. fallow agent install detects Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. Then it writes the files that each harness reads:
fallow agent status shows what is installed. fallow agent uninstall removes exactly what fallow wrote.

fallow agent install --dry-run # show the plan first
fallow agent install # wire every detected harness
fallow agent status --format json
Review next_actions after installation. Approve the project and its hooks in your harness when prompted.
fallow init --agents, fallow hooks install --target agent, and the hand-written MCP snippet still work. agent install combines them. It does not replace them.

Without --harness, fallow selects a harness when one or more of its signals is present. When no signal exists, fallow writes nothing for that harness. For example, a Cursor-only repository never gets a .claude/ directory.

When fallow detects no harness, it writes only the harness-neutral files (AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/fallow). The output then names the --harness values that you can pass. AGENTS.md is not a detection signal, because every harness and fallow write it.

Skills. The step writes two skills: fallow for analysis, and fallow-setup to set up code-quality tooling in a project. It reports one skill row for each skill in each skill directory. When the project has node_modules/fallow/skills/<name>, the installed skill is a small pointer to that copy. The skill thus always matches the fallow version that the project pins. Without that directory, fallow writes the skill from the binary, which matches the binary version. Fallow selects the source of each skill separately. An older npm package without fallow-setup thus gets the copy from the binary for that skill. If a skill named fallow or fallow-setup exists and fallow did not write it, that step is refused (skill_name_taken), unless you pass --force. Fallow still writes the other skill.
MCP. Before it writes anything, fallow checks that the server command can start. It tries these commands:
npx --no fallow-mcp for an npm-installed project
the running binary, when it is the npm multicall build

When none of them exists, fallow skips the step with mcp_entry_unavailable. It does not write a registration that cannot start. A project-level .codex/config.toml applies only after Codex trusts the project. The output thus starts with the codex mcp add fallow -- ... command, which works immediately.

Gate. For Claude Code and Codex, the step installs a PreToolUse hook that runs fallow audit before git commit and git push, and blocks the command on a fail verdict. Both harnesses run the same gate script. The Codex handler in .codex/hooks.json uses the matcher ^Bash$. Codex runs a project hook only after you trust it in /hooks. The AGENTS.md block tells agents to use fallow and names the hook as the enforcement layer. Claude Code hooks has the details.

Approval. Claude Code asks before it starts a project-scoped MCP server. --approve records that approval for you: it lists fallow in .claude/settings.local.json. The flag is opt-in. Fallow refuses it when git tracks that file.
Each file or block that fallow writes has a <!-- fallow:agent-install v1 ... --> marker. A second run gives the same bytes and reports every step as unchanged.
Fallow never overwrites a file that it did not write, unless you pass --force.
A fallow MCP entry belongs to fallow only when its command is one that fallow writes. Fallow refuses a hand-written entry (mcp_entry_foreign) and keeps it.
--force on a config file that fallow cannot parse first saves the old bytes as <file>.fallow-bak.
uninstall removes managed blocks and entries, and deletes a config file that it emptied. It deletes AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md only while the file still matches what fallow wrote.

The root is the git toplevel of the current directory, unless you pass --root. A run from a monorepo package thus still writes where the harnesses read. The first line of output shows the chosen root.
Human output groups paths under "Shared with your team (commit these)" and "Local to you".
With --format json, the envelope has kind (agent-install, agent-uninstall, agent-status), schema_version, and fallow_version. Each step has:
status: written, removed, unchanged, skipped, refused, or failed
a reason, when the step was skipped or refused

Fallow does not write, back up or delete a project path when the path, or a directory on the way to it, is a symlink that resolves outside the project root, or a dangling link. The step then has the status skipped and the reason symlinked_path. A link that stays inside the project, such as CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md, still works. --user targets still follow symlinks.
After the steps comes next_actions. An action is flagged mutating when it would write harness config. The next_steps of the analysis commands are read-only.

A --dry-run of agent install that plans at least one write puts an agent-install-apply action first in next_actions[]. The human output shows it first in the Next: list. Its command applies the plan: it drops --dry-run and repeats the flags that change the plan (--harness, --user, --without, --force, --approve, --gitignore-claude, and --root). A harness that detection found is repeated as --harness, because detection reads the session environment and $HOME. A run of the command in another shell then writes the same plan.
The exit code is 2 when a step is refused or failed. All other steps still run.

agent status reports a different shape: surfaces[], each with harness, step, path, and a state of absent, installed, stale, or foreign. stale means that the surface needs a refresh, or that its runtime is missing or unverified. foreign means that the file or entry exists, but fallow did not write it. fallow agent install --force replaces a foreign surface. Without --force, fallow leaves it alone.
For Codex, the hooks step covers the gate script and the AGENTS.md routing block. Check detail and next_actions[] for a stale gate:

Status inventories project launchers and package managers without executing them. It does not verify project trust or hook activation. Branch on state and the action ID. A missing reader makes the gate print a notice and exit 0 without auditing.

fallow agent install --format json --quiet
fallow agent status --format json
fallow agent uninstall --dry-run

Install the fallow skill in your coding agent.
