pages.title: fallow config: print the resolved configuration
items: fallow config: print the resolved configuration
Print the resolved fallow configuration and the file that fallow loaded, to find out why a setting is not applied. It works like eslint --print-config.

Use fallow config when fallow does not apply your config as you expect. The command prints the resolved configuration and the path of the loaded config file. This helps most in a monorepo with more than one .fallowrc.json file.

By default, the command prints the loaded config path to stderr. Then it prints the config as JSON to stdout, with extends resolved. On a zero-config project, the stderr line is no config file found, using defaults:
The command obeys the global --config <path> flag. If you pass it, fallow loads that path directly and does not search the directory tree.
Verify which config the LSP/CLI picked up
In a monorepo, run fallow from inside a sub-package:

cd packages/app
fallow config --path
# /repo/.fallowrc.json (root config inherited, sub-package has none of its own)
If a sub-package has its own config, fallow prints that path. The first match wins.
Pipe to jq for further inspection
The loaded config: ... line goes to stderr, so stdout has only the JSON document. See Loaded config disclosure.

if ! fallow config --path > /tmp/fallow-cfg-path 2>/dev/null; then
 echo "no fallow config found, will use defaults"
fi
See the supported config file names and the full schema.
Learn how config discovery works in workspaces.

pages.title: fallow telemetry: control opt-in telemetry
items: Control what fallow sends and see the exact payload first. fallow telemetry manages opt-in telemetry, off by default: status, enable, disable, or inspect.

Use fallow telemetry to check, turn on, or turn off opt-in product telemetry, and to see the exact payload. Telemetry is off by default. Its purpose is to improve agent, CI, JSON, MCP, and editor workflows.
Telemetry & privacy is the data and privacy contract. It says what fallow never collects, what one event contains, and how fallow sends it. To opt out on one machine, run fallow telemetry disable.
if telemetry is on or off
what decided that: an admin env var, a shell env var, the user config, or the default
Turn telemetry on or off in the user-level config file. A person must do this explicitly. Agents and wrappers must not turn on telemetry automatically.

fallow telemetry enable
fallow telemetry disable
enable fails when DO_NOT_TRACK or FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED is set.
Explain inspect mode, or print documented example payloads with the purpose of each field.

fallow telemetry inspect # explain how to inspect a real run
fallow telemetry inspect --example # print an example payload + field purposes
To see the exact payload that a real command would send, without sending it, put FALLOW_TELEMETRY=inspect before the command:
Fallow prints the payload to stderr. The normal output of your command does not change, including --format json on stdout.

DO_NOT_TRACK / FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED (admin/fleet kill switch)
> FALLOW_TELEMETRY_DEBUG (forces inspect mode)
> FALLOW_TELEMETRY (per-shell override)
> CI: off unless FALLOW_TELEMETRY is set
> user telemetry config (fallow telemetry enable/disable)
> default: off
In CI, telemetry is off unless FALLOW_TELEMETRY is explicitly set in that CI environment. When a developer runs fallow telemetry enable locally, telemetry in the CI of the organization stays off.
If the user already turned on telemetry, an agent or wrapper can tag the run with its own name. Use one value from the fixed list below:

Accepted values: codex, claude_code, cursor, copilot, opencode, aider, roo, windsurf, gemini (aliases gemini_cli / antigravity), cline, continue, zed, goose, other_known, unknown, none. Fallow normalizes hyphen aliases such as claude-code. Fallow ignores an unrecognized value and does not upload it. Agents that are not on the list, for example enterprise IDE assistants, go under other_known. FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE never turns on telemetry by itself, and it uploads no codebase content.

When more than one agent environment is present, fallow guesses which one is calling. The guess can depend on the order in which fallow checks them. For a reliable result, set FALLOW_AGENT_SOURCE to name the agent yourself.
Read what fallow collects, what it never collects, and how it sends events.
See every environment variable that fallow reads.

pages.title: fallow report: render saved results for CI
items: fallow report: render saved results for CI
Analyze once, then render every CI output from the saved JSON result. fallow report writes summaries, PR comments, annotations, and inline reviews.

Run the analysis one time, and produce each CI output from that one result.
fallow report renders a saved --format json results file in another format
without re-running analysis. The JSON file stays the record of what the run
found, and each CI output comes from it.

fallow dead-code --type-aware --format json -o results.json
fallow report --from results.json --format github-annotations
fallow report --from results.json --format pr-comment-github > comment.md
fallow report --from results.json --format review-github > review.json

fallow report reads the kind field of the saved envelope, so it can render
any saved fallow result: dead-code, architecture, dupes, health, audit,
security, or the bare combined run. The supported targets are:

The PR-comment and review targets keep the saved audit conclusion, diff
positions, ownership grouping, and repository path prefix. For type-aware
dead-code and audit results, fallow renders the final findings after
semantic refinement, and not the earlier syntactic candidates. When the run
requires semantic evidence and the evidence is incomplete, the analysis run
fails closed. It does not save a result that only looks clean.

A re-render also repeats the verdicts of the saved envelope, so a rendered body
says what the run said:

The PR-comment and review bodies repeat the baseline advisory, the gate
verdicts, and the request outcomes.

github-summary and github-annotations repeat the gate verdicts and the
request outcomes.

The comment and review targets also report a diff filter that did not apply
during the re-render. These bodies use the diff that you give fallow report.
They do not use the diff of the analysis run.

The combined pull-request comment of the bare fallow run
(--format pr-comment-github or pr-comment-gitlab) also shows the status note,
for example a diff filter that did not apply. The review summary body of the
bare run (--format review-github or review-gitlab) shows the same note. For a
saved combined envelope, fallow report --from renders the generic body with
the same note.

fallow report keeps the level that the analysis run gave each finding. It reads the effective_severity field of each dead-code finding, each complexity finding, and each prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, and duplicate-prop-shape finding. The github-annotations, sarif, and codeclimate levels are therefore the same as in the direct run. See Levels in CI formats.
A saved report from an older version has no effective_severity:
Complexity findings keep the earlier levels from the band.

The other findings take their levels from the base rules of the config. When fallow finds no config for this fallback, it prints a note on stderr. It also prints the note when the SARIF default levels of the default rules differ from the saved levels. Pass --config with the config of the original run to use its rules. --quiet removes both notes.
A saved --group-by dead-code or architecture envelope with no findings has an empty groups list. fallow report --from renders zero findings for it and exits 0.

GitHub annotations and summaries go to the job log, so they work on fork PRs
without a write token. PR-comment and review envelopes still need the posting
step for your provider. See CI integration.

--mutation-report adds the results of a fallow mutation run to the pr-comment-github, pr-comment-gitlab, review-github, review-gitlab, github-summary, github-annotations and codeclimate formats. Another format exits with code 2.

fallow mutation --changed-since main --min-score 80 --format json -o mutation.json
fallow --format json -o results.json
fallow report --from results.json --mutation-report mutation.json --format pr-comment-github

Each survived mutant on a changed line becomes a finding of the rule fallow/mutation-survived, in the Tests group of the comment, as an annotation, as an inline review comment and as a CodeClimate issue.
The comment, the review summary and the job summary get a "Mutation testing" section with the counts, the score and the state of the run, for example a partial run.
A --min-score result of the run becomes the mutation-min-score gate, so the gate lines and the check run show it.
Paths in the mutation report are relative to the root of the mutation run. Use the same --root for both commands. A survivor in a file that changed after the run is not shown.
--mutation-not-run renders the reason when the CI job did not run mutation testing.
The GitHub Action and the GitLab template pass these flags for you.

fallow report exits 0, also when the saved file contains findings. The analysis run that wrote the file does the gating, with --fail-on-issues or the audit verdict. In CI, use the exit code of that run, and use report only to render.
An unsupported --format value exits with code 2.

A saved file from a failed run ("error": true) renders nothing. fallow report prints the saved message, code and help, and exits with the saved exit_code. When the saved code is missing or below 2, it exits with code 2.
The GitHub Action, GitLab template, and native workflow formats

pages.title: fallow ci: post PR and MR feedback from CI
items: fallow ci: post PR and MR feedback from CI
Reference for fallow ci: post or update the sticky PR comment, post inline reviews, resolve fixed review threads, and post GitHub Check Runs from rendered fallow output.

fallow ci posts fallow feedback to a pull request (GitHub) or a merge request (GitLab). The GitHub Action and the GitLab CI template call these commands for you. Use them directly when you build your own CI integration.
Each command reads a file that an earlier fallow run rendered. It does not analyze the project.

fallow dead-code --format pr-comment-github --quiet > fallow-comment.md
fallow ci post-pr-comment --provider github --pr 42 \
 --body fallow-comment.md --marker-id fallow-results

The API base URL is --api-url. The GitHub default is github.com. The GitLab default is CI_API_V4_URL, else https://gitlab.com/api/v4. The GitLab CI_JOB_TOKEN cannot create or update MR notes, so fallow does not use it.
These environment variables also change the behavior:
Computes what to do with a sticky summary comment. It does not call a provider API. Use it when your own script posts the comment.
The output is JSON with an action: create, update, or skip. A skip has a skip_reason: clean_no_existing_comment (a clean run with no comment to update) or unchanged (the body did not change).
Finds the existing sticky comment, then creates, updates, or skips it. The rules are the same as in plan-pr-comment.
The command prints the plan as JSON on stdout.

Posts a review envelope to the pull request or merge request. On GitHub, the comments go into one review. On GitLab, each comment is a discussion on the diff. The command posts only the comments whose fingerprint is not in an open fallow thread. It also resolves the fallow threads of findings that are not in the envelope any more, as reconcile-review does.

The JSON result gives comments_posted, comments_skipped, stale_fingerprints, and threads_resolved. A comment that the provider rejects goes into post_errors, and the command still exits 0. See CI integration for the fingerprint markers.
Checks a review envelope and computes a stable plan. Then it resolves the fallow threads of findings that are not in the envelope any more.
Posts a GitHub Check Run from a PR decision file. Only GitHub is supported. --provider gitlab exits with code 2.

FALLOW_PR_DECISION_FILE=fallow-pr-decision.json \
 fallow dead-code --format pr-comment-github --quiet > fallow-comment.md
fallow ci post-check-run --provider github --decision fallow-pr-decision.json \
 --repo acme/app --head-sha "$GITHUB_SHA" --split-gates
Use --split-gates to make each gate a separate required check. See Gates.
With --format json, an error is a JSON object with "error": true on stdout.
Set up the GitHub Action or the GitLab CI template.
Print or vendor the GitLab CI template.
Render saved JSON as GitHub or CodeClimate output.
Gate a pull request on the changed code.

pages.title: fallow ci-template: print or vendor the GitLab CI template
items: fallow ci-template: print or vendor the GitLab CI template
Print the fallow GitLab CI template, or vendor it with its helper scripts into your repository so pipelines run without a download from GitHub.
fallow ci-template prints a CI integration template, or writes it into your repository with its helper scripts. It has one subcommand, gitlab.

fallow ci-template gitlab # print the template on stdout
fallow ci-template gitlab --vendor # write the template and the helper scripts
fallow ci-template gitlab --vendor ci-dir # write them below another directory
The template is the one that the bundled fallow version ships. For the setup and the template variables, see GitLab CI.
Without --vendor, the command prints gitlab-ci.yml on stdout.
With --vendor, the command writes these files:
The vendored template uses the local scripts. A pipeline then downloads nothing from raw.githubusercontent.com for MR comments and inline review. Commit the files, and include the local template:

A file that is equal to the bundled version is not a conflict, so you can run the command again. When a file exists with other content, the command stops with exit code 2 and names the file. Pass --force to overwrite it. Run the command again after you update fallow, so that the vendored files match the new version.
The command accepts the global flags. They do not change the template.
Set up the GitLab CI template and its variables.
Post MR comments and reviews from your own pipeline.

pages.title: fallow hooks: install Git and agent hooks
items: fallow hooks: install Git and agent hooks
Install, remove, and inspect the fallow-managed Git pre-commit hook and the Claude Code and Codex gate that runs fallow audit before git commit and git push.
fallow hooks manages two kinds of hooks. Both run fallow audit on the changed code:
The Git target writes a shell-level pre-commit hook. It checks the commits of people.
The agent target writes a PreToolUse gate for Claude Code and Codex. It blocks an agent git commit or git push when the audit verdict is fail.

fallow hooks status
fallow hooks install --target git
fallow hooks install --target agent
fallow hooks uninstall --target agent
Shows the state of four hook surfaces: the Git pre-commit hook (git), the Claude Code gate (claude), the Codex AGENTS.md routing block (codex), and the Codex gate (codex_gate).

fallow hooks status
fallow hooks status --format json

Git hook: installed (.git/hooks/pre-commit)
Claude hook: not installed
Codex hook: not installed
Codex block: not installed
For the JSON fields, see Inspect hook state. An agent reads user_edited before it changes a hook. When user_edited is true, the agent asks before it overwrites the file.
fallow hooks install --target git finds your hook manager:
With Lefthook (a .lefthook/ directory, lefthook.yml, or lefthook.json), it writes no file. It prints the pre-commit command to add to your Lefthook config.
fallow init --hooks does the same. For what the generated hook runs, see Pre-commit hook.
The fallback base ref of the hook is the --branch value. Without --branch, it is the default branch of origin, else main.

When the pre-commit file exists, the command stops with exit code 2. This is also true for a hook that fallow wrote earlier. The command then prints the block to add to your hook by hand. To replace the file, pass --force.

fallow hooks install --target agent writes .claude/settings.json and .claude/hooks/fallow-gate.sh. When the project has a .codex/ directory, it also writes the Codex gate and an AGENTS.md routing block. When neither .claude/ nor .codex/ exists, it installs the Claude Code gate. For the gate behavior, the block message, and the version floor, see Claude Code hooks.
fallow agent install installs the same gate together with the skill and the MCP registration.
Uninstall removes only what fallow wrote. Handlers and hooks that you added stay. A second run prints unchanged or not present and exits 0.

Fallow does not write, back up or delete a project path when the path, or a directory on the way to it, is a symlink that resolves outside the project root, or a dangling link. A link that stays inside the project still works. .git/hooks and --user targets still follow symlinks.
Read how the agent gate blocks commits and pushes.
Create a config, and read what the Git pre-commit hook runs.
Wire fallow into each agent harness in one pass.
Read the verdicts that both hooks use.

pages.title: fallow schema: print the capability manifest
items: fallow schema: print the capability manifest
Print the full fallow capability manifest as one JSON document: commands, issue types, MCP tools, plugins, and environment variables, for agents and tooling.
fallow schema prints the complete capability manifest of fallow as JSON. An AI agent or a doc generator reads this one source to learn what fallow can do:
The output is always JSON, whatever the value of --format.

The agent-skill tables also come from the manifest. At release time, the command, issue-type, and MCP-tool tables in the bundled SKILL.md of the npm package regenerate from it. For agents, this docs site also serves an auto-generated llms.txt index.
Each issue_types entry describes one reportable issue type:
Nullable fields are always present. When a field does not apply, its value is null.
Get the rationale, examples, and fix guidance for one issue type.
See the MCP tools from the manifest, with full input schemas.
Read about each variable in the manifest.
See the discovered files, entry points, and active plugins of your project.

pages.title: fallow plugin-schema: print the plugin JSON Schema
items: fallow plugin-schema: print the plugin JSON Schema
Print the JSON Schema of external fallow plugin files. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation while you write a fallow-plugin file.

fallow plugin-schema prints the JSON Schema of an external plugin definition. An external plugin is a fallow-plugin-* file, a file in .fallow/plugins/, or a path in the plugins config field. The schema describes every plugin field, for example enablers, entryPoints, and manifestEntries.
The output is always JSON on stdout, whatever the value of --format. The command does not read your project or your config file.
Use the schema in your editor
Point the $schema field of a JSON plugin file at the schema:
The npm package does not include this schema. To get the schema of the fallow version that you installed, use the local file.
fallow plugin-schema has no flags of its own. The global flags do not change the output.
The MCP server serves the same schema as the fallow://schema/plugin resource.
Read the plugin file format and the field reference.
Do a dry run of your plugins and see what each rule seeds.
Print the JSON Schema of the fallow config file.
Print the JSON Schema of rule pack files.

pages.title: fallow plugin-check: debug a custom plugin
items: fallow plugin-check: debug a custom plugin
See why a custom fallow plugin does not activate or seeds no entries. plugin-check is a read-only dry run that shows the matches of each manifestEntries rule.

Use fallow plugin-check to debug an external plugin while you write it. The command does a dry run of your external plugins and does not run a full analysis. For each plugin, it tells you if the plugin activated, and what each manifestEntries rule matched and seeded. The command is read-only, so you can run it again after each change to a fallow-plugin-* file.

plugin-check is advisory, and never a gate. It always exits 0, and it rejects the output-gating flags (--ci, --fail-on-issues, --sarif-file, --output-file) with exit code 2. Use it to debug why a plugin does not activate or seeds nothing. Do not use it to fail CI.

fallow plugin-check
fallow plugin-check --format json
fallow plugin-check --format json --root packages/app

fallow list --plugins tells you if a plugin is active. For an active plugin, plugin-check also shows what each manifestEntries rule matched and seeded. For the plugin file format, the field reference, and manifestEntries interpolation, see Custom plugins.
Fallow finds external plugins in the plugins config field, the .fallow/plugins/ directory, and fallow-plugin-* files in the project root. For each of these plugins, it reports:
active. For an inactive plugin, an activation_requirement string names the unmet condition. A plugin with a failing detection thus shows why it did not activate.

For an active plugin with manifestEntries, a report for each rule:

the manifests that the glob matched (manifests_matched)
the result of the when gate for each matched manifest (when_passed)
the seeded entries, each a resolved path with a path_exists flag
The output is deterministic and sorted. --format json gives the same bytes on each machine, so you can diff it in CI or use it as a test snapshot.

path_exists reports if a file on disk matches the seeded glob. false means that the entry is broken for certain. true is necessary but not sufficient. It does not prove that the entry became reachable, because file discovery still removes gitignored files and files with the wrong extension.

Each manifestEntries rule reports typed warnings[]. When a rule seeds nothing, read these warnings first. Agents branch on the kebab-case kind. Each warning has only the fields for its kind: glob, field_path, manifest, or entry. The two limit warnings also have a limit number.
Global flags such as --no-cache and --threads still apply. See global flags.
This example shows both shapes in one run:
an inactive plugin, with its activation_requirement
an active plugin with a rule that seeded an entry that does not exist on disk yet (path_exists: false). The rule reports a seeded-paths-missing warning.
A healthy active plugin reports when_passed: true, path_exists: true for each seeded entry, and an empty warnings array.
plugin-check is a CLI-only tool for plugin authors. The MCP server does not expose it.
The plugin file format, the manifestEntries rule shape, and ${dotted.field} interpolation.
fallow list --plugins shows which plugins are active.
fallow plugin-schema prints the plugin-file schema for IDE autocomplete.

pages.title: fallow rule-pack: create, list, and test rule packs
items: fallow rule-pack: create, list, and test rule packs
Manage declarative fallow rule packs (policy as code). Create a pack from a template, list the configured rules, and test a pack against your project.

A rule pack is a JSON or JSONC file with project policy rules, for example a banned import, a banned call, or a banned side effect. The rulePacks config key lists the packs. Fallow reports a broken rule as a policy-violation finding in fallow architecture and in fallow dead-code.
fallow rule-pack helps you write and check packs. It has four subcommands:

fallow rule-pack init
fallow rule-pack test rule-packs/team-policy.jsonc
fallow rule-pack list --format json
For the pack format and the rule kinds, see the rulePacks config key and Policy violations.
Creates a pack file from a built-in template. Then it adds the path of the file to rulePacks in your config file.

The command writes <DIR>/<NAME>.jsonc. When that file exists, the command stops with exit code 2 and does not overwrite it. Keep pack files in a committed directory. Do not put them in .fallow/, because that directory is gitignored.

When the project has no config file, the command prints the rulePacks line to add by hand. It updates .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, and .fallow.toml. When it cannot update the file safely, it prints the line to add.
Lists the configured packs. For each pack, it shows the source file, the description, and each rule with its id, effective severity, kind, and patterns.

fallow rule-pack list
fallow rule-pack list --format json

The JSON output has kind: "rule-pack-list" and one entry in packs[] for each pack. Each rule has id, kind, severity, patterns, files, exclude, and message. A banned-import rule with allowNames also has that field. With no configured packs, packs is an empty array and the command exits 0.
Runs pack rules against the project and prints each match. Use it while you write a pack.

fallow rule-pack test # all configured packs
fallow rule-pack test rule-packs/team-policy.jsonc # one pack file, also when the config does not list it
fallow rule-pack test --format json

The output groups the matches by rule, with the path, line, column, and matched token of each match. It also lists the rules with no match. With --format json, the output has kind: "rule-pack-test", a rules[] summary with the finding count for each rule, and a findings[] list.
When rules.policy-violation is off in your config, the test run uses warn for that run. The command then prints a note on stderr, and the JSON output has forced_severity: true.

rule-pack test exits 0 when it reports matches. It is a tool to write packs, not a gate. It exits 2 when no pack is configured and you pass no [PACK], and when a pack file is not valid. To fail CI on policy violations, run fallow architecture --policy. An error-severity finding then exits with code 1.
Prints the JSON Schema of pack files. The output is equal to fallow rule-pack-schema.
The subcommands accept the global flags, for example --root, --config, --format (human or json), and --quiet. --config selects the config file that init updates and that list and test read.
Gate policy violations, cycles, and boundaries in CI.
See the rule-pack policies that apply to a file before you edit it.
Read what a policy violation means and how to fix it.
Print the JSON Schema of rule pack files.

pages.title: fallow rule-pack-schema: print the rule pack JSON Schema
items: fallow rule-pack-schema: print the rule pack JSON Schema
Print the JSON Schema of fallow rule pack files. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation of the policy rules in a rule pack.

fallow rule-pack-schema prints the JSON Schema of a rule pack file. A rule pack is a JSON or JSONC file that the rulePacks config key lists. The schema describes the pack fields and every rule kind, for example banned-import, banned-call, and banned-effect.
The output is always JSON on stdout, whatever the value of --format. The command does not read your project or your config file. fallow rule-pack schema prints the same schema.
Use the schema in your editor
Point the $schema field of the pack file at one of these sources:
The npm package also exports the file as fallow/rule-pack-schema.json. The output of fallow rule-pack-schema is equal to the file in the npm package of the same version.
fallow rule-pack-schema has no flags of its own. The global flags do not change the output.
The MCP server serves the same schema as the fallow://schema/rule-pack resource.
Create, list, and test rule packs.
Read the rulePacks config key and the rule kinds.
