Print the JSON Schema of external plugin files.

pages.title: fallow config-schema: print the config JSON Schema
items: fallow config-schema: print the config JSON Schema
Print the JSON Schema of the fallow config file. Use it for editor autocomplete and validation of .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, and fallow.toml.

fallow config-schema prints the JSON Schema of the fallow configuration. The schema describes every config field, with its type, default, and description. Editors use it for autocomplete and validation. An agent reads it to learn the valid keys before it writes a config.
The output is always JSON on stdout, whatever the value of --format. The command does not read your project or your config file.
Use the schema in your editor
Point the $schema field of a JSON config file at one of these sources:
The npm package also exports the file as fallow/schema.json. The output of fallow config-schema is equal to the file in the npm package of the same version.
fallow config-schema has no flags of its own. The global flags do not change the output.
The MCP server serves the same schema as the fallow://schema/config resource.
Read the reference for every config field.
Show the resolved config and the config file that fallow loaded.
Get a project-tailored config proposal for an agent to author.
Print the capability manifest of the CLI.

pages.title: fallow baselines prune: remove stale baseline entries
items: fallow baselines prune: remove stale baseline entries
Remove stale entries from committed fallow baselines. One whole-project run prunes the dead-code, health, and duplication baselines and never adds an entry.

Use fallow baselines prune after you fix findings that a committed baseline holds. A fixed finding leaves its entry in the file. A run with --fail-on-stale-baseline in the mode of the file then fails until someone updates the file. Prune removes the entries that match no current finding, so the stale gate passes again.

Pruned 1 entry from the dead-code baseline baselines/dead-code.json (12 -> 11)
 unused_files: unused-file:src/legacy/export.ts
health baseline baselines/health.json: nothing to prune (40 entries)
Pruned 1 entry from the dupes baseline baselines/dupes.json (9 -> 8)
 normalized_clone_fingerprints: dup:4e50b434:2
Prune keeps exactly the entries that --baseline matches. A pruned file hides the same findings as before.

Prune never adds an entry. A new finding stays outside the baseline, and the normal gates report it. To record new findings on purpose, use fallow dead-code --save-baseline, fallow health --save-baseline or fallow dupes --save-baseline.
Prune keeps the order of the file and writes a file only when it removes an entry. It writes through a temporary file and a rename, and it does not write through a symbolic link.

Health buckets keep the slots that cover current findings. A slot of a higher severity can cover a finding of a lower severity, as with --baseline. An identity bucket that follows a moved file keeps its saved key.
Prune does not change the runtime-coverage keys or the refactoring target keys of a health baseline.
When the run still reports a function whose identity bucket loses all its slots, the bucket stays as an empty object. This keeps the move matching of --baseline as it was.
Prune reads the paths in the config, the same paths that fallow audit reads:
The paths resolve against the project root. A flag overrides the config path for one file. Prune runs only the analyses that the files need.

Prune analyzes the whole project. A narrowed run would remove entries for findings that it did not see. So prune exits 2 on --changed-since, --workspace, --changed-workspaces, --diff-file, --diff-stdin and the FALLOW_DIFF_FILE environment variable, and it ignores workspaces.changedSince. Production mode is not a narrowed run for prune. Pass --production, or set production mode in the config as for fallow audit.
Prune also exits 2 on the global baseline flags --baseline, --save-baseline, --fail-on-baseline-growth and --baseline-base. Name the files with the prune flags or the config.

CRAP scores in a health baseline depend on coverage. Prune reads the coverage input of the config and of FALLOW_COVERAGE. When you saved the health baseline with --coverage, pass the same input to prune.

A prune runs in one mode, and the file must be saved in the same mode. Two modes change which findings exist: --production and --include-entry-exports. A run in another mode does not see the findings of the file, so it would remove valid entries.
Pass --production to prune a baseline saved with --production.
Pass --include-entry-exports to prune a baseline saved with --include-entry-exports.
Pass no mode flag to prune a baseline saved without them.
Prune refuses a file that it cannot match to the mode of the run. It leaves the file as it is, exits 2, and prints the command to use. The refusal has the reason_code scope-mismatch.

A file may have no record of a mode that the run uses. This happens with a file saved before fallow recorded the mode, and with a whole-project file. Prune refuses it as well, so --check can exit 2 for a project that sets production mode in the config. Review the findings of the file, then save it again in that mode:
The dead-code, health and duplication baselines record production mode when you save them with --production.

Prune does not change a file that it cannot match entry by entry. It reports the file as skipped, prints the command that saves it again, and exits 2. The other files are still pruned. A file that does not exist or cannot be read gets the status error, and the other files are still pruned. A file is skipped when:
it uses an older key form, for example a dead-code baseline without identity;
it was saved by a type-aware run;
it has fields that this version does not know, for example from a newer fallow version;
it is a duplication baseline with the clone keys that older versions shared between unrelated groups. See migrating collision handles.
The stale-baseline warning and the --fail-on-stale-baseline message print the prune command for the file, with an absolute path.
Install a pre-commit hook that prunes before the audit:

Prune analyzes the working tree, not the staged content. A partial commit (git commit -p) can then carry a pruned file that the commit does not support. So the hook runs the prune only when the working tree has no unstaged changes and no untracked files, and it stages the files that the prune wrote. Otherwise it prints a note and skips the prune. It also skips the prune for a commit with paths (git commit <path> or --only), because git builds a temporary index for such a commit. A failed prune never blocks the commit, because the audit is the gate. The prune analyzes the whole project, so it adds the time of a full run to each commit.
For a hook manager such as Lefthook, or an existing hook, the install command prints the block to add.
--format json prints the baselines-prune envelope (schema version 1). Paths are relative to the project root.
status is pruned, would-prune (with --check), unchanged, refused (skipped) or error (the file cannot be read or written).
reason is a sentence for people. It is set for refused and error, and null for the other statuses.

reason_code names why a file is skipped: parse-error, not-this-kind, legacy-keys, unknown-key-scheme, incompatible-identity, shared-clone-keys, unknown-fields or scope-mismatch. It is null for error and for the other statuses.

actions holds stage-baselines for written files, prune-baselines after a --check run with entries to prune, and resave-baseline with the save command for each skipped file. For a scope-mismatch refusal, the action holds the command to run. It is prune-baselines with the mode flags of the file when the run can prune the file, and resave-baseline when the file has no record of a mode that the run uses.

pages.title: fallow coverage: find unused code with runtime coverage
items: fallow coverage: find unused code with runtime coverage
Runtime coverage shows which code runs in production and which code you can delete. fallow coverage analyzes it and uploads source maps and the inventory.

Static analysis tells you what code can run. Runtime coverage tells you what code did run in production, so you can delete cold code with more confidence and review hot paths with more care. fallow coverage groups the commands for runtime coverage, which is part of Fallow Cloud, the paid product. A single local capture is free. Continuous or multi-capture monitoring needs a license. The cloud commands need a Fallow Cloud API key:

fallow coverage setup # resumable first-run flow
fallow coverage setup --cloud # Fallow Cloud plan: beacon, CI steps, one commit SHA
fallow coverage analyze --cloud --repo owner/repo
fallow coverage upload-inventory # push a static function inventory
fallow coverage upload-source-maps # upload build source maps for bundled code
fallow coverage review-packet # production facts of the changed functions
fallow coverage deployment-changes # what changed in production between two deployments
You can stop and resume the setup flow. Run it once to start, follow the generated recipe, and then run it again after you capture traffic. It does four steps:
write a framework-specific collection recipe to docs/collect-coverage.md
if coverage already exists, run fallow health --runtime-coverage <path> directly

fallow coverage setup
fallow coverage setup --non-interactive
fallow coverage setup --yes
fallow coverage setup --yes --json
fallow coverage setup --yes --json --explain
fallow coverage setup --cloud --json
fallow coverage setup --cloud --wait --git-sha "$DEPLOYED_SHA"

Fallow Cloud joins runtime coverage to your code only when five things name the same commit SHA: the beacon, the static inventory, the source maps, the deployment registration, and the first runtime data. fallow coverage setup --cloud writes a plan that gives each step that SHA:

Beacon snippets. The snippets send coverage over HTTP with coverageOrigin: "production". A server reads commitSha from FALLOW_COMMIT_SHA, VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA, RENDER_GIT_COMMIT, or RAILWAY_GIT_COMMIT_SHA. A browser bundle reads VITE_FALLOW_COMMIT_SHA, which the build sets. In a workspace, each member gets its own runtimeSurface tag.

CI steps. cloud.ci.steps holds GitHub Actions steps for the job that builds and deploys: a checkout with fetch-depth: 0 (the inventory reads git history), upload-inventory, upload-source-maps for each bundled member, and the deployment registration. All of them use $GITHUB_SHA. cloud.ci.workflows_detected names the workflow files that look like a deploy.
Keys. The plan names the variables (FALLOW_API_KEY for CI and the server, VITE_FALLOW_API_KEY for an ingest-only browser key). It never holds a key value.
The plan does not prompt, write files, or make network calls. With --json, the setup envelope gets a cloud object. Without --cloud, the envelope does not change.

After the deploy, --wait reads the setup state of the deployed SHA every 10 seconds and prints each change. It retries a network error, a rate limit, or a server error. It exits 0 when every step is done, 1 when --wait-timeout passes first, and 2 on an auth, key scope, or input error. A browser key (fallow_pub_k1_) cannot read the setup state: use a full key. With --json, cloud.wait holds the outcome (complete, timeout, or error) and the last setup state from Fallow Cloud. That state can get new step ids and states, so read it as open data. Its next field names the step to do now and, where one exists, a command.
fallow coverage setup reads package.json, lockfiles, and scripts, and writes instructions for your project:
If the project matches no built-in framework recipe, fallow still writes a fallback docs/collect-coverage.md. It links to the public coverage docs, so you can do the setup by hand.
Agents start with fallow coverage setup --yes --json. The payload is deterministic and does not change between runs. --explain adds the optional _meta keys and does not change schema_version.
This example is a workspace monorepo with an Elysia API at the root and two Vite browser apps in dashboard/ and site/:

{
 "schema_version": "1",
 "framework_detected": "plain_node",
 "package_manager": "bun",
 "runtime_targets": ["node", "browser"],
 "members": [
 {
 "name": "fallow-cloud",
 "path": ".",
 "framework_detected": "plain_node",
 "runtime_targets": ["node"],
 "files_to_edit": [{"path": "src/index.ts", "reason": "..."}],
 "snippets": [{"label": "Node entrypoint", "path": "src/index.ts", "content": "..."}],
 "dockerfile_snippet": "ENV FALLOW_TRANSPORT=fs\nENV FALLOW_WRITE_TO_DIR=/tmp/fallow-coverage",
 "warnings": []
 },
 {
 "name": "fallow-dashboard",
 "path": "dashboard",
 "framework_detected": "vite",
 "runtime_targets": ["browser"],
 "files_to_edit": [{"path": "dashboard/src/main.ts", "reason": "..."}],
 "snippets": [{"label": "Vite browser entry", "path": "dashboard/src/main.ts", "content": "..."}],
 "dockerfile_snippet": null,
 "warnings": []
 }
 ],
 "config_written": null,
 "commands": ["bun add @fallow-cli/beacon", "bun add -d @fallow-cli/fallow-cov"],
 "files_to_edit": [{"path": "src/index.ts", "reason": "..."}],
 "snippets": [{"label": "Node entrypoint", "path": "src/index.ts", "content": "..."}],
 "dockerfile_snippet": "ENV FALLOW_TRANSPORT=fs\nENV FALLOW_WRITE_TO_DIR=/tmp/fallow-coverage",
 "next_steps": [...],
 "warnings": []
}
framework_detected uses canonical ids (nextjs, nestjs, nuxt, sveltekit, astro, remix, vite, plain_node, unknown).
In a workspace project, members[] has one entry for each workspace that runs code. Each entry has its own framework_detected, runtime_targets, files_to_edit, snippets, and dockerfile_snippet.

The top-level fields copy the first runtime member. This is the root when the root is a runtime app, and otherwise the first runtime workspace. In a monorepo with a browser app at the root and a Node child, agents must read the dockerfile_snippet of each member, not the top-level one.
A single-app project has a members array of length 1 (path "."), so scripts can handle members[] the same way for all projects.

Some repos only aggregate other packages. Their only runtime sign is a Turbo- or Nx-style dev script that calls the children, plus build-only library packages. Fallow does not treat these repos as runtime code and returns an empty payload: framework_detected: "unknown", runtime_targets: [], members: [], and a warnings entry of "No runtime workspace members were detected; emitted install commands only.". To detect this case, agents can check members.length === 0 (or framework_detected === "unknown") and skip the step that applies snippets.
A generated docs/collect-coverage.md recipe usually looks like this:

1. Remove any old dump directory: rm -rf ./coverage
2. Build the app
3. Start the app with NODE_V8_COVERAGE=./coverage ...
4. Exercise the routes or jobs you care about
5. Stop the app and run: fallow coverage setup
Fallow uses your existing build, start, or preview scripts when they exist. Otherwise, it uses the common commands of your framework.

fallow license activate --trial --email you@company.com
fallow coverage setup

# Follow docs/collect-coverage.md, then run setup again.
# With coverage present it hands off to `fallow health --runtime-coverage ./coverage`.
fallow coverage setup
Use local mode when you have a coverage artifact on disk:
Use cloud mode to get the latest fallow.cloud runtime context for a repo:

FALLOW_API_KEY=fallow_live_... \
 fallow coverage analyze --cloud --repo owner/repo --format json
FALLOW_API_KEY alone never selects cloud mode. You must pass --cloud or --runtime-coverage-cloud, or set FALLOW_RUNTIME_COVERAGE_SOURCE=cloud.

Cloud analysis gives the same runtime_coverage JSON block as local mode. Its summary includes data_source: "cloud", last_received_at, and a capture_quality computed from the fetched runtime window. When fallow cannot match a cloud function to the local AST or static index, it leaves the function out of the findings and reports it in a cloud_functions_unmatched warning.
The join works even when the two sides name a function differently. It uses these steps:
Fallow first matches on stable ids.
For a runtime path such as /app/src/a.ts from a containerized service, fallow maps the path onto the local tree. It compares the file name and then the path segments from the end.

Some functions have a runtime name that differs from the static index, for example an anonymous callback reported as map, then, or get, or an accessor that keeps its get prefix. Fallow matches these on their position in the resolved file.
Steps 2 and 3 refuse to guess when the answer is ambiguous. In these cases, the function stays unmatched:
two local files match one runtime path equally well
two definitions start on the same line, with no end line between them
To list the functions that stay unmatched, pass --debug-unmatched.

The actions[].type of each finding uses canonical kebab-case values: delete-cold-code for verdict=safe_to_delete, and review-runtime for verdict=review_required. The sidecar can add other protocol-specific values. Treat an unknown value as a future extension, not as a schema violation.

The runtime_coverage block holds the joined findings. In cloud mode, each finding and each hot path also has a cloud_context object. It holds the fields of the cloud runtime-context row that fallow does not read itself, for example errors, performance.cpu, performance.browser, branches, covered_by_test and test_hit_count. A blast-radius entry from the cloud has production_callers, caller_sites and the caller counts in its cloud_context. runtime_coverage.cloud_context holds the top-level fields of the response, for example capabilities and page. These signals are context only and do not change a verdict. A null count or an untracked state means not measured, never zero. The MCP tool get_cloud_runtime_context runs this command, so it returns them too. The hosted MCP server and review-packet also read these fields.

fallow coverage review-packet reads the production facts of the changed code from Fallow Cloud. It sends a set of files or functions to POST /v1/coverage/:repo/review-packet and prints the cloud answer as JSON. It runs no local analysis and does not fetch the runtime context of the full repository, so the answer stays small. Use it in a code review or in a pull request job.

# The source files changed against the base
fallow coverage review-packet

# Selected files and functions
fallow coverage review-packet --file src/checkout.ts --function src/cart.ts:addItem
Without --file and --function, fallow sends the source files that changed against the base. Fallow finds the base like fallow audit does:
The merge-base with the upstream branch or the remote default branch
When no source file changed, the command stops with exit code 2. Pass --file, --function or --base.

The JSON has one row per function in functions. Each row has the tracking_state, period_tracking_state, hit_count, repo_path, covered_by_test, errors, blast radius, complexity and churn of the function. The answer also has an evidence_window and a prod_hot_untested list: functions that ran in production and that no test called. Files and functions that Fallow Cloud does not know go into not_found. See the runtime-context fields for the meaning of each field.
fallow coverage deployment-changes reads how production behavior changed between two deployments. It reads GET /v1/coverage/:repo/deployments/:sha/changes and prints the cloud answer as JSON.

# The deployment of HEAD against the previous deployment with production runtime
fallow coverage deployment-changes

# One deployment against a selected base, only the functions that stopped
fallow coverage deployment-changes --sha <deploy-sha> --base <base-sha> --change stopped
Each function gets one change kind:

When the two deployments cannot be compared, comparable is false and reason tells why. Examples are a deployment that ran for less than 6 hours, or too little runtime on one side. Then the report lists only new functions that already ran. It never reports a stop or a rate change on that evidence. newErrorGroups lists the error groups that the deployment saw first.
Exit codes of the cloud reads
review-packet and deployment-changes use the same exit codes. On an error, they print a JSON object with error, message and exit_code.
If fallow-cov is missing, setup tells you what it checked and gives the install command for your package manager, for example:

To skip auto-discovery, set one of the two override env vars to a binary path. Fallow checks FALLOW_COV_BIN first, then FALLOW_COV_BINARY_PATH, then project-local auto-discovery. If the configured path does not exist, both env vars fail with a clear error. They never go to the next step silently. Use FALLOW_COV_BINARY_PATH for air-gapped enterprise installs, Linux distro-packaged sidecars, and Docker multi-user setups where ~/.fallow/bin is not writable.

Each time fallow starts the sidecar, it checks the Ed25519 signature against the public key built into fallow. The sidecar binary must have a <binary>.sig file next to it. A missing, wrong-length, or invalid signature fails with exit code 4, and fallow does not run the binary. There is no mode that warns and runs, and no env var to turn the check off. If the check fails, reinstall the signed distribution with the install command above.

fallow coverage upload-inventory lets the dashboard show the functions that never ran in production. It reads each JS and TS source file in the project and POSTs a static function inventory to Fallow Cloud, with one row per declaration, expression, arrow, or method. For the matching git SHA, the server computes inventory − runtime-seen = untracked. The result fills the Untracked filter in the dashboard.

With --with-callers, the upload body (version 4) has a top-level routes array and a routeIds array for each function. Fallow takes each route pattern from the file name or the source code, never from a request path.

File-based routes. The nextjs, remix, sveltekit and nuxt plugins find the route files. A route handler gives one route for each exported HTTP method. A TanStack Router route file gives its pattern in the argument of createFileRoute("/repo/$repo"). These routes have no HTTP method.

Elysia routes. Fallow reads calls such as app.get("/v1/repos/:repo", handler) in each file that imports elysia. It joins the prefixes of the app, of .group("/v1", ...) and of each mounted plugin, and it gives the route to the file of its handler. A route with a path or a prefix that is not a string literal stays out of the upload.
Reach follows the runtime imports of the module graph. So a route in routeIds means that the route can reach the function, not that a request did reach it.

The upload keeps at most 500 routes and at most 50 route ids for each function. When the total grows too large, fallow lowers the cap for each function. Each cut shows in the routeLimits field of the upload body and in a warning.
Inventory entries use the same names as oxc-coverage-instrument, byte for byte, so the runtime join works. Fallow picks the name in this order:
Parent context (method key, variable binding, property key, export default).
The function's own id (function foo() {}, named function expression).
(anonymous_N) where N is a file-scoped monotonic counter.
Fallow skips TypeScript declaration files (*.d.ts, *.d.mts, *.d.cts, *.d.tsx) and overload signatures with no body. They never run, so they would always show as untracked in the dashboard.

The runtime beacon reports the V8 filePath as V8 sees it at runtime. In a container, that is the path inside the image (for example, /app/src/foo.ts when the Dockerfile sets WORKDIR /app). The static inventory runs in CI on the checkout and gives repo-relative paths (src/foo.ts) by default. The server joins runtime and inventory on the exact (filePath, functionName) pair. If the paths on the two sides have different prefixes, the Untracked filter stays empty and the dashboard shows a mismatched state.
To fix this, pass a --path-prefix that matches your deployed WORKDIR:

After the upload, the server checks up to 100 recent runtime rows and reports their overlap with the inventory. If the overlap is below 50%, the CLI prints a yellow warning with an example mismatch. Until you correct the prefix, the repo detail page in the dashboard shows a configuration-needed state.

- name: Upload function inventory to Fallow Cloud
 run: |
 npx fallow coverage upload-inventory
 env:
 FALLOW_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.FALLOW_API_KEY }}

fallow coverage upload-inventory (dry run)
 project-id: acme/web
 git-sha: a1b2c3d4e5f6...
 functions: 14,280
 endpoint: https://api.fallow.cloud/v1/coverage/acme/web/inventory

first 5 of 14,280 entries:
 src/index.ts:1 bootstrap
 src/index.ts:12 (anonymous_1)
 src/user.ts:3 createUser
 src/user.ts:18 default
 src/user.ts:42 (anonymous_5)
 ... and 14,275 more

For bundled or compiled code, source maps let Fallow Cloud show runtime coverage on your original source files. Compiled code includes a Node service that tsc builds to dist/. The production beacon reports coverage against the deployed JavaScript files. The cloud resolver uses the uploaded source maps to map those bundle positions back to the original source files. fallow coverage upload-source-maps finds the source maps in a build output directory and POSTs each map to Fallow Cloud under the current repo and git SHA.

FALLOW_API_KEY=fallow_live_... \
 fallow coverage upload-source-maps --dir dist --repo my-app --git-sha "$GITHUB_SHA"
Fallow reads the API key only from FALLOW_API_KEY. There is no --api-key flag on purpose, so secrets do not get into shell history or process lists.

When CI needs a custom PEM trust bundle for Fallow Cloud, set FALLOW_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/bundle.pem. The bundle replaces the default WebPKI roots. In private-CA environments, pass a complete bundle with the public roots and the private CA. Relative bundle paths resolve from the working directory of the process.

Fallow tries each upload up to three times on network failures, HTTP 429, and HTTP 502/503/504. On HTTP 429, fallow follows Retry-After in delta seconds or as an HTTP date, up to 60 seconds. When fallow cannot set up the HTTP client, or when every map fails with a network error, fallow exits 7. When only some maps fail, or when an upload fails with an HTTP error, fallow exits 1.

- name: Build
 run: npm run build

- name: Upload source maps to fallow
 run: npx fallow coverage upload-source-maps --dir dist --git-sha "$GITHUB_SHA"
 env:
 FALLOW_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.FALLOW_API_KEY }}

upload_source_maps:
 stage: deploy
 script:
 - npm run build
 - npx fallow coverage upload-source-maps --dir dist --git-sha "$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
 variables:
 FALLOW_API_KEY: $FALLOW_API_KEY

- run: npm run build
- run:
 name: Upload source maps to fallow
 command: npx fallow coverage upload-source-maps --dir dist --git-sha "$CIRCLE_SHA1"

A Node service that runs tsc output needs no extra flags. Fallow Cloud matches the absolute path that the beacon reports, for example /usr/app/dist/consumers/base/index.js, to the map at dist/consumers/base/index.js.map.
Run upload-source-maps from the repository root, so that each map gets its path in the repository.

Do not set sourceRoot in tsconfig.json. With rootDir: "src", sourceRoot: "/" removes the src/ segment from each source path, so no runtime function resolves to a file in the repository. upload-source-maps warns about this before it uploads.
Before the first upload, run the command with --dry-run. Fix each warning about sources that do not resolve to files in the repository.

After the deployed service has had traffic, run fallow coverage analyze --cloud --repo <repo>. A coverage_unresolved warning means that runtime positions did not map to source for this commit. Make sure that you uploaded the maps for the same --git-sha that the beacon reports.
Start a trial, refresh a token, or inspect feature status.
What runtime coverage adds, and how it differs from static reachability.

pages.title: fallow cloud: log in to Fallow Cloud from the CLI
items: fallow cloud: log in to Fallow Cloud from the CLI
Log in to Fallow Cloud from the CLI without copying an API key. fallow cloud login runs the device flow and stores a read-only key in the OS keychain.

Use fallow cloud login to give the CLI a Fallow Cloud key on your machine. You do not copy or paste a key. The CLI shows a code, you approve it in the dashboard, and Fallow Cloud creates a read-only API key for you, your organization and this machine.

fallow cloud login
fallow cloud logout

Open https://fallow.cloud/device and enter the code ABCD-EFGH
This creates a read-only API key for "build-box". Waiting for approval...
Logged in. Stored the read-only key fallow_read_k1_ab... in the OS keychain.
Open the URL and sign in to the dashboard.
Make sure that the code is the same as the code in your terminal.
Approve the request. The dashboard shows the machine name of the key.

Only an organization owner can approve a key. When a member approves the code, Fallow Cloud signs the member in but creates no key. The CLI then says that only an owner can approve a key, stores nothing, and exits with code 2. Ask an owner to approve the code, or to create a read-only key for FALLOW_API_KEY.

The key starts with fallow_read_k1_. It can read production data, for example for fallow inspect --cloud, but it cannot upload or change data. The key shows in Settings > API keys with the name fallow cloud login (<machine name>). Revoke it there like any other key.
Only a person can approve a login. A coding agent must not run fallow cloud login for you.
The CLI stores the key in the OS keychain, with the service fallow-cloud and the API base URL as the account:
The CLI never prints the key.
Every fallow command that reads production data from Fallow Cloud uses the same order. This includes the cloud tools of the fallow MCP server, which run these commands:
--api-key, when the command has this flag.
The key in the OS keychain.
The key in the credentials file.
$FALLOW_API_KEY always wins over the stored key, so CI keeps the key that you set on the runner.

Upload commands (fallow coverage upload-inventory, upload-static-findings, upload-source-maps) and fallow coverage setup --cloud --wait need a live key. They read only --api-key and $FALLOW_API_KEY, because the stored key is read-only and Fallow Cloud refuses it for these routes.
fallow cloud logout removes the stored key from the keychain and from the credentials file. The key stays valid in Fallow Cloud until you revoke it in Settings > API keys.
Add production data per function to the evidence of one file.
Upload inventories and read Fallow Cloud runtime coverage.

pages.title: fallow license: activate a trial or license
items: fallow license: activate a trial or license
Activate a fallow trial or license to turn on continuous runtime coverage. fallow license also shows status, refreshes a license, or removes the local token.
Use fallow license to manage the local license for runtime coverage, which is part of Fallow Cloud, the paid product.

You need a license only for continuous or multi-capture runtime monitoring. A single local capture is free and needs no license. All static analysis is free and open source (MIT). For pricing and tiers, see fallow.tools/pricing.
Fallow verifies the license offline, against an Ed25519 public key in the binary. Only the trial and refresh flows send network requests to api.fallow.cloud.
Activate a local JWT or start a 30-day email-gated trial.

fallow license activate --trial --email you@company.com
fallow license activate eyJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
fallow license activate --from-file ./license.jwt
cat ./license.jwt | fallow license activate --stdin
Fallow reads the JWT from the first source that is present:
Fallow normalizes whitespace before verification, so a copied multiline token still works.
Print the current license status, tier, seats, enabled features, and expiry state.

license: VALID, tier=trial seats=1 features=runtime_coverage days_until_expiry=29
 → runtime_coverage: ENABLED
If the token is expired but still in the grace window, fallow says so and tells you to refresh it. If no token is present, the command suggests a trial.

api.fallow.cloud can set a refresh_after claim in the JWT, at iat + 15 days. When that time has passed, status adds a one-line refresh hint. The hint is not an error. It comes while the license is still valid, so you can refresh early.
Fetch a fresh JWT for the currently active license.
Use refresh to renew a token before it reaches the hard-fail window.

Fallow first sends the stored license JWT. When no JWT is stored, or the server reports it as too stale to refresh, fallow tries again with a full-access API key. Generate the key at fallow.cloud/settings.

By default, fallow stores the local token at ~/.fallow/license.jwt. On Unix, fallow writes the file with mode 0600 (only the owner can read and write). Other users on the same host thus cannot read the bearer token. On Windows, the ACL of the parent directory controls access.
Fallow looks for the license in this order:
On a shared CI runner where you do not want to write to a home directory, use FALLOW_LICENSE.
When a license expires, fallow gives you a grace period before it blocks runtime coverage:
Commands that take --runtime-coverage (health, audit, security, and coverage analyze) check the license before they start the sidecar:
With no license, the run continues. A single local capture works. The sidecar rejects continuous or multi-capture input.

With a license present, fallow checks it also for a single capture. A token that is not valid, a license more than 30 days past expiry, or a license without the runtime_coverage feature stops the run with exit code 3.
To go back to the free single-capture mode, run fallow license deactivate and unset FALLOW_LICENSE and FALLOW_LICENSE_PATH.
When the backend returns a structured error envelope, fallow shows a specific hint for each known code value. It does not print the raw HTTP body:
For an unknown code, fallow prints the message field from the backend. If that field is missing, fallow prints the raw body.
License verification rejects a JWT when its iat (issued-at) claim is more than 24 hours in the future, relative to the local system clock. The same check finds skew in both directions:
a JWT signed with a clock that is ahead
a local machine with a clock that is behind

On rejection, fallow prints a license appears to be issued <duration> in the future error and exits non-zero. Licensed features thus fail closed. Fallow does not accept a license that the local clock cannot validate.
Common causes that are not user errors:
Machines with a dead BIOS battery.
A laptop clock that drifts after a long sleep.

For an environment with predictable drift, first make sure that the system clock is correct. Then set FALLOW_LICENSE_SKEW_TOLERANCE_SECONDS=<seconds> to change the default 24h window. Fallow parses this value leniently. An unset, empty, unparsable, or negative value falls back to the default, so a typo in a runner env block cannot cause a license verification failure by itself.
See what runtime coverage adds to health analysis.
Run the guided first-run setup. It sets up the sidecar and writes a collection recipe.

pages.title: fallow recommend: get a proposed fallow config
items: fallow recommend: get a proposed fallow config
Get a proposed fallow config for your project and review it before you write it. fallow recommend is read-only and explains each decision behind the proposal.

Get a config proposal for your project, with the reasons for each setting, before anything is written. fallow recommend examines the frameworks, workspace layout, and tooling of the project. It writes nothing, and it reports:
A person or an agent can thus review the reasons, and does not have to trust a generated file.

Zero config is a valid end state. The fallow defaults are strong, and fallow fully supports a project with no config. recommend is for projects that want a config, and for agents that must write the config with the user and not guess.
fallow init writes a config file. recommend is read-only. An agent uses it in these steps:
Tell the user about the default decisions.
Ask the user about the taste decisions.
Write the result, or run init.
When fallow detects TypeScript, the default decisions point to optional type-aware analysis. They do not add it to proposed_config.
Each proposed setting has a tier and a rationale:

fallow recommend has no flags of its own. If you pass an existing config with
--config, the command reads it and takes it into account. Global flags such as --root,
--format, --quiet, --no-cache, and --threads apply.

This example is for a single-package TypeScript project with Vitest. It shows two of the decisions. A real run also has taste decisions (for example ci-strictness) with an open question, and more default decisions.

{
 "kind": "recommendation",
 "schema_version": "1",
 "detected": {
 "is_monorepo": false,
 "workspace_tool": null,
 "workspace_patterns": [],
 "has_typescript": true,
 "test_framework": "Vitest",
 "test_framework_ambiguous": false,
 "ui_framework": null,
 "frameworks_present": [],
 "heterogeneous_frameworks": false,
 "has_storybook": false,
 "package_manager": null
 },
 "proposed_config": {
 "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/schema.json",
 "entry": ["src/index.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}", "src/main.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}"]
 },
 "decisions": [
 {
 "setting": "entry",
 "value": ["src/index.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}", "src/main.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}"],
 "rationale": "Assumes the src/index or src/main entry convention. Adjust for framework-routed apps or DI-wired entry points (fallow also auto-honors package.json exports/main/module for libraries).",
 "kind": "auto",
 "question": null
 },
 {
 "setting": "typeAware.enabled",
 "value": null,
 "rationale": "Detected TypeScript. For exact symbol use across aliases, re-exports, class contracts, packages, or tests, run `fallow dead-code --type-aware` or set `typeAware.enabled` to true. This starts a slower semantic pass and does not replace tsc or Oxlint. Guide: https://fallow.tools/docs/analysis/type-aware/",
 "kind": "default",
 "question": null
 }
 ],
 "note": "proposed_config is the safe, detection-derived baseline; resolve every taste decision with the user before finalizing. For the full set of valid config keys and their shapes, run `fallow config-schema`. Zero config is a valid stop: fallow's defaults are strong, so writing no config at all is fully supported.",
 "config_schema_command": "fallow config-schema"
}
A taste decision has a question object with a header, the question text, and options. Each option has a label and a description.
Fallow reads package_manager only from the packageManager field in package.json. frameworks_present and heterogeneous_frameworks show if frameworks are in workspace packages and not in the root.
Write the config file, and also AGENTS.md and git hooks.
Print the full JSON schema for every config key.
Read about the optional semantic pass for TypeScript.
Call the read-only recommend MCP tool from an agent.

pages.title: Global CLI flags for every fallow command
items: Global CLI flags for every fallow command
Global CLI flags that work the same on every fallow command: project root, config, output format, scope, cache, workspaces, score, trend, and snapshot options.

These flags work the same way across fallow commands, so you learn them once. They set the project root, the config, the output format, the scope, the cache, and the CI gates. Some commands reject a flag that has no meaning for them.
The --dupes-* flags apply to combined mode. When you do not set one, fallow uses the config value. Each one works like the fallow dupes flag with the same name.
The save flags (--save-baseline, --save-regression-baseline, --save-snapshot) and the report flags (--output-file, --sarif-file) write only inside these directories:
its Git work tree, when the working directory is also inside that tree
the CI workspace: GITHUB_WORKSPACE and GitLab CI_PROJECT_DIR, when they are set

Before the analysis runs, fallow resolves the file that each flag writes, and resolves symlinks first. A path outside these directories, for example ../outside.json, exits 2. The check also applies to the default destinations: .fallow/snapshots for a bare --save-snapshot, and the config file for a bare --save-regression-baseline. A committed .fallow or config symlink therefore cannot move the write. A relative path still resolves against the working directory.

Fallow writes a .gitignore with * into its cache directory (.fallow/ by default), so Git does not commit a file there. When the --save-baseline path of bare fallow, dead-code, architecture, dupes or health is in the cache directory, fallow prints a warning on stderr. The warning names a path that you can commit, for example fallow-baselines/dead-code.json. The save still happens, and the exit code does not change.

The CI workspace keeps a GitHub Action job working that checks out into a subdirectory (actions/checkout with path: app) and sets root: app. The job runs from the workspace, which is outside the Git work tree of the root.

An existing character device or named pipe is always allowed, because a write to it creates no file. So -o /dev/null, --sarif-file /dev/stdout, and process substitution keep working. When stdout is a regular file, /dev/stdout resolves to that file, and the directory rule applies to it. On Windows, NUL writes to the null device, in any case and with an optional colon, and so does \\.\NUL. A name with an extension, such as NUL.txt, stays a normal file name.

Fallow checks the resolved path again right before each write, and does not follow a symlink at the last path component. This makes the window for a swapped path smaller, but does not remove it for an intermediate directory. On Windows, the last check and the open are two steps.

When the default cache directory .fallow resolves outside these directories, for example through a committed symlink, the run does not use the cache and prints one note on stderr. The run does not fail. FALLOW_CACHE_DIR, cache.dir, and --no-cache do not change.
The MCP save_baseline, save_regression_baseline, and save_snapshot parameters return a tool error for the same paths.
A quiet run (--quiet, --ci or FALLOW_QUIET) hides progress output. It also hides the stderr warnings that repeat a workspace_diagnostics[] entry or describe the analysis inputs, for example:
a graph cache that fallow cannot use

The JSON output does not change, so a script can still read every entry. To show these warnings in a quiet run, set RUST_LOG, for example RUST_LOG=warn. Config warnings, such as an unknown rule name, and the stderr lines of gates and baselines still print.

By default, a source file that fallow cannot parse does not change the exit code. The parser also rejects valid syntax that is newer than the parser, so the gate is off by default. To fail the run on such a file, pass --fail-on-parse-error or set failOnParseError: true in the config.

When the gate is on and a file has a source-parse-degraded or source-nesting-too-deep diagnostic, the run exits 1 in every output format. A file that ignoreFindings covers has no such diagnostic, so it does not count. The gate_outcomes["parse-error"] entry has a files array. Each entry names a file and its parser error count. The human output prints one line per file.

Fallow does not parse a file that nests brackets deeper than the parser cap (1024 levels) or that needs more stack than fallow reserves. Such a file can be valid code, so it gets the source-nesting-too-deep diagnostic instead of source-parse-degraded, with the cap in limit. Its entry in files has reason: "nesting-too-deep", and the human output, the GitHub Action and the GitLab template say that the file nests too deep to parse. Add a generated file of this kind to ignoreFindings.

A TypeScript, JSX or MDX file whose < tokens can nest as type-argument lists more than 10 levels deep gets the same diagnostic. The TypeScript parser tries each such level again, so the parse time grows exponentially with the level. The limit field still shows the bracket cap. Real code stays well below this cap.

A stylesheet that nests more than 8 color functions, such as rgb( or light-dark(, is not parsed by the CSS parser either, because its parse time also grows exponentially with that depth. Such a stylesheet gets no diagnostic: its CSS Modules classes come from the plain class scan, and it has no CSS analytics.
health --report-only shows the verdict and does not fail.

fallow audit checks every file that it parsed, not only the changed files. A file that was already unparseable therefore fails every audit with the gate on, also with --gate new-only. The audit verdict does not include this gate. Read gate_outcomes for the exit reason.
The GitHub Action and the GitLab template fail the job when the gate fails. They have no input for this gate: set the config key, or pass the flag in args or FALLOW_ARGS.
An older fallow version rejects failOnParseError as an unknown key. When you commit the key, also set minimumVersion.

--baseline and --fail-on-stale-baseline pass when a change adds a finding and saves the baseline again in the same commit. --fail-on-baseline-growth stops this. It compares each loaded baseline with the same file at a base ref:
A key that the base file does not have is growth. The run exits 1 and lists each new key per category on stderr.
A renamed file gives a new key, so it counts as growth.
In a dead-code baseline with line-free keys ("identity": "dc1"), one more occurrence of a key also counts as growth. A moved line does not. The dupes and health baseline keys did not change.
A baseline that the base ref does not have is a new baseline. The gate passes and prints a note.
A base ref that git cannot resolve exits 2, for example in a shallow clone. Fetch the full history (fetch-depth: 0 on GitHub Actions).
A default base that resolves to HEAD exits 2, because a comparison with HEAD cannot fail. This happens on a branch that tracks its own pushed copy. Pass --baseline-base origin/main in CI.
Without --baseline-base, the gate uses the fallow audit base: --changed-since (alias --base), then FALLOW_AUDIT_BASE, then the merge-base with the upstream or the remote default branch.

The gate applies to the dead-code, dupes and health baselines, to the three baselines of the bare run, and to --dead-code-baseline, --dupes-baseline and --health-baseline of fallow audit. health --report-only and the review brief do not run the gate and say so on stderr. A command that loads no baseline rejects the flags.

A commit can rewrite a dead-code baseline from an earlier release into the line-free form. When the base file has no identity and the head file is dc1, the gate translates each old key to its new key and compares by key and count. A commit that removes one finding and adds another in the same rewrite therefore still fails. Some old keys have no safe translation, for example keys with a line or bare package names. The gate compares the categories with such keys by their entry count.
JSON output reports the verdict as gate_outcomes["baseline-growth"]. observed is the number of new keys and threshold is 0.

To get findings for one file or directory only, pass a path as the first
argument. The bare fallow command and these commands accept it:
check, dupes,
health, audit, security,
fix, list and similar-code.

fallow src/components
fallow health src/api/client.ts
fallow fix src/legacy

Fallow still builds the graph of the whole project, so cross-file facts such as
reachability, re-export chains and importer counts stay correct. Fallow narrows
only the reported findings to the file or directory. fix plans and applies
only the fixes that touch files in scope.

CI platforms resolve file paths against the repository root. GitHub annotations, CodeClimate reports in GitLab, and inline review comments reject or misplace paths that are relative to another directory.

When --root points at a subdirectory of a git repository (a monorepo package like packages/app/), fallow writes repository-root-relative paths in the CI formats: github-annotations, github-summary, codeclimate, pr-comment-github, pr-comment-gitlab, review-github, and review-gitlab. Fallow detects the offset between --root and the git toplevel and adds it in front of each path automatically, so annotations land on the correct lines.
In containerized or vendored checkouts, the git toplevel can differ from the CI workspace. Use --report-path-prefix to override the detected offset.
An empty string (--report-path-prefix '') disables the offset and gives --root-relative paths again.
--annotations-path-prefix is the old name of --report-path-prefix. Fallow still accepts it as an alias, with the same behavior.

For supplied diffs (--diff-file, --diff-stdin, FALLOW_DIFF_FILE), fallow works in the other direction. It detects if the paths in the diff are repository-root-relative or --root-relative, and filters findings to match. A diff that parses but touches no analyzable files (deletion-only, binary-only, or empty) filters the report to zero findings. Only when fallow cannot place the paths of a diff at all does it fall back to the full-scope report, with a warning.

--changed-since, a supplied diff and --sarif-file ask a run to narrow its report, or to write a file next to it. When the run cannot apply one of them, it continues and the exit code does not change. --format json tells you the result of each request in a root object, keyed by request name. gate_outcomes uses the same shape for the gate results of the run:
The object also lists the requests that the run applied. An absent request_outcomes means that the run received no request. It never means that nothing failed.

Expect new keys, status values and affects values in later releases. Read a name, a status or a class that you do not recognize as one more request and one more outcome. Do not read it as an error, and never as applied or as scope. Select on affects and not on a list of names, because a request added later has its own class. A diff that parsed but names no analyzable file reports applied with scope_size: 0, because the run applied the filter over an empty scope.
A request that the run did not apply also prints a warning on stderr. Fallow records the entry in the envelope with or without --quiet, so a script can rely on the envelope.
fallow audit has no request_outcomes object. It exits 2 when its --base does not resolve, and it never widens the report.

fallow security records sarif-file as applied with the path it wrote. You can then tell a run that wrote the document from a run that asked for none. If the write fails, the run exits 2 with an error document, so no envelope has that entry as not applied.
fallow flags and fallow suppressions have only the changed-since entry, because neither applies a diff filter.
Formats other than json show the object as one line:

A request that narrows the report can apply over an empty scope. The line then adds a clause: the report is clean because nothing in it was analyzable. The clause also tells you to check the diff or the ref that you gave the run.

The GitHub Action and the GitLab template expose the affects: "scope" requests that the run could not apply. The Action uses a job output, and the template writes a dotenv variable. Both also print a warning on an empty scope. See CI integration.
When fallow loads a config file (auto-discovered or from --config), it prints one line to stderr:
In a monorepo with more than one config, this line tells you which .fallowrc.json fallow uses. Fallow does not print the line when:

--format is anything other than human (json, sarif, compact, markdown, codeclimate, gitlab-codequality, pr-comment-github, pr-comment-gitlab, review-github, review-gitlab, badge, github-annotations, github-summary)
To see the resolved config with extends merged, use the fallow config subcommand.

# Analyze a project in a different directory
fallow dead-code -r /path/to/project

# Use a specific config file
fallow dead-code -c configs/fallow-strict.json

# JSON output with no progress messages
fallow dead-code -f json --quiet

# Limit parallelism to 4 threads
fallow dead-code --threads 4

# Scope to a single workspace package
fallow dead-code -w @myorg/ui

# Scope to whichever workspaces changed since origin/main (CI primitive)
fallow --changed-workspaces origin/main

# Show timing breakdown
fallow dead-code --performance

# Group issues by CODEOWNERS ownership (see Grouped output below)
fallow dead-code --group-by owner

# Health score in combined mode
fallow --score

# Save a snapshot and track trends
fallow --save-snapshot
fallow --trend

# Let a trusted config file extend an HTTPS URL
fallow dead-code --allow-remote-extends

# Match a health baseline per function, not per file and category
fallow health --save-baseline fallow-baselines/health.json --baseline-mode identity
fallow health --baseline fallow-baselines/health.json --baseline-mode identity

# Add TypeScript checker evidence, and fail when it is incomplete
fallow dead-code --type-aware --type-aware-project tsconfig.json --type-aware-require complete

# Keep one run syntactic when the config turns type-aware analysis on
fallow dead-code --no-type-aware

With the per-analysis production flags, you can turn on production mode for one analysis and keep the other analyses on the full tree. Bare combined runs (fallow with no subcommand) and fallow audit accept three of these flags:

# Treat health as production-only, leave dead-code and dupes in full-tree mode
fallow --production-health

# Audit changed files with production-only health
fallow audit --base main --production-health

The matching environment variables FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DEAD_CODE, FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH, and FALLOW_PRODUCTION_DUPES accept the same values as FALLOW_PRODUCTION (true, false, 1, 0, yes, no, on, off). The production config field also accepts a per-analysis object:
Fallow uses this order of precedence, from highest to lowest:
Per-analysis env var (FALLOW_PRODUCTION_HEALTH, and the others)
The legacy boolean form (--production, production: true, FALLOW_PRODUCTION=true) did not change and still applies to every analysis.

With a subcommand other than audit, fallow rejects the per-analysis CLI flags (for example, fallow dead-code --production-health gives an error). In that case, use the bare command or the per-analysis env vars.

With --group-by, each team or package sees its own issues. The flag splits all issues into labeled groups. It works with the analysis subcommands, and with the formats that can show groups. fallow flags ignores it.
With --format json, the output shape changes to a grouped envelope:
fallow architecture --group-by writes the same shape with kind: "architecture-grouped".

Each finding goes to the group of its file. A fact about the whole project stays on the root. For example, unused_load_data_keys_global_abstain: true is on the root when the unused-load-data-key rule could not run safely for the project.

The opt-in prop-drilling, thin-wrapper, and duplicate-prop-shape findings are in their groups, but they do not count toward total_issues. In human and markdown output, the group header names them next to the issue count, for example src (0 issues; 3 health signals: 3 duplicate prop shapes).
For --group-by section, each group also has an owners array with the default owners of the section:
owner puts all sections that share a lead reviewer into one group. section keeps the [Section] headers as group keys, and these keys stay the same when reviewers change.
If your CODEOWNERS file is not in a standard location, set its path in the codeowners field in .fallowrc.json.
Fallow caches parsed file data between runs, so later runs are faster. On the second run, fallow parses only the changed files and loads the rest from the cache.
The cache works in three steps:
Fallow hashes each file with xxh3, a fast non-cryptographic hash.
If the hash matches the cached version, fallow skips the parse.
Fallow builds the module graph from the cached data and the newly parsed data.
To find the cause of a slow run, use --performance. It shows the cache hit rates and the time of each stage.

Discovery 12ms (142 files)
 Parsing 48ms (23 parsed, 119 cached)
 Resolution 15ms
 Analysis 8ms
 Total 83ms
To parse all files again, use --no-cache. This helps after large refactors, or when you debug unexpected results.

To move the persistent cache out of .fallow/cache.bin, set cache.dir in the project config or FALLOW_CACHE_DIR in the environment. When you set both, the env var wins. cache.dir must be a directory inside the project. For a directory outside the project, use FALLOW_CACHE_DIR.
Set defaults for format and quiet mode via environment variables.
The config file reference for project-level settings.

pages.title: fallow migrate: convert knip, jscpd or stylelint config
items: fallow migrate: convert knip, jscpd or stylelint config
Migrate from knip, jscpd, or stylelint to fallow and keep your settings. fallow migrate converts your existing configuration to the fallow config format.
Keep the settings you already made in knip, jscpd, or stylelint when you move to fallow. fallow migrate reads your current config, converts it to the fallow format, and writes a new config file.
If more than one source config exists in your project, fallow merges them into a single config.

fallow migrate converts only the settings that have a fallow equivalent, for example entry points, ignore patterns, ignored dependencies, rule severities, and duplication thresholds. It does not follow every option of the source tools. Fallow shows a warning for each setting that it does not convert, so no setting is lost without a message.

Without --jsonc or --toml, fallow uses the extension of the source file. A knip.jsonc migration writes .fallowrc.jsonc, and a knip.json migration writes .fallowrc.json. The fallow config parser accepts comments in both extensions.

For stylelint, fallow maps the selector complexity rules (for example max-nesting-depth and selector-max-id) to the css-selector-complexity rule and turns on CSS analysis in audit. Formatting, ordering, naming, syntax, and vendor prefix rules stay in stylelint. Fallow shows a warning for each of these rules that your config turns on. See Migrating from stylelint.
Fallow detects TypeScript config files (knip.ts, knip.config.ts), but it cannot parse them. Convert the file to knip.json first, then run migrate again.

# Detect config files and migrate
fallow migrate

# Preview without writing
fallow migrate --dry-run
Fallow shows a warning for each config field that it cannot migrate automatically.

pages.title: Verify fallow security candidates with an agent
items: Verify fallow security candidates with an agent
Verify fallow security candidates with a coding agent and keep only the survivors that a verifier cannot dismiss. fallow itself makes no model calls.

Use this recipe to turn raw fallow security candidates into a shorter list of survivors that you can act on. A coding agent or an external harness checks each candidate and dismisses the ones that the evidence does not support.
fallow security produces deterministic candidates only. It does not call a model, it does not decide exploitability, and it does not report verified vulnerabilities.
Use the CLI when you want a standalone JSON file:
Use MCP when an agent is already in an edit loop:
The MCP parameters work as follows:
surface: true forwards --surface and adds the top-level attack_surface[] entries.
gate set to new returns candidates on changed lines. gate set to newly-reachable returns candidates that became reachable from entry points. newly-reachable requires changed_since.
paths forwards repeated --file filters. Fallow returns only candidates whose anchor, trace hops, source-trace hops, or unresolved-callee diagnostics match.

Each candidate has a severity field with a review-priority tier (high, medium, or low). The tier is not a verified vulnerability verdict. When reachability.taint_confidence is present, use it to tell arg-level source association apart from the weaker module-level reachability.
For each security_findings[] item, build one packet. The packet holds the deterministic fallow evidence and the source windows that you collect:
Read the source windows from disk after the scan. Keep them out of the fallow output, so that the fallow output stays deterministic, compact, and independent of any model provider.

blind_spots.unresolved_callee_diagnostics can hold a copy of the top-level diagnostics from the fallow output. Copy it when the verifier needs sample locations to follow up on dynamic dispatch. It is bounded metadata and is not proof of a vulnerability.
Ask the verifier to dismiss candidates unless the supplied evidence supports a real exploit path:

You are verifying one fallow security candidate.

Fallow is a deterministic candidate producer, not a vulnerability oracle.
Use only the supplied candidate, trace, attack-surface entry, and source windows.
Do not assume data flow beyond the provided code.

Check:
1. Is the input attacker-controlled?
2. Does the value reach the reported sink?
3. Is the reported boundary relevant to exploitability?
4. What concrete impact would remain if the candidate is real?
5. Is there an existing defensive control that dismisses it?

Return only JSON matching fallow-security-verdict/v1.
If attack_surface.defensive_boundary.verification_prompt is present, add it to the prompt as an extra question. Do not treat it as a verdict.

attack_surface.defensive_boundary.controls lists control patterns that fallow found in files on the import trace. A listed control does not prove that the control runs before the reported sink or that it protects the same input. Before you dismiss a candidate because of a control, check the execution order and the value flow in the source windows.

A control with callee: "origin-equality-guard" records a strict .origin comparison against a known string, where the mismatch branch returns or throws at once. It does not prove that the object is a built-in URL, that the checked value reaches the sink unchanged, or that redirects are safe. Verify these points in the source. Controls do not remove candidates, and they do not lower the taint confidence or the severity.
Ask the verifier for a compact JSON verdict:

{
 "schema_version": "fallow-security-verdict/v1",
 "finding_id": "9a705395d3b50465",
 "verdict": "survivor",
 "reason": "The request query value reaches execSync without validation.",
 "impact": "Command injection through the id query parameter.",
 "evidence_checked": {
 "source": true,
 "sink": true,
 "boundary": true,
 "trace": true,
 "source_window": true
 },
 "dismissal_reason": null,
 "fix_direction": "avoid-shell"
}
survivor: the verifier could not dismiss the candidate from the supplied evidence.
dismissed: the candidate is not exploitable from the supplied evidence.
needs-human-review: the evidence is incomplete, contradictory, or blocked by missing context.

Store the verifier output next to the original fallow JSON. Set the finding_id of each verdict to the stable_finding_id of the candidate, so the verdict stays valid after edits that move the sink. Do not write verdict fields back into the fallow output.

A finding_id contains the rule, the project-relative path, the line, and the column. Two sinks on the same line therefore get different IDs. An edit above a sink changes its finding_id. The JSON output and the visualization use the same ID as partialFingerprints["fallowSecurity/v2"] in the security SARIF output. When you select fewer files, the remaining findings keep their IDs.
When you upgrade from line-only IDs, every security finding gets a new ID, including findings that did not collide before. To migrate:
Regenerate the candidate files and the verdicts together.
Refresh the evaluation labels that you key by finding_id.
Keep old candidate and verdict pairs together for replay. Do not match old verdicts to new candidates by path and line alone.
fallow security survivors exits 2 when a verdict names an ID that is not in the candidate file. An old verdict file with a new candidate file therefore fails.
The stable_finding_id of a finding does not contain the line or the column. It hashes the rule, the project-relative path, and a name of the finding that does not depend on the line:

For a sink in script code, the name is the exact source text of the full sink expression. For an assignment, that is the full assignment with the assigned value. For a call, that is the full call with all its arguments. Whitespace, comments, line endings, a byte order mark, and a trailing comma before a closing bracket do not count. The text inside string, template, and regex literals counts as it is. For a JSX attribute sink such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML, the text is the attribute and not the element. Two such attributes with the same text get the same base ID, also on different elements or next to different other attributes.

For a hard-coded secret, the name is the name of the variable or property and the kind of the match: the provider (for example Stripe key) or a high-entropy value. The secret value is never part of the hash. A new value with the same kind of match keeps the ID and its verdict: one high-entropy value in place of another, or one key in place of another key of the same provider. Only a new kind of match gives a new ID, for example a known provider key in place of a high-entropy test value.

For a client-server leak, the name is the paths of the client file and of the module with the secret or the server-only code, and the names of the env secrets that the module reads (for example process.env.DATABASE_PASSWORD). A read of a different secret gives a new ID.

fallow security survivors accepts the stable ID in the finding_id field of a verdict. A verdict file keyed by stable_finding_id stays valid after edits above a sink and after a rebase. It also stays valid after a reformat that changes only whitespace, comments, line breaks, or trailing commas. A change to the sink text or a file rename gives a new ID. A new quote style changes the text of a string literal, so it also gives a new ID. A verdict for the old ID then fails with exit code 2 and does not apply to another candidate.

A finding has no stable_finding_id when fallow does not know the exact sink text. This is the case for a sink in Vue, Svelte, or Angular template markup, for a sink whose text does not parse on its own (for example an expression with yield), and for a file that fallow cannot read. Key the verdict of such a finding by finding_id.

The hash does not include the enclosing function. When two sinks in one file have the same text, the first one in source order gets the base ID, and the next ones get the suffix ~1, ~2, and so on. When you delete the first sink, the second sink gets the base ID, and the verdict of the deleted sink applies to it. A new identical sink above an existing one moves the suffixes in the same way. Review such sinks again after an edit that adds or removes one of them. An inline suppression comment does not move the suffixes: the suppressed sink keeps its place in the order, so its verdict does not apply to the next identical sink.

Stored review history does not transfer automatically. SARIF tools can close and reopen each security alert once. Fallow no longer emits the legacy fallowSecurity/v1 fingerprint, because that fingerprint can merge separate sinks again.
To show only the candidates that the verifier kept, join the candidates and the verdict file with fallow security survivors:

fallow security --format json --quiet > candidates.json
# (verifier writes verdicts.json keyed by stable_finding_id)
fallow security survivors --candidates candidates.json --verdicts verdicts.json

The command reports summary.unverdicted, so candidates without a review stay visible. To fail CI when a candidate has no verdict, add --require-verdict-for-each-candidate. To see where the structural trace stopped, run fallow security blind-spots. It lists the unresolved callees that the verifier must inspect by hand.

Candidate quality depends on how accurate the source and the trace are. Fallow gates HTTP-input source patterns on the receiver, so a broad *.query pattern does not collide with unrelated APIs. Framework-specific request aliases can still need the judgment of the verifier.

reachability.taint_confidence tells arg-level source association apart from module-level source association. Use severity and taint_confidence to order the triage. Before you report a survivor, use the source windows to verify:
that an attacker controls the source
Find security candidates and render the survivors.

pages.title: knip alternative: migrate from knip to fallow
items: knip alternative: migrate from knip to fallow
Migrate from knip to fallow. One command converts your knip config to a fallow config. See what the command migrates and what to check after the move.
The fallow migrate command translates your knip configuration to a fallow config. This page shows the steps, the field mapping, and the settings that need a manual check.

1Preview the migrationRun fallow migrate --dry-run to see the generated config. The command writes no files.fallow migrate --dry-runfallow looks for knip.json, knip.jsonc, .knip.json, .knip.jsonc, knip.ts, knip.config.ts, and the knip field in package.json. Fallow detects the TypeScript config files (knip.ts, knip.config.ts) but cannot parse them. Convert them to knip.json first.{
 "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fallow-rs/fallow/main/schema.json",
 // Migrated from knip.json
 "entry": [
 "src/index.ts",
 "src/cli.ts"
 ],
 "ignoreFindings": [
 "**/*.generated.ts"
 ],
 "ignoreDependencies": [
 "@types/node"
 ]
}

Migrated from: knip.json

Warning (1):
 [knip] `project`: Fallow auto-discovers project files

Note: knip and fallow use different glob engines; verify migrated entry /
ignoreFindings with `fallow dead-code` before relying on CI.
https://fallow.tools/docs/migration/from-knip/

Note: knip's ignore also suppresses dependency and manifest issues by file
path; fallow's ignoreFindings never hides manifest-owned findings such as
unused dependencies.
https://fallow.tools/docs/migration/from-knip/

2Generate the configWhen the preview looks correct, run the migration:fallow migrate # Write .fallowrc.json
fallow migrate --toml # Or output as fallow.toml
3Review the configOpen the generated config. Check the translated entry points, ignore patterns, and plugin mappings. Fallow shows a warning for each field that it could not migrate automatically.

4Run your first analysisRun the dead code analysis and examine the findings. Then run the other analyses:fallow dead-code # Unused code + circular deps + boundaries
fallow dupes # Code duplication
fallow health # Complexity hotspots + maintainability scores
fallow # All of the above in one pass

A trailing ! marks an entry pattern as a production entry. When the config marks at least one pattern, the migration writes the marked patterns to entry and the other patterns to supportEntry. So fallow dead-code --production uses only the marked entries plus the framework production entries, and a normal run uses all of them. When no pattern has the marker, every pattern goes to entry.

A workspace section can set ignoreDependencies and includeEntryExports. The migration writes them to workspaces.settings, keyed by the workspace path, so they keep their workspace scope. The root workspace . uses the global keys.

Only the most specific workspace section applies in the source config. Fallow merges the ignoreDependencies lists of every matching key. When a glob section such as packages/* has a list and a more specific section also matches, the migration warns, because the more specific workspace now also ignores the glob entries. For includeEntryExports, the migration writes the root value to a more specific section that does not set it, so the result does not change.
fallow migrate warns about each setting that it cannot translate, so you do not lose a setting without notice.

Unknown rule names. Your knip rules, exclude, or include entries can reference a key that fallow does not know. The cause can be a typo, a future knip rule, or an issue type that the migrator does not know yet. The migration then prints a warning like this one:

Warning (1):
 [knip] `rules.unsued-files`: unknown knip issue type `unsued-files`; not migrated (suggestion: check for a typo or report the missing mapping at https://fallow.tools/docs/migration/from-knip/)

The binaries issue type maps to the unlisted-binaries rule. Some keys are on the documented list of keys that cannot be mapped: optionalPeerDependencies, and similar issue types that knip reports and fallow does not. For these keys, the warning reads issue type \X` has no fallow equivalent` and has no suggestion.

Glob-engine drift. knip and fallow use different glob engines. The migration copies entry and ignoreFindings verbatim, but they can match a slightly different set of files than in knip. When the migrated config has either field, the migrate command prints:

Note: knip and fallow use different glob engines; verify migrated entry /
ignoreFindings with `fallow dead-code` before relying on CI.
https://fallow.tools/docs/migration/from-knip/

Common patterns (brace expansion {ts,tsx}, double-star **, src/**) match the same files in both engines. ignoreFindings keeps a leading ! as an exception to the earlier patterns. Run fallow dead-code on a representative subset before you use the migrated globs in CI.

Dependency regexes. knip reads an ignoreDependencies entry as a regex when it contains one of * + \ ( | { ^ $. Fallow reads ignoreDependencies entries as exact names or as globs, see ignoreDependencies. The migration converts a regex to a glob only when the glob matches exactly the same package names:

A regex that has no exact glob form stays out of the config, for example an alternation such as ^(react|vue)$, a character class such as ^@acme/[a-z]+$, or .+ in the middle of a name. The migration prints a warning for each such entry:

Warning (1):
 [knip] `ignoreDependencies`: regex pattern `^(react|vue)$` skipped (no glob matches the same packages) (suggestion: rewrite it as a glob such as `@scope/*`, or add each dependency name)

Add the skipped entries by hand as globs or as exact names. After the migration, fallow dead-code names every ignoreDependencies glob that matches no declared dependency, so a glob with a typo does not go unnoticed. See Unmatched config patterns.

Ignore scope. knip's ignore also hides dependency and manifest issues by file path. Fallow's ignoreFindings never hides manifest-owned findings, such as unused dependencies. The migrate command prints a note about this difference for every knip migration.

fallow migrate reads your knip config and writes a new fallow config. It does not change or delete the knip config. After the migration, fallow reads only its own config file, so make new changes in .fallowrc.json or fallow.toml. You can delete the knip config when you no longer run knip.
Yes. Each tool reads its own config. Fallow knows knip as a tooling dependency, so it does not report knip in devDependencies as unused.

fallow migrate does not overwrite a config. When .fallowrc.json, .fallowrc.jsonc, fallow.toml, or .fallow.toml exists, the command stops with an error. Remove the file first, or run fallow migrate --dry-run and copy the fields that you need.
No. Fallow detects knip.ts and knip.config.ts, but it does not run TypeScript config files. Convert the file to knip.json, then run fallow migrate again.

Not always. The two tools use different glob engines and different framework plugins, and fallow has issue types that knip does not have. Run fallow dead-code after the migration and compare the result before you use it in CI. To adopt fallow on a codebase with existing findings, save a baseline. See Baselines.
Build plugins for frameworks that fallow does not cover yet.
Read the full CLI reference for fallow migrate.

pages.title: ts-prune alternative: find unused exports with fallow
items: ts-prune alternative: find unused exports with fallow
Compare ts-prune with fallow for unused exports in TypeScript. See which ts-prune option maps to which fallow setting, and how the two tools resolve symbols.

ts-prune reads your tsconfig.json and reports exports that no other file in the project appears to use. Fallow reports unused exports too, together with unused files, types, dependencies, and members. This page maps the ts-prune options to fallow settings, and lists what each tool does better.

The ts-prune repository is not archived. The project status section of its README says that the project "has been resurrected after a long hiatus". The newest release on npm is still 0.10.3, from December 2021.
fallow migrate does not read .ts-prunerc files or the ts-prune field in package.json. The table below shows the fallow setting for each option, so you can write the config by hand.
ts-prune options take JavaScript regular expressions. The fallow settings take globs.
How the two tools resolve symbols

ts-prune is built with ts-morph, and it uses the TypeScript compiler to find the references to each export. Fallow parses the code with Oxc and does not run the TypeScript compiler. It builds a module graph from the entry points and follows imports and re-export chains through that graph.
When a delete depends on exact TypeScript symbol identity, add --type-aware. Fallow then confirms each candidate with the TypeScript checker:
Compiler-based references by default. ts-prune uses the TypeScript compiler on each run. Fallow uses the TypeScript checker only with --type-aware.
One task, small output. ts-prune does only one thing, and each result is one file:line - exportName line. Fallow runs more checks, and you filter them with flags such as --unused-exports.
Regular expressions. ts-prune filters with regular expressions. Fallow filters with globs and export names.
Unused files and dependencies. Fallow also reports unused files, unused dependencies, unlisted dependencies, and unused enum and class members.

Framework entry points. Built-in plugins find the entry points of frameworks such as Next.js and Vite. ts-prune sees only the uses inside the configured project, so a framework export that a convention loads can show as unused.
Automatic removal. fallow fix removes unused exports and unused dependencies. ts-prune only reports. See Auto-fix.
A native binary. Fallow does not need Node.js for its default analysis. The current ts-prune README requires Node.js 22.18 or newer.
More analyses in one run. Fallow also reports import cycles, duplication, and complexity hotspots.
Move a ts-prune check to fallow
A typical CI step runs ts-prune --error. To do the same with fallow, run:
To adopt the check on a codebase that already has unused exports, save a baseline first. See Baselines.
Find unused files, exports, and dependencies.
Confirm unused symbols with the TypeScript checker.
Suppress one finding with an inline comment.
