pages.title: stylelint and fallow: migrate selector complexity rules
items: stylelint and fallow: migrate selector complexity rules
Convert the selector complexity rules of your stylelint config to fallow styling analysis. See what fallow migrates and which rules stay in stylelint.

The fallow migrate command reads your stylelint configuration and turns on the matching fallow styling analysis. Fallow does not replace stylelint. Stylelint keeps the formatting, ordering, naming, syntax, and vendor prefix rules. Fallow adds project-wide styling findings, for example unused styling and broken references. This page shows the steps, the rule mapping, and the limits of the conversion.

2Generate the configWhen the preview looks correct, run the migration:fallow migrate # Write .fallowrc.json
fallow migrate --toml # Or output as fallow.tomlTo migrate one specific file, pass its path:fallow migrate --from config/.stylelintrc.json
3Keep stylelintDo not remove stylelint. The warnings list the rules that only stylelint enforces. Keep them in your stylelint config and in your lint step.

4Run the styling analysisRun the styling analysis and examine the findings:fallow health --css # Styling findings and CSS analytics for the project
fallow audit # Styling findings for the changed files
Fallow maps a rule only when your config turns it on. A rule with the value null, false, or an empty array is off, and fallow ignores it.

Thresholds do not transfer. Fallow does not copy the limit of a stylelint rule. For example, "selector-max-id": 2 and "selector-max-id": 0 give the same fallow config. css-selector-complexity uses its own fixed limits: an id selector, a nesting depth of 3 or more, a !important use, or a structurally complex selector. See Selector complexity.

Shared configs are not followed. Fallow reads only the rules object of your own config file. Rules that come from extends, for example stylelint-config-standard, do not count. When your config has no rules object, the migration writes no styling settings and prints this warning:

Warning (1):
 [stylelint] `rules`: no Stylelint rules object found to map (suggestion: keep Stylelint for formatting and syntax linting)

JavaScript configs must be static. Fallow does not run stylelint.config.js, .cjs, or .mjs. It reads the text from the first { to the last } as one object literal. A config that uses require(), variables, or spread syntax does not parse, and the command exits with code 2. A brace before the object also stops the parse, for example the /** @type {import('stylelint').Config} */ comment. In these cases, convert the config to .stylelintrc.json, or pass a JSON copy with --from.

Other rules give no warning. Fallow warns only about a fixed list of formatting, naming, ordering, vendor prefix, and syntax rules. Other rules, for example most plugin rules, get no warning, and fallow does not migrate them.
Severity. Fallow writes css-selector-complexity as warn. A warn finding shows in the output but does not fail the run. To fail the run on these findings, set the rule to error. See Rules.

pages.title: madge alternative: compare madge with fallow
items: madge alternative: compare madge with fallow
Compare madge with fallow for circular dependencies, orphan files, and dependency graphs in TypeScript and JavaScript. See which madge command maps to which fallow command.

madge makes a visual graph of your module dependencies and finds circular dependencies. Fallow also finds circular dependencies and draws the import graph. It also reports unused code, duplication, and complexity in the same run. This page maps the madge commands to fallow commands, and lists what each tool does better.

fallow migrate does not read .madgerc or the madge field in package.json. Most madge options control the graph style or the module resolution, and fallow has no equivalent settings for them. Fallow finds the entry points and the tsconfig.json path aliases automatically.
To find the shortest chain of imports between two files, run fallow trace --path <from> <to>. See fallow trace.
madge reports an orphan when no other module depends on it. Fallow reports an unused file when no entry point reaches it. The two lists are different:

A file that nothing imports, but that is an entry point, is a madge orphan. Fallow does not report it. Fallow finds entry points from package.json, from scripts, and from the built-in framework plugins.
A group of files that import each other, but that no entry point reaches, has no madge orphan. Fallow reports each file in the group as unused.

Graph image in one step. madge --image writes an SVG or a PNG directly, with configurable colors and layout. Fallow writes DOT or Mermaid text, and you render it with Graphviz or a Mermaid tool. The default fallow viz output is an interactive HTML map instead.
Leaves. madge --leaves lists the modules with no dependencies. Fallow has no such list.
Full graph as JSON. madge --json prints the full dependency tree, and --stdin reads it back. Fallow has no JSON dump of the full graph.

Other module formats. madge reads AMD modules, and it follows the dependencies of Sass, Stylus, and Less files. Fallow reads ES modules and CommonJS in JavaScript and TypeScript, and the imports in Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX, and HTML files. See Non-JS file types. For styles, fallow tracks @import, @use, and @forward in CSS and SCSS. See CSS and SCSS extraction.
JavaScript API. madge has a promise-based Node.js API with methods such as circular() and orphans(). Fallow has Node.js bindings with a different shape.
Unused code. Fallow reports unused exports, types, dependencies, enum members, and class members. madge does not.
Boundaries. Fallow checks the imports between architecture zones that you define. See Boundaries.
Entry points without a path argument. Fallow finds the entry points of the project, so you do not pass a source directory or a tsConfig option.
More analyses in one run. Fallow also reports duplication and complexity hotspots. Run fallow without a subcommand to get all analyses in one pass.
CI formats. Fallow writes JSON, SARIF, CodeClimate, and pull request comments. See CI integration.
Move a madge check to fallow
A typical CI step runs madge --circular and fails when it finds a cycle. To do the same with fallow, run:

The command exits with code 1 when it finds a cycle, because circular-dependencies has the default severity error. See Exit codes. To adopt the check on a codebase that already has cycles, save a baseline first. See Baselines.
Find import cycles and boundary violations.
Draw the import graph as HTML, DOT, or Mermaid.
Find unused files, exports, and dependencies.
Compare fallow boundaries with dependency-cruiser rules.

pages.title: jscpd alternative: migrate to fallow duplication
items: jscpd alternative: migrate to fallow duplication
Migrate from jscpd to fallow. One command converts your jscpd config to fallow duplication settings for TypeScript and JavaScript. See how detection modes map.
The fallow migrate command translates your jscpd configuration to the duplicates section of a fallow config. This page shows the steps, the field mapping, and the detection mode mapping.
1Preview the migrationRun fallow migrate --dry-run to see the generated config. The command writes no files.fallow migrate --dry-runfallow looks for .jscpd.json and the jscpd field in package.json.

2Generate the configWhen the preview looks correct, run the migration:fallow migrate # Write .fallowrc.json
fallow migrate --toml # Or output as fallow.toml
3Review the configOpen the generated config. Check the translated thresholds, token counts, and ignore patterns.
4Run fallow dupesRun your first duplication analysis:fallow dupes
jscpd v5 has strict, mild, and weak modes. For exact token matching, the closest fallow mode is strict.
Fallow uses mild mode by default. This mode normalizes syntax variations, so a migrated project can show clones that strict mode does not report. To report only exact token matches, use strict mode:
To also match clones with renamed variables, use semantic mode:
The same binary runs the other fallow analyses:

pages.title: dependency-cruiser alternative: compare with fallow
items: Compare dependency-cruiser rules with fallow boundaries, cycles, and dependency checks for TypeScript and JavaScript. See which rules map and which have no fallow equivalent.

dependency-cruiser validates the dependencies of a project against your own rules, and it draws dependency graphs. Fallow checks import cycles, architecture boundaries, and the dependencies in package.json. It also reports unused code, duplication, and complexity in the same run. This page maps the dependency-cruiser rules to fallow, and lists what each tool does better.

fallow migrate does not read .dependency-cruiser.js or other dependency-cruiser configs. A dependency-cruiser rule is a set of regular expressions and conditions. Fallow boundaries use named zones with an allow list. The two models do not convert one to one, so write the fallow zones by hand. See Boundaries.
These are the rules that npx dependency-cruiser --init writes, and the fallow rule that reports the same kind of problem:

Fallow also reports problems that dependency-cruiser does not: unused dependencies, unused exports and types, type-only and test-only production dependencies, and package cycles between workspace packages.

A dependency-cruiser forbidden rule says which dependencies are not allowed. A fallow boundary rule says which zones a zone can import from. All other imports between zones are violations. For example, this dependency-cruiser rule forbids an import from src/ui into src/db:
In fallow, give each directory a zone, and list the zones that ui can import from:

Fallow patterns are globs, not regular expressions. A file that matches no zone has no restriction. For common layouts, start from a preset. To give each feature directory its own zone, like a dependency-cruiser rule with $1 group matching, see Auto-discovered feature zones.

dependency-cruiser reports an orphan when a module has no incoming dependencies and no outgoing dependencies. Fallow reports an unused file when no entry point reaches it. Fallow finds entry points from package.json, from scripts, and from the built-in framework plugins. So the two checks find different files:
A file that nothing imports, but that imports other files, is not an orphan. Fallow reports it when it is not an entry point.
A file that nothing imports and that imports nothing is an orphan. Fallow does not report it when it is an entry point.
A group of files that only import each other has no orphans. Fallow reports the group when no entry point reaches it.

Rule conditions. A rule can match on dependency types (for example npm-dev or type-only), on dynamic imports, on licenses, on reachability, on the number of dependents, and on module stability. Fallow boundaries match on the zone of the source file and the zone of the target file. The one dependency-type condition is allowTypeOnly, which allows type-only imports from a zone that is not in allow.

Regular expressions with group matching. A rule can capture part of the from path and reuse it in the to path with $1. Fallow has auto-discovered feature zones for the common case, but no general group matching.
Required dependencies. A required rule says that a module must depend on another module. Fallow has no such rule.
Cycle filters. A circular rule can use via and viaOnly to match only some cycles. Fallow reports every import cycle, and you can ignore lazy imports or suppress one cycle with a comment.

Reporters. dependency-cruiser writes text, err, JSON, CSV, HTML, DOT, and Mermaid. Fallow draws the graph with fallow viz as HTML, DOT, or Mermaid, and writes findings as JSON, SARIF, CodeClimate, and other formats. Fallow has no CSV output.
More languages. dependency-cruiser also reads CoffeeScript and LiveScript.
No rules to write for the basics. Fallow reports cycles, unresolved imports, and unlisted dependencies with no config.
Unused code. Fallow reports unused files, exports, types, dependencies, enum members, and class members, and fallow fix can remove some of them. See Auto-fix.
Framework entry points. Built-in plugins find the entry points of frameworks such as Next.js and Vite, so fallow knows which files are used.
Forbidden calls and rule packs. Fallow can also forbid calls and imports with rule packs.
More analyses in one run. Fallow also reports duplication and complexity hotspots.
Move a dependency-cruiser check to fallow
A typical CI step runs dependency-cruiser on the source directory and fails on an error rule. To check the same kinds of problems with fallow, run:

fallow architecture # Import cycles and boundary violations
fallow dead-code # Unused files, unresolved imports, and dependency findings

To adopt the checks on a codebase that already has findings, save a baseline first. See Baselines. Fallow does not report the dependency-cruiser config file as unused. When dependency-cruiser is a dependency, the built-in dependency-cruiser plugin marks .dependency-cruiser.js, .cjs, .mjs, and .json as used.
